"Albula, drunk by God," Ovid; understood, water. "Sad wolf to the stalls," Virgil; understood, animal. To this also belongs: "Three thousand of the Samnites slain," Livy. "Two thousand fixed to crosses," Curtius.

units.la: Zeugma nominis, <bl>die Zufügung des Nammens/</bl> est cum diversis substantivis Adjectivum additur, quod cum propiore tantum consentit: ut, Sociis & Rege recepto, Virgilius. Caper tibi salvus & haedi, Virgilius.
units.tr: Zeugma of a noun (the addition of the name) is when an adjective is added to different substantives and agrees only with the nearer one: as, "With the allies and the king received," Virgil. "Your goat safe, and the kids," Virgil.

units.la: Prima Syllepsis Nominis, <bl>die erste Begreiffung des</bl> <bl>Nammens/</bl> est quando substantivis singularibus, vel plurali & singulari, subjicitur Substantivum vel Adjectivum plurale: ut, Procles & Cyristhenes Reges, Cicero. Thestylis allia & Serpillum herbas contundit olentes, Virgilius. Fratribus & Matre inspicientibus, 2.Machabaeor.7.
units.tr: The first syllepsis of a noun is when a plural substantive or adjective is subjoined to singular substantives, or to a plural and a singular: as, "Procles and Cyristhenes, kings," Cicero. "Thestylis pounds garlic and wild thyme, pungent herbs," Virgil. "With the brothers and the mother looking on," 2 Maccabees 7.

units.la: Secunda Syllepsis Nominis est, quando Substantivis diversorum generum, subjicitur Adjectivum vel Substantivum plurale, quod generi digniori respondet: ut, pater & mater mortui, Terentius. Ptolemaeū & Cleopatram reges, Caesar. Masculinum genus dignius est foeminino: Et foeminino dignius est neutro.
units.tr: The second syllepsis of a noun is when a plural substantive or adjective is subjoined to substantives of different genders and agrees with the more worthy gender: as, "The father and mother are dead," Terence. "Ptolemy and Cleopatra, kings," Caesar. The masculine gender is more worthy than the feminine, and the feminine more worthy than the neuter.

units.la: Tertia Syllepsis Nominis est, quando Substantivis rerum inanimatarum Adjectivum plurale neutrum subjicitur: ut, Divitiae, decus, gloria, in oculis sita sunt, Salust. Interdum cum Substantivis rerum inanimatarum Adjectivum plurale in genere convenit: ut, prudentia intelligentiaq;, interpretatio somniorum, & ostensio secretorum, ac solutio ligatorum inventae sunt in eo, hoc est in Daniele, Daniel.5.
units.tr: The third syllepsis of a noun is when a plural adjective of the neuter gender is subjoined to substantives of inanimate things: as, "Riches, honour and glory lie in the eyes," Sallust. Sometimes with substantives of inanimate things the plural adjective agrees in gender: as, "Insight and understanding, the interpretation of dreams, and the disclosure of secrets, and the loosing of bonds were found in him, that is, in Daniel," Daniel 5.

units.la: Quarta Syllepsis Nominis est, quando Adjectiva singularia conveniunt in genere & casu cum Substantivo plurali: ut, De Aegyptio & Cretico Labyrinthis jam dictum est. Plinius. Sic primum & secundum capita Evangelistę Johannis perlegi. Propheta Ezechiel tricesimo octavo & tricesimo nono capitibus de Magogi interitu vaticinatur.
units.tr: The fourth syllepsis of a noun is when singular adjectives agree in gender and case with a plural substantive: as, "Concerning the Egyptian and Cretan Labyrinths it has already been said," Pliny. So I have read through the first and second chapters of the Evangelist John. The prophet Ezekiel, in chapters thirty-eight and thirty-nine, prophesies about the destruction of Gog of Magog.

units.la: Quæ est quinta Regula?
units.tr: What is the fifth Rule?

units.la: Adjectivum partitionem significans regit Genitivum pluralem, qui exponitur per De, è, ex, vel inter: ut, Nemo hominum. Aliter horum Animantium aliae coriis rectae sunt, aliae villis vestitae, aliae spinis hirsutae, Cicero. Uter, alter, neuter horum, de duobus dicuntur: Quis, nemo, nullus, de pluribus.
units.tr: An adjective signifying a part governs the genitive plural, which is explained by de, e, ex, or inter: as, "none of men." Otherwise, Cicero: "Of these animals, some are covered with hides, some clothed with fur, some bristly with spines." Uter, alter and neuter horum are said of two; quis, nemo and nullus of more than two.

units.la: Quæ est sexta Regula?
units.tr: What is the sixth Rule?

units.la: Adjectivum copiae vel inopiae regit Genitivum vel Ablativum: ut, plenus rimarum, Terent. Crura thymo plena, Virgil. Macte virtute esto, Cicero, <bl>wolan</bl> <bl>seyn an tugent fürtreffenlich</bl>. Macti ingenio esse, Plin. <bl>wolan seid am verstande fürtreffenlich vnd gemehrt</bl>.
units.tr: An adjective of plenty or want governs the genitive or the ablative: as, "full of cracks" (Terence); "legs full of thyme" (Virgil); "be excellent in virtue" (Cicero), German wolan seyn an tugent fürtreffenlich; "to be excellent in intellect" (Pliny), German wolan seid am verstande fürtreffenlich vnd gemehrt.

units.la: Quæ est septima Regula?
units.tr: What is the seventh Rule?

units.la: Adjectivum, quod memoriam, desiderium, notitiam, metum, aut contrà significat, regit Genitivum: ut, vive memor letbi[?], Persius. Natura hominum novitatis avida, Plin. Peritus linguæ Latinæ. Græcarum literarum rudis.
units.tr: An adjective signifying memory, desire, knowledge, fear, or their opposites governs the genitive: as, "live mindful of death" (Persius); "the nature of men eager for novelty" (Pliny); "skilled in the Latin language"; "untrained in Greek letters."

units.la: Quæ est octava Regula?
units.tr: What is the eighth Rule?

units.la: Adjectivum, quod affinitatem, similitudinem, aut contrà significat, regit Genitivum vel Dativum: ut, Affinis suspicionis vel suspicioni, Cicero. Proprium virtutis, Cicero: proprium tibi, Plautus. Reus voti, cædis, capitis, & reus stipulando, promittendo. Commune omnium, vel omnibus vel commune mihi cum cæteris. Adjectivum cōmoditatis, facilitatis, vel contrà: Et Adjectivum verbale in Bilis, & Dus, regit Dativum tantùm. Utilis, inutilis, idoneus, aptus, huic rei & ad hanc rem.
units.tr: An adjective signifying kinship or likeness, or their opposites, governs the genitive or the dative: as, "related to suspicion, or to suspicion" (Cicero); "peculiar to virtue" (Cicero), "peculiar to you" (Plautus); "liable for a vow, for murder, for a capital charge," and "liable by stipulation, by promise"; "common to all," either to all or "common to me with the rest." An adjective of convenience or ease, or the contrary, and a verbal adjective in -bilis and -dus, governs the dative only: "useful, useless, suitable, fit for this thing, and to this thing."

units.la: Quæ est nona Regula?
units.tr: What is the ninth Rule?

units.la: Dignus & indignus regunt Ablativum sæpiùs, quàm Genitivum: ut, Audc[?] aliquid brevibus Gyaris & carcere dignum, Si vis esse aliquid, probitas laudatur & alget, Juvenalis. Indignus avorum, Virgilius.
units.tr: Dignus and indignus govern the ablative more often than the genitive: as, "you dare to do something worthy of the short isles of Gyaros and a prison" (Juvenal); "if you wish to be somebody, honesty is praised and left to freeze" (Juvenal); "unworthy of ancestors" (Virgil).

units.la: Interdum Dignus & Indignus regunt infinitum: ut, non sum dignus intueri & aspicere altitudinem cœli, inquit Manasses.
units.tr: Sometimes dignus and indignus govern the infinitive: as, "I am not worthy to look up and behold the height of heaven," says Manasseh.

units.la: Quæ est decima Regula?
units.tr: What is the tenth Rule?

units.la: Adjectiva quædam regunt Infinitum, quædam Gerundium in Di, quædam supinum in u, Verbi passivi: ut, Soli cantare periti, Virgilius. Cupidus videndi, Terentius. O rem tum auditu crudelem, tum visu nesariam, Cicero.
units.tr: Some adjectives govern the infinitive, some the gerund in -di, and some the supine in -u of a passive verb: as, "skilled to sing alone" (Virgil); "eager to see" (Terence); "O thing cruel to hear and unspeakable to see" (Cicero).

units.la: Quæ est undecima Regula?
units.tr: What is the eleventh Rule?

units.la: Comparativus regit Ablativum, qui exponitur per Quàm: ut, Vilius argentum est auro, virtutibus aurum, Horatius. Comparativus partitione significans regit Genitivum: ut, Dextra est agilior manuum.
units.tr: The comparative governs the ablative, which is explained by quam: as, "silver is cheaper than gold, gold than virtues" (Horace). A comparative signifying a part governs the genitive: as, "the right hand is the more nimble of the hands."

units.la: Quæ est duodecima Regula?
units.tr: What is the twelfth Rule?

units.la: Superlativus regit Genitivum pluralem, vel collectivi nominis singularem, qui exponitur per De, e, ex, vel inter: ut, Scævola Jurisperitorum eloquentissimus, Cicero. Optimus plebis. Est autem Nomen collectivum quod in singulari numero multa significat: ut, Turba, Gens, Pars, Populus.
units.tr: The superlative governs the genitive plural, or the singular of a collective noun, which is explained by de, e, ex, or inter: as, "Scaevola, the most eloquent of the jurists" (Cicero); "best of the commons." A collective noun is one that in the singular number signifies many, such as turba, gens, pars, populus.

units.la: Interdum Comparativus & Superlativus casum positivi retinent: ut, Cibi aliquanto avidior. Servantissimus æqui, Virgil. Dies mihi optatissimus, Cicer.
units.tr: Sometimes the comparative and superlative keep the case of the positive: as, "somewhat more eager for food"; "most observant of justice" (Virgil); "the day most desired by me" (Cicero).

units.la: Quæ est decimatertia Regula?
units.tr: What is the thirteenth Rule?

units.la: Adjectiva participialia regunt casus suorum Verborum: ut, videns Romam, visurus Romam: Quia verbum, Video, regit Accusativum. Potitus imperij vel imperio: Quia verbum, Potior, regit Genitivum vel Ablativum.
units.tr: Participial adjectives govern the cases of their verbs: as, "seeing Rome" and "about to see Rome," because the verb video governs the accusative; "having gained possession of the empire" or "of the empire," because potior governs the genitive or ablative.

units.la: Interdum Adjectiva participialia verborum suorum constructionem non imitantur: ut, patiens inediæ. Fugitans litium. Sitiens famæ. Lapsus animi. Victus animi.
units.tr: Sometimes participial adjectives do not imitate the construction of their verbs: as, "enduring hunger," "avoiding lawsuits," "thirsting for fame," "fallen in spirit," "beaten in spirit."

units.la: Quæ est decimaquarta Regula?
units.tr: What is the fourteenth Rule?

units.la: Nominativus præcedit verbum finitum, simili numero & persona: ut, ego amo, tu amas, ille amat. Nos amamus, vos amatis, illi amant. Ego & nos primæ, Tu & vos secundæ, Nominativi reliquorum nominum tertiæ personæ habentur.
units.tr: The nominative precedes a finite verb, agreeing in number and person: as, I love, you love, he loves; we love, you love, they love. Ego and nos are regarded as the first person, tu and vos as the second; the nominatives of all other nouns are regarded as third person.

units.la: Utimur verbis primæ vel secundæ personæ dissimulatis pronominibꝰ, Ego, Tu, Nos, Vos, quæ nunquā fere ponuntur, nisi discretionis aut emphasis causâ.
units.tr: We use verbs of the first or second person with the pronouns ego, tu, nos and vos left out, since these are almost never expressed except for distinction or emphasis.

units.la: Infinitum, aut tota oratio infinita, Gerundium in dum & Supinum in um verbi impersonalis & interdum Verbi Deponentis, ac aliæ quædam voces, sunt loco Nominativi tertiæ personæ: ut, Adde, quod ingenuas didicisse fideliter artes, Emollit mores nec finit esse feros,Ovid. Non facile est æqua commoda mente pati,Ovidius Vigilandum est. Vigilatum est. Utendum est Quod Tyranni vivunt est malum.
units.tr: An infinitive, or a whole infinitive clause, a gerund in -dum and a supine in -um of an impersonal verb, and sometimes of a deponent verb, along with certain other words, stand in place of a third-person nominative: as, "Add that to have learned the liberal arts faithfully softens the manners and does not let them be savage" (Ovid); "it is not easy to bear good fortune with an even mind" (Ovid); "one must keep watch"; "there was keeping watch"; "one must use"; "that tyrants live is an evil."

units.la: Evocatio est cùm Nominativus tertiæ personæ, Verbo primæ vel secundæ præponitur: ut,Ego Virgilius lego Tu Apollonius scribis.Nos poma natamus.
units.tr: Evocation is when a third-person nominative is placed before a verb of the first or second person: as, "I, Virgil, read; you, Apollonius, write"; "we apples swim."

units.la: Synthesis Verbi est cùm Nomini multitudinis singularis subjicitur verbum plurale: ut, pars epulis onerant mensas,Virgilius. Aliquando Synthesis & Evocatio concurrunt: ut, pars veniemus, Virgil. Aliquis aperite.Terent.
units.tr: Synthesis of the verb is when a plural verb is joined to a noun of singular multitude: as, "some part load the tables with feasts" (Virgil). Sometimes synthesis and evocation occur together: as, "some part of us will come" (Virgil); "someone, open up!" (Terence).

units.la: Zeugma Verbi est cùm diversis nominativis Verbum adjungitur, quod cum propiore tantum consentit: ut,Semper honos,nomenq; tuû, laudesq; manebunt. Hic illius arma,hic currus fuit,Virgilius.
units.tr: Zeugma of the verb is when one verb is joined to different nominatives and agrees only with the nearer one: as, "honour, your name and your praises will remain; here were his arms, here his chariot" (Virgil).

units.la: Prima Syllepsis Verbi est,quando Nominativis singularibus, vel plurali & singulari subjicitur Verbum plurale: ut,furor iraque mentem præcipitant,Virgil. Milites & Imperator pugnant,Livius.
units.tr: The first syllepsis of the verb is when a plural verb is subjoined to singular nominatives, or to a plural and a singular: as, "rage and fury overwhelm the mind" (Virgil); "soldiers and the general fight" (Livy).

units.la: Secunda Syllepsis Verbi est quando Nominativis diversarum personarum subjicitur Verbum plurale, quod personæ digniori respondet: ut, Ego & suavif[?]simus Cicero valemus, si tu & Tullia lux nostra valetis,Cicero. Hæc si neq; ego,neq; tu fecimus,non sivit egestas facere nos,Terentius. Prima persona dignior est secundâ: Et secunda dignior tertiâ.
units.tr: The second syllepsis of the verb is when a plural verb is subjoined to nominatives of different persons and agrees with the more worthy person: as, "I, most sweet Cicero, and you and Tullia, our light, are well" (Cicero); "if neither I nor you have done these things, poverty did not allow us to do them" (Terence). The first person is more worthy than the second, and the second than the third.

units.la: Tertia Syllepsis Verbi est, quando Nominativo & Ablativo inter se cohærentibus subjicitur Verbum plurale: ut, Remo cum fratre Quirinus jura dabant, Virgil.Cùm alter ab altero discederimus.Castalio.
units.tr: The third syllepsis of the verb is when a plural verb is subjoined to a nominative and an ablative that are joined together: as, "Quirinus with his brother Remus gave laws" (Virgil); "since we have departed from one another" (Castalio).

units.la: Prolepsis est cùm Nominativo & Verbo pluralis numeri subjiciuntur alij Nominativi, Verbo non repetitô: ut, Milites redeunt, hic ex Hispaniis, ille ex Galliis.Ambo defessi sumus,ego vapulando, ille verberando,Terent.
units.tr: Prolepsis is when other nominatives are subjoined to a nominative and a verb of plural number, the verb not being repeated: as, "the soldiers return, this one from Spain, that one from Gaul"; "we are both worn out, I by being beaten, he by beating" (Terence).

units.la: Prior Enallage est cùm in narrando, infinito, pro primo imperfecto utimur: ut, Facile omnes perferre ac pati, Terent. Pro, perferebat ac patiebat.
units.tr: The first enallage is when, in narrating, we use the infinitive for the first imperfect: as, "all to endure and suffer easily" (Terence), for "they endured and suffered easily."

units.la: Posterior Enallage est cùm verbum, Sum, aut quod ejus vim obtinet, duobus Nominativis diversorum numerorum appositum convenit cum Nominativo posteriore: ut, Amantium irae amoris redintegratio est, Terent. Pro Amantium irae sunt redintegratio.
units.tr: The second enallage is when the verb sum, or a word that has its force, is placed between two nominatives of different numbers and agrees with the later nominative: as, "the anger of lovers is a renewal of love" (Terence), for "the anger of lovers are a renewal of love."

units.la: Quæ est decimaquinta Regula?
units.tr: What is the fifteenth Rule?

units.la: Vocativus in numero cum verbo secundae personae convenit: ut, Eripe nate fugam, finemque impone labori, Virgil. Interdum Vocativi singulares, vel Vocativus nominis multitudinis convenit verbo secundae personae plurali: ut, Simalio, Donax, Syrisce, sequimini, Teren. Attendite omnis multitudo, Castalio.
units.tr: A vocative in the singular agrees with a verb of the second person: as, "Eripe nate fugam, finemque impone labori" (Virgil). Sometimes a singular vocative, or the vocative of a collective noun, agrees with a plural verb of the second person: as, "Simalio, Donax, Syrisce, sequimini" (Terence). "Attendite omnis multitudo" (Castalio).

units.la: Quæ est decimasexta Regula?
units.tr: What is the sixteenth Rule?

units.la: Verbum activum, neutrum, vel Deponens, regit Accusativum: ut, virum malum vel mus mordeat. Hos accusando, illos occidendo civitatem labefactasti. Cicero. Venio salutatum amicos. Aro terram. Bibo vinum. Vereor hominem. Sequor illum.
units.tr: An active or neuter verb, or a deponent, governs the accusative: as, "virum malum vel mus mordeat" (let a mouse bite a bad man). "Hos accusando, illos occidendo civitatem labefactasti" (Cicero). "Venio salutatum amicos" (I come to greet my friends). "Aro terram" (I plough the land). "Bibo vinum" (I drink wine). "Vereor hominem" (I fear the man). "Sequor illum" (I follow him).

units.la: Sed Gaudeo, polleo, vivo, victito, utor, fruor, fungor, vescor, lætor, dignor, delector, regunt Ablativū. Potior, regit Genitivum vel Ablativum. Interdum vivo, utor, fungor, potior, lætor, regunt Accusativum: Lætor, invenitur etiam cum Genitivo: ut, Nec veterum memini lætorve malorum, Virgilius. Pluit lapides & lapidibus.
units.tr: But gaudeo, polleo, vivo, victito, utor, fruor, fungor, vescor, lætor, dignor and delector govern the ablative. Potior governs the genitive or the ablative. Sometimes vivo, utor, fungor, potior and lætor govern the accusative. Lætor is also found with the genitive, as in Virgil: "Nor do I remember the old sorrows, nor rejoice in evils." "It rains stones and with stones."

units.la: Quæ est decimaseptima Regula?
units.tr: What is the seventeenth Rule?

units.la: Verbum patiendi, prohibendi, abstinendi, distandi, aut Verbum vi Compositionis regit Ablativum cum Adverbio, vel sine Adverbio: ut, laudatur ab his, culpatur ab illis, Horatius. Fortes creantur fortibus, Horat. Ignavum fucos pecus a præsepibus arcent, Virgilius. Est virtus placitis abstinuisse bonis, Ovidius. Supersedeas hoc labore itineris, Cicero. Et villa adhuc egressi non fumus, Cicero. Pedem porta non exulit, Suetonius. Verbum passivum aliquando pro Ablativo Dativum regit: ut, Neque cernitur ulli, Virgilius. Pro ab ullo. Neq; senatui,neq; populo probatur, Cicero. Pro a senatu,a populo.
units.tr: A verb of suffering, forbidding, abstaining or differing, or a verb that takes this sense from its compound form, governs the ablative, with or without a preposition: as in Horace, "He is praised by these men and blamed by those." Horace: "Brave men are born of brave." Virgil: "The drones keep the idle herd away from the stalls." Ovid: "It is virtue to have abstained from pleasant goods." Cicero: "You may spare yourself this labour of the journey." Cicero: "We have not yet gone out of the villa." Suetonius: "He has not set foot outside the gate." A passive verb sometimes governs the dative in place of the ablative with a preposition: as in Virgil, "It is seen by no one," that is, "by anyone." Cicero: "It is approved neither by the senate nor by the people," that is, "by the senate, by the people."

units.la: Quæ est decimaoctava Regula?
units.tr: What is the eighteenth Rule?

units.la: Verbum, animi perturbationem significans, regit Genitivum vel Ablativum: ut, pendeo animi vel animis,Cicero. Discrucior animi vel animo, Terentius.
units.tr: A verb signifying a disturbance of the mind governs the genitive or the ablative: as, "pendeo animi vel animis" (Cicero). "Discrucior animi vel animo" (Terence).

units.la: Miserebor,misereris, <bl>ich erbarme mich</bl> regit Genitivum, & in sacris literis etiam Dativum. At miseror,miseraris,<bl>ich be[?]weine oder beklage</bl> regit Accusativum.
units.tr: Miserebor, misereris, "ich erbarme mich" (I have mercy) governs the genitive, and in the sacred writings also the dative. But miseror, miseraris, "ich beweine oder beklage" (I bewail or lament) governs the accusative.

units.la: Quæ est decimanona Regula?
units.tr: What is the nineteenth Rule?

units.la: Verbum memoriæ vel oblivionis regit Genitivum vel Accusativum: ut, Memini hujus rei vel hanc rem. Obliviscor nominis tui vel nomen tuum. Dicimus: Venit mihi in mentem ea res,ejus rei,de ea re.
units.tr: A verb of remembering or forgetting governs the genitive or the accusative: as, "Memini hujus rei vel hanc rem" (I remember this thing). "Obliviscor nominis tui vel nomen tuum" (I forget your name). We say: "Venit mihi in mentem ea res", "ejus rei", or "de ea re" (that matter came into my mind).

units.la: Quæ est vicesima Regula?
units.tr: What is the twentieth Rule?

units.la: Verbum attribuendi, adimendi, comparandi, imperandi, serviendi, declarandi,promittedi,assentiendi,aut repugnandi, regit Dativum: ut, Dat veniam corvis, vexat censura columbas, Juvenalis. Collegæ suo imperium abrogavit,Cicero.Homo homini quid præstat? Terentius. Dicimus,antecello omnibus vel omnes. Antecedo huic,& antecedo ætate Gracchum, Dominor victis Argis, Virgilius. Dominor in animalia, Ovidius: Dominor in urbe,Cicero: Dominor illius,in Sacris literis.
units.tr: A verb of giving, taking away, comparing, commanding, serving, declaring, promising, assenting or resisting governs the dative. Juvenal: "He grants pardon to the crows; censure harasses the doves." Cicero: "He stripped his colleague of his command." Terence: "What does one man excel another in?" We say antecello omnibus or antecello omnes, "I surpass everyone." Virgil: "I surpass him, and I excel Gracchus in age." Virgil: "I rule over the conquered Argos." Ovid: "I rule over the animals." Cicero: "I rule in the city." "I rule over him, in the Sacred Letters."

units.la: Quæ est vicesimaprima Regula?
units.tr: What is the twenty-first Rule?

units.la: Verbum rogandi vel docendi, & alia quædam verba regunt duos Accusativos: ut,illud te oro, Terent. Quid nū te, Asine,literas docebā? Non opus est verbis, sed fustibus, Cicero. Idipsum me monet, Cicero. Duxit virginem uxorem. Dicimus, induo tibi vestem, induo te vestem, & induo te veste. Sic & Exuo. Celo tibi hanc rem, & celo te hanc rem, & celo te de hac re, [illegible, ~14 letters] dir. In passiva forma posterior casus manet: ut, per legatos cuncta edocetur. Ego doctus sum abs te Dialecticam.
units.tr: A verb of asking or teaching, and certain other verbs, govern two accusatives: as, "illud te oro" (I ask you this; Terence). "Quid nū te, Asine, literas docebā?" "Non opus est verbis, sed fustibus" (Cicero). "Idipsum me monet" (Cicero). "Duxit virginem uxorem" (he took the maiden as his wife). We say "induo tibi vestem", "induo te vestem", and "induo te veste" (I dress you in clothing). So also "exuo". "Celo tibi hanc rem", "celo te hanc rem", and "celo te de hac re" [illegible, about fourteen letters] ... In the passive form the second accusative remains: as, "per legatos cuncta edocetur" (he is taught everything through envoys). "Ego doctus sum abs te Dialecticam" (I have been taught dialectic by you).

units.la: Quæ est Vicesimasecunda Regula?
units.tr: What is the twenty-second Rule?

units.la: Verbum copiæ, inopiæ, æstimationis aut mercaturæ, regit Ablativum: ut, Abundat doctrina. Data magno æstimas, accepta parvo, Seneca. Nihil carius constat, quàm quod precibus emitur. At egeo, indigeo, careo, impleo, recipiunt Ablativum vel Genitivum. Valeo recipit Ablativum sæpius, quàm Accusativum. Verum æstimationis aut mercaturæ regit etiam hosce Genitivos: Quanti, tanti, magni, maximi, pluris, plurimi, parvi, minoris, minimi, æqui, boni, flocci, nihili, nauci, pili, assis, teruntij.
units.tr: A verb of plenty, want, valuation or trade governs the ablative. "Learning abounds." Seneca: "You value what was given at a high price, and what was received at a low price." "Nothing costs more than what is bought with prayers." But egeo, indigeo, careo and impleo take the ablative or the genitive. Valeo takes the ablative more often than the accusative. Verbs of valuation or trade also govern these genitives: how much, so much, much, very much, more, most, little, less, least, equal, good, a whit, nothing, nought, a hair, a farthing, a penny.

units.la: Quæ est Vicesimatertia Regula?
units.tr: What is the twenty-third Rule?

units.la: Verbum judiciale regit Genitivum vel Ablativum: ut, Verrem insimulat avaritiæ & audaciæ, Cicero. Absolvere aliquem improbitatis. Crimine liberare. Dicimus etiam: Accusare de negligentia, ex Cicerone. Non dicimus: utrius, sed tantùm utro accusatus est, furti an cædis? Respondemus: utroq;, neutro.
units.tr: A verb of judgment governs the genitive or the ablative: as, "Verrem insimulat avaritiæ & audaciæ" (Cicero). "Absolvere aliquem improbitatis" (to acquit someone of wickedness). "Crimine liberare" (to free from a charge). We also say "accusare de negligentia" (to accuse of negligence), from Cicero. We do not say "utrius", but only "utro accusatus est, furti an cædis?" (on which of the two charges was he accused, theft or murder?). We answer "utroq;" (on both) or "neutro" (on neither).

units.la: Quæ est Vicesimaquarta Regula?
units.tr: What is the twenty-fourth Rule?

units.la: Verbum sum, aut quod ejus vim obtinet, & alia quædam verba, regunt post se Nominativum: ut, ira est furor brevis, Horat. Manus nostræ sunt oculatæ, credunt quod vident. Plaut. Aristæus dicitur inventor oliviæ. Incedit sordidatus. Redeo inde iratus, Terentius.
units.tr: The verb "sum", or a word that takes its force, and certain other verbs, govern a nominative after them: as, "ira est furor brevis" (anger is a brief madness; Horace). "Manus nostræ sunt oculatæ, credunt quod vident" (our hands are sharp-eyed, they believe what they see; Plautus). "Aristæus dicitur inventor oliviæ" (Aristaeus is said to be the discoverer of the olive). "Incedit sordidatus" (he walks about in squalid clothes). "Redeo inde iratus" (I return thence angry; Terence).

units.la: Verbum sum, aut quod ejus vim obtinet, possessionem vel proprietatē significans, regit Genitivum: ut, sive vivimus, sive morimur, Domini sumus, Paulus. Hæc vestis est patris. Boni pastoris est tondere pecus, non deglubere.
units.tr: The verb "sum", or a word that takes its force, signifying possession or ownership, governs the genitive: as, "sive vivimus, sive morimur, Domini sumus" (whether we live or die, we are the Lord's; Paul). "Hæc vestis est patris" (this coat is my father's). "Boni pastoris est tondere pecus, non deglubere" (it is the good shepherd's part to shear the flock, not to flay it).

units.la: Sed verbum Sum regit pro Genitivis, mei, tui, sui[?], nostri, vestri, possessiva, meum, tuum, suum, nostrum, vestrum: ut, Non est meum contra aliquem dicere[?], Cicero. Tuum est, si quid præter spem evenit, mihi ignoscere, Terent.
units.tr: But the verb sum governs these genitives in place of the possessive forms: mei, tui, sui[?], nostri and vestri, with the possessives meum, tuum, suum, nostrum and vestrum. Cicero: "It is not mine to speak against anyone[?]." Terence: "It is yours, if something happens beyond hope, to pardon me."

units.la: Verbum, Sum, si pro habeo usurpetur, regit Dativum: Est mihi namq; domi pater, est injusta noverca[?], Virgilius.
units.tr: If the verb "sum" is used for "habeo" (to have), it governs the dative: "Est mihi namq; domi pater, est injusta noverca" (for I have a father at home, and an unkind stepmother; Virgil).

units.la: Verbum, Sum, & alia quædam verba regunt duos Dativos: ut, Sunt exitio Reipublicis[?] intestinæ dissensiones. Dedit mihi pecuniam fœnori, librum pignori, dono usui. Dicimus: Est mihi nomen Pomponius, vel Pomponii, vel Pomponio, qua ultima formula maxime delectantur eruditi. Interdum verbum, Sum, regit unum Dativum: ut, canicies est indicio, Castalio.
units.tr: The verb "sum", and certain other verbs, govern two datives: as, "Sunt exitio Reipublicis intestinæ dissensiones" (internal quarrels are ruinous to the commonwealths). "Dedit mihi pecuniam fœnori, librum pignori, dono usui" (he gave me money to lend at interest, a book as a pledge, a gift for use). We say "Est mihi nomen Pomponius", "Pomponii", or "Pomponio" (my name is Pomponius); learned men are especially fond of the last form. Sometimes the verb "sum" governs a single dative: as, "canicies est indicio" (grey hair is a sign; Castalio).

units.la: Verbum Sum, regit Substantivum nomen in Genitivo vel Ablativo cum Adjectivo descriptionis: ut, Asinus est amplissimi corporis, cervice valida, Columella. Cicero erat tenuissima valetudine, Cæsar.
units.tr: The verb "sum" governs a substantive in the genitive or the ablative, with an adjective of description: as, "Asinus est amplissimi corporis, cervice valida" (the ass is of very large body, with a strong neck; Columella). "Cicero erat tenuissima valetudine" (Cicero was of very weak health; Caesar).

units.la: Casus, qui Infinitum esse vel fuisse, sequitur, convenit cum casu præcedente: ut, Nobis non licet esse tam disertis, Martialis. Cave te tristem esse sentiat, Te-rentius.
units.tr: A case that follows an infinitive, to be or to have been, agrees with the preceding case: as, "Nobis non licet esse tam disertis" (we are not allowed to be so eloquent; Martial). "Cave te tristem esse sentiat" (take care that he does not perceive you to be sad; Terence).

units.la: Quæ est vicesimaquinta Regula?
units.tr: What is the twenty-fifth rule?

units.la: Verbum significans voluntatem[?], sensum, inceptionem, aut facultatem, vel ejusmodi quid, regit Infinitum: ut, in animo habet navem conscendere. Coeperunt interrogare. Fœlix qui potuit rerum cognoscere causas, Virgilius. Non dubito affirmare. Puer erubescat impudica audire & loqui.
units.tr: A verb signifying will, intention, beginning, or ability, or something of that kind, governs the infinitive: as, he intends to board the ship; they began to ask. "Happy is he who has been able to know the causes of things," Virgil. "I do not hesitate to affirm." "Let a boy blush to hear and to speak shameless things."

units.la: Quæ est vicesimasexta Regula?
units.tr: What is the twenty-sixth rule?

units.la: Verbum motus ad locum regit Supinum in um:
units.tr: A verb of motion towards a place governs the supine in -um.

units.la: ut, Spectatum veniunt, veniunt spectentur ut ipsæ, Ovid. Interdum verbum motus regit Græco more Infinitum: ut, inde venit judicare vivos & mortuos. Pro judicatum, seu ad judicandum, seu judicaturus, quæ postrema formula omnium est eruditissima.
units.tr: As, "They come to see, they come to be looked at themselves," Ovid. Sometimes a verb of motion governs the infinitive in the Greek manner: as, "He came thence to judge the living and the dead." This stands for judicatum, or ad judicandum, or judicaturus, the last of which is the most learned form of all.

units.la: Verbum motus e loco rexit olim supinum in u: ut, paterfamilias primus cubitu surgat, postremus cubitum eat, Cato. Obsonatu redeo, Plautus.
units.tr: A verb of motion formerly governed the supine in -u from a place: as, "Let the head of the household rise first from his bed, and let the last one go to bed," Cato. "I return from the market," Plautus.

units.la: Quæ est vicesimaseptima Regula?
units.tr: What is the twenty-seventh rule?

units.la: Verbum Infinitum regit ante se Accusativum, qui exponitur per Quod vel Ut, post se autem casum sui verbi: ut, Meum natum rumor est amare Terentius. Id est, Rumor est quod meus natus amet.
units.tr: A verb in the infinitive governs an accusative before it, which is explained by that or so that, and after it the case of its own verb: as, "Rumour has it that my son is in love," Terence. That is, "It is rumoured that my son loves."

units.la: Post verba, Loco, <bl>ich verdinge[?]/conduco</bl>, <bl>ich</bl> <bl>dinge/bestelle</bl>/mando, <bl>ich befehle</bl>/curo, <bl>ich verschaffe/</bl> <bl>ich lasse</bl>/habeo, <bl>ich muß</bl>/& si qua sunt alia, non ponitur Accusativus cum infinito, sed Adjectivum participiale in dus, quod cum substantivo convenit: ut, loco faciendam sepulturam. Conduxit columnam faciendam. Gladiatores vi rapiendos, reservandosque mandabat. Curavit jaciendos lapides. Habeo eos consolandos. Hæc ex Vallæ elegantiar. lib.1.cap.27.
units.tr: After the verbs loco (I let out for hire), conduco (I hire), mando (I order), curo (I see to), habeo (I have), I must, and any others of the kind, the accusative with the infinitive is not used; instead the participial adjective in -dus is used, agreeing with the noun: as, "to have the burial carried out"; "he hired a column to be erected"; "he ordered the gladiators to be seized by force and kept back"; "he saw to the stones being thrown"; "I have them to be consoled." These examples are from Valla's Elegantiae, book 1, chapter 27.

units.la: Quæ est vicesimaoctava Regula?
units.tr: What is the twenty-eighth rule?

units.la: Interest, <bl>es ist daran gelegē</bl> / & refert, <bl>es gehet an</bl>/ regunt Genitivum, & hosce Ablativos, mea, tua, sua, nostra, vestra & cuja: ut, interest omnium recte facere, Cicero Reipublicæ refert conservari literas. Tua quod nihil refert, percontari desinas, Terentius. Non Tui. Permagni nostra refert. Non Nostri.
units.tr: Interest (it concerns, it matters) and refert (it is of importance) govern the genitive, and these ablatives: mea, tua, sua, nostra, vestra and cuja: as, "It is in everyone's interest to act rightly," Cicero; "it matters to the republic that letters be preserved"; "Since it is of no concern to you, stop asking," Terence (not tui); "it matters greatly to us" (not nostri).

units.la: Quæ est vicesimanona Regula?
units.tr: What is the twenty-ninth rule?

units.la: Miseret, <bl>es jammert mich</bl> / <bl>miserescit, es erbarmet</bl> <bl>mich</bl> / <bl>tædet, es verdreust mich</bl> / <bl>piget, es verdreust</bl> <bl>mich</bl> / <bl>pœnitet, es reuet mich</bl> / <bl>pudet, ich schäme mich</bl>. regunt Accusativum, cum Genitivo vel Infinito: ut,
units.tr: Miseret (it moves to pity), miserescit (it has pity), taedet (it wearies), piget (it grieves), paenitet (it repents), pudet (it shames): these govern the accusative, with the genitive or the infinitive: as,

units.la: Nonne te miseret mei? Terentius. Sunt homines, quos libidinis infamiæque suæ, neque pudeat, neque tædeat, Cic. Nec te pœniteat, calamo trivisse labellum, Virgil.
units.tr: "Does pity for me not move you?" Terence. "There are men whom neither shame at their lust nor at their infamy shames or wearies," Cicero. "Let it not grieve you to have worn down your lip on the pen," Virgil.

units.la: Quæ est tricesima Regula?
units.tr: What is the thirtieth rule?

units.la: Post Decet, es stehet wol / delectat, es <bl>belustiget</bl> / juvat, es <bl>erfreuet</bl> / oportet, es <bl>muß</bl> / es <bl>gehöret sich</bl> / ponitur Accusativus cum Infinito: ut, omnes homines summa ope niti decet, ne vitam silentio transigant, veluti pecora, Sallustius. Te animo hilari esse valde me juvat, Cicero. Oportet mendacem esse memorem. Antiquum est quod Cicero dixit: Quandoque id deceat prudentiæ tuæ.
units.tr: After decet (it becomes, it is fitting), delectat (it delights), juvat (it pleases, it helps), oportet (it is necessary, one ought) the accusative with the infinitive is used: as, "All men ought to strive with all their might not to pass their lives in silence, like cattle," Sallust. "It greatly pleases me that you are cheerful," Cicero. "A liar must have a good memory." It is an old saying that Cicero used: "Whenever it befits your prudence."

units.la: Quæ est tricesimaprima Regula?
units.tr: What is the thirty-first rule?

units.la: Quædam ex impersonalibus Activæ formæ regunt Dativum cum Infinito, vel Infinitum tantum: ut, Non cuivis homini contingit adire Corinthum, Horatius. Licet dicere. Expedit facere. Nec numeros comprehendere refert, Virgilius.
units.tr: Some impersonal verbs in the active form govern the dative with the infinitive, or the infinitive alone: as, "It does not fall to every man to go to Corinth," Horace. Licet dicere (it is permitted to say). Expedit facere (it is expedient to do). "Nor does it matter to grasp the rhythms," Virgil.

units.la: Interdum post impersonalia activæ formæ ponitur particula, Ut, cum verbo secundi temporis: ut, Expedit ei ut suspendatur mola asinaria in collo ejus, Matth. 18. Interdum particula, ut, eleganter omittitur: ut, Ex rerum cognitione efflorescat oratio, Cicero.
units.tr: Sometimes after impersonal verbs in the active form the particle ut is placed, with a verb of the second tense: as, "It is expedient for him that a millstone be hung about his neck," Matthew 18. Sometimes the particle ut is elegantly omitted: as, "Let eloquence flourish from knowledge of things," Cicero.

units.la: Quæ est tricesimasecunda Regula?
units.tr: What is the thirty-second rule?

units.la: Impersonalia passivæ formæ regunt Dativum aut Ablativum cum Adverbio vel sine Adverbio, aut absolutè ponuntur: ut, occurritur nobis, & quidem à doctis, Cicero. Vivitur ex rapto. Vivitur ingenio, cætera mortis erunt. Statur. Pugnatur. Egetur.
units.tr: Impersonal verbs in the passive form govern the dative or the ablative, with or without an adverb, or are used absolutely: as, "We encounter it, and indeed from learned men," Cicero. "One lives by plunder." "One lives by wit; all else will be for death." "It is stood." "It is fought." "It is needed."

units.la: Gerundium in Dum verbi impersonalis vel Deponentis cum verbo Est, regit Dativum sæpius, quàm Accusativum vel Ablativum: ut, Vigilandum est nobis, Sperandum est vivis. Respondendum est mihi Adversario. Petendum est pacem à Trojano Rege, Virgil. Pro quo hodie dicimus: petenda est pax. Carendum est libro. Utendum est ætate, Ovidius. Supinum in unum[?] cum verbo, est, regit Datiuum[?]: ut, Huic quoque rei subventum est, ejus orationi reclamatum est, Cicero.
units.tr: The gerund in -dum of an impersonal or deponent verb, with the verb est, governs the dative more often than the accusative or ablative: as, "We must keep watch"; "the living must hope"; "I must reply to my opponent"; "he must seek peace from the Trojan king," Virgil. Where today we say, "peace is to be sought." "One must do without a book." "One must use one's youth," Ovid. The supine in -um with the verb est governs the dative: as, "Help was given to this matter too"; "his speech was opposed," Cicero.

units.la: Quæ est tricesimatertia Regula?
units.tr: What is the thirty-third rule?

units.la: Adverbia adjunguntur[?] nominibus, verbis, & ipsis Adverbiis ad explicandas eorum circunstantias: ut, Mulier infigniter impudens. Festina lente. Satis imprudenter.
units.tr: Adverbs are joined to nouns, to verbs, and to adverbs themselves, to explain their circumstances: as, "a remarkably shameless woman"; "make haste slowly"; "quite carelessly."

units.la: Quæ est tricesimaquarta Regula?
units.tr: What is the thirty-fourth rule?

units.la: Adverbia numeri conveniunt distributivis nominibus: ut, Bis bina quid sint Epicurus non didicit, Cicero.
units.tr: Adverbs of number agree with distributive numerals: as, "What twice two makes, Epicurus did not learn," Cicero.

units.la: Quæ est tricesimaquinta Regula?
units.tr: What is the thirty-fifth rule?

units.la: Adverbium Quàm pro quantum additur positivo; pro valde Superlativo. Quo & eo comparativis adduntur, Quanto,tanto,multo,longe,alias comparativis,alias superlativis conveniunt.
units.tr: The adverb quam is added to a positive in place of quantum; valde is added to a superlative. Quo and eo are added to comparatives; quanto, tanto, multo, longe: some agree with comparatives, others with superlatives.

units.la: Quæ est tricesimasexta Regula?
units.tr: Which is the thirty-sixth Rule?

units.la: Adverbium Derivatum primitivi casum retinet: ut, Similiter huic vestitus. Melius corvo canit Galerita. Omnium elegantissime scripsit.
units.tr: A derived adverb keeps the case of its primitive: for example, "similarly to this, a garment" (Similiter huic vestitus); "the crested lark sings better than a crow" (Melius corvo canit Galerita); "he wrote most elegantly of all" (Omnium elegantissime scripsit).

units.la: Quæ est tricesimaseptima Regula?
units.tr: Which is the thirty-seventh Rule?

units.la: Adverbium loci, temporis, aut quantitatis, regit Genitivum: ut, ubicunque terrarum Cicero. Pridie ejus dici, Cicero. Postridie natalis Christi. Satis eloquentiæ, sapientiæ parum, Salustius. Quoad ejus fieri potest. Cicero. Eo insolentiæ processit. Huc dementiæ pervenit.
units.tr: An adverb of place, time or quantity governs the genitive: for example, "wherever in the world" (ubicunque terrarum), Cicero; "the day before that" (Pridie ejus dici), Cicero; "the day after Christmas" (Postridie natalis Christi); "enough eloquence, little wisdom", Sallust; "as far as it can be done" (Quoad ejus fieri potest), Cicero; "he has gone so far in insolence" (Eo insolentiæ processit); "he has come to such madness" (Huc dementiæ pervenit).

units.la: Instar regit Genitivum: ut, instar montis equum, divina Palladis arte, ædificant, Virgilius.
units.tr: Instar governs the genitive: for example, "they built a horse like a mountain by the divine art of Pallas", Virgil.

units.la: Quæ est tricesimaoctava Regula?
units.tr: Which is the thirty-eighth Rule?

units.la: Adverbia En, & Ecce, regunt Nominativum, Dativum, vel Accusativum.
units.tr: The adverbs En and Ecce govern the nominative, the dative or the accusative.

units.la: Adverbia, O,Proh,& Hem. regunt Nominativum, Accusativum vel Vocativum.
units.tr: The adverbs O, Proh and Hem govern the nominative, the accusative or the vocative.

units.la: Vah regit Nominativum: Heu regit Nominativum vel Accusativum: Hei & Væ regunt Dativum: Heus, Ah & Ohe regunt Vocativum. Usus spectandus.
units.tr: Vah governs the nominative; Heu governs the nominative or the accusative; Hei and Væ govern the dative; Heus, Ah and Ohe govern the vocative. Usage is to be observed.

units.la: Quæ est tricesimanona Regula?
units.tr: Which is the thirty-ninth Rule?

units.la: Unum & triginta Adverbia sunt, quæ Accusativum regunt, ut, Ad, <bl>zu.</bl> Apud, <bl>bey.</bl> Ante, <bl>vor.</bl> Adversus, <bl>zuwider.</bl> Cis, <bl>disseit.</bl> Citra, <bl>disseit.</bl> Ultra, <bl>vber/jenseit.</bl> Intra, <bl>in/innerhalb.</bl> Extra, <bl>draussen.</bl> Circum, <bl>vmb.</bl> Circa, <bl>herumb.</bl> Circiter, <bl>vmb oder bey/ad tempus &</bl> numerum referrtur. Contra, <bl>wider.</bl> Erga, <bl>gegen.</bl> Inter, <bl>zwischen/vnter.</bl> Infra, <bl>vnder.</bl> Supra, <bl>droben/ober.</bl> Juxta, <bl>bey/nach.</bl> Ob, <bl>von wegen.</bl> Per, <bl>durch.</bl> Prope, <bl>bey oder nahe.</bl> Præter, <bl>ohn/vber/wider.</bl> Propter, <bl>von</bl> <bl>wegen.</bl> Post, <bl>hinder.</bl> Penes, <bl>in gewalt/bey.</bl> Secundum, <bl>bey/nach.</bl> Trans, <bl>hinüber/jenseit.</bl> Pone, <bl>hinder/zu</bl> <bl>rück.</bl> Secus, <bl>neben/bey.</bl> Usq; <bl>bis.</bl> Versus, <bl>gegen.</bl> Ex his nonnulla absq; casu usurpantur. Gerundium in Dum est Accusativi loco: ut, Mitto illum ad speculandum arcem.
units.tr: There are thirty-one adverbs that govern the accusative: ad (to), apud (at, by), ante (before), adversus (against), cis (on this side), citra (on this side), ultra (beyond), intra (within), extra (outside), circum (around), circa (about), circiter (about, said of time and number), contra (against), erga (towards), inter (between, among), infra (below), supra (above), juxta (near, according to), ob (on account of), per (through), prope (near), praeter (beyond, besides, against), propter (on account of), post (behind), penes (in the power of, with), secundum (near, according to), trans (across, beyond), pone (behind, back), secus (beside, near), usque (until), versus (towards). Some of these are used without a case. A gerund in -dum stands in place of the accusative: for example, "I send him to spy out the citadel."

units.la: Quæ est quadragesima Regula?
units.tr: Which is the fortieth Rule?

units.la: Quatuordecim Adverbia sunt, quæ Ablativum regunt: ut, A, <bl>von/nach/wider.</bl> Ab, <bl>von.</bl> Abs, <bl>von.</bl> Absque, <bl>ohn.</bl> Cum, <bl>mit.</bl> Clam, <bl>ohn wissen.</bl> Coram, <bl>vor/in beiwesen.</bl> De, <bl>von/auß/von wegen.</bl> E, <bl>auß.</bl> Ex, <bl>auß.</bl> Pro, <bl>vor/in/nach/von wegen/für.</bl> Præ, <bl>vor/von wegen.</bl> Sine, <bl>ohn/</bl> & Tenues, <bl>biß an/</bl>quod semper postponitur. A & E regunt Ablativum incipientem a consona: ut, a te. a Jove, e conspectu. Ab regit Ablativum incipientem a Vocali vel L, vel R, vel jod: ut, ab alio, ab lege, ab Rege, ab Jove. Abs regit Ablativum incipientem a Q vel T: ut, Abs quivis homine, abs te. Græcum est, crurum tenus, Virgil. Cumarum tenus, in Epistol.
units.tr: Fourteen adverbs govern the ablative: a (from, after, against), ab (from), abs (from), absque (without), cum (with), clam (without the knowledge of), coram (before, in the presence of), de (from, concerning, on account of), e (out of), ex (out of), pro (before, in, after, on account of, for), prae (before, on account of), sine (without), and tenus (as far as), which is always placed after its noun. A and E govern an ablative beginning with a consonant: a te, a Jove, e conspectu. Ab governs an ablative beginning with a vowel, or with L, R or J: ab alio, ab lege, ab Rege, ab Jove. Abs governs an ablative beginning with Q or T: abs quivis homine, abs te. It is a Greek construction: "as far as the thighs" (crurum tenus), Virgil; "as far as Cumae", in the Epistles.

units.la: Quæ est quadragesima prima Regula?
units.tr: Which is the forty-first Rule?

units.la: Adverbia, in, <bl>inn</bl>. Sub, <bl>under/unb/nach</bl>. Super, <bl>auff/uber/</bl> & Subter, <bl>under/</bl> regunt cum voce motus Accusatiuum: cum voce quietis Ablatiuum. Hoc non perpetuó in sacris literis observatur.
units.tr: The adverbs in (in), sub (under, after), super (upon, above) and subter (under) govern the accusative with a verb of motion, and the ablative with a verb of rest. This is not always observed in Holy Scripture.

units.la: Gerundium in Do est Ablativi loco: ut, in tribuendo suum cuiq; versatur justitia, Cicero.
units.tr: A gerund in -do stands in place of the ablative: for example, "justice consists in giving each person his due", Cicero.

units.la: Quæ est quadragesima secunda Regula?
units.tr: Which is the forty-second Rule?

units.la: Sine Adverbio. Ablativus causæ, instrumenti, materiæ, formæ, vel similis circunstantiæ, Nomini aut Verbo frequenter apponitur: ut, Lassus cura. Oderunt peccare boni virtutis amore, oderunt peccare mali formidine pœnæ, Horatius. Ferit illum gladio, Duplicem gemmis auroque coronam, Virgilius. Ennius ingenio maximus, arte rudis, Ovidius. Scilicet ab ingenio, ab arte, id est, quod attinet ad ingenium ad artem, Gerundium in Do sine Adverbio sæpe usurpatur: ut, defessus sum ambulando, Terentius.
units.tr: Without a preposition, an ablative of cause, means, matter, form or a similar circumstance is often attached to a noun or verb: for example, "weary with care"; "good men refrain from sin for love of virtue, bad men for fear of punishment", Horace; "he strikes him with a sword"; "a double crown of gems and gold", Virgil; "Ennius, great in genius, rough in art", Ovid. That is, "in respect of genius, in respect of art". A gerund in -do is often used without a preposition: for example, "I am tired of walking", Terence.

units.la: Quæ est quinquagesima tertia Regula?
units.tr: Which is the fifty-third Rule?

units.la: Sine Adverbio, Accusativus aut Ablativus mensuræ vel spacii, nomini aut verbo frequenter adjungitur: ut, floreæ quatuor pedes latæ, Cæsar. Longum sesquipede, Plinius. Francofurtum ad Mænum Marpurgo distat decem milliaria vel milliaribus.
units.tr: Without a preposition, an accusative or ablative of measure or extent is often attached to a noun or verb: for example, "four feet wide", Caesar; "a foot and a half long", Pliny. Frankfurt on the Main is ten miles from Marburg.

units.la: Quæ est quadragesima quarta Regula?
units.tr: Which is the forty-fourth Rule?

units.la: Cum Quando, Adverbium interrogandi, expresse vel tacite præcedit; Nomen temporis in Ablativo ponitur: ut, Quando revertuntur Ciconiæ? primo vere. Superioribus diebus veni in Cumanum, Cicero. Dicimus etiam, De nocte vigilare, ex Cicerone. De nocte surgere, ex Horat.
units.tr: When the interrogative adverb "quando" (when) precedes, expressly or tacitly, the noun of time is put in the ablative: for example, "When do the storks return? In early spring." "I came in the other day to Cumae", Cicero. We also say "to keep watch at night" after Cicero, and "to rise at night" after Horace.

units.la: Quæ est quadragesima quinta Regula?
units.tr: Which is the forty-fifth Rule?

units.la: Cum Quamdiu, Adverbium interrogādi, expresse vel tacitè præcedit; Nomen temporis in Accusativo vel Ablativo ponitur: ut, Quamdiu duravit bellum Trojanum? decem annos. Noctes atque dies patet atri janua Ditis, Virgil. Vixit Adam centum triginta annis, Genesis 5. Hæc constructio frequens est in Bibliis.
units.tr: When the interrogative adverb "quamdiu" (how long) precedes, expressly or tacitly, the noun of time is put in the accusative or ablative: for example, "How long did the Trojan war last? Ten years." "Night and day the gate of black Dis stands open", Virgil. "Adam lived a hundred and thirty years", Genesis 5. This construction is frequent in the Bible.

units.la: Quæ est quadragesimasexta Regula?
units.tr: Which is the forty-sixth Rule?

units.la: Si aliquid in loco esse seu fieri significetur, proprium Nomen urbis aut insulæ primæ vel secundæ Declinationis in Genitivo singulari ponitur: Tertiæ vero, vel imparisyllabæ Declinationis in Dativo vel Ablativo: Quodvis proprium nomen urbis pluralis numeri tantum, in Ablativo: ut, Hierosolymæ Filius Dei flagellatus est. Tarenti degit Archytas, qui ligneam columbam volatilem fecit, Gellius. Samia mihi mater fuit, ea habitabat Rhodi, Terentius. Sum Neapoli. Sum Carthagini vel Carthagine. Marcus Ciceronis filius audivit Philosophum Cratippum Athenis.
units.tr: If something is signified as being or happening in a place, the proper name of a city or island of the first or second declension is put in the genitive singular; of the third (or imparisyllabic) declension, in the dative or ablative; and any proper name of a city that is plural only is put in the ablative: for example, "in Jerusalem the Son of God was scourged"; "Archytas lived at Tarentum, who made a wooden dove that could fly", Gellius; "my mother was from Samos, and she lived at Rhodes", Terence; "I am at Naples"; "I am at Carthage" or "at Carthage"; "Marcus, the son of Cicero, heard the philosopher Cratippus at Athens."

units.la: Quæ est quadragesimaseptima Regula?
units.tr: What is the forty-seventh rule?

units.la: Si motus ad locum significetur, proprium nomen urbis ponitur in Accusativo: Sin motus per locum, vel è loco fit, in Ablativo: ut proficiscar Romam. Epistolas ad me Servilius Tharso misit, Cicero. Athenis habuit iter Paulus.
units.tr: If motion toward a place is meant, the proper name of a city is put in the accusative. If the motion is through a place, or from a place, it is put in the ablative: as, I shall set out for Rome. Servilius sent letters to me from Tarsus, Cicero. Paul made his journey from Athens.

units.la: Hæc appellativa: Militia, Humus, Rus, Domus; constructionem propriorum nominum imitantur: ut, una semper militiæ & domi fuimus, Cicero. Jacet humi. Sternit juvenem humi, non humum. Tollitur humo. Sum rure vel rure. Eo rus. Redeo rure. Sum domi. Eo domum, Venio domo. Offendes etiam alia nomina in simili Syntaxi: ut, Belli rempublicam augeant, Cicero.
units.tr: These appellatives, militia, humus, rus and domus, imitate the construction of proper names: as, we were always together in the field and at home, Cicero. He lies on the ground. He strikes the young man to the ground (humum, not humo). He is lifted from the ground. I am in the country. I go into the country. I come back from the country. I am at home. I go home. I come home from home. You will find other nouns in a similar syntax: as, they increase the commonwealth by war, Cicero.

units.la: Cū Domi & Domū, adjectiva, mea, tua, sua, nostra, vestra, aliena, in casu conveniunt: ut, Malo esse cum timore domi meæ, quàm cum periculo domi alienæ, Cicero. Balbus à porta domum meam venit, Cicero.
units.tr: With domi and domum, the adjectives mea, tua, sua, nostra, vestra and aliena agree in case: as, I would rather be in fear at home, in my own house, than in danger in someone else's house, Cicero. Balbus came from the gate to my house, Cicero.

units.la: Quæ est quadragesima octava Regula?
units.tr: What is the forty-eighth rule?

units.la: Adverbia: ubi, <bl>nach dem</bl>. Cum, <bl>wenn / dieweil</bl>. Dum, <bl>bis</bl>. Donec, <bl>biß daß</bl>. Non, <bl>nit</bl>. Simulac, <bl>so bald</bl>. Simulatq;, <bl>so bald als</bl>. Postquam, <bl>nach dem</bl>. Quoad, <bl>so lange biß</bl>. Ut, <bl>wie</bl>. Quemadmodum, <bl>gleich wie</bl>. Utcunq;, <bl>Gott gebe wie</bl>. Sicut, <bl>als</bl>. Antequâ, <bl>ehe dann</bl>. Priusquam, <bl>ehe dann</bl>. Verbis primorum vel secundorum temporum adjunguntur. Ne, an, num, utrùm, <bl>was?</bl> Non, <bl>nicht?</bl> Adverbia interrogandi: ut, <bl>nach</bl> <bl>dem</bl> / Verbis primorum temporum tantùm conveniùt. Ne, an, num, utrùm, ob. Adverbia dubitandi. Utinam, <bl>wolt Gott</bl>. Quasi, <bl>gleich als</bl>. Ceu, <bl>gerad als</bl>. Tanquam, <bl>als ob</bl>. Perinde acsi, <bl>gleich als wenn</bl>. Haud secus ac si, <bl>nicht anderst als wen</bl> / Verbis secundorum temporum tantùm conveniunt. Ne pro Non, verbis secundorum temporum, aut verbis tertii futuri convenit: ut, Ne metuas. Ne feceris. Meretrix coronam auream ne habeto, Cicero.
units.tr: Adverbs: ubi, after; cum, when or since; dum, until; donec, until; non, not; simulac, as soon as; simulatque, as soon as; postquam, after; quoad, as long as, until; ut, as; quemadmodum, just as; utcunque, however; sicut, as; antequam, before; priusquam, before. These are joined to verbs of the first or second tenses. Ne, an, num, utrum, what? Non, not? These are interrogative adverbs: as, ... They agree only with verbs of the first tenses: ne, an, num, utrum, whether. Adverbs of doubt: utinam, would that; quasi, as if; ceu, just as if; tanquam, as though; perinde ac si, just as if; haud secus ac si, no differently than if. These agree only with verbs of the second tenses. Ne for non agrees with verbs of the second tenses or of the third future: as, Do not fear. Do not do it. A prostitute shall not wear a golden crown, Cicero.

units.la: Quæ est quadragesima nona Regula?
units.tr: What is the forty-ninth rule?

units.la: Conjunctio, aut similes casus, aut similia tempora, aut Adverbia conjungit: ut, Nox & amor vinumque nihil moderabile suadent, Ovidius. Multa tulit fecitque puer, sudavit & alsit, Horatius. Scortari & potare & fores effringere est flagitium, Terentius. Impudenter & petulanter. Interdum casus vel tempus conjunctionem sequens cum priori discordat: ut, Fui Romæ & Thebis. Plenus vini & cerevisia. Revertimini ad me, & revertar ad vos, dicit Dominus exercituum.
units.tr: A conjunction joins cases, tenses or adverbs alike: as, night and love and wine urge nothing moderate, Ovid. The boy endured and did much, sweated and was cold, Horace. To whore around, to drink and to break down doors is a disgrace, Terence. Shamelessly and wantonly. Sometimes the case or tense that follows a conjunction differs from the one before it: as, I was at Rome and at Thebes. Full of wine and beer. Turn back to me, and I will turn back to you, says the Lord of hosts.

units.la: Quæ est quinquagesima Regula?
units.tr: What is the fiftieth rule?

units.la: Conjunctiones: Ni, <bl>wa[?] nicht</bl>. Nisi, <bl>wo nicht / es sey</bl> <bl>dann</bl>. Si, <bl>wann</bl>. Siquidem, <bl>sintemal</bl>. Etiamsi, <bl>wiewol</bl>. Quòd, daß. Quoniam, dann / darum daß. Quia, die-weil. Quippe, als das. Utpote, als nemlich. / Verbis primorum vel secundorum temporum conveniunt.
units.tr: Conjunctions: ni, unless; nisi, unless or except; si, if; siquidem, since indeed; etiamsi, although; quod, that; quoniam, since, because; quia, because; quippe, as being; utpote, namely as. These agree with verbs of the first or second tenses.

units.la: Quanquam, Etsi, Tametsi, wiewol. Quando, sintemal. Quandoquidem, dieweil / verbis primorum temporum tantum conveniunt.
units.tr: Quanquam, etsi, tametsi, although; quando, since; quandoquidem, since. These agree only with verbs of the first tenses.

units.la: Quamvis, wiewol. Licèt, ob schon. Ut, wiewol. Ut, auff daß. Ne, / daß nicht. Quin, das nicht / Verbis secundorum temporum tantum conveniunt.
units.tr: Quamvis, although; licet, though; ut, although; ut, so that; ne, that not; quin, that not. These agree only with verbs of the second tenses.

units.la: Conjunctionum aliæ præponuntur, ut, Nam, quare, at, ac, ast, nec, si, quin, nisi, sin, seu, sive: Aliæ postponuntur, ut, Quoq; ; q;, enim, autem, verò: Aliæ indifferenter præponuntur & postponuntur, ut, Ergo, igitur, itaq;, quoniam, tamen.
units.tr: Some conjunctions are placed before the word they govern, as nam, quare, at, ac, ast, nec, si, quin, nisi, sin, seu, sive. Others are placed after, as quoque, que, enim, autem, vero. Others may be placed either before or after, as ergo, igitur, itaque, quoniam, tamen.

units.la: Si verbum primi præsentis præcedat, sequens verbum secundi præsentis esse solet: Sin verbum primorum præteritorum præcesserit, sequens verbum in secundo imperfecto plærunq; ponitur: ut, jubeo, ut facias. Jubebam, jussi, jussêram ut faceres.
units.tr: If a verb of the first present comes first, the following verb is usually of the second present. If a verb of the first past comes first, the following verb is usually put in the second imperfect: as, I order you to do it; I ordered you to do it; I had ordered you to do it.

units.la: Post Rogo, jubeo, facio: efficio, fio, curo, laboro, tam, quàm, tantus, talis, adeò, tot, sic, ita, ponitur Ut, non Quòd.
units.tr: After rogo, iubeo, facio, efficio, fio, curo, laboro, tam, quam, tantus, talis, adeo, tot, sic and ita, ut is used, not quod.

units.la: Post metuo, timeo, paveo, vereor, Ut, negat: Ne, affirmat. Metuo ut Rector veniat, ich fürchte daß der Rector nit komme. Metuo ne Rector veniat, ich fürchte daß der Rector komme.
units.tr: After metuo, timeo, paveo and vereor, ut expresses denial and ne expresses affirmation. I fear that the rector will not come. I fear that the rector will come.

units.la: Recita figuras Grammaticæ.
units.tr: Recite the figures of grammar.

units.la: Prosthesis est vel literæ vel syllabæ ad vocis principium appositio: ut, Gnatus, pro Natus. Tetuli, pro tuli.
units.tr: Prosthesis is the addition of a letter or syllable at the beginning of a word: as, gnatus for natus; tetuli for tuli.

units.la: Aphæresis est vel literæ vel syllabæ à vocis principio ablatio: ut, Ruit, pro Eruit. Temnere pro contemnere.
units.tr: Aphaeresis is the removal of a letter or syllable from the beginning of a word: as, ruit for eruit; temnere for contemnere.

units.la: Syncope est quoties aliquid è vocis medio excinditur : ut, Nummûm, pro nummorum. Amafti, pro amavisti.
units.tr: Syncope is when something is cut out of the middle of a word: as, nummum for nummorum; amasti for amavisti.

units.la: Epenthefis est quoties aliquid vocis medio apponitur:ut, Relligio pro Religio. Induperator, pro Imperator.
units.tr: Epenthesis is when something is inserted into the middle of a word: as, relligio for religio; induperator for imperator.

units.la: Apocope est è vocis fine amputatio : ut, dic,duc, fac,fer, pro dice,duce,face, fere.
units.tr: Apocope is the cutting off of something from the end of a word: for example, dic, duc, fac, fer, for dice, duce, face, fere.

units.la: Paragoge est cum ad vocis finem quippiam accedit:ut,Dicier,pro dici. Poteftur, pro potest.
units.tr: Paragoge is when something is added to the end of a word: as, dicier for dici; poteftur for potest.

units.la: Antimeria est cum vox pro voce ponitur : ut, Ubi pro postquam. Ibi,pro tum,apud Terentium.
units.tr: Antimeria is when one word is put for another: as, ubi for postquam; ibi for tum, in Terence.

units.la: Pleonafmus est cum aliquid abundat : ut, Hisce meis oculis vidi. Pleonafmus Conjunctionum dicitur Polyfyndeton.
units.tr: Pleonasm is when something is superfluous: as, I saw with these my own eyes. Pleonasm of conjunctions is called polysyndeton.

units.la: Anaftrophe est cum Adverbium casui suo postponitur ut,Quibus cum,pro cum quibus. Ante postpositum regit Ablativum : ut, paucis diebus ante, <bl>vor</bl> <bl>wenig tagen.</bl>
units.tr: Anastrophe is when an adverb is placed after its case: as, quibus cum, for cum quibus. An adverb placed after its noun governs the ablative: as, paucis diebus ante, a few days before.

units.la: Tmefis est cum vox composita dividitur:ut,Expergetefacias, pro Expergefacias te. Sic Antequâ,priusquàm,postquàm, non solùm, non tantùm, non modò, sæpissimè ab authoribus dividuntur.
units.tr: Tmesis is when a compound word is divided: as, expergetefacias for expergefacias te. So antequam, priusquam, postquam, non solum, non tantum and non modo are very often divided by authors.

units.la: Antiptosis est cum casus pro casu ponitur: ut, populo ut placerent,quas fecissét fabulas,Terentius pro Fabulæ.
units.tr: Antiptosis is when one case is put for another: as, populo ut placerent, quas fecisset fabulas, Terence, for fabulae.

units.la: Ellipsis est cùm aliquid deest : ut, Urbs antiqua fuit, Tyrii tenuere coloni. Deest, Relativum Quam. Vixit annos viginti unum. Deest, Etannum. Non sum solvendo. Non est ferendo oneri. Cibus non est esui. In his deest, Sufficiens, Idoneus, Aptus, aut simile quid. Dedit Pamphilo filiam suam vxorem. Deest in. Sumpsit te judicem. Deest, in. Ajunt, dicunt, ferunt, perhibent. Deest, Homines. Ellipsis conjunctionum dicitur Asyndeton. Usus, usus, inquam, magister artium omnium spectandus.
units.tr: Ellipsis is when something is missing: as, the ancient city was, which the Tyrian colonists held; the relative quam is missing. He lived twenty-one years; "et annum" is missing. I am not able to pay. It is not bearable for the burden. Food is not for eating. In these examples something like sufficient, fit, suitable is missing. He gave his daughter to Pamphilus as wife; in is missing. He took you as judge; in is missing. They say, they tell, they report, they claim; homines (men) is missing. Ellipsis of conjunctions is called asyndeton. Use, use, I say, is the master of all arts and must be looked to.

units.la: Quid praeterea superest? Tractatio Commatis, Coli, & Periodi. Quid est Comma?
units.tr: What remains besides? The treatment of the comma, the colon and the period. What is a comma?

units.la: Comma est sententia imperfecta, cujus finis notatur semicirculo ad imum literae posito, sic. Finis vero sententiae imperfectae, cui contrarii aliquid opponitur, notatur puncto & subjecto semicirculo, sic;
units.tr: A comma is an incomplete sentence, whose end is marked by a semicircle placed at the foot of the letter, thus: ,. But the end of an incomplete sentence to which something contrary is opposed is marked by a point and a semicircle below it, thus: ;

units.la: Quid est Colon?
units.tr: What is a colon?

units.la: Colon est sententia pene perfecta, ita tamen, ut animus audientis nondum conquiescat: cujus finis duobus signatur punctis, altero ad summum, altero ad imum literae posito, hoc modo:
units.tr: A colon is a sentence nearly complete, yet in such a way that the mind of the hearer does not yet come to rest; its end is marked by two points, one placed at the top of the letter and the other at the foot, in this manner: :

units.la: Quid est Periodus?
units.tr: What is a period?

units.la: Periodus est oratione sententia perfecta ac completa, cujus initium majore litera signatur, & finis puncto ad imum literae posito, hoc modo. Interrogationis signum hoc est? Admirationis signum hoc! Parenthesis signum hoc ( ) Unius syllabae in duas divisae signum hoc ·· Vocis in fine versus disjunctae signū hoc-vel hoc*[?]
units.tr: A period is a complete and rounded sentence in speech, whose beginning is marked by a capital letter and whose end by a point placed at the foot of the letter, in this manner. The sign of a question is this: ? The sign of exclamation is this: ! The sign of a parenthesis is this: ( ) The sign of a syllable of one word divided in two is this: ·· The sign of a word divided at the end of a line is this: - or this: *[?]

units.la: Quæ est prima Regula de vocibus in fine lineæ recte disjungendis?
units.tr: What is the first rule concerning the proper division of words at the end of a line?

units.la: Consonae, quae in principio alicujus vocis possunt conjungi, nunquam disjungatur: ut, No-ster, A-ptus, I-gnis. Nam dicimus: Sterno, Ptolemæus, Gnarus.
units.tr: Consonants which can be joined at the beginning of any word must never be separated: as, No-ster, A-ptus, I-gnis. For we say: Sterno, Ptolemaeus, Gnarus.

units.la: Quæ est secunda Regula?
units.tr: What is the second rule?

units.la: Quando consonae geminantur, prior ad præcedentem syllabam, posterior ad sequentem referatur: ut, Ar-ra, Ar-ma.
units.tr: When consonants are doubled, the first is assigned to the preceding syllable, the second to the following: as, Ar-ra, Ar-ma.

units.la: Quæ est tertia Regula.
units.tr: What is the third rule?

units.la: Consona inter duas vocales posita, posteriori adscribatur: ut, A-ra, A-nus.
units.tr: A consonant placed between two vowels is assigned to the latter: as, A-ra, A-nus.

units.la: Quæ est quarta Regula?
units.tr: What is the fourth rule?

units.la: In Compositis vocibus unaquæq; pars sejungatur: ut, Abs—traho, præter—eo.
units.tr: In compound words each part is separated: as, Abs—traho, præter—eo.

units.la: Hisce Grammatices Latinæ brevibus quidem præceptis, absolutis tamen, non contenti, Domini Philippi Melanchthonis Grammaticam, Petri Rami, vel Prisciani, succisivis horis legunto.
units.tr: Not content with these brief but complete precepts of Latin grammar, let them read through the Grammar of Philip Melanchthon, or that of Peter Ramus or Priscian, in their spare hours.

units.la: Qui autem omnium Latinarum vocum significationes scire volunt, Dasypodium, Calepinum vel Frisium evolvunto.
units.tr: And those who wish to know the meanings of all Latin words, let them turn over Dasypodius, Calepinus or Frisius.

units.la: GRAMMATICA GRAECA.
units.tr: GREEK GRAMMAR.

units.la: Quid est Grammatica Græca?
units.tr: What is Greek Grammar?

units.la: GRAMMATICA Græca est ars purè loquendi Græcè. <bl>Die Griechische</bl> <bl>Spra-chekunst ist eine kunst seuberlich Griechisch</bl> <bl>zu sprächen.</bl>
units.tr: Greek grammar is the art of speaking Greek correctly. (German gloss: The art of Greek grammar is the art of speaking Greek properly.)

units.la: Quot sunt ejus partes?
units.tr: How many parts does it have?

units.la: Duæ: Etymologia & Syntaxis, <bl>zwey: die stimmer-klär-</bl> <bl>ung und stimmsetzung.</bl>
units.tr: Two: Etymology and Syntax. (German gloss: two: the explanation of sounds and the setting of sounds.)

units.la: Quid est Etymologia?
units.tr: What is Etymology?

units.la: Etymologia est prima pars Grammaticæ, in qua de singularum vocum proprietate agitur.
units.tr: Etymology is the first part of grammar, in which the properties of individual words are discussed.

units.la: Quid est Vox?
units.tr: What is a word (vox)?

units.la: Vox est Nota, qua unaquæq; res vocatur.
units.tr: A word is a mark by which each thing is called.

units.la: Unde fit Vox?
units.tr: How is a word formed?

units.la: E litera & syllaba.
units.tr: From a letter and a syllable.

units.la: Quot sunt literæ apud Græcos?
units.tr: How many letters are there in Greek?

units.la: Quatuor & viginti, sequentibus figuris scriptæ: A, α, ἄλφα, | A, Alpha. B, β, ϐ[?], βῆτα, | B, Beta, Vulgò Vita. Γ, γ, γ[?], γάμμα, | G, Gamma, Δ, δ, δέλτα, | D, Delta. E, ε, ἐψιλόν, | E, Epsilon, sicut, e, in Germanica voce, <bl>ewig</bl>/æternum. Ζ, ζ, ζ, ζῆτα, | Z, Zeta, Vulgò Zita. H, η, ἦτα, | E, Eta, sicut e, in voce Germanica, schemen/pudore, Vulgò ita. Θ, ϑ, θ, θῆτα, | Th, Theta, Vulgò Thita. I, ι, ἰῶτα, | J[?], iota, vel i, iota, trisyllabum. Κ, κ, κάππα, | K, Kappa. A, λ, λάμβδα, L, Lambda. M, μ, μῦ, M, My, N, ν, νῦ, N, Ny. Ξ, ξ, ξι, X, Xi. O, o, ὀμικρὸν, O, Omicron. Π, π, πι, P, Pi. P, ϱ, ῥω, R, Rho. Σ, σ, ς, σίγμα, S, St, Sigma. T, τ, ταυ, T, Tau, Vulgò Taf. Y, υ, ὖψιλὸν, Y, Ypsilon, sicut, ü, in voce Germanica, wünschen / optare, Vulgò sicut i. Φ, φ, φι, Phi, Phi. X, χ, χι, Ch, Chi. Ψ, ψ, ψι, Psi, Psi. Ω, ω, ὦμέγα, O, Omega.
units.tr: Twenty-four, written with the following forms: A, alpha; B, beta, commonly called "Vita"; G, gamma; D, delta; E, epsilon, sounded like the e in the German word "ewig" (eternal); Z, zeta, commonly called "Zita"; E, eta, sounded like the e in the German word "Schemen" (shame), commonly called "ita"; Th, theta, commonly called "Thita"; I, iota, or i, a trisyllable; K, kappa; L, lambda; M, my; N, ny; X, xi; O, omicron; P, pi; R, rho; S, sigma; T, tau, commonly called "Taf"; Y, upsilon, sounded like the ü in the German word "wünschen" (to wish), commonly called like i; Ph, phi; Ch, chi; Ps, psi; O, omega.

units.la: Unde probas veteres dixisse Beta, & non Vita?
units.tr: How do you prove that the ancients said Beta and not Vita?

units.la: Ex Cratino, qui sic ait: ὁ δ' ἀλίσκω, ὥστε ... βῆ, βῆ, λέγων βαυλίζει. Hoc est, Is fatuus autem perinde ac ovis Be, Be, dicens incedit. Si illud βῆ, βῆ, veteres legissent Vi, Vi: sequeretur oves veterum tempore Vi, Vi, balavisse.
units.tr: From Cratinus, who says: "But the fool goes along like a sheep, saying Be, Be" [ὁ δ' ἀλίσκω, ὥστε ... βῆ, βῆ, λέγων βαυλίζει]. That is: "The fool, however, walks just like a sheep, saying Be, Be." If the ancients had read "Be, Be" as "Vi, Vi," it would follow that sheep in the time of the ancients bleated "Vi, Vi."

units.la: Atqui consequens valdè ridiculum est: Quippe quum oves nunquam balaverint Vi, Vi, sed semper Be, Be. Ergo & Antecedens: Ac per consequens, veteres nullo modo legerunt Vita, sed Beta.
units.tr: But the consequence is very absurd, since sheep never bleat "Vi, Vi," but always "Be, Be." Therefore the antecedent is also false, and consequently the ancients by no means read "Vita" but "Beta."

units.la: Γ ante γ, ξ, χ, quomodo sonat?
units.tr: How is gamma sounded before gamma, xi, and chi?

units.la: Secundum Grammaticos sonat perinde ut n: ἀγγελος, angelos, Angelus. λύγξ, lynx, ἔγχος, enchos, hasta. Sic γ ante × sonat ut n, sed ipsum × pronuntiandum ut g: πίφαγγα, pephanga, apparui.
units.tr: According to the grammarians it sounds like n: angelos (ἄγγελος), Angelus; lynx (λύγξ), lynx; enchos (ἔγχος), spear. So gamma before kappa sounds like n, but the kappa itself must be pronounced as g: pephanga (πέφαγγα), I have appeared.

units.la: Quotuplex est litera?
units.tr: How many kinds of letter are there?

units.la: Duplex: Vocalis aut Consona.
units.tr: Two: vowel or consonant.

units.la: Quot sunt Vocales?
units.tr: How many vowels are there?

units.la: Septem:η & ω, longæ: ε & ο, breves:α,ι,υ, ancipites. Ex his fiunt Diphthongi duodecim: αι,αω,ει,αυ,ου propriæ:α, cum jota subscripto, η,ω,ηυ,υ,ωυ, impropriæ.
units.tr: Seven: eta and omega, long; epsilon and omicron, short; alpha, iota, and upsilon, common (doubtful). From these are formed twelve diphthongs: the proper ones, ai, ao, ei, au, ou; alpha with iota subscript, eta, ō, ēu, u, ōu, which are improper.

units.la: Quomodo dividuntur Consonantes?
units.tr: How are consonants divided?

units.la: In mutas & Semivocales.
units.tr: Into mutes and semivowels.

units.la: Quot sunt Mutæ?
units.tr: How many mutes are there?

units.la: Novem: Tenues, Mediæ, Aspiratæ. π. | β. | φ. κ. | γ. | χ. τ. | δ. | θ.
units.tr: Nine: the smooth, the middle, and the aspirated: p, b, ph; k, g, ch; t, d, th.

units.la: Quomodo dividuntur semivocales?
units.tr: How are semivowels divided?

units.la: In liquidas quatuor: λ, μ, ν, ρ: & Duplices tres: ζ, ξ, ψ.
units.tr: Into four liquids: l, m, n, r; and three double letters: z, x, ps.

units.la: Quot sunt Spiritus?
units.tr: How many breathings are there?

units.la: Duo: Lenis sive Tenuis: ut, ἐγώ, Ego. Asper sive densus: ut ἅμα, simul.
units.tr: Two: the smooth or thin, as in egō (ἐγώ), I; and the rough or thick, as in hama (ἅμα), together.

units.la: Semper autem Vocalis aut Diphthongus initio dictionis alterû possidet è spiritibus. Consonans ρ in principio perpetuò aspiratur. Excipe, ῥάξ[?], Ceres, ῥαδ[?]ος[?], puer, infans, ῥάχ[?]ος[?], robustus. ῥωξός[?], vehemens. In medio verò si ρ geminetur, priore loco lævigatur, posteriore aspiratur: ut, πέρρω[?], longè.
units.tr: A vowel or diphthong at the beginning of a word always has one of the breathings. The consonant rho at the beginning is always aspirated. Exceptions: rhax, Ceres; rhadios, boy, infant; rhachos, robust; rhōxos, vehement. But in the middle, if rho is doubled, the first is left smooth and the second is aspirated, as in pherrō (πέρρω), far off.

units.la: Quid est Apostrophus?
units.tr: What is an apostrophe?

units.la: Est nota rejectæ vocalis, α,ε,ι,ο, aut Diphthongi, αι, οι: Quod fit ob sequentem vocalem, quæ si aspiretur, migrat præcedens tenuis in aspiratam: ut, νύχ' ὅλῳ, νύχθ' ὅλῳ, noctem totam. ἀπ' ἕ, ἀφ' ἕ, à quo.
units.tr: It is the mark of a dropped vowel: alpha, epsilon, iota, omicron, or a diphthong, ai or oi. This happens because of a following vowel which, if it takes a rough breathing, causes the preceding smooth consonant to pass into the aspirated one: as nyk' holō, nykth' holō, the whole night. ap' hē, aph' hē, from which.

units.la: Quot sunt Accentus?
units.tr: How many accents are there?

units.la: Tres: Acutus, ut, Θεὸς, Deus: Gravis, ut, τιμὴ, honor: circunflexus, ut, τιμῶ, facio.
units.tr: Three: the acute, as in Theos (Θεὸς), God; the grave, as in timē (τιμὴ), honour; the circumflex, as in timō (τιμῶ), I honour.

units.la: Quæ est prima Regula de Accentibus?
units.tr: What is the first rule about accents?

units.la: Nominativi accentus in prima, secunda, tertia, vel quarta syllaba, manet in eâdem etiam in cæteris casibus,nisi quòd sæpè accentus in accentu mutetur propter infrà traditas regulas:ut ἡ μέσα[?], cantus, τῆς μέσης. ἡ τιμή[?], honor, τῆς τιμῆς. ὁ Πλάτων, Plato, τὸ Πλάτωνο[?]. ὁ αἰὼν, æternitas, τὸ αἰῶνο[?]. ἡ ἀκροχορδῶν[?], verruca, τῆς ἀκροχορδῶνο[?].
units.tr: The accent of the nominative, whether on the first, second, third, or fourth syllable, remains on the same syllable in the other cases as well, except that the accent is often changed by the rules given below: as hē mesa (ἡ μέσα), the middle, gen. tēs mesēs; hē timē, honour, gen. tēs timēs; ho Platōn, Plato, to Platōno; ho aiōn, eternity, to aiōno; hē akrochordōn, wart, tēs akrochordōno.

units.la: Excipe primò, Quando Nominativus trium syllabarum in prima,vel Nominativus plurium in secunda accentum habet: tum casus crescentes ipsum protrudunt: ut, τὸ εὐδαιμον[?], beatum, τὸ εὐδαιμόνο[?]. ἡ φιλοπάτρι[?], patriæ studiosus, ὁ φιλοπατρίδης[?].
units.tr: Make an exception first when the nominative of three syllables has the accent on the first, or the nominative of more syllables has it on the second: then the oblique cases push it forward, as to eudaimon, happy, to eudaimono; hē philopatri, a lover of one's country, ho philopatridēs.

units.la: Deinde, quando ultima est longa, & nullo accentu notata: tum semper penultima acuitur: ut, ὁ ἔνδοξος, clarus, τὸ ἔνδοξον[?]. Græcus, τὸ ἑλλήνω[?], G. & D. Dualis, τὼ ἑλλήνοιν[?]. G. Pluralis, τῶν ἑλλήνων[?].
units.tr: Next, when the last syllable is long and has no accent mark, then the penultimate is always acuted: as ho endoxos, famous, to endoxon; Hellēnos (Græcus), to Hellēnō, genitive and dative dual, tō Hellēnoin; genitive plural, tōn Hellēnōn.

units.la: Quæ est secunda Regula?
units.tr: What is the second rule?

units.la: Cùm Nominativus primæ vel secundæ Declinationis in ultima accentum habet: tum Genitivi & Dativi in omni numero ac genere circumflectuntur: reliqui casus Nominativi accentum retinent:ut, ἡ τιμή, τῆς τιμῆς. Vide primam Declinationem.
units.tr: When the nominative of the first or second declension has the accent on the last syllable, the genitive and dative in every number and gender take the circumflex; the remaining cases keep the accent of the nominative: as, ἡ τιμή, τῆς τιμῆς. See the first declension.

units.la: Quæ est tertia Regula?
units.tr: What is the third rule?

units.la: A nominativo monosyllabo, Genitivi & Dativi habent gravem in ultima: Genitivus verò dualis & pluralis circumflexum in ultima: Reliqui casus habent accentum in priore: ut, ἡ χείρ, manus, τῆς χειρός, τῇ χειρί, τὴν χεῖρα. N. & A. Dualis, τὼ χεῖρε. G. & D. τοῖν χεροῖν. οἱ & ὦ χεῖρες, τῶν χειρῶν, τὰς χεῖρας, τὰς χερσί. Excipe θεῖς[?], ponens, θεὶς[?], ὤν, existens, ὤν[?]: Et alia nonnulla.
units.tr: From a monosyllabic nominative, the genitive and dative have the grave accent on the last syllable; but the genitive dual and plural have the circumflex on the last syllable. The remaining cases have the accent on the first syllable: as, ἡ χείρ, hand, τῆς χειρός, τῇ χειρί, τὴν χεῖρα. Nominative and accusative dual, τὼ χεῖρε. Genitive and dative, τοῖν χεροῖν. οἱ and ὦ χεῖρες, τῶν χειρῶν, τὰς χεῖρας, τὰς χερσί. Except θεῖς, placing, θεὶς, ὤν, being, ὤν; and some others.

units.la: Quæ est quarta?
units.tr: What is the fourth?

units.la: Natura longa ante finalem natura brevem vel positione longam, circumflectitur: ut, δῆμος, populus. βῆμα, suggestum, <bl>ein Predigstul</bl>. σῶμα, corpus. αὖλαξ, sulcus, <bl>ein furch oder grub</bl>.
units.tr: A long vowel naturally before a final syllable that is short by nature or long by position takes the circumflex: as, δῆμος, people. βῆμα, a platform, <bl>a preaching-stool</bl>. σῶμα, body. αὖλαξ, a furrow, <bl>a furrow or ditch</bl>.

units.la: Interdum hæc regula à prima impeditur: ut, ἡ ἄλων, Area, Arca ein plon oder plat3/τῆς ἁλῶν@, non ἁλῶν@.
units.tr: Sometimes this rule is hindered by the first: as, ἡ ἄλων, threshing floor, Area, Arca, a floor or flat place, genitive τῆς ἁλῶν, not ἁλῶν.

units.la: Quæ est quinta Regula.
units.tr: What is the fifth rule?

units.la: Brevis ante finalem brevem, aut brevis seu longa ante finalem longam semper acuitur: ut, λόγῳ, sermo, ἥρως amor, ἥρως Heros, κοquorum tabula. Interdum hæc regula etiam à prima impeditur: ut, ἀλώπηξ vulpes, τῆς ἀλώπηκος, non ἀλώπηκος.
