units.la: Metonymia adjuncti, <bl>die Namm verblümung des zu</bl> <bl>gefügten /</bl> est cum res adjuncta usurpatur, & res subjecta intelligitur: ut, Non auferetur sceptrū de Juda, & dux de fœmore ejus,donec veniat qui mittendus est, & ipse erit expectatio gentium,Genef.49. Sceptrum, id est, regnum non auferetur. Hic tropus est in voce Sceptro. Quando autem signo per copulam attribuitur res significata ,hoc modo : Sceptrum est Regnū; tum neq; in sceptro,neq; in regno est tropus,sed tantum in copula,seu attributionis genere. Nam de sceptro, primo Disparato, non potest regnum , alterum disparatum,proprie praedicari, sed omnino tropice.
units.tr: Metonymy of the adjunct (German gloss: the naming of the attached thing) is when the attached thing is used and the thing to which it is attached is understood, as in: "The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet, until he come whose right it is, and the gathering of the people shall be his," Genesis 49. "Sceptre," that is, kingdom, shall not be taken away. The trope here lies in the word "sceptre." But when the thing signified is attributed to the sign through a copula, in this way: "The sceptre is kingdom," then there is no trope either in "sceptre" or in "kingdom," but only in the copula, or kind of attribution. For "sceptre," a disparate term, cannot properly be predicated of "kingdom," another disparate term, but only tropically.

units.la: Quid est Ironia?
units.tr: What is irony?

units.la: Ironia, <bl>die verspottung/</bl>est tropus a contrario bono usurpato ad contrarium malum intelligendum, & contra: ut,Fecit quoq; Dominus Deus Adę & uxori ejus tunicas pelliceas,& induit eos. Et ait, Ecce Adam quasi unus ex nobis factus est, sciens bonum & malum,Genesis3. Id est,non factus est, Heus bone vir curasti probè,Terentius. Id est, Heus male vir,curasti male.
units.tr: Irony (German gloss: mockery) is a trope in which a good word is used to mean the contrary evil, and the reverse, as in: "And the Lord God made for Adam and for his wife coats of skins, and clothed them. And he said, Behold, Adam has become as one of us, knowing good and evil," Genesis 3. That is, he has not become so. "Well, good sir, you have taken good care of it," Terence. That is, "Well, bad sir, you have taken bad care of it."

units.la: Est & ironia, quæ prætéritio a quibusdam dicitur, ut in his formulis,prætereo,mitto.
units.tr: There is also irony which some call preterition, as in these formulas: "I pass over," "I say nothing."

units.la: Ironia denique est,quæ negatio dicitur: ut, non agam tecum jure summo (scilicet) : non dicam quod fortasse obtinerem,Cicero. Sarcasmus est, cùm hostis calamitatem exprobrat hosti : ut, Ave rex Judæorum, si filius Dei es,descende de cruce.Matth.27.
units.tr: Finally, there is the irony which is called negation, as in: "I will not deal with you by strict right" (that is, "I will not say what I might perhaps obtain"), Cicero. Sarcasm is when an enemy reproaches an enemy with his calamity, as in: "Hail, King of the Jews! If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross," Matthew 27.

units.la: Quid est Metaphora?
units.tr: What is metaphor?

units.la: Metaphora, <bl>die gleichliche übersetzung /</bl> est in una voce contracta similitudo : ut, si in viridi ligno hæc faciunt : in arido quid fiet ? Lucæ 23. Id est, si in homine Christo hæc faciunt,qui similis est viridis ligni: quid fiet in reliquis hominibus, qui similes sunt aridi ligni?
units.tr: Metaphor (German gloss: the like translation) is a likeness contracted into a single word, as in: "If they do these things in the green tree, what shall be done in the dry?" Luke 23. That is, if they do these things to Christ, who is like a green tree, what will be done to the rest of men, who are like dry wood?

units.la: Hyperbole,id est, supra fidē amplificatio, (vulgō Auxesis) & Allegoria, id est, continuatio troporum, in Metaphoris præcipuam laudem obtinent: Atque ex hyperbolica metaphora oritur mira sublimitas orationis cùm rebus inanimatis actum quendam, & animos damus: ut, parietes, ut mihi videntur, hujus curiae tibi gratias agere gestiunt, Cicero.
units.tr: Hyperbole, that is, amplification beyond belief (commonly called auxesis), and allegory, that is, a continued series of tropes, obtain the chief praise among metaphors. And from hyperbolical metaphor arises a wonderful sublimity of speech when we give inanimate things an action and feelings, as in: "The walls, as they seem to me, are eager to give you thanks, of this senate house," Cicero.

units.la: Quid est Synecdoche?
units.tr: What is synecdoche?

units.la: Synecdoche, <bl>Die begreiffung/</bl> est cum pars usurpatur & totum intelligitur, aut contrà. Synecdoche est quadruplex: Membri, speciei, integri, aut generis.
units.tr: Synecdoche (German gloss: the comprehension) is when a part is used and the whole understood, or the reverse. Synecdoche is fourfold: of the member, of the species, of the whole, or of the genus.

units.la: Quid est Synecdoche membri?
units.tr: What is synecdoche of the member?

units.la: Synecdoche membri, <bl>Die begreiffung des stücks/</bl> est quando membrum usurpatur, & integrum intelligitur: ut, anima sæpe ponitur in Bibliis, & intelligitur totus homo. sic tectum ponitur pro domo, mucro, <bl>ein spiţ[?] am gewehr/</bl> pro gladio.
units.tr: Synecdoche of the member (German gloss: the comprehension of the piece) is when a member is used and the whole understood, as "soul" is often put in the Bible and the whole man is understood. So "roof" is put for house, and "mucro" (German gloss: a spike on a weapon) for sword.

units.la: Quid est Synecdoche speciei?
units.tr: What is synecdoche of the species?

units.la: Synecdoche speciei, <bl>Die begreiffung einer eigent-</bl> <bl>lichen substanz oder dinges/</bl> est quando species usurpatur, & genus intelligitur: ut, Si fueris Thrafo, non deerit tibi Gnatho. Id est, Si fueris homo gloriosus non deerit tibi assentator.
units.tr: Synecdoche of the species (German gloss: the comprehension of a particular substance or thing) is when a species is used and the genus understood, as: "If you are a Thraso, a Gnatho will not be lacking to you." That is, "If you are a boastful man, a flatterer will not be lacking to you."

units.la: Quid est Synecdoche integri?
units.tr: What is synecdoche of the whole?

units.la: Synecdoche integri, <bl>Die begreiffung des ganzen/</bl> est quando integrum usurpatur, & membrum intelligitur: ut, pabula gustassent Trojae, Xanthumq; biberent, Virgilius. Hic intelligis & partem pabuli, & partem Xanthi fluvij.
units.tr: Synecdoche of the whole (German gloss: the comprehension of the whole) is when the whole is used and a member understood, as: "They had tasted the Trojan fodder and drunk from the Xanthus," Virgil. Here you understand both part of the fodder and part of the river Xanthus.

units.la: Quid est Synecdoche generis?
units.tr: What is synecdoche of the genus?

units.la: Synecdoche generis, <bl>Die begreiffung des gemei-</bl> <bl>nen/</bl> est quando genus usurpatur, & species intelligitur: ut, Apostolus, pro Paulo. Imperator pro Justiniano. Orator pro Cicerone aut Demosthene. Poeta pro Virgil. aut Homero. Vulgus Antonomasiam vocat, Sic pluralis numerus pro singulari: ut, Nos populo imposuimus, & Oratores visi sumus, Cicero.
units.tr: Synecdoche of the genus (German gloss: the comprehension of the common thing) is when a genus is used and a species understood, as "Apostle" for Paul, "Emperor" for Justinian, "Orator" for Cicero or Demosthenes, "Poet" for Virgil or Homer. The common people call this antonomasia. So too the plural number is used for the singular, as: "We have imposed on the people, and we seemed to be orators," Cicero.

units.la: Quid est Figura?
units.tr: What is a figure?

units.la: Figura est elocutio, qua orationis habitus à vulgari consuetudine cum quadam suavitate mutatur: <bl>Die zierliche gestalt ist eine rede zierung/damit</bl> <bl>der rede eigentliche form vom gemeinen brauch mit einer lieblichkeit verändert wird.</bl>
units.tr: A figure is a mode of speech by which the form of the discourse is changed from ordinary usage with a certain charm (German gloss: an ornamental form is an embellishment of speech, by which the proper form of speech is changed from common usage with a certain pleasantness).

units.la: Quotuplices sunt figurae?
units.tr: How many kinds of figures are there?

units.la: Duplices: Vocum & Sententiarum. Figurae vocum sunt novem: Epizeuxis, Anadiplosis, Climax, Anaphora, Epistrophe, Symploce, Epanalepsis, Paronomasia, Polyptoton.
units.tr: Two kinds: figures of words and figures of sentences. There are nine figures of words: epizeuxis, anadiplosis, climax, anaphora, epistrophe, symploce, epanalepsis, paronomasia, polyptoton.

units.la: Quid est Epizeuxis?
units.tr: What is epizeuxis?

units.la: Epizeuxis, die widerholung einer stim / est figura, in qua idem sonus continuè iteratur: ut, Et respondens dixit illi Dominus, Martha, Martha, sollicita es, & turbaris erga plurima. Lucae 10.
units.tr: Epizeuxis (German gloss: the repetition of a word) is a figure in which the same sound is repeated continuously, as: "And the Lord answered and said to her, Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things," Luke 10.

units.la: Et hora nona exclamavit Jesus voce magna dicens: Eloi, Eloi, lamma sabachthani? quod est interpretatu, Deus meus, Deus meus, ut qd dereliquisti me? Mar.15.
units.tr: "And at the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani? which is, being interpreted, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" Mark 15.

units.la: Quid est Anadiplosis?
units.tr: What is anadiplosis?

units.la: Anadiplosis, <bl>die zweyfaltigung</bl> / est figura, in qua idem sonus in fine praecedentis & principio sequentis sententiæ iteratur: ut, Hic tamen vivit: vivit? imò vero etiam in senatum venit, Cicero.
units.tr: Anadiplosis (German gloss: the doubling) is a figure in which the same sound is repeated at the end of one sentence and at the beginning of the next, as: "Yet he lives: lives? Nay indeed, he even comes into the senate," Cicero.

units.la: Quid est Climax?
units.tr: What is Climax?

units.la: *Climax, <bl>die aufsteigung</bl> / est figura, in qua oratio per gradus ita progreditur, ut antecedens sequenti loco repetatur: ut, Sed & gloriamur in tribulationibus, scientes quod tribulatio patientiam operatur, patientia autem probationem, probatio verò spem. Spes autem non confundit. Roman.5.
units.tr: Climax, the ascent, is a figure in which the speech advances by steps, so that the preceding word is repeated in the next place: as, "But we also glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation works patience, patience probation, and probation hope. And hope does not disappoint." Romans 5.

units.la: Quid est Anaphora?
units.tr: What is Anaphora?

units.la: Anaphora, <bl>die widerbringung einer stim am an-</bl> <bl>fang</bl> / est figura, in qua idem sonus iteratur in principiis diversarum sententiarum: ut, Beati pauperes spiritu: quoniam ipsorum est regnû cœlorum. Beati mites: quoniam ipsi possidebunt terram. Beati qui lugent: quoniam ipsi consolabuntur. Beati qui esuriût, & sitiunt justitiâ: quoniam ipsi saturabuntur. Beati misericordes: quoniam ipsi misericordiâ cósequentur. Beati mundo corde: quoniam ipsi Deum videbunt. Beati pacifici: quoniâ filij Dei vocabuntur. Beati qui persecutionem patiuntur propter justitiam: quoniâ ipsorum est regnû cœlorû. Beati estis cûm maledixerint vobis, & persecuti vos fuerint, & dixerint omne malum adversus vos mentientes, propter me, Matth.5.
units.tr: Anaphora, the repetition of a word at the beginning, is a figure in which the same sound is repeated at the beginnings of successive sentences: as, "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are the meek: for they shall possess the earth. Blessed are those who mourn: for they shall be comforted. Blessed are those who hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be satisfied. Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy. Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God. Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the sons of God. Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are you when they shall revile you and persecute you, and shall say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake." Matthew 5.

units.la: Quid est Epistrophe?
units.tr: What is Epistrophe?

units.la: Epistrophe, <bl>Die wiederkehrung am ende</bl> / est figura, in qua idem sonus in clausulis iteratur: ut, Quid faceret? senatum obsideret? cives indemnatos expelleret? bona diriperet? ædes incenderet? tecta disturbaret? templa Deorum immortalium inflammaret? Cicero. Homœoptoton est Epistrophe in casibus: Homœoteleuton Epistrophe in verbis: ut, Est enim hæc, judices, non scripta, sed nata lex, quam non didicimus, accepimus, legimus: verum ex natura ipsa arripuimus, hausimus, expressimus: ad quam nô doc-ti, sed facti, non instituti sed imbuti sumus: ut si vita nostra in aliquas insidias, si in vim, in tela aut latronû aut inimicorum incidisset, omnis honesta ratio esset expediendæ salutis. Cicero pro Milone.
units.tr: Epistrophe, the return at the end, is a figure in which the same sound is repeated at the ends of clauses: as, "What would he do? Would he besiege the senate? Would he expel uncondemned citizens? Would he plunder goods? Would he burn houses? Would he tear down roofs? Would he set fire to the temples of the immortal gods?" Cicero. Homoeoptoton is epistrophe in cases; homoeoteleuton is epistrophe in verbs: as, "For this, judges, is not a written law but a born one, which we have not learned, received or read, but have seized, drawn in and absorbed from nature itself; to which we have been formed not by teaching but by making, not instructed but steeped. So that if our life had fallen into some ambush, or into violence, or into the weapons of robbers or enemies, every honourable means of securing safety would be justified." Cicero, for Milo.

units.la: Quid est Symploce?
units.tr: What is Symploce?

units.la: Symploce, <bl>Die verbindung</bl> / est figura, in qua Anaphora & Epistrophe conjunguntur: ut, Quis Dei filius? Christus. Quis pro nobis mortuus? Christus. Quis pro nobis resurrexit? Christus.
units.tr: Symploce, the combination, is a figure in which anaphora and epistrophe are joined: as, "Who is the Son of God? Christ. Who died for us? Christ. Who rose again for us? Christ."

units.la: Quid est Epanalepsis seu Epanodos?
units.tr: What is Epanalepsis or Epanodos?

units.la: Epanalepsis seu Epanodos, <bl>Die widerholung</bl> / est figura, in qua idem sonus in principio & clausula repetitur : ut, Multa super Priamo rogitans, super Hectore multa, Virgilius. Multi & graves dolores inventi, parentibus & propinquis multi, Cic.
units.tr: Epanalepsis or Epanodos, the repetition, is a figure in which the same sound is repeated at the beginning and at the end: as, "Asking many things about Priam, and many about Hector," Virgil. "Many and grievous pains have been found, for parents and many kinsfolk," Cicero.

units.la: Quid est Paronomasia?
units.tr: What is Paronomasia?

units.la: Paronomasia, Die <bl>Zusammenung</bl>[?] est figura, in qua voces diversae, aliquot syllabis inter se consonant: ut, Qui fuit Saulus, factus est Paulus, Actor.9. Inceptio est amentium, non amantium, Terentius. Non est orator, sed arator.
units.tr: Paronomasia, the juxtaposition, is a figure in which different words agree with one another in some syllables: as, "He who was Saul has become Paul," Acts 9. "It is the beginning of madmen, not of lovers," Terence. "He is not an orator but a ploughman (arator)."

units.la: Quid est Polyptoton?
units.tr: What is Polyptoton?

units.la: Polyptoton, Die <bl>mancherley fälle hat</bl> / est figura, in qua voces ejusdem originis finibus dissimilibus variantur: ut, Littora littoribus contraria, fluctibus undas Imprecor, arma, armis, Virgil. Non ut edam, vivo: sed ut vivam, edo. Quintilianus.
units.tr: Polyptoton, the many cases, is a figure in which words of the same origin are varied in different endings: as, "Shores against shores, I call down waves on waves, arms on arms," Virgil. "I do not live in order to eat, but I eat in order to live," Quintilian.

units.la: Quot sunt figurae sententiarum?
units.tr: How many are the figures of thought?

units.la: Undecim : Exclamatio, Epiphonema, Epanorthosis, Aposiopesis, Apostrophe, Prosopopœia, Addubitatio, Comunicatio, Prolepsis, Permissio, Concessio.
units.tr: Eleven: exclamation, epiphonema, epanorthosis, aposiopesis, apostrophe, prosopopoeia, addubitatio, communicatio, prolepsis, permissio, concessio.

units.la: Quid est Exclamatio?
units.tr: What is Exclamation?

units.la: Exclamatio, Die <bl>ausschreyung</bl>[?] / est figura in qua Adverbium exclamandi exprimitur vel intelligitur: ut, o altitudo divitiarum sapientiae & scientiae Dei! Roman.11. Aliquando Exclamatio fit per interrogationem: ut, Quis cognovit sensum Domini?
units.tr: Exclamation, the outcry, is a figure in which an adverb of exclaiming is expressed or understood: as, "O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God!" Romans 11. Sometimes exclamation is made by means of a question: "Who has known the mind of the Lord?"

units.la: Quid est Epiphonema?
units.tr: What is Epiphonema?

units.la: Epiphonema, Die <bl>zuschiebung</bl>[?] / est species exclamationis, quae ad finem rei narratae & explicatae addi solet: ut,tantæ molis erat Romanam condere gentem, Virgilius.
units.tr: Epiphonema, the added remark, is a kind of exclamation which is customarily added at the end of a narrated and explained matter: as, "So great was the effort required to found the Roman race," Virgil.

units.la: Quid est Epanorthosis?
units.tr: What is Epanorthosis?

units.la: Epanorthosis, Die <bl>widerruffung</bl> / est figura, in qua antecedens aliquid revocatur: ut, Filium unicum adolescentulum habeo, ah ! quid dixi habere me? Imo habui Chreme, nunc habeam nec'ne, incertum est, Terentius.
units.tr: Epanorthosis, the retraction, is a figure in which something said before is taken back: as, "I have an only son, a young man. Ah, what did I say, that I have him? Nay, rather I had him, Chremes. Whether I have him now or not is uncertain," Terence.

units.la: Quid est Aposiopesis?
units.tr: What is Aposiopesis?

units.la: Aposiopesis, <bl>Die verschweigung</bl> est figura, in qua cursus sententiæ inchoatæ ita revocatur, ut aliquid non dictum intelligatur: ut, Quos ego: sed motos præstat componere fluctus, Virgilius. Intelligitur puniam vel simile quid.
units.tr: Aposiopesis, the breaking off, is a figure in which the course of a begun sentence is broken off so that something unspoken is understood: as, "Those whom I... but it is better to calm the stirred-up waves," Virgil. It is understood: "I will punish them," or something similar.

units.la: Quid est Apostrophe?
units.tr: What is Apostrophe?

units.la: Apostrophe, <bl>Die abwendung</bl> est figura, qua oratio inter dicendum ad alienam personam convertitur: ut, In nova, fert animus mutatas dicere formas, corpora. Dij coeptis (nam vos mutastis & illas) Aspirate meis, primaq; ab origine mundi, Ad mea perpetuum deducite tempora carmen, Ovid. Interdum Apostrophe fit ad nos ipsos: ut, infere nunc Melibœe pyros, pone ordine vites, Virgil.
units.tr: Apostrophe, the turning away, is a figure by which, in the course of speaking, the speech is turned to another person: as, "Of forms changed into new bodies my mind bids me speak. Gods, for you also changed those forms, breathe on my undertaking, and from the first origin of the world lead my song down to my own times without end," Ovid. Sometimes apostrophe is made to ourselves: "Now graft the pears, Melibous; set the vines in rows," Virgil.

units.la: Quid est Prosopopœia?
units.tr: What is Prosopopoeia?

units.la: Prosopopœia, <bl>Die einfuhrung der person</bl> est figura, qua nostra oratione alienam personam loquetem introducimus: ut, Et nunc si quis vobis dixerit, Ecce, hic est Christus, ecce illic: ne credideritis, Marci 13. Interdum nostram personam loquentem introducimus: ut, Veni hodie ad fontem aquæ, & dixi: Domine Deus Domini mei Abraham, Genef.24.
units.tr: Prosopopoeia, the introduction of a person, is the figure by which we introduce another person speaking in our oration: for example, "And if anyone then says to you, 'Look, here is Christ, or there,' do not believe it" (Mark 13). Sometimes we introduce ourselves speaking: for example, "I came today to the spring of water and said, 'O Lord, God of my lord Abraham'" (Genesis 24).

units.la: Quid est Addubitatio?
units.tr: What is Addubitatio?

units.la: Addubitatio, <bl>Die halbzweifflung</bl> est deliberatio nobiscum: ut, Ait autem villicus intra se: quid faciam, quia Dominus meus aufert à me villicationē? fodere non valeo, mendicare erubesco. Scio quid faciam, ut, cùm amotus fuero à villicatione, recipiant me in domos suas, Lucæ 16.
units.tr: Addubitatio, the half-doubt, is deliberation with oneself: for example, "Then the steward said within himself, 'What shall I do, since my lord is taking away from me the stewardship? I am not strong enough to dig, and I am ashamed to beg. I know what I shall do, so that when I am removed from the stewardship, they may receive me into their houses'" (Luke 16).

units.la: Quid est Communicatio?
units.tr: What is Communicatio?

units.la: Communicatio, <bl>Die rahtsfragung</bl> est deliberatio cum aliis: ut, Nunc ego, Judices, jam vos consulo, quid mihi faciendum putetis, Cicero.
units.tr: Communicatio, consulting others, is deliberation with others: for example, "Now I consult you, judges, as to what you think I should do" (Cicero).

units.la: Quid est Prolepsis?
units.tr: What is Prolepsis?

units.la: Prolepsis, die zuuorkommung[?]/ist interrogationis occupatio: ut, Dicet aliquis, hæc igitur est tua disciplina? sic tu instituis adolescentes? Cicero.
units.tr: Prolepsis, anticipation, is the forestalling of an objection by a question: for example, "Someone will say, 'Is this then your teaching? Is this how you instruct the young?'" (Cicero).

units.la: Quid est Permissio?
units.tr: What is Permissio?

units.la: Permissio, die nachlassung / est cum licentia facti condonatur: ut, i, sequere Italiam ventis; pete regna per undas, Virgil.
units.tr: Permissio, granting leave, is when a deed is allowed with permission: for example, "Go, follow Italy on the winds; seek your kingdom across the waves" (Virgil).

units.la: Quid est Concessio?
units.tr: What is Concessio?

units.la: Concessio, die nachgebung/ est cum dicto aliquod aut argumentum conceditur: ut, Sit sacrilegus, sit fur, sit flagitiorum omnium vitiorumq; princeps, Cic.
units.tr: Concessio, concession, is when something is granted for the sake of argument, either by a statement or by a reason: for example, "Let him be a sacrilegious man, let him be a thief, let him be the chief of all crimes and vices" (Cicero).

units.la: Quid est Pronuntiatio?
units.tr: What is Pronunciation?

units.la: PRonuntiatio est secunda pars Rhetoricae, qua oratio tropis vel figuris exornata, apte enūtiatur. <bl>Die rede außsagung ist das ander theil der Rede-</bl> <bl>kunst / damit die rede mit verblümungen vnd zierli-</bl> <bl>chen gestalten außgebutzet / geschicklich außgesaget</bl> <bl>wird.</bl> Ejus partes duae sunt: Vox, & Gestus.
units.tr: Pronunciation is the second part of rhetoric, by which a speech, adorned with tropes or figures, is fittingly delivered. Die rede außsagung ist das ander theil der Redekunst, damit die rede mit verblümungen vnd zierlichen gestalten außgebutzet, geschicklich außgesaget wird. Its two parts are voice and gesture.

units.la: Quodnam est præceptum Vocis?
units.tr: What is the precept concerning Voice?

units.la: Ut omnia sono vocis, rebus accommodato, proferantur.
units.tr: That everything be uttered with a sound of voice suited to the matter.

units.la: Quid est Gestus seu Actio?
units.tr: What is Gestus, or Actio?

units.la: Gestus seu Actio est corporis sermo: Estq; vel totius corporis, vel partium corporis.
units.tr: Gesture, or action, is the speech of the body, and it is either of the whole body or of its parts.

units.la: Quomodo fit Gestus totius corporis?
units.tr: How is the gesture of the whole body made?

units.la: Totius corporis status sit secundum naturam erectus & excelsus.
units.tr: The posture of the whole body should be upright and erect, according to nature.

units.la: Quomodo fit Gestus partium corporis?
units.tr: How is the gesture of the parts of the body made?

units.la: Oculorum, & manuum, ac omnium membrorum, magna debet esse moderatio, ne quid ineptum, aut vultuosum in orationibus habendis appareat.
units.tr: There must be great restraint in the eyes, the hands, and all the limbs, so that nothing awkward or grimacing appears when we are speaking.

units.la: Lecturi praecepta prolixiora videant Rhetoricam Domini Philippi Melanchthonis, & libros quatuor Rhetoricorum ad Herennium.
units.tr: Those who want fuller precepts should see the Rhetoric of Master Philip Melanchthon, and the four books of Rhetoric to Herennius.

units.la: Hactenus est Rhetorica explicita.
units.tr: So far the Rhetoric has been set out.

units.la: DE POETICA.
units.tr: ON POETRY.

units.la: Quid est Poetica?
units.tr: What is poetry?

units.la: POETICA est ars bene versificandi, <bl>Die reymekunst ist eine kunst wol sprüche</bl> <bl>mit abgemessen silben zu stellen.</bl>
units.tr: Poetry is the art of composing verse well: "The rhyming art is the art of setting out well-formed lines with measured syllables."

units.la: Quot sunt consideranda in versibus?
units.tr: What must be considered in verses?

units.la: Tria: Quantitas Syllabarum, Pedes, & Metrum.
units.tr: Three things: the quantity of syllables, the feet, and the metre.

units.la: Quid de quantitate Syllabarum dicis?
units.tr: What do you say about the quantity of syllables?

units.la: Omnis syllaba, aut est longa, aut brevis, aut communis.
units.tr: Every syllable is either long, short, or common.

units.la: Quænam Syllaba est longa?
units.tr: Which syllable is long?

units.la: Primò, omnis diphthongus est longa, ut prima syllaba in ætas, <bl>ein jetlichs</bl> alter / audio, <bl>ich höre</bl> / coena, <bl>ein nachtmal</bl> / euge, ei <bl>wolan.</bl>
units.tr: First, every diphthong is long, as the first syllable in aetas, "each one's age"; in alter / audio, "I hear"; in coena, "a supper"; in euge, and ei, "well then."

units.la: Secundò, omnis positio est longa. Est autem positio, quando vocalem sequuntur duæ cõsonæ, aut duplex: ut, Ast, aber / pax, friede / gaza, <bl>ein schatz</bl> / ajo, <bl>ich</bl> <bl>sage.</bl> Cæterum cum prioris vocis ultima syllaba definit in vocalem, & in proxima voce sequuntur duæ vel plures consonæ, aut duplex, nulla fit inde necessaria positio: ut, jam medio apparet fluctu nemorosa Zacynthus, Virgil. <bl>Es erscheinet mitten in den was-</bl> <bl>sern die waldechtige Insel im Meer Jonio.</bl>
units.tr: Second, every syllable followed by a position is long. A position occurs when a vowel is followed by two consonants, or by a double consonant: as in ast, "but"; pax, "peace"; gaza, "a treasure"; ajo, "I say." But when the last syllable of a word ends in a vowel, and the next word begins with two or more consonants, or with a double consonant, no necessary position arises: as in jam medio apparet fluctu nemorosa Zacynthus, Virgil: "Now in the middle of the waves there appears the wooded island of Zacynthus in the Ionian sea."

units.la: Si aut prioris vocis ultima definit in consonã, & in proxima voce cõsona aut duplex sequitur, positio locum habet: ut, nec te collaudes, nec te culpaveris ipse, Hoc faciunt stulti, quos gloria vexat inanis, <bl>Du solt Dich sel[?]</bl> mit loben/ noch dich selber schelten/ das thun <bl>Narren/</bl> welche die <bl>ewel ehre</bl> plaget[?].
units.tr: If the last syllable of a word ends in a consonant, and the next word begins with a consonant or a double consonant, position does apply: as in nec te collaudes, nec te culpaveris ipse, and Hoc faciunt stulti, quos gloria vexat inanis: "You should neither praise yourself nor blame yourself [?]; fools do this, whom empty glory plagues."

units.la: Tertiò, praeterita & supina dissyllaba habent priorem longam: ut, liqui, ich habe verlassen/ fugi, ich bin geflohen/ feci, ich habe gethan/ cudi, ich habe geschmi- det/ fivi, ich habe gestattet/ cretum, zu wachsen/ cusum, zu schmiden/ fusum, zu giessen/ lusum, zu spie- len. Excipiuntur haec praeterita & supina, quae priore brevem habent: ut, bibi, ich habe getruncken/ dedi, ich habe gegeben/ fidi, ich habe gespalten/ scidi, ich habe geschnitten/ steti, ich bin gestanden/ tuli, ich habe getragen/ Datum, zu geben/ ratum, zu meinen/ satum, zu säyen/ itum, zu gehen/ litum, zu salben/ quitum, zu können/ situm, zu gestatten/ citum, zu bewegen/ a cieo, statum, zu stehen/ in quibusdam producitur, in quibusdam corripitur.
units.tr: Third, perfects and supines of two syllables have the first syllable long: liqui, "I have left"; fugi, "I have fled"; feci, "I have done"; cudi, "I have hammered"; fivi, "I have permitted"; cretum, "to grow"; cusum, "to hammer"; fusum, "to pour"; lusum, "to play." The following perfects and supines are exceptions, having the first syllable short: bibi, "I have drunk"; dedi, "I have given"; fidi, "I have split"; scidi, "I have cut"; steti, "I have stood"; tuli, "I have carried"; datum, "to give"; ratum, "to think"; satum, "to sow"; itum, "to go"; litum, "to anoint"; quitum, "to be able"; situm, "to permit"; citum, "to move," from cieo; statum, "to stand." In some of these the syllable is lengthened, in others shortened.

units.la: Quartò, Adverbia, à, è, de, di, fe, co, longa sunt: ut A cane non magno sæpè tenetur aper: amando, ich schicke wohin/ averto, ich wende ab/ eligo, ich erwehle/ depono, ich lege ab/ deficio, ich gebreste/ diluo, ich vermische/ lehne ab/ diduco, ich ziehe von einander. Excipe di breve in Dirimo, ich scheide von einander/ & difertus, wol beredt. Dicta Adverbia brevia sunt, sequente vocali: ut, deamo, ich habe fast lieb.
units.tr: Fourth, the prefixes a, e, de, di, fe, and co are long: as in a cane non magno saepe tenetur aper; amando, "I send somewhere"; averto, "I turn away"; eligo, "I choose"; depono, "I lay down"; deficio, "I fail"; diluo, "I mix / I decline"; diduco, "I draw apart." Make an exception for di in dirimo, "I separate from one another," and in difertus, "well spoken," where it is short. These prefixes are short when a vowel follows: as in deamo, "I almost love."

units.la: Quintò, i, u, n, c, as, es, os, in vocis fine longa sunt: ut, veni, manu, Titan, die Sonne/ hymen, ein braut- lied/ein Gott der hochzeit/ halec, ein häring/ hic, hie/ amas, doces, aries, ein schaffsbock/ dem nicht ausgeh- awen ist/ paries, ein wand/ abies, ein Tannenbaum/ Ceres, die Göttin der frücht/ fides, trew und glaube/ hæres, ein erbe/ pes, ein fuß/ res, ein ding/ locuples, reich an ligende gütern/ spes, hoffnung/ bos, ein rind/ honor, ehr/ os, oris, der mund.
units.tr: Fifth, the final syllables i, u, n, c, as, es, and os are long: veni, manu, Titan, "the sun"; hymen, "a wedding song, a god of marriage"; halec, "a herring"; hic, "here"; amas, doces, aries, "a ram that is not yet full-grown"; paries, "a wall"; abies, "a fir tree"; Ceres, "the goddess of fruits"; fides, "faith, trust"; heres, "an heir"; pes, "a foot"; res, "a thing"; locuples, "rich in landed property"; spes, "hope"; bos, "an ox"; honor, "honour"; os, oris, "the mouth."

units.la: Primò excipiuntur Græcorum Dativi & Vocativi in i breves: ut, Palladi, der Göttinnen guter künste Auß des Jovis haupt geboren / ô Pari, ô Sohn des Königes Priami. Sic Nisi, quasi.
units.tr: First, the Greek datives and vocatives in -i are exceptions and are short: Palladi, "of the goddess of the good arts"; "Born from the head of Jove, O Paris, O son of King Priam." So too nisi, quasi.

units.la: Secundo, neutra, & masculina latina in en, habentia inis, in Genitivo, corripiuntur: ut, Nomen, carmen, pecten, tubicen. Sic forsan, forsitan, tamen, attamen, in, dein, <bl>Darnach</bl>/ exin, proin, <bl>Darumb</bl>/ an, <bl>was</bl>. Sic Nomina Graeca in on per o parvum, Accusativi Graeci in in, & in an a nominativis in a, corripiuntur.
units.tr: Second, neuter and masculine Latin nouns in -en, which have -inis in the genitive, are short: nomen, carmen, pecten, tubicen. So too forsan, forsitan, tamen, attamen, in, dein, "afterwards"; exin, proin, "therefore"; an, "what." Likewise Greek nouns in -on with short o, Greek accusatives in -in, and accusatives in -an formed from nominatives in -a, are short.

units.la: Tertio, nec, donec, lac, & hoc, nominativi & accusativi casus, corripiuntur. Fac & hic pronomen, communia sunt.
units.tr: Third, nec, donec, lac, and hoc are short in the nominative and accusative cases. Also the pronoun hic; these are common.

units.la: Quarto, Nominativi in as, quorum Genitivus in dos definit, corripiuntur. Sic Accusativi Graeci in as, quorum Genitivus singularis definit in os.
units.tr: Fourth, nominatives in -as whose genitive ends in -dos are short. So too Greek accusatives in -as whose singular genitive ends in -os.

units.la: Quinto, in es, quae Genitivo crescunt, brevia sunt: ut, seges, miles, dives. Sic Es à Sum cum compositis, penes, hippomanes, cacoethes, brevia sunt. Item Nominativi Graeci plurales in es corripiuntur.
units.tr: Fifth, nouns in -es which lengthen in the genitive are short: seges, miles, dives. So too es, from sum, with its compounds, and penes, hippomanes, cacoethes, are short. Likewise Greek plural nominatives in -es are short.

units.la: Sexto, Graeca in os parvum corripiuntur. Sic os offis.
units.tr: Sixth, Greek words in short -os are short. So too os, offis.

units.la: Quaenam syllaba est brevis?
units.tr: What is a short syllable?

units.la: Primo, vocalis ante vocalem in Latinis vocibus corripitur: ut, prima syllaba in Deus, pius, scio. Sic & diphthongus ante vocalem corripitur: ut, ver praeit aestatem, cur aestas ipsa senescit. Virgilius.
units.tr: First, a vowel before a vowel is shortened in Latin words, as the first syllable in Deus, pius, scio. Likewise a diphthong before a vowel is shortened: "ver praeit aestatem, cur aestas ipsa senescit" (Virgil).

units.la: Excipe aer, fio in disyllabis, Dius, <bl>Göttlich</bl>/ac Genitivos in ei, ut, species, progenici.
units.tr: Excepted are aer, fio in disyllables, Dius (divine), and genitives in -ei, such as species and progenies.

units.la: Secundo, prima in praeteritis geminatis corripitur: ut, pependi, totondi, momordi.
units.tr: Second, the first syllable of perfects with reduplication is short: pependi, totondi, momordi.

units.la: Tertio, a, e, y, b, d, l, m, r, t, is, us, in vocis fine brevia sunt: ut, Musa, ita, quia, age, ecce, euge, moly, <bl>ein</bl> <bl>traut vom Homero gepreiset</bl> / ab, apud, nihil, templum, jubar, caput, tristis, bonus.
units.tr: Thirdly, the vowels a, e, y and the consonants b, d, l, m, r, t, and the endings is and us, are short at the end of a word. Examples: Muse, thus, because, go, behold, well done, moly, <bl>ein traut vom Homero gepreiset</bl> (a trusted one praised by Homer); from, near, nothing, temple, brightness, head, sad, good.

units.la: Primo excipiuntur nomina masculina Graeca in as, quae in vocativo a longum habent: ut, Aenea, Psalla. Sic nomina primae declinationis, habent in Ablativo a longum, ut, à Poeta, à musa. Verba quoq; tertij futuri a producunt, ut, canta. Sic Antea, frustra, infra, supra, intra, extra, interea, præterea, ultra, a producunt. Numeralia in ginta, communem habent ultimam, ut, triginta, quadraginta, quæ tamen rectius producuntur.
units.tr: First, the exceptions are Greek masculine nouns in -as, which have a long a in the vocative: Aenea, Psalla. Likewise nouns of the first declension have a long a in the ablative: à Poeta, à musa. Verbs of the future perfect in the third person also lengthen the a, as canta. Antea, frustra, infra, supra, intra, extra, interea, praeterea, ultra also make the a long. Numerals in -ginta have a common last syllable, as triginta and quadraginta, though these are more correctly lengthened.

units.la: Secundò excipiuntur Græca in e longum. ut, <bl>Mu-</bl> <bl>fice, mele, gesänge / cete, walfische</bl>/ Ablativi in e, à Genitivo ei, producuntur, ut, die fide. Sic hodie, quare, fame. Verba tertij futuri, secundæ cōjugationis, producunt e, ut salve, manc. Adverbia in e, formata à Dativo in o, producuntur, ut, belle, pulchre: sic valde, fere, ferme, ohe, <bl>hola genug</bl>. Male vero bene corripiuntur. Monosyllaba hæc, me, te, se, & ne, pro non, longa sunt.
units.tr: Second, Greek words in long e are excepted (glosses: music, song; whales). Ablatives in -e, formed from a genitive in -ei, are long: die, fide. So too hodie, quare, fame. Verbs of the future perfect of the second conjugation lengthen the e: salve, mane. Adverbs in -e, formed from a dative in -o, are long: belle, pulchre; likewise valde, fere, ferme, ohe, hola (enough). But bene is shortened wrongly. These monosyllables, me, te, se, and ne (for non), are long.

units.la: Tertiò, peregrina in el fere producuntur, ut Michael, Daniel, Sic pol, sol, & nil, longa sunt.
units.tr: Third, foreign words in -el are generally long: Michael, Daniel. Likewise pol, sol, and nil are long.

units.la: Quartò, Græca in Er, quæ Genitivum per Eris formant, producuntur, ut, aer, æther, character. Monosyllaba, far, nar, lar, ver, cur, fur, par cum compositis, compar, impar, & reliquis producuntur.
units.tr: Fourth, Greek words in -er, which form their genitive in -eris, are long: aer, aether, character. The monosyllables far, nar, lar, ver, cur, fur, par, with their compounds compar, impar, and the rest, are long.

units.la: Quintò, Nomina in is declinationis imparisyllabæ, quæ Genitivum per entis, inis, iris, itis, penultima longa faciunt, producuntur, ut, Simois, Simoentis, <bl>ein</bl> fluß <bl>in</bl> Phrygia/ Salamis, Salaminis, <bl>ein Insel</bl> <bl>im Euboischen Meer</bl>/ <bl>glis, ein Endhohn oder Hasel-</bl> <bl>mauß</bl>/ <bl>lis, sauck [?]</bl> / & vis <bl>gewalt</bl>. Dativi & Ablativi plurales in is producuntur, ut, musis, Dominis. Verba secundæ personæ singularis primi præsentis, quartæ conjugationis, producūt is, ut, venis, ab is, nescia. Velis, malis, nolis: vis à volo, cum omnibus compositis, quamvis, quidvis, quivis: fis cum compositis producuntur.
units.tr: Fifth, nouns of the third declension with an unequal number of syllables, which form their genitive in -entis, -inis, -iris, -itis and have a long penultimate syllable, are long: Simois, Simoentis (a river in Phrygia); Salamis, Salaminis (an island in the Euboean Sea); glis (a dormouse or hazel-mouse); lis; and vis (force). The datives and ablatives plural in -is are long: musis, dominis. The second person singular of the present indicative of fourth-conjugation verbs ends in a long -is: venis, nescia. Velis, malis, nolis are long; vis, from volo, with all its compounds, is long, as are quamvis, quidvis, quivis; fis with its compounds is long.

units.la: Sextò, Fœminina in us quæ Genitivũ per u penultima longa faciunt, producunt us, ut, virtus, tellus. Sic monosyllaba, ut, mus, plus, pus, rus, sus, thus, habent us longum. Præter nominativum singularem, casus in us, declinationis imparisyllabæ, producuntur, ut hujus manus, hæ, has & ô manus. Græca in us longa sunt, ut, Panthus, <bl>ein sohn Otrei</bl> / <bl>ein bruder</bl> <bl>Hecube</bl> / Amathus, Amathuntis, <bl>ein Statt</bl> in <bl>Cypern</bl>.
units.tr: Sixth, feminine nouns in -us which form their genitive in -us with a long penultimate syllable have a long u: virtus, tellus. Likewise the monosyllables mus, plus, pus, rus, sus, thus have a long u. Apart from the nominative singular, the cases in -us of the third declension with an unequal number of syllables are long: huius manus, hae, has, and o manus. Greek words in -us are long: Panthus (a son of Otreus), a brother of Hecuba; Amathus, Amathuntis (a city in Cyprus).

units.la: Quænam syllaba est communis?
units.tr: What is a common syllable?

units.la: Syllaba est communis seu anceps, quam sequitur muta cum liquida, ut, terebrum, vel terebrum, <bl>ein</bl> <bl>boier</bl>[?]. Tenebræ vel tenebræ, <bl>finsternisse</bl>[?]. Excipe quando præcedens vocalis natura longa est, tum eam muta cum liquida nequit reddere communem, ut simulacrum, <bl>ein bildnuß</bl>, perpetuò a longum habet: quia est à simulare, cujus a natura longum est.
units.tr: A syllable is common, or doubtful, when a mute is followed by a liquid, as in terebrum or terebrum (a kind of ...), and tenebrae or tenebrae (darkness). The exception is when the preceding vowel is long by nature; then a mute followed by a liquid cannot make it common, as in simulacrum (a likeness), which always has a long a, because it comes from simulare, whose a is long by nature.

units.la: In Genitivis secundæ declinationis, i ante us commune est, ut, illius vel illius, ipsius vel ipsius. Sed corripis alterius, semper producis Alius.
units.tr: In genitives of the second declension, the i before -us is common: illius or illius, ipsius or ipsius. But you shorten alterius, and always lengthen Alius.

units.la: Tertiò, o in fine est commune, ut, Virgo, nolo, medicando. Sed Dativi & Ablativi secundæ Declinationis o tantùm producunt, ut Domino, Deo, bono: sic adeò, falsò, tantò, quantò, meritò, ideò, do, flo, no, sto, ô. At duo, scio, nescio, citò, ego, illicò, modò, quomodo, o tantùm corripiunt.
units.tr: Third, a final o is common: Virgo, nolo, medicando. But the datives and ablatives of the second declension lengthen the o only: Domino, Deo, bono; so also adeo, falso, tanto, quanto, merito, ideo, do, flo, no, sto, o. But duo, scio, nescio, cito, ego, illico, modo, quomodo shorten the o only.

units.la: Quartò, communia sunt hæc in i, ut mihi, tibi, sibi, ubi, ibi.
units.tr: Fourth, these words ending in -i are common: mihi, tibi, sibi, ubi, ibi.

units.la: Quintò, verba secundi futuri in is communia sunt, ut, amaveris, docueris, legeris, audiveris, tuleris, fueris. Hinc amaverimus, pœnul. longa, vel amaverimus, pœnult. brevi.
units.tr: Fifth, verbs of the future perfect ending in -is are common: amaveris, docueris, legeris, audiveris, tuleris, fueris. Hence amaverimus, with the penultimate long, or amaverimus, with the penultimate short.

units.la: Quæ autem syllabæ ex dictis regulis longæ aut breves judicari nequeunt, eæ ex illustribus Poetis sunt cognoscendæ.
units.tr: Those syllables which cannot be judged long or short by the rules given above must be learned from the famous poets.

units.la: Quid est pes?
units.tr: What is a foot?

units.la: Pes est certa syllabarum constitutio. Estque duplex: Bisyllabus, ut Spondæus, Trochæus, Pyrrychius, Iambus, aut Trisyllabus, ut Dactylus, Anapæstus, & Molossus.
units.tr: A foot is a fixed arrangement of syllables. There are two kinds: the disyllabic, such as the spondee, trochee, pyrrhic, and iamb, and the trisyllabic, such as the dactyl, anapaest, and molossus.

units.la: Quid est Spondæus?
units.tr: What is a spondee?

units.la: Est pes ex duabus longis syllabis constans : ut, Musas.
units.tr: A spondee is a foot made of two long syllables, as in "Musas" (Muses).

units.la: Quid est Trochæus?
units.tr: What is a trochee?

units.la: Est pes è longa & brevi constans : ut, annus.
units.tr: A trochee is a foot made of a long syllable and a short one, as in "annus" (year).

units.la: Quid est Pyrrychius?
units.tr: What is a pyrrhic?

units.la: Est pes è duabus brevibus constans: ut, Deus.
units.tr: A pyrrhic is a foot made of two short syllables, as in "Deus" (God).

units.la: Quid est Iambus?
units.tr: What is an iamb?

units.la: Est pes è brevi & longa constans: ut, tenax.
units.tr: An iamb is a foot made of a short syllable and a long one, as in "tenax" (tenacious).

units.la: Quid est Dactylus?
units.tr: What is a dactyl?

units.la: Est pes è longa & duabus brevibus constans : ut, Tityre.
units.tr: A dactyl is a foot made of one long syllable and two short ones, as in "Tityre" (Tityrus).

units.la: Quid est Anapæstus?
units.tr: What is an anapaest?

units.la: Est pes ex duabus brevibus & longa constans : ut, Domini.
units.tr: An anapaest is a foot made of two short syllables and a long one, as in "Domini" (of the Lord).

units.la: Quid est Molossus?
units.tr: What is a molossus?

units.la: Est pes ex tribus longis constans: ut, verbosos.
units.tr: A molossus is a foot made of three long syllables, as in "verbosos" (wordy, accusative).

units.la: Quid est Metrum?
units.tr: What is a metre?

units.la: Metrum est numerus poeticus, certos pedes, certis locis collocatos continens. Cujus affectiones duæ sunt: Ecthlipsis & Synaloepha, utraq; elisio vocatur, cum scilicet vel M, vel vocalis aliqua elidi/tur in fine vocis, quando sequens incipit à vocali: ut, Audendum est, fortes adjuvat ipsa Venus, Tibullus. Non facile est æqua commoda mente pati, Ovidius. In scandendo legitur, Audend' est, Facil' est. Metrorum autem duo genera præcipua sunt: Hexametrum sive Heroicum, & Pentametrum sive Elegiacum.
units.tr: A metre is a poetic rhythm containing feet arranged in fixed places. It has two features, ecthlipsis and synaloepha, both called elision, which occurs when either M or a vowel is cut off at the end of a word when the following word begins with a vowel. For example: "Audendum est, fortes adjuvat ipsa Venus" (Tibullus), and "Non facile est aequa commoda mente pati" (Ovid). In scansion these are read as "Audend' est" and "Facil' est". There are two main kinds of metre: the hexameter, or heroic, and the pentameter, or elegiac.

units.la: Quid est Hexametrum?
units.tr: What is a hexameter?

units.la: Hexametrum est metrum, quod constat sex regionibus, sed ita ut prima regione Spondæum vel Dactylum, stylum, secunda Spondæum vel Dactylum, tertia Spondæum vel Dactylum, quarta Spondeum vel Dactylum, quinta Dactylum tantùm, sexta Spondæum vel Trochæum habeat: ut, 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 ——— | ——— | ——— | ——— | ——— | ——— — vv | — vv | — vv | — vv | — vv | — v
units.tr: A hexameter is a metre consisting of six feet, arranged so that the first foot is a spondee or dactyl, the second a spondee or dactyl, the third a spondee or dactyl, the fourth a spondee or dactyl, the fifth a dactyl only, and the sixth a spondee or trochee: 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 ——— | ——— | ——— | ——— | ——— | ——— — vv | — vv | — vv | — vv | — vv | — v

units.la: Ex sequentibus versiculis Catonis præceptor studiosos poeticè examinato.
units.tr: Let the teacher have his students examine the following little verses of Cato as poetry.

units.la: Si Deus est animus nobis ut Carmina dicunt:
units.tr: If God is a mind to us, as the poets say,

units.la: Hic tibi præcipuè sit pura mente colendus.
units.tr: let him be worshipped above all by you with a pure mind.

units.la: Plus vigila semper, nec somno deditus esto,
units.tr: Keep watch always, and do not give yourself over to sleep,

units.la: Nam diuturna quies vitiis alimenta ministrat.
units.tr: for long rest supplies food to vices.

units.la: Primam virtutem esse puta compescere linguam,
units.tr: Consider the first virtue to be restraining the tongue,

units.la: Proximus ille Deo, qui scit ratione tacere.
units.tr: and the one nearest to God is he who knows how to keep silent with reason.

units.la: Si vitam inspicias hominum, si deniq; mores,
units.tr: If you look into the life of men, and finally into their manners,

units.la: Dum culpent alios, nemo sine crimine vivit.
units.tr: while they blame others, no one lives without fault.

units.la: Contra verbosos noli contendere verbis.
units.tr: Do not contend with words against the wordy.

units.la: Sermo datur multis, animi sapientia paucis.
units.tr: Speech is given to many, but wisdom of mind to few.

units.la: Rumores fuge, ne incipias novus author haberi,
units.tr: Avoid rumours, lest you begin to be thought a new author,

units.la: Nam nulli tacuisse nocet, nocet esse locutum.
units.tr: for keeping silent harms no one, but speaking does harm.

units.la: Cùm quis te laudat, Judex tuus esse memento.
units.tr: When someone praises you, remember that he is your judge.

units.la: Plus aliis de te, quàm tu tibi credere noli.
units.tr: Do not trust yourself more than others trust you.

units.la: Ne cures si quis tacito sermone loquatur.
units.tr: Do not care if someone speaks in a quiet voice.

units.la: Conscius ipse sibi de se putat omnia dici.
units.tr: Conscious of himself, each man thinks everything is said about him.

units.la: Cùm dubia & fragilis sit nobis vita tributa,
units.tr: Since life given to us is uncertain and fragile,

units.la: In mortem alterius spem tu tibi ponere noli.
units.tr: do not place your hope in another's death.

units.la: Exiguum munus cùm dat tibi pauper amicus,
units.tr: When a poor friend gives you a small gift,

units.la: Accipito placidè, plenè & laudare memento.
units.tr: accept it gladly, and remember to praise it fully.

units.la: Infantem nudum cùm te natura creârit,
units.tr: When nature has created you a naked infant,

units.la: Paupertatis onus patienter ferre memento.
units.tr: remember to bear the burden of poverty patiently.

units.la: Qui simulat verbis, nec corde est fidus amicus,
units.tr: He who pretends with words, and is not a faithful friend in his heart,

units.la: Tu quoq; fac simile, sic ars deluditur arte.
units.tr: you too do the same; so art is deceived by art.

units.la: Si tibi sint nati, nec opes, tunc artibus illos
units.tr: If you have children, but no wealth, then teach them the arts

units.la: Instruc, quo possint inopem defendere vitam.
units.tr: by which they can defend their life when it is poor.

units.la: Quæ culpare soles, ea tu ne feceris ipse
units.tr: Do not do yourself what you are accustomed to blame,

units.la: Turpe est Doctori, cùm culpa redarguit ipsum.
units.tr: for it is shameful for a teacher when his fault rebukes him.

units.la: Iratus de re incerta contendere noli,
units.tr: Do not contend when angry about an uncertain matter,

units.la: Impedit ira animum, ne possit cernere verum.
units.tr: for anger hinders the mind from being able to see the truth.

units.la: Quod nimium est fugito, parvo gaudere memento,
units.tr: Avoid what is excessive, and remember to be glad with little,

units.la: Tuta mage est puppis modico quæ flumine fertur.
units.tr: for a boat carried by a shallow stream is safer.

units.la: Corporis exigui vires contemnere noli,
units.tr: Do not despise the strength of a small body,

units.la: Consilio pollet, cui vim natura negavit.
units.tr: for he who has been denied strength by nature excels in counsel.

units.la: Quid Deus intendat, noli perquirere sorte,
units.tr: Do not inquire by lot what God intends,

units.la: Quid statuat de te, sine te deliberat ipse.
units.tr: for what he decides about you he deliberates without you.

units.la: Est animo forti, cùm sis damnatus iniquè,
units.tr: It is the mark of a brave mind, when you have been unjustly condemned,

units.la: Nemo diu gaudet, qui judice vincit iniquo.
units.tr: that no one rejoices for long who wins before an unjust judge.

units.la: Utere quæsitis modicè, cùm sumptus abundat,
units.tr: Use what you have acquired moderately, when there is abundance of expense,

units.la: Labitur exiguo, quod partum est tempore longo.
units.tr: for what was gained over a long time slips away in a short time.

units.la: Quod peccas ignoscere tu tibi noli,
units.tr: Do not allow yourself to pardon your own sins,

units.la: Nam nullum crimen vini est, sed culpa bibentis,
units.tr: for there is no fault in wine, but in the one who drinks it.

units.la: Cùm recte vivas, ne cures verba malorum,
units.tr: Since you live rightly, do not care about the words of evil men,

units.la: Arbitrij nostri non est, quid quisquam loquatur.
units.tr: for it is not within our power what anyone says.

units.la: Interpone tuis interdum gaudia curis,
units.tr: Sometimes interpose joys among your cares,

units.la: Ut possis animo quemvis sufferre laborem.
units.tr: so that you may be able to bear any labour in your mind.

units.la: Disce aliquid, nam cùm subito fortuna recedit,
units.tr: Learn something, for when fortune suddenly withdraws,

units.la: Ars remanet, vitamque hominis non deserit unquam.
units.tr: art remains, and never deserts the life of man.

units.la: Disce sed à doctis, indoctos ipse doceto,
units.tr: Learn, but from the learned, and teach the unlearned yourself,

units.la: Propaganda etenim rerum doctrina bonarum.
units.tr: for the teaching of good things is to be spread abroad.

units.la: Demissos animo, ac tacitos vitare memento,
units.tr: Remember to avoid the downcast and the silent in spirit,

units.la: Quò flumen placidum est forsan latet altius unda.
units.tr: for a calm stream runs perhaps deeper, where the water lies hidden.

units.la: Quid est Pentametrum?
units.tr: What is the pentameter?

units.la: Pentametrum est metrum, quod constat quinque regionibus, sed ita ut prima regione spondeum vel Dactylum, secunda Spondæum vel Dactylū habeat cum longa syllaba subspensa, tertia Dactylum tantum, quarta Trochæum, quinta Pyrrhychium vel Jambum: ut, 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 (metrical scheme: — ∪∪ | — ∪∪ | — ∪∪ | — ∪ | ∪∪ — ∪) Vulgus amicitias utilitate probat. Jupiter exiguo tempore inermis erit. A cane non magno saepe tenetur aper. Ignorans Christum bellua totus homo est. Non venit ad Christum qui puer esse negat. Ante tuos oculos nil nisi culpa sumus. Praesentemq; refert una vel herba Deum.
units.tr: The pentameter is a metre made up of five parts. The first part has a spondee or a dactyl; the second has a spondee or a dactyl, with a long syllable left hanging at its end; the third has only a dactyl; the fourth has a trochee; and the fifth has a pyrrhic or an iamb. For example: (1) The common crowd judges friendships by their usefulness. (2) Jupiter will be unarmed for a short time. (3) The boar is often caught by a dog that is not large. (4) Not knowing Christ, a man is wholly a beast. (5) He does not come to Christ who says he is no child. (6) Before your eyes we are nothing but guilt. (7) Even a single herb reveals God present.

units.la: Praecepta horis succisivis lecturus prolixiora, videat tres libros Prosodiae Latinae, Graecae & Hebraicae Johannis Claji Hirtzbergensis.
units.tr: Whoever wishes to read the fuller rules in his spare hours should look at the three books of the Prosody of Latin, Greek and Hebrew by Johannes Clajus of Hirschberg.

units.la: Praecedentes artes ipsas duntaxat rerum voces tractant: Sequitur Dialectica, q; ipsissimas res considerat.
units.tr: The preceding arts deal only with the words for things; dialectic follows, which considers the things themselves.

units.la: DE DIALECTICA.
units.tr: ON DIALECTIC.

units.la: Quid est Dialectica seu Logica?
units.tr: What is Dialectic or Logic?

units.la: DIALECTICA est ars bene ratione utendi. Cujus partes duae sunt: Inventio & Dispositio. <bl>Die vernunfftes kunst ist</bl> <bl>eine kunst wol der vernunfft zu gebrau-</bl> <bl>chen. welcher zwey theile seind: die Ding erfindung</bl> <bl>und die Ding setzung.</bl>
units.tr: Dialectic is the art of using reason well. It has two parts: Invention and Disposition. (German: The art of reason is the art of using reason well. It has two parts: the finding of things and the setting out of things.)

units.la: Quid est Inventio?
units.tr: What is Invention?

units.la: Inventio est prima pars Dialecticae de inveniendis argumentis, <bl>Die Ding erfindung ist das erste theil &</bl> <bl>vernunfftes kunst von den zeige dingen zu erfinde.</bl>
units.tr: Invention is the first part of Dialectic, concerning the finding of arguments. (German: Invention is the first part of the art of reason, concerning the finding of things to be shown.)

units.la: Quid est Argumentum?
units.tr: What is an Argument?

units.la: Argumentum est omne ens vel verum vel fictum, quod ad aliquid arguendum affectum est. Mutua autem argumentorum affectio non habeatur pro uno argumento, sed in qualibet affectione duo argumenta ad se invicem affecta considerentur: ut,Deus creavit coelum & terram. In hoc enunciato duo sunt argumenta ad se invicem affecta, Deus nimirum est argumentum à vera causa efficiente, creavit coelum & terram, est argumentum à vero effecto sumptum.
units.tr: An argument is any being, real or fictional, that is related to something so as to prove it. The mutual relation of arguments should not be counted as a single argument. Rather, in any relation there are two arguments related to one another, and both should be considered. For example: "God created heaven and earth." In this statement there are two arguments related to each other. God, of course, is an argument drawn from the true efficient cause. "Created heaven and earth" is an argument drawn from the true effect.

units.la: At Jupiter transformatus in cygnum, est argumentum à ficta causa efficiente, Ledam uxorem Regis Tyndari vitiavit, est argumentum à ficto effecto sumptum. Quod autem rei dubiae fidem facit, appellatur à Ramo argumentum tertium. <bl>Ein zeige ding ist ein</bl> <bl>jedes wesen entweder warhafftig oder erdichtet/</bl> <bl>welches auff etwas zu zeigen verwandt ist. Es muss</bl> <bl>aber die gleiche gegen verwandtschafft der zeige dingen nicht geachtet werden für ein zeige ding/ sondern in einer jeden gegen verwandtschafft müssen zwey zeige dinge/ ein dem</bl> <bl>andern verwant betrachtet werden: als Gott hat geschaffen Himel und Erde. In diesem aussspruch sind zwey zeige dinge ein dem andern verwandt/ Gott nemlich ist ein zeige</bl> <bl>wesen von der wahren wirckenden ursach/ hat geschaffen Himmel und Erd/ ist ein zeige</bl> <bl>ding von der wahren werck genommen. Aber der Heidnische Gott Jupiter in</bl> <bl>ein schwan verwandlet/ ist ein zeige ding von der</bl> <bl>erdichteten wirckenden ursach/ hat die Ledam ein</bl> <bl>hausfrawe des Königs Tyndari geschwecht/ ist</bl> <bl>ein zeige ding von dem erdichteten werck genommen.</bl> <bl>Welches aber ein zweiffelhafftig ding glaublich</bl> <bl>macht/ wird vom Ramo geheissen dz dritte zeige ding.</bl>
units.tr: But "Jupiter transformed into a swan" is an argument drawn from a fictional efficient cause, and "he violated Leda, the wife of King Tyndareus" is an argument drawn from a fictional effect. What gives credit to a doubtful matter is called by Ramus the third argument. (German: An argument is any being, whether true or invented, that is related to something in order to show it. The mutual relation of arguments, however, is not to be regarded as one argument; rather, in every mutual relation two arguments related to one another should be considered, as: "God created heaven and earth." In this statement there are two arguments related to one another: God is an argument from the true efficient cause, and "created heaven and earth" is an argument taken from the true work. But the heathen god Jupiter changed into a swan is an argument from a fictional efficient cause, and "he violated Leda, the wife of King Tyndareus" is an argument taken from a fictional work. What makes a doubtful matter credible is called by Ramus the third argument.)

units.la: Quot sunt argumentorum loci seu sedes?
units.tr: How many places or seats of arguments are there?

units.la: Octo: Causa primum locum occupat: Effectum, secundum: Subjectum, tertium: Adjunctum, quartum: Diffentaneum, quintum: Comparatum, sextum: Ortum, septimum: Testimonium, octavum.
units.tr: Eight. Cause occupies the first place; effect the second; subject the third; adjunct the fourth; the discordant the fifth; the compared the sixth; origin the seventh; testimony the eighth.

units.la: Quid est Causa, primum Argumentorum locum occupans?
units.tr: What is Cause, which occupies the first place among the arguments?

units.la: Causa est cujus vi res est. <bl>Die Ursach ist auss wel-</bl> <bl>c[?]her trafft ein Ding entstehet.</bl> Estq; duplex: Externa aut interna. Externa, quae extra effectum manet, ut causa finalis & Efficiens: Interna, quae effectum ingreditur, ut causa materialis & formalis.
units.tr: A cause is that by whose force a thing comes into being. It is twofold: external or internal. External is that which remains outside the effect, such as the final and efficient cause; internal is that which enters into the effect, such as the material and formal cause.

units.la: Quid est causa finalis?
units.tr: What is the final cause?

units.la: Causa finalis, <bl>die entl[?]che vrsach[?]</bl> / est cujus gratia efficiens agit: ut, Gloria Dei fuit causa finalis, cujus gratia Deus ex terrae massa homine creavit, Genes.2.
units.tr: The final cause is that for whose sake the efficient cause acts. For example: the glory of God was the final cause, for whose sake God created man from a mass of earth, Genesis 2.

units.la: Recta gubernatio utriusq; temporis & bellorum & pacis fuit causa finalis, cujus gratia imperator Justinianus suam majestatem armis decoravit, & legibus armavit, in proœm. Instit.
units.tr: The right government of both times, of war and of peace, was the final cause, for whose sake the Emperor Justinian adorned his majesty with arms and armed it with laws, in the preface of the Institutes.

units.la: Ostende usum argumentandi?
units.tr: Show the use of arguing.

units.la: Si Deus propter suam gloriam tanquam causam finalem, omnia creavit: sequitur Deum nequaquam frustra quippiam fecisse.
units.tr: If God created all things for the sake of his glory as the final cause, it follows that God has by no means done anything in vain.

units.la: At universa propter semetipsum operatus est Dominus, Proverb.16. Ergo Deus nequaquam frustra quippiam fecit.
units.tr: But the Lord has worked all things for himself, Proverbs 16. Therefore God has by no means done anything in vain.

units.la: Si Imperator Justinianus propter rectam gubernationem belli & pacis suam majestatem armis decoravit & legibus armavit: sequitur ipsum non fecisse hoc eo, ut tyrannidem erga subditos armis exerceret, & legibus magnum aeris & auri acervum coraderet. At propter gubernationem fecit. Ergo non propter tyrannidem nec pecuniam. Hanc consequentiam confirmat elegans textus in l.1. Quas gratias, §.5. Optamus C. de officio praefecti praetorio Africae: Ergo, inquit, Imperator, jubemus omnes violentias & omnem avaritiam cessare, & justitiam atq; veritatem circa omnes nostros tributarios reservari.
units.tr: If the Emperor Justinian adorned his majesty with arms and armed it with laws for the sake of the right government of war and peace, it follows that he did not do this in order to exercise tyranny over his subjects by arms, or to heap up a great pile of bronze and gold by means of laws. But he did it for good government. Therefore not for tyranny, nor for money. An elegant text confirms this inference, in law 1, Quas gratias, §5, Optamus, C. de officio praefecti praetorio Africae: "Therefore," says the Emperor, "we order that all violence and all avarice cease, and that justice and truth be observed toward all our taxpayers."

units.la: Quo syllogismo probas causam finalem omnino debere caeteras causas antegredi?
units.tr: By what syllogism do you prove that the final cause ought altogether to precede the other causes?

units.la: Hoc sequenti: Quod non solùm movet & impellit efficientem, sed etiam caeteras causas omnes trahit ac ducit, ut vim suam exerant, quare hoc non antegrederetur? At causa finalis non solum movet & impellit efficientem, sed etiam caeteras causas omnes trahit ac ducit, ut vim suam exerant, sicut Beurhusius recte disputat parte 2. Disputation. Dialecticarum pag.624. Quare igitur causa finalis non antegrederetur? quum Ramus etiam in nonnullis editionibus caeteris causis praepositerit. Qui vero autumant, finem, id est, effectae rei usum esse causam finalem, hallucinantur: quippe quum finis seu usus effectum non constituat, sed effectam rem sequatur.
units.tr: By the following: what not only moves and impels the efficient cause, but also draws and leads all the other causes so that they exert their force, why should this not precede them? But the final cause not only moves and impels the efficient cause, but also draws and leads all the other causes so that they exert their force, as Beurhusius rightly argues in part 2 of his Disputations on Dialectic, p. 624. Why then should the final cause not precede? Ramus himself, in some editions, placed it before the other causes. Those who maintain that the end, that is, the use of the thing effected, is the final cause are mistaken. For the end or use does not constitute the effect; rather, it follows the thing effected.

units.la: Quid est causa efficiens?
units.tr: What is an efficient cause?

units.la: Causa efficiens, <bl>Die wirckende Ursach</bl>/ est a qua res est: ut, Noe fuit causa efficiens Arcae, Genef.6. Consensus est causa efficiens nuptiarum, l.30. Nuptias, ff. de diverf. Regulis Jur. Nuptias non concubitus, sed consensus facit, inquit ibi Ulpianus.
units.tr: An efficient cause (German: "Die wirckende Ursach") is that from which a thing comes to be: thus Noah was the efficient cause of the ark, Gen. 6. Consent is the efficient cause of marriage, l. 30, Nuptias, ff. de diversis regulis juris. It is not intercourse but consent that makes a marriage, says Ulpian there.

units.la: Quinam sunt modi causae efficientis?
units.tr: What are the kinds of efficient cause?

units.la: Primò, Efficiens est aut procreans, aut conservans, aut corrumpens, aut labefactans.
units.tr: First, an efficient cause is either generating, or preserving, or destroying, or weakening.

units.la: Secundò, Efficiens est aut solitaria, aut cum aliis. Efficiens cum aliis est aut principalis, aut instrumentalis. Principalis est, quae instrumentalem in efficiendo regit & gubernat. Instrumentalis est, qua principalis utitur ad rem efficiendam. Instrumentalis est duplex: aut Adjuvans movens, quae ita a principali movetur, ut ipsa interim seipsam etiam propria ac inhaerente vi moveat, ut equi, boves in arando ab aratore quidem moventur, interim tamen seipsos inhaerente potentia movent: aut adjuvans quieta, quae in efficiendo, propria ac inhaerente quadam vi, seipsam non movet, sed tantum movetur a principali, ut, Malleus opificis tantum movetur a principali & in efficiendo accepta quędam & infusa virtute se haudquaquam movet. Sic corpus hominis tantùm movetur ab anima, & in laborando, infusa quadam vi ab anima, se non movet.
units.tr: Second, an efficient cause is either solitary or works together with others. An efficient cause that works with others is either principal or instrumental. The principal is that which directs and governs the instrumental cause in producing the effect. The instrumental is that which the principal uses to bring the thing about. The instrumental cause is of two kinds. It is either a helping moving cause, which is moved by the principal in such a way that, meanwhile, it also moves itself by its own inherent power, as horses and oxen in ploughing are indeed moved by the ploughman but also move themselves by an inherent power. Or it is a helping resting cause, which in producing the effect does not move itself by any proper and inherent power but is only moved by the principal, as the hammer of the craftsman is moved only by the principal and, in working, by a certain power received and infused into it, does not move itself at all. So the human body is moved only by the soul, and in labouring, by a certain power infused by the soul, it does not move itself.

units.la: Tertiò, Efficiens est per se, aut per accidens. Per se, quæ consilio vel natura facit: per accidens, quæ vel necessitate agit, vel Fortuna, quando scilicet efficiens causa præter suum scopū effectū aliquod producit.
units.tr: Third, an efficient cause is either per se or per accidens. Per se is that which acts by design or by nature; per accidens is that which acts either by necessity or by chance, namely when an efficient cause produces some effect beyond its aim.

units.la: Ostende usum argumentandi?
units.tr: Show the use of the argument?

units.la: Si Christus suum populum salvum facit à peccatis: sequitur valdè hallucinari Jesuvitas, qui dicunt bona opera homines à peccatis liberare. Ratio à causa solitaria, quæ adjuvantes causas in æternum non admittit. At scriptum est Matth. 1. Joseph fili David, noli timere accipere Mariam conjugem tuam: quod enim in ea natum est, de Spiritu sancto est. Pariet autem filium, & vocabis nomen ejus Jesum. Ipse enim salvum faciet populum suum à peccatis eorum. Ergo Jesuvitæ valdè hallucinantur, qui dicunt bo[?]a opera, quæ in hac vita varijs peccatis contaminantur, à peccatis liberare homines.
units.tr: If Christ saves his people from their sins, it follows that the Jesuits are greatly mistaken who say that good works free men from sins. The argument is from the solitary cause, which admits no helping causes at all. But it is written, Matt. 1: "Joseph, son of David, fear not to take Mary your wife; for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Spirit. And she shall bring forth a son, and you shall call his name Jesus, for he shall save his people from their sins." Therefore the Jesuits are greatly mistaken who say that good works, which in this life are contaminated by various sins, free men from sins.

units.la: Si Imperator Justinianus opera Triboniani, Theophili, Dorothei & aliorum virorum illustrium, immensa veteris prudentiæ volumina, hoc est, duo penè millia librorum conscripta, & plus quàm trecentis decem millia versuum à veteribus effusa, (ut dicitur in Constitut. Tanta. §.1. omnia igitur, de Confirmatione digestorum, & C. de veteri jur. enucleando) in quinquaginta Pandectarum libros redegit: sequitur non solum Justinianum propterea esse honorandum, sed etiam cæteros illustres viros, tanquam causas adjuvantes. Ratio: quia principalis causa communicare debet honorem cum causis adjuvantibus. At verum est Antecedens ex Constit. Tanta. §.9. Quæ omnia. de Confirm. digest. Consequens igitur.
units.tr: If the Emperor Justinian reduced the works of Tribonian, Theophilus, Dorotheus and other illustrious men, the immense volumes of ancient wisdom, that is, nearly two thousand books, composed and poured out by the ancients in more than three hundred and ten thousand verses (as is said in the constitution Tanta §1, Omnia igitur, de confirmatione digestorum, and C. de veteri jure enucleando), into fifty books of the Pandects, it follows that not only Justinian is to be honoured for this, but also the other illustrious men, as helping causes. The reason: because the principal cause must share its honour with the helping causes. But the antecedent is true, from the constitution Tanta §9, Quae omnia, de confirmatione digestorum. Therefore the consequent.

units.la: Quid est caussa materialis?
units.tr: What is a material cause?

units.la: Caussa materialis, <bl>Die materische Vrsach</bl>/ est ex qua res est: ut, Ex semine Abrahæ Christi sanctum corpus creatum est.
units.tr: A material cause (German: "Die materische Ursach") is that from which a thing is: thus, from the seed of Abraham the holy body of Christ was created.

units.la: Ex vino & melle conficitur mulsum.
units.tr: Mead is made from wine and honey.

units.la: Ostende usum argumentandi?
units.tr: Show the use of the argument?

units.la: Christi sanctum & verum corpus est ex semine Abrahæ creatum, & ex Maria virgine in lucem editum. Atqui corpus, quod ex panis substantia in Missa creari,fieri,nasci, Jesuvitæ docent,non est ex semine Abrahæ factum, nec ex Maria virgine natum. Ergo illud corpus, quod in missa ex substantia panis Jesuvitæ creant, non est Christi sanctum & verum corpus: Et per consequens salsissimum & horrendum dogma Jesuvitarum de transubstantiatione est rejiciendum.
units.tr: Christ's holy and true body was created from the seed of Abraham and brought into the light from the Virgin Mary. But the body which the Jesuits teach is created, made and born in the Mass from the substance of bread was not made from the seed of Abraham, nor born of the Virgin Mary. Therefore the body which the Jesuits create in the Mass from the substance of bread is not Christ's holy and true body; and consequently the most false and horrible dogma of the Jesuits on transubstantiation is to be rejected.

units.la: Dominus Doctor Hefshusius[?] inquit: Si consecratione conficitur & creatur corpus Christi in cœna, sequeretur, & plura esse corpora Christi, quàm unū, & majestas creationis attribueretur creaturæ, quod est absurdissimum. Vide tertiam partem Methodorū Dom. Doct. Simonis Pauli de Cœna Dom.
units.tr: Doctor Heshusius says: If the body of Christ is made and created in the Supper by consecration, it would follow that there are more bodies of Christ than one, and the majesty of creation would be attributed to a creature, which is most absurd. See the third part of the Methods of Doctor Simon Paulus on the Lord's Supper.

units.la: Qui vinum & mel habent, mulsum conficere possunt, ut ex verbis Imperatoris colligitur. §. si duorum. inst. de rer. Division. At Titius & Mevius vinum & mel habent. Ergo Titius & Mevius mulsum conficere possunt. Negativè sic: Qui vinum & mel non habent, mulsum conficere haud possunt. Ratio: quia si materia non sit, effectum materiatum à causis secundis effici nequit. Deus, ut obiter hoc dicam, est prima causa, omnes reliquæ creaturæ aliquid efficientes causæ secundæ appellantur. At Titius & Mevius vinum & mel nō habent. Ergo Titius & Mevius mulsum conficere haud possunt.
units.tr: Those who have wine and honey can make mead, as is gathered from the words of the Emperor, §si duorum, Inst. de rerum divisione. But Titius and Maevius have wine and honey. Therefore Titius and Maevius can make mead. Negatively: those who do not have wine and honey cannot make mead. The reason: if the matter does not exist, a material effect cannot be produced by secondary causes. God, by the way, is the first cause; all the remaining creatures that produce something are called secondary causes. But Titius and Maevius do not have wine and honey. Therefore Titius and Maevius cannot make mead.

units.la: Quid est caussa formalis?
units.tr: What is the formal cause?

units.la: Caussa formalis, <bl>Die gestaltende Vrsach</bl>/ est, per quam res est, id quod est, & à cæteris rebus omnibus distinguitur: ut, celebrare cœnam Domini sub utraque specie est ejus[?] essentialis forma à Christo præscripta, per quam à cæteris sacris actionibus distinguitur & dignoscitur.
units.tr: The formal cause (German: the forming cause) is that through which a thing is what it is and is distinguished from all other things. For example, celebrating the Lord's Supper under both kinds is its essential form, prescribed by Christ, through which it is distinguished and recognised apart from all other sacred actions.

units.la: Emptionis & venditionis forma est utriusq; partis de pretio consensio, per quam Emptio & Venditio à cæteris contractibus distinguuntur.
units.tr: The form of buying and selling is the agreement of both parties about the price, through which buying and selling are distinguished from other contracts.

units.la: Ostende usum Argumentandi?
units.tr: Show the use of the argument.

units.la: Qui essentialem Cœnæ Dominicæ formam sub utraq; specie communicandi à Christo præscriptam tollunt, & formam cœnæ sub una communicandi specie à Papa introductam, hominibus proponunt: illi non distribuunt hominibus cœnam Domini, sed cœnam Papæ. Ratio est inexpugnabilis: Quia mutata essentiali forma alicujus rei, ipsa res formata quoq; mutatur, & aliud nomen sortitur.
units.tr: Those who abolish the essential form of the Lord's Supper, which Christ prescribed for communion under both kinds, and put before people the form of the supper under one kind, introduced by the Pope, do not distribute the Lord's Supper to people but the Pope's supper. The reasoning is unassailable: when the essential form of something is changed, the formed thing itself is also changed and takes on another name.

units.la: Atqui Jesuvitæ essentialem cœnæ Dominicæ formam sub utraq; specie communicandi à Christo præscriptam tollunt, & formam cœnæ sub una communicandi specie à Papa introductam, hominibus proponunt.
units.tr: But the Jesuits abolish the essential form of the Lord's Supper, which Christ prescribed for communion under both kinds, and put before people the form of the supper under one kind introduced by the Pope.

units.la: Ergo Jesuvitæ non distribuunt hominibus cœnam Domini, sed cœnam Papæ. Si autem Jesuvitæ adeo impudentes fuerint, ut dicant, manere nihilominus cœnam Domini, licet forma à Christo præscripta nonnihil immutetur: tum omnes sanæ mentis homines istis impostoribus contradicent: quippe quum mutata essentiali forma alicujus rei, ipsa res necessario mutetur & aliud nomen sortiatur: ut, exempli gratia, Forma uxoris Lothi mutabatur in statuam salis, Genes.19. Nunc quærimus ex Jesuvitis an mutata uxoris Lothi forma, statua salis vere uxor Lothi esse potuerit? Nequaquam. Quæ est ratio? quia essentialis forma mutata est, idcoq; res ipsa alia facta est. Sic ubi mutata est essentialis forma Cœnæ Domini ȷ[?] Christo præscripta, non amplius est Cœna Domini, sed Cœna Papæ.
units.tr: Therefore the Jesuits do not distribute the Lord's Supper to people but the Pope's supper. But if the Jesuits are so shameless as to say that the Lord's Supper nevertheless remains, even though the form prescribed by Christ is somewhat altered, then all men of sound mind will contradict these impostors. For when the essential form of a thing is changed, the thing itself necessarily changes and takes on another name. For example, the form of Lot's wife was changed into a pillar of salt (Gen. 19). Now we ask the Jesuits: since Lot's wife's form was changed, could the pillar of salt truly have been Lot's wife? By no means. What is the reason? Because its essential form has been changed, and so the thing itself has become something else. Likewise, when the essential form of the Lord's Supper prescribed by Christ has been changed, it is no longer the Lord's Supper but the Pope's supper.

units.la: Væ igitur omnibus illis,qui Papæ Cœnam sub una specie celebrant, & Christi Cœnam sub utraq; specie celebrare nolunt.
units.tr: Woe, therefore, to all those who celebrate the Pope's supper under one kind and are unwilling to celebrate Christ's supper under both kinds.

units.la: Si inter utraq; partem de pretio non est confensio : Emptio & Venditio etiam non contrahuntur. Ratio: quia sublata forma, res quoque formata tollitur. Atqui inter Titium & Mevium de pretio non est consensio. Ergo inter Titium & Mevium emptio & venditio non contrahuntur.
units.tr: If there is no agreement between the two parties about the price, then buying and selling are not contracted either. The reason: when the form is removed, the thing formed by it is also removed. But between Titius and Mevius there is no agreement about the price. Therefore between Titius and Mevius no buying and selling is contracted.

units.la: Quid est Effectum secundum argumentorum locum occupans?
units.tr: What is the effect, which occupies the place of the second argument?

units.la: Effectum,<bl>Das wirckt</bl>/ est quod è caussis existit : ut, Effecta sunt claudos, cæcos, & cæteros insanabiles morbos sanare.
units.tr: An effect (German: what is produced) is that which exists from causes, for example: to heal the lame, the blind and other incurable diseases are the effects of [the Lord's power].
