units.la: Barbaricas gentes sub juga redigere, & constitutiones confusas in luculentam erigere cōsonantiam sunt Justiniani effecta.
units.tr: To bring barbarian nations under the yoke and to raise confused laws into a splendid harmony are the achievements of Justinian.

units.la: Ostende usum argumentandi?
units.tr: Show the use of the argument.

units.la: Qui sua omnipotentia æterna cæcos,surdos,claudos, & cæteros insanabiles sanat, is est secundum Isaiam verus Messias. Sic enim Isaias 35. scribit: Deus ipse veniet & salvabit vos. Tunc aperientur oculi cæcorum, & aures surdorum patebunt. Tunc salict[?] sicut cervus claudus, & aperta erit lingua mutorum.
units.tr: He who by his eternal omnipotence heals the blind, the deaf, the lame and other incurable people is, according to Isaiah, the true Messiah. For Isaiah 35 writes thus: God himself will come and save you. Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will be unstopped. Then the lame will leap like a deer, and the tongue of the dumb will be loosed.

units.la: At Jesus Nazarenus sua omnipotentia æterna, cæcos, surdos, claudos ac cæteros insanabiles sanavit, testibus Matthæo 11. Marco 5. Luca 7. Johan. 5. Ergo Jesus Nazarenus est verus Messias.
units.tr: But Jesus of Nazareth by his eternal omnipotence healed the blind, the deaf, the lame and other incurable people, as witnessed by Matthew 11, Mark 5, Luke 7, John 5. Therefore Jesus of Nazareth is the true Messiah.

units.la: Qui barbaricas gentes sub juga sua redigit, & constitutiones confusas in luculentam erigit consonantiam, is est bonus Imperator. Ratio : quia qualis efsectus, fœtus, talis plerunque & caussa. Opus commendat opificem, vulgò dicitur.
units.tr: He who brings barbarian nations under his yoke and raises confused laws into a splendid harmony is a good emperor. The reason: as the effect or product is, so for the most part is the cause. The work commends the workman, as is commonly said.

units.la: At Justinianus barbaricas gentes sub juga sua redegit, & constitutiones confusas in luculentam erexit [?] consonantiam. §.1. quorum utranq; & §.2. Et cùm sacratissimas, in procem. Instit.
units.tr: But Justinian brought barbarian nations under his yoke and raised confused laws into a splendid harmony (Inst., proem., §1, both of which, and §2, "And since most sacred..."].

units.la: Ergo Justinianus fuit bonus Imperator.
units.tr: Therefore Justinian was a good emperor.

units.la: Quid est Subjectum tertium argumento- rum locum occupans?
units.tr: What is the subject, which occupies the place of the third argument?

units.la: <bl>Subjectum</bl>, <bl>Das Vnderworffene</bl> [?] / est quod adjuncto subjicitur: ut, An nescitis quoniam membra vestra, templum sunt spiritus sancti, qui in vobis est, quem habetis à Deo? 1. Corinth. 6.
units.tr: The subject (German: that which is placed under) is that to which an adjunct is attached, for example: "Do you not know that your bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit, who is in you, whom you have from God?" 1 Corinthians 6.

units.la: Constituitur autem usufructus non tantùm in fundo & ædibus, verum etiam in servis, & jumentis, & cæteris rebus: Exceptis ijs quæ ipso usu consumuntur. §.2. Constituitur, Inst.2. de usufructu.
units.tr: A usufruct is established not only on land and buildings but also on slaves, beasts of burden and other things, except those which are consumed by the very use. Inst. 2, de usufructu, §2 ("A usufruct is established...").

units.la: Ostende usum Argumentandi?
units.tr: Show the use of the argument.

units.la: Qui membra habent humana, etiam Spiritum sanctum habere possunt. Nam Paulus dicit membra nostra esse templum Spiritus sancti.
units.tr: Those who have human members can also have the Holy Spirit. For Paul says that our members are the temple of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: At infantes membra habent humana. Ergo infantes etiam Spiritum sanctum, non otiosum, sed fidem operantem habere, non est impossibile. Ratio: quia cui tribuitur subjectum, ei etiam ipsius subjecti Adjunctum tribuendum est.
units.tr: But infants have human members. Therefore it is not impossible for infants also to have the Holy Spirit, not idle but working through faith. The reason: to whom the subject is attributed, to him the adjunct of that same subject must also be attributed.

units.la: Eo amplius constat, si ædes incendio con-sumptæ fuerint, vel etiam terræmotu, vel vitio suo corruerint: extingui usumfru-ctum, & ne areæ quidem usumfructum deberi, inquit Imperator §.2. finitur. Instit.2. de usufruct. Ratio: quia sublato Subjecto, tollitur quoque Adjunctum. Atqui Titij ædes sunt incendio consumptæ. Ergo in Titij ædibus usufructus quoque extinctus est.
units.tr: Furthermore it is established that if houses are consumed by fire, or even by an earthquake, or fall down through their own defect, the usufruct is extinguished, and not even a usufruct over the site is owed, says the Emperor in Inst. 2, de usufructu, §2 ("finitur"). The reason: when the subject is removed, the adjunct is removed too. But Titius's houses were consumed by fire. Therefore the usufruct on Titius's houses has also been extinguished.

units.la: Quid est Adjunctum, quartum argumentorum locum occupans?
units.tr: What is the Adjunct, which occupies the fourth place among the arguments?

units.la: <bl>Das Zugefügte[?]</bl> est quod subjecto adjungitur: ut, Naturalis amor erga filium est adjunctum, quod verae matri tanquam proprio subjecto adjungitur, 3.Regum 3. Jus de jure respondendi à Cæsare Jurisconsulto datum est. Jus respondendi est Adjunctum, quod Jurisconsulto tanquam subjecto adjungitur, §.8. Responsa, Instit. 1. de jure natural. gent. & civil.
units.tr: The added (German: Das Zugefügte[?]) is what is joined to a subject. For example, natural love toward a son is an adjunct, which is joined to the true mother as to its proper subject (3 Kings 3). The right to give legal opinions was granted by Caesar to a jurisconsult. The right to give opinions is an adjunct, which is joined to the jurisconsult as to its subject (§8 Responsa, Institutes 1, On Natural and Civil Law).

units.la: Ostende usum argumentandi?
units.tr: Show the use of the argument.

units.la: Mulier, quæ naturalem habet amorem erga filium, illa vera est mater. Ratio: quia cui tribuitur adjunctum, ei etiam est ipsius Adjuncti subjectum tribuendum. Atqui mulier, 3.Reg.3. cujus filius erat vivus, dixit ad regem (Salomonem:) commota sunt quippe viscera ejus super filio suo. Obsecro Domine, date illi infantem vivum, & nolite interficere eum. Ergo mulier cujus viscera commota sunt, super infante vivo, vera mater fuit: ideoque respondit rex, & ait: Date huic infantem vivum, & non occidatur: Hæc est enim mater ejus. Audivit itaq; omnis Israel judicium (scilicet ab Adjuncto) quod judicasset rex, & timuerunt regem, videntes sapientiam Dei esse in eo ad faciendum judicium. Hinc studiosi adolescentes observent, acutè ac verè argumentari posse, esse sapientiā Dei, non ut quidā impudenter calumniantur, res serias humanis & philosophicis rationib. metiri.
units.tr: A woman who has natural love toward a son is the true mother. The reason: to whom an adjunct is attributed, to him the subject of that adjunct must also be attributed. But the woman in 3 Kings 3, whose son was alive, said to the king (Solomon): "Her bowels were moved over her son. Please, Lord, give her the living infant, and do not kill him." Therefore the woman whose bowels were moved over the living infant was the true mother. So the king answered and said: "Give her the living infant, and do not let him be killed, for she is his mother." Thus all Israel heard the judgment (namely from the adjunct) which the king had given, and they feared the king, seeing that the wisdom of God was in him to do judgment. Hence let studious young men observe that one can argue acutely and truly, and that the wisdom of God is not, as some shamelessly slander, to be measured by human and philosophical reasons in serious matters.

units.la: Cui jus de jure respondendi à Cæsare datum est, ipse est Jurisconsultus. Atqui Triboniano jus de jure respondendi à Cæsare datum est. Ergo Tribonianus est jurisconsultus. Ratio: quia cui attribuitur
units.tr: He to whom the right to give legal opinions has been granted by Caesar is a jurisconsult. But the right to give legal opinions was granted by Caesar to Tribonian. Therefore Tribonian is a jurisconsult. The reason: to whom an adjunct is attributed,

units.la: Adjunctum, ei etiam est ipsius Adjunđti subjectum attribuendum.
units.tr: to him the subject of that adjunct must also be attributed.

units.la: Quid est Dissentaneum, quintum Argumen- torum locum occupans?
units.tr: What is the Dissonant, which occupies the fifth place among the arguments?

units.la: Dissentaneum est argumentum, quod à re, quam arguunt dissentit. <bl>Das mißhellige ist ein zeige ding/</bl> <bl>welches mit dem Dinge / darauff es zeiget/ mißhellig</bl> <bl>ist.</bl> Estq; Disparatum aut contrarium.
units.tr: The dissonant is an argument which dissents from the thing it argues about. (German: Das mißhellige ist ein zeige ding, welches mit dem Dinge, darauff es zeiget, mißhellig ist.) And it is either disparate or contrary.

units.la: Quid est Disparatum?
units.tr: What is the Disparate?

units.la: Disparatum, <bl>Das vnderscheidene</bl> est Dissentaneum, quod multis pariter opponitur: ut, Domus precationis non potest esse secundum idem & ad idem, & eodem tempore, domus mercatus, nec spelunca latronum. Comedere & bibere non potest esse offerre pro vivis & mortuis, nec adorare, nec circumgestare. Servitus aquae ducendae, non potest esse servitus aquae hauriendae, nec pecoris ad aquam appellendi. Homo non potest esse proprie Asinus, nec vulpes, nec lepus, nec lupus, nec leo, nec stipes.
units.tr: The disparate (German: Das vnderscheidene) is a dissonant which is opposed to several things equally. For example: a house of prayer cannot at the same time, in the same respect and in the same way, be a house of merchandise, nor a den of robbers. Eating and drinking cannot be offering for the living and the dead, nor adoring, nor carrying about. Servitude of drawing water cannot be servitude of drawing up water, nor of bringing cattle to the water. A man cannot properly be an ass, nor a fox, nor a hare, nor a wolf, nor a lion, nor a stump.

units.la: Leo non potest esse vacca, nec piscis, nec avis, nec lapis, nec lignum, nec ferrum.
units.tr: A lion cannot be a cow, nor a fish, nor a bird, nor a stone, nor wood, nor iron.

units.la: Grammatica non potest esse Rhetorica, nec Dialectica, nec Physica, nec Medicina, nec Musica.
units.tr: Grammar cannot be Rhetoric, nor Dialectic, nor Physics, nor Medicine, nor Music.

units.la: Ostende usum argumentandi?
units.tr: Show the use of the argument.

units.la: Domus supplicationis, nō potest esse domus mercatus, nec spelunca latronum. At templum Dei est Domus supplicationis. Ergo templum Dei non est domus mercatus, nec spelunca latronum.
units.tr: A house of worship cannot be a house of merchandise, nor a den of robbers. But the temple of God is a house of worship. Therefore the temple of God is not a house of merchandise, nor a den of robbers.

units.la: Si panis sacramentalis, de quo distributo Christus dixit: Hoc est corpus meum: accipiendus est & comedendus: nullo modo debet offerri pro vivis & mortuis, nec adorari, nec instar Persici ignis circumgestari. At verum est Antecedens ex Matthaeo 26. Marco14. ex Luca 22. & ex Paulo 1. Corint. 11. Consequens igitur. Vide tertiam partem Doctor. Simon. Pauli de Coena Domini. Servitus aquæ ducendæ, non servitus est aquæ hauriendæ, nec pecoris ad aquam appellendi. At hæc est servitus aquæ ducendæ. Ergo hæc non est servitus aquæ hauriendæ, nec pecoris ad aquam appellendi.
units.tr: If the sacramental bread, of which Christ said when he distributed it, "This is my body," is to be received and eaten, it must in no way be offered for the living and the dead, nor adored, nor carried about like the Persian fire. But the antecedent is true, from Matthew 26, Mark 14, Luke 22 and Paul, 1 Corinthians 11. Therefore the consequent holds. See the third part of Doctor Simon Paulus on the Lord's Supper. Servitude of drawing water is not servitude of drawing up water, nor of bringing cattle to the water. But this is servitude of drawing water. Therefore this is not servitude of drawing up water, nor of bringing cattle to the water.

units.la: Horum syllogismorum ratio est: quia posito uno disparato, omnia alia disparata removentur. Veruntamen in Sacrosanctis Bibliis sæpe disparatum de disparato enunciatur seu prædicatur, non quidem proprie, sed omnino tropicè: ut, Herodes est vulpes, id est, similis vulpis. Johannes est Elias, id est, similis Eliæ. Christus est agnus, id est, similis agni. Deus autem, inquit Dominus Philippus, unum admirandum exemplum dissimile toti reliquo ordini naturæ proposuit, videlicet copulationem Divinæ & Humanæ naturæ in Filio Domino nostro Jesu Christo, de quo tamen Ecclesia peculiaria recipit Enunciata: ut Deus est homo. Verbum caro factum. Ecclesia autem non dicit: Divinitas est humanitas. Humanitas est Divinitas.
units.tr: The reason for these syllogisms is this: once one disparate is posited, all other disparates are removed. Nevertheless, in the Holy Bible a disparate is often stated or predicated of a disparate, not properly indeed, but wholly tropically. For example: "Herod is a fox," that is, like a fox. "John is Elijah," that is, like Elijah. "Christ is a lamb," that is, like a lamb. Yet God, says Master Philip, has set forth one wonderful example unlike the whole rest of the order of nature, namely the joining of the divine and human natures in the Son, our Lord Jesus Christ. Of this the Church nonetheless receives particular propositions, such as: "God is man," "The Word was made flesh." But the Church does not say: "Divinity is humanity," or "Humanity is divinity."

units.la: Quid est Contrarium?
units.tr: What is the Contrary?

units.la: Contrarium, <bl>das widerstreitende</bl> / est diffentaneum, quod uni tantum opponitur.
units.tr: The contrary (German: das widerstreitende) is a dissonant which is opposed to only one thing.

units.la: Est q; vel adversum, vel relatum, vel contradicens, vel privans.
units.tr: It is either adverse, or relative, or contradictory, or privative.

units.la: Quid est Adversum?
units.tr: What is the Opposite?

units.la: <bl>Adversum, das widerstehende</bl> / est contrarium quod alteri velut e regione perpetuo adversatur: ut, Lex est Adversum, Euangelium est alterum Adversum, Liber est Adversum, Servus est alterum Adversum.
units.tr: An opposite, the resisting thing, is a contrary that is always set against another as if from across: for example, Law is an opposite, Gospel is the other opposite; Free is an opposite, Slave is the other opposite.

units.la: Ostende usum argumentandi?
units.tr: Show the use in argument.

units.la: Nos Christiani aut propter legem, aut propter Filium Dei mediatorem sola fide in gratiam a Deo recipimur. At non propter legem: quia omnis homo mendax, mēndax, Romanor.3. Ergo propter Filium Dei sola fide recipimur, sicut Euangelium docet.
units.tr: We Christians are received into grace by God, through faith alone, either because of the Law or because of the Son of God as Mediator. But not because of the Law, since every man is a liar (Rom. 3). Therefore we are received through the Son of God, through faith alone, as the Gospel teaches.

units.la: Sempronius aut est liber, aut servus At Sempronius est liber. Ergo Sempronius non est servus. Horum syllogismorum ratio est: quia Adversorum posito uno, removetur alterum: Et contra.
units.tr: Sempronius is either free or a slave. But Sempronius is free. Therefore Sempronius is not a slave. The reason for these syllogisms is that when one of two opposites is posited, the other is removed, and conversely.

units.la: Quid est Relatum?
units.tr: What is the Relative?

units.la: <bl>Relatum, Das gegenzeigende</bl>[?]<bl>/</bl> est, quod è mutua alterius relati affectione constat: ut, Pater est Relatum, Filius est alterum Relatum. Dominus est Relatum, Servus est alterum Relatum.
units.tr: A relative, the thing that points back, is that which consists in the mutual relation of one correlate to the other: for example, Father is a relative, Son is the other relative; Lord is a relative, Servant is the other relative.

units.la: Ostende usum argumentandi?
units.tr: Show the use in argument.

units.la: Qui pater est, habet filium. At Deus ab æterno fuit pater. Ergo Deus ab æterno habuit filium.
units.tr: Whoever is a father has a son. But God was a Father from eternity. Therefore God had a Son from eternity.

units.la: Omnis Dominus habet servum. At Sempronius non habet servum. Ergo Sempronius non est Dominus. Ratio est: quia Relatorum posito uno, ponitur & alterum: ac sublato uno, tollitur & alterum.
units.tr: Every lord has a servant. But Sempronius does not have a servant. Therefore Sempronius is not a lord. The reason is that when one of two relatives is posited, the other is posited too, and when one is removed, the other is removed too.

units.la: Quid est Contradicens?
units.tr: What is the Contradictory?

units.la: Contradicens, <bl>Das widersprechende</bl> / est quod eidem affirmato negando contradicit: ut, Credidit, non credidit. Matrimonium contraxit, non contraxit.
units.tr: A contradictory, the contradicting thing, is that which denies what is affirmed of the same thing: for example, he believed, he did not believe; he contracted marriage, he did not contract marriage.

units.la: Ostende usum argumentandi?
units.tr: Show the use in argument.

units.la: Qui credidit & Baptizatus fuit, de eo vere dici nequit, quod non crediderit, nec baptizatus fuerit. At vir Aethiops, Eunuchus potens Candaces Reginæ Aethiopum credidit & baptizatus fuit à Philippo, Actor.8. Ergo de illo viro Aethiope vere dici nequit, quod non crediderit, nec baptizatus fuerit.
units.tr: Whoever believed and was baptized cannot truly be said not to have believed or not to have been baptized. But the Ethiopian man, a eunuch of great authority under Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, believed and was baptized by Philip (Acts 8). Therefore it cannot truly be said of that Ethiopian man that he did not believe or was not baptized.

units.la: Qui matrimonium non contraxit, de eo vere dici nequit, quod contraxerit. At Titius matrimonium non contraxit. Ergo de Titio vere dici nequit, quod matrimonium contraxerit. Ratio est: quia dequo affirmatum praedicatur, de eodem negatum vere dici nequit: Et contrà.
units.tr: Whoever has not contracted marriage cannot truly be said to have contracted it. But Titius has not contracted marriage. Therefore it cannot truly be said of Titius that he contracted marriage. The reason is that what is affirmed of a thing cannot truly be denied of the same thing, and conversely.

units.la: Quid est Privans?
units.tr: What is the Privative?

units.la: Privans, <bl>das beraubende/</bl>est, quod habitum in eo tantum subjecto, in quo inesse potest, privat: ut, Loqui posse est habitus, mutum esse est privans. Ratione uti est habitus, furiosum esse est privans.
units.tr: A privative, the depriving thing, is that which deprives a subject of a habit only in that subject in which the habit can be present: for example, being able to speak is a habit, being mute is a privation; using reason is a habit, being insane is a privation.

units.la: Ostende usum Argumentandi?
units.tr: Show the use in argument.

units.la: Qui mutus est, ipse loqui non potest. At Zacharias est mutus, Lucæ 1. Ergo Zacharias loqui non potest.
units.tr: Whoever is mute cannot himself speak. But Zacharias was mute (Luke 1). Therefore Zacharias cannot speak.

units.la: Qui furiosus est, ratione non utitur. At Mevius est furiosus. Ergo Mevius ratione non utitur.
units.tr: Whoever is insane does not use reason. But Mevius is insane. Therefore Mevius does not use reason.

units.la: Horum syllogismorum ratio est: quia posito-privante, removetur habitus. In quo autem habitus non est natura possibilis, in eodem etiam nequit esse privans. Ubi vero privans est, ibi habitus fuit, aut esse potuit. At in talpis, lapidibus & aliis rebus non est videndi habitus natura possibilis. Ergo talpae, lapides, & aliae res, caecae dici nequeunt.
units.tr: The reason for these syllogisms is that when the privative is posited, the habit is removed. Where the habit is not naturally possible in a thing, the privation cannot be there either. Where a privation is, there the habit was, or could have been. But in moles, stones and other such things, the habit of sight is not naturally possible. Therefore moles, stones and other such things cannot be called blind.

units.la: Quid est Comparatum, sextum argumentorum locum occupans?
units.tr: What is the Compared, which occupies the sixth place among the arguments?

units.la: Comparatum est, quod cum altero cōparato confertur. <bl>Das vergleichte ist/ welches mit dem andern</bl> <bl>vergleichten vergleichet wird.</bl> Estq; Majus vel Minus, Simile vel Dissimile.
units.tr: The compared is that which is set beside another compared thing. The thing compared is that which is compared with another thing compared. And it is either Greater or Less, Similar or Dissimilar.

units.la: Quid est Majus?
units.tr: What is the Greater?

units.la: Majus, <bl>das grössere /</bl> est comparatum, quod excedit Minus: ut, Anima & Corpus Majus est: Alimentum & Vestitus est Minus, Dispositio totorum bonorum in Testamento est Majus, Dispositio servorum in ultima voluntate est Minus.
units.tr: The greater, the larger thing, is the compared which exceeds the less: for example, soul and body is the greater; food and clothing is the less. The disposition of all one's goods in a will is the greater; the disposition of servants in a last will is the less.

units.la: Quomodo argumentamur a Majori?
units.tr: How do we argue from the Greater?

units.la: Affirmativè & Negativè: ut, Si pater coelestis discipulis Christi animam & corpus dedit: dabit etiam illis proculdubio escam & vestimentum. Ratio a Majori affirmato ad Minus affirmandum: quia anima, inquit Christus Matthæi 6. plus est quàm esca: Et corpus plus quàm vestimentum. Qui igitur Majus dedit, dabit etiam Minus. At verum Antecedens. Consequens igitur.
units.tr: Affirmatively and negatively. For example: If the heavenly Father has given to the disciples of Christ soul and body, he will certainly also give them food and clothing. The argument is from the greater affirmed to the less affirmed, because the soul, says Christ (Matt. 6), is more than food, and the body more than clothing. Therefore he who has given the greater will also give the less. But the antecedent is true. Therefore the consequent.

units.la: Si Deus incredulis Judæis, naturalibus ramis, Romanor. II. non pepercit: Turcis etiam incredulis & reliquis Ethnicis non parcet. Ratio a Majori negato, ad minus negandum.
units.tr: If God did not spare the unbelieving Jews, the natural branches (Rom. 11), he will not spare the unbelieving Turks and the other heathen either. This is an argument from the greater denied to the less denied.

units.la: At Deus incredulis Judæis non pepercit. Ergo etiam Turcis incredulis & reliquis ethnicis non parcet.
units.tr: But God did not spare the unbelieving Jews. Therefore he will not spare the unbelieving Turks and other heathen either.

units.la: Si Domino minori viginti annis totorum suorum bonorum in Testamento dispositio permissa est: ipsi etiam servorum in ultima voluntate dispositio permitti debet. Ratio a Majori affirmato ad Minus affirmandum: cui enim licet quod plus est, licebit quoq; quod Minus est. At verum antecedens ex §.7. cum ergo, verf.quod non erat, Instit.1. Quibus ex causis manum non licet. Consequens igitur.
units.tr: If to a lord under twenty years of age the disposition of all his goods in a will has been permitted, then the disposition of servants in a last will ought also to be permitted to him. This is an argument from the greater affirmed to the less affirmed: for whatever is permitted in the greater case will also be permitted in the lesser. But the antecedent is true, from §.7, with "cum ergo" and the words "quod non erat", Institutes 1. (on the grounds on which manumission is not permitted). Therefore the consequent.

units.la: Quid est Minus?
units.tr: What is the Lesser?

units.la: Minus, <bl>bas geringere</bl> / est Comparatum, quod excedit ur à Majori: ut, Homines mali, Minus est: Pater cœlestis Majus. Imperatores, Minus est: Papa Romanus, Majus.
units.tr: The lesser (German: the lower, the inferior) is the compared term that falls short of the greater. For example, "evil men" is the lesser, and "the heavenly Father" the greater. "Emperors" is the lesser, and "the Roman Pope" the greater.

units.la: Quomodo argumentamur à minori?
units.tr: How do we argue from the lesser?

units.la: Etiam affirmative & negative: ut, Si vos homines cùm sitis mali, nostis bona data dare filiis vestris, quanto magis pater vester de cœlo dabit spiritum bonum petentibus se, Lucæ 11. Ratio a minori affirmato ad Majus affirmandum.
units.tr: Both affirmatively and negatively. For example: "If you, though you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give the good Spirit to those who ask him?" (Luke 11). This is an argument from the lesser affirmed to the greater affirmed.

units.la: At vos homines nostis bona data dare vestris filiis. Hujus assumptionis prosyllogismus est in his verbis Christi: Quis autem ex vobis patrem petit panem, nunquid lapidem dabit illi? aut piscem: nunquid pro pisce serpentem dabit illi? aut si petierit ovum: nunquit porriget illi scorpionem?
units.tr: But you men know how to give good gifts to your children. The prosyllogism of this assumption is in the words of Christ: "Which of you, if his son asks for bread, will give him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, will he give him a serpent instead of a fish? Or if he asks for an egg, will he give him a scorpion?"

units.la: Ergo pater vester coelestis etiam dabit spiritum bonum petentibus se. Hunc immotum Christi syllogismum rancido Diabolo precaturi objiciamus, qui piorum auribus insusurrat: frustrà clamas, pater tuus coelestis te non exaudiet.
units.tr: Therefore your heavenly Father will also give the good Spirit to those who ask him. Let us put this unshakable syllogism of Christ before the rancid Devil, who whispers to the ears of the godly: "You cry out in vain; your heavenly Father will not hear you."

units.la: Si Deus passeres non deserit: nec vos meos discipulos deferet. Ratio à minori negato, ad Majus negative concludendum. At Deus passeres non deserit. Nonne quinq; passeres veneunt dipondio? & unus ex illis non est in oblivione coram Deo, Lucæ 12. Ergo Deus vos meos discipulos non deferet. Nam multis passeribus pluris estis: sed & capilli capitis vestri omnes numerati sunt, inquit Christus.
units.tr: If God does not forsake the sparrows, he will not forsake you, my disciples. This is an argument from the lesser denied to the greater denied. But God does not forsake the sparrows. Are not five sparrows sold for two farthings? And not one of them is forgotten before God (Luke 12). Therefore God will not forsake you, my disciples. For you are worth more than many sparrows; indeed, even the hairs of your head are all numbered, says Christ.

units.la: Si Imperatores civili & naturali ratione suadente consensum parentum in matrimonio contrahendo omnino necessarium in suis legibus requirunt: sequitur ipsum Romanū Papam etiam, qui longe vult Imperatoribus sanctitate antecellere, debere consensum in nuptiis necessarium requirere, & nequaquam mandatum Domini: Honora patrem & matrem, suo jure canonico, alicubi parentum consensum non necessarium esse docente, irritum reddere, Ratio à Minori ad Majus concludendum.
units.tr: If emperors, prompted by civil and natural reason, require in their laws that the consent of parents be entirely necessary for contracting marriage, it follows that the Roman Pope himself, who wishes to surpass the emperors far in holiness, ought to require the consent of parents as necessary in marriage. He ought not, by his canon law, which in some places teaches that parental consent is not necessary, render void the command of the Lord: "Honour your father and mother." This is an argument from the lesser to the greater.

units.la: At antecedens probatur ex princip. justas, Instit.1. de nuptiis: Dum tamen si filij familiarum sint, consensum habeant parentum, quorum in potestate sunt. Nam hoc fieri debere, & civilis & naturalis ratio suadet: in tantum, ut jussus parentis praecedere debeat. Item ex l. 2. Nuptiae. ff. de ritu nuptiarum: Nuptiae consistere non possunt, nisi consentiant omnes, id est, qui coeunt, quorumq; in potestate sunt. Item ex §.1. Et si quidem, C. de raptu virginum seu viduar. nec non sanctimoniales. Oportet enim, inquit Imperator, ut quicunque uxorem ducere voluerit, sive ingenuam, sive libertinam: secundum nostras leges & ANTIQUAM CONSUETUDINEM, parentes vel alios, quos decet, petat, ut cum eorum voluntate fiat legitimum conjugium. Ergo Romane Papa Consequens merito agnosceres.
units.tr: But the antecedent is proved from the law of the Institutes, de nuptiis, the principle "Provided, however, that if they are sons of a household, they have the consent of their parents, in whose power they are." For both civil and natural reason persuade that this must be done, to such an extent that the command of the parent must come first. Likewise from Digest 23.2.2, de ritu nuptiarum: "Marriage cannot exist unless all consent, that is, those who come together and those under whose power they are." Likewise from the first section of Codex 9.13 (de raptu virginum seu viduarum, nec non sanctimonialium): "For it is fitting, says the Emperor, that whoever wishes to take a wife, whether freeborn or freedwoman, should, according to our laws and the ancient custom, ask for the parents or others who are fitting, so that the lawful marriage is made with their will." Therefore, Roman Pope, you ought rightly to acknowledge the consequence.

units.la: Quid est Simile?
units.tr: What is the Similar?

units.la: Simile, <bl>das gleiche</bl> / est comparatum, quod cum altero simili eandem qualitatem habet: ut, sicut Sara, Rachel, Rebecca, suis maritis subditae fuerunt, primum simile: ita etiam Christianorum uxores suis conjugibus pareant, alterum simile.
units.tr: The similar (German: the same) is the compared term that has the same quality as another similar term. For example: just as Sarah, Rachel and Rebecca were subject to their husbands (the first similar), so too the wives of Christians should obey their spouses (the second similar).

units.la: Hujus senis studium juris discendi simile est studio jurisconsulti Pomponij.
units.tr: This old man's study of learning the law is similar to the study of the jurist Pomponius.

units.la: Ostende usum argumentandi?
units.tr: Show the use of the argument.

units.la: Si Sara, Rachel, Rebecca, & aliae pię uxores maritis in veteri Testamento subditae fuerunt: etiam Christianorum uxores suis conjugibus parere debent. At prius. Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: If Sarah, Rachel, Rebecca and the other godly wives were subject to their husbands in the Old Testament, then the wives of Christians also ought to obey their spouses. But the first is true. Therefore the second is also true.

units.la: Si Jurisconsulto Pomponio seni honestum fuit leges addiscere: etiam huic seni studium legum civilium honestum erit. At verum prius ex l.20. Apud Julianum ff. de fideicommissar. libertatib. Nam ego, inquit Pomponius, discendi cupiditate, quam solam vivendi rationem optimam in octavum & septuagesimum annum ætatis duxi, memor sum ejus sententiae, qui dixisse fertur: κατὰ τὴν ἑτέραν ποδὰ ἐν τῇ σωρῷ ἔχω[?], ἀποσμιγθεὶς[?] τῇ βλοίμῳ[?], id est, Etsi alterum pedem in tumulo haberem: non pigeret aliquid addiscere. Posterius igitur.
units.tr: If it was honourable for the old jurist Pomponius to learn the laws, then the study of civil laws will also be honourable for this old man. But the first is true, from Digest 36.1.20, "Apud Julianum," de fideicommissariis libertatibus. For I, says Pomponius, having a desire for learning, which I have judged to be the only best way of living into my seventy-eighth year, remember the saying of one who is said to have spoken: "kata tēn heteran poda en tō sōrō echō, aposmigtheis tē bloimō," that is, "Even though I had one foot in the grave, it would not grieve me to learn something." Therefore the second is true.

units.la: Horum syllogismorum ratio est: quia de similibus seu paribus idem fertur judicium, quando scilicet collatio fit in his partibus, quae congruunt. Nam si fiat earum partium collatio, quae dissimiles sunt, nihil cohæret. Idcò crebrò dici solet: simile non est idem: omnis similitudo claudicat. Item, simile non currit quatuor pedibus. Similitudo nihil probat.
units.tr: The reason for these syllogisms is this: the same judgment is given about similar or equal things, namely when the comparison is made in those parts which agree. For if the comparison is made of those parts which are dissimilar, nothing coheres. Therefore it is often said: the similar is not the same; every similitude limps. Likewise, a similar thing does not run on four feet. A similitude proves nothing.

units.la: Quid est Dissimile?
units.tr: What is the Dissimilar?

units.la: Dissimile, [illegible, ~2 words] est comparatum, quod cum altero dissimili diversam qualitatem habet: ut, Reges Gentium dominantur, primum dissimile: Christi autem discipuli non sic,alterum dissimile.
units.tr: The dissimilar ([illegible]) is the compared term that has a different quality from another dissimilar term. For example: "The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them" is the first dissimilar; "but it shall not be so among the disciples of Christ" is the second dissimilar.

units.la: Juris Tyrones initio Institutiones discant,primum dissimile: non autem Digesta, Codicem, Novellas, alterum dissimile.
units.tr: Beginners in law should learn the Institutes first, that is the first dissimilar; but not the Digest, the Code and the Novels, which is the second dissimilar.

units.la: Ostende usum argumentandi?
units.tr: Show the use of arguing?

units.la: Si Christus regibus gentium dominandi potestatem concedit, non autem suis discipulis: sequitur illos Doctores rectè facere, qui seculare brachium magistratui remittunt: Papam verò Romanum, qui vult Christi discipulus esse, Cardinales, Episcopos & reliquos Papæ gregales graviter peccare, qui, officio verbi Divini annuntiandi relicto, gladium secularem portant, cibis opiparis, vinoq; optimo sese ingurgitant, chartis lusoriis tempus transfigentes, Veneri fruges & munera sacra libando inserviunt. At verum Antecedens ex Luca 22. Ergo & Consequens.
units.tr: If Christ grants the power of ruling to the kings of the nations but not to his disciples, it follows that those teachers act rightly who hand the secular arm over to the magistrate. But the Roman Pope, who wishes to be a disciple of Christ, and the cardinals, bishops and the rest of the Pope's flock sin gravely: having abandoned the office of announcing the divine Word, they carry the secular sword, gorge themselves on rich foods and the finest wine, pass their time with playing cards, and serve Venus while offering the sacred fruits and gifts. But the antecedent is true, from Luke 22. Therefore the consequent too.

units.la: Si juris Tyrones initio Institutiones discant, non autem Digesta, Codicem, Novellas: sequitur eos, quibus imperatoris admonitio cordi est, rectè facere: reliquos verò, qui juris cunabulis repudiatis, vasto Digestorum, Codicis & Novellarum Oceano se temerè committunt, & Imperatori non audientes esse, & suis non satis prudenter consulere studiis. At verum Antecedens ex Constitut. Omnem, verf. Itaque, de juris docendi ratione. Consequens igitur.
units.tr: If beginners in law learn the Institutes first, but not the Digest, the Code and the Novels, it follows that those who heed the emperor's admonition act rightly. The rest, who reject the cradle of law and rashly entrust themselves to the vast ocean of the Digest, the Code and the Novels, are disobedient to the emperor and do not consult their studies prudently enough. But the antecedent is true, from the constitution Omnem, verse Itaque, on the method of teaching law. Therefore the consequent.

units.la: Horum syllogismorum ratio est: quia de dissimilibus diversum est judicium.
units.tr: The reasoning behind these syllogisms is this: because a different judgment is due to things that are dissimilar.

units.la: Quid est Ortum, septimum argumentorum locum occupans?
units.tr: What is Ortum, the seventh place of arguments?

units.la: <bl>Ortum, das entstandene</bl> / est argumentum, quod perinde affectum est ad arguendum, sicut argumentum primum, unde ortum existit. Discrimen vero primi & orti est, quòd in prioribus locis, Causa, Essectum, Subjectum, Adjunctum, subtiliter & per se explicetur: In hoc vero septimo loco, Causa, Effectum, Subjectum, Adjunctum, in Conjugato, Notatione, Distributione & Definitione comprehendantur.
units.tr: Ortum (the arisen) is an argument that is framed for proving in the same way as the first argument from which it arises. The difference between the first argument and the ortum is that in the earlier places, cause, effect, subject and adjunct are explained subtly and in themselves, whereas in this seventh place they are comprehended under the conjugate, notation, distribution and definition.

units.la: Quid est Conjugatio?
units.tr: What is Conjugation?

units.la: <bl>Conjugatum, das abgeleitete</bl> / est, cujus vox ab aliquo principio, quod improprie conjugatum dicitur, deducta est: ut, Benignitas est causa conjugata, agere benignissimè est effectum conjugatum. Hæreditas est causa conjugata. Hæres est effectum conjugatum. Nam quod quis hæres dicitur, id fit propter hæreditatem.
units.tr: The conjugate (the derived) is a word derived from some principle, which is improperly called the conjugate. For example: goodness is a conjugate cause; acting most kindly is a conjugate effect. Inheritance is a conjugate cause; heir is a conjugate effect, since someone is called an heir on account of the inheritance.

units.la: Ostende usum argumentandi?
units.tr: Show the use of arguing?

units.la: Qui nobiscum benignissimè agit, in eo est benignitas. Hic ab Effecto ad causam disputatur. At Deus nobiscum benignissimè agit. Ergo in Deo est summa benignitas. Ratio: quia alicui tributo aut remoto conjugatorum uno, tribuitur vel removetur etiam alterum.
units.tr: He who deals most kindly with us has goodness in him. Here the argument runs from effect to cause. But God deals most kindly with us. Therefore there is supreme goodness in God. The reason: when one of the conjugates is attributed to or removed from something, the other is also attributed or removed.

units.la: Si hæreditas nihil aliud est, quàm successio in universum jus, quod defunctus habuit tempore mortis: sequitur hæredem etiam in jus universum succedere, quod defunctus mortis tempore habuit. At prius: posterius igitur. Ratio: quia quod uni, id etiam alteri Conjugatorum tribuitur vel detrahitur.
units.tr: If inheritance is nothing other than succession into the whole right that the deceased possessed at the time of death, it follows that the heir also succeeds to the whole right that the deceased possessed at the time of death. But the first is true; therefore the second is too. The reason: what is attributed to or taken away from one of the conjugates is also attributed or taken away from the other.

units.la: Quid est Notatio?
units.tr: What is Notation?

units.la: Notatio, <bl>die Stimmerforschung</bl> / est qua ex aliquo argumento primo quarundam vocum interpretatio redditur: ut, Notatio hominis, redditur ex materia Humo. Notatio pandectarum redditur e Subjecto πᾶν δέχεσθαι[?], omne capere.
units.tr: Notation (etymology, the study of a word) is that by which the interpretation of certain words is given from some primary argument. For example, the notation of "man" is given from its matter, humus (earth). The notation of "pandects" is given from its subject, "to receive all" [πᾶν δέχεσθαι], that is, to hold everything.

units.la: Ostende usum à Notatione argumen- tandi?
units.tr: Show the use of arguing from notation?

units.la: Is rectè homo dicitur, qui ex humo factus est. At Angelus non est ex humo factus. Ergo Angelus non recte homo dicitur. Ratio: quia negata causa materiali, effectum quoq; negatur.
units.tr: He is rightly called a man who is made from earth. But an angel is not made from earth. Therefore an angel is not rightly called a man. The reason: when the material cause is denied, the effect is denied too.

units.la: Si pandectæ dicuntur ὡς τὰ πᾶν δεχόμενα[?], quod est omne continere: sequitur Pandectas omnes Disputationes & decisiones in se habere legitimas, ut Imperator inquit in Const. Tanta. §. omnia verf. postea vero de Confirm. Digest. At prius: Posterius igitur.
units.tr: If the pandects are so called as things receiving all [ὡς τὰ πᾶν δεχόμενα], that is, containing everything, it follows that the Pandects contain within themselves all lawful disputations and decisions, as the emperor says in the constitution Tanta, §. omnia, verse postea vero, On the confirmation of the Digest. But the first is true; therefore the second is too.

units.la: Quid est Distributio?
units.tr: What is Distribution?

units.la: Distributio, <bl>Die theilung</bl> / est qua totum in partes distribuitur. Totum est quod continet partes: partes sunt quæ continentur à toto.
units.tr: Distribution is that by which a whole is divided into parts. The whole is that which contains parts; the parts are those which are contained by the whole.

units.la: Collectio partium ad constituendum totum, Inductio dicitur: ut, vinum Creticum calefacit, vinum Italicum calefacit, vinum Rhenanum calefacit, nec ullum dissimile exemplum monstrari potest. Ergo omne vinum calefacit. Distributio est aut ex causis, effectis, subjectis, aut adjunctis.
units.tr: The collection of parts to constitute a whole is called induction: for example, Cretan wine warms, Italian wine warms, Rhenish wine warms, and no dissimilar example can be shown; therefore all wine warms. Distribution is from causes, from effects, from subjects, or from adjuncts.

units.la: Quid est Distributio ex causis?
units.tr: What is distribution from causes?

units.la: Quando partes sunt causæ totius: ut, Scriptura sacra partim à Moyse & Prophetis, partim ab Evangelistis & Apostolis exarata est.
units.tr: When the parts are causes of the whole: for example, Holy Scripture was written partly by Moses and the Prophets, partly by the Evangelists and Apostles.

units.la: Quid est Distributio ex Effectis?
units.tr: What is distribution from effects?

units.la: Quando partes sunt Effecta: ut, primus dixit ei, villam emi, alter dixit quinq; juga boum emi, alius dixit, uxorem duxi, & ideo non possum venire, Luc. 14.
units.tr: When the parts are effects: for example, "The first said to him, I have bought a field; the second said, I have bought five yoke of oxen; another said, I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come." Luke 14.

units.la: Distributio generis in species hic excellit.
units.tr: Distribution of a genus into its species excels here.

units.la: Quid est Genus?
units.tr: What is Genus?

units.la: Quod speciebus communem essentiam tribuit: ut, Animal, genus hominis & bestiæ dicitur, quia animalis essentia, nempe corporea, animata, sentiens, bestiæ & homini æqualiter inest: Estque aut generalissimum, cujus nullum est Genus superius: ut Ens, aut Subalternum, quod species hujus, illius autem Genus est: ut, Homo species est animalis: Petri vero & Pauli Genus.
units.tr: The genus is that which gives a common essence to its species. For example, animal is said to be the genus of man and beast, because the essence of animal, namely bodily, animate and sentient, is equally present in both beast and man. A genus is either the most general, having no higher genus, such as being; or subaltern, which is the species of one thing but the genus of another: for example, man is a species of animal, but the genus of Peter and Paul.

units.la: Quid est Species?
units.tr: What is a species?

units.la: Quæ præter Generis essentiam propriam formam sustinet: ut, Homo & Bestia, species animalis dicuntur: quia præter animalis essentiam propriam formam in se habent: Estque aut subalterna, aut specialissima, quæ nequit dividi in species inferiores: ut, hic Petrus, hic Paulus, hic Johannes.
units.tr: That which, beyond the essence of its genus, carries its own distinct form. Thus man and beast are called species of animal, because, beyond the essence of animal, they have their own distinct forms. A species is either subaltern or most specific, the most specific being one that cannot be divided into lower species: for example, this Peter, this Paul, this John.

units.la: Quid est Distributio è subjectis?
units.tr: What is distribution from subjects?

units.la: Quando partes sunt subjecta: ut, Sapientia tùm in Deo tùm in Angelis, tùm in Hominibus elucet.
units.tr: When the parts are subjects: for example, wisdom shines forth in God, in the angels, and in men.

units.la: Quid est Distributio ex Adjunctis?
units.tr: What is distribution from adjuncts?

units.la: Quando partes sunt Adjuncta: ut, Regnum cœlorum simile est decem virginibus. Quinque autem ex eis erant fatuæ, & quinque prudentes.
units.tr: When the parts are adjuncts: for example, "The kingdom of heaven is like ten virgins. Five of them were foolish, and five were wise."

units.la: Ostendeusum[?] à toto & Genere argu- mentandi?
units.tr: How is the argument from the whole and from the genus used?

units.la: Si totum judicium est res approbata à Deo: sequitur accusare, defendere, & sententiam pronunciare licitum esse. At verum Antecedens. Consequens igitur.
units.tr: If the whole judgment is a matter approved by God, it follows that it is lawful to accuse, to defend, and to pronounce sentence. But the antecedent is true. Therefore the consequent.

units.la: Si Titius Domum legavit, etiam fundamentum, tectum & parietes.At illud: Hoc igitur.
units.tr: If Titius bequeathed the house, he also bequeathed the foundation, the roof and the walls. But the first is true. Therefore the second.

units.la: Horum syllogismorum ratio est: quia toto posito & concesso, partes quoq; ponuntur & conceduntur.
units.tr: The reason for these syllogisms is this: when the whole is posited and granted, the parts are also posited and granted.

units.la: Quisquis crediderit in Jesum Nazarenum, remissionem peccatorum per nomē ejus accipiet, id quod omnes prophetæ testantur, Actor.10. Atqui vir Cæsariæ, nomine Cornelius, credidit in Jesum Nazarenū. Ergo Cornelius remissionem peccatorum accepit.
units.tr: Whoever believes in Jesus of Nazareth will receive forgiveness of sins through his name, as all the prophets testify (Acts 10). But a man of Caesarea named Cornelius believed in Jesus of Nazareth. Therefore Cornelius received forgiveness of sins.

units.la: Si Sempronius huic mulieri omne argentum legavit: etiam numeratam pecuniam.
units.tr: If Sempronius bequeathed all the silver to this woman, he also bequeathed the coined money.

units.la: At verum Antecedens: Consequens igitur.
units.tr: But the antecedent is true. Therefore the consequent.

units.la: Horum syllogismorum ratio est: Quia affirmato seu posito genere universè, species etiam quaelibet affirmatur.
units.tr: The reason for these syllogisms is this: when the genus is affirmed universally, every species is also affirmed.

units.la: Quid est Definitio?
units.tr: What is a definition?

units.la: Definitio, [illegible, ~12 letters] est qua explicatur quid res fit: Eftq; perfecta vel imperfecta.
units.tr: A definition is that by which what a thing is becomes clear; and it is either perfect or imperfect.

units.la: Quid est Definitio perfecta?
units.tr: What is a perfect definition?

units.la: Quæ constat è solis causis essentiam constituentibus: quales causæ genere & forma comprehenduntur: ut, peccatum est defectus, vel inclinatio, vel actio, pugnans cum lege Dei.
units.tr: One that consists solely of the causes that constitute the essence, which causes are comprehended in genus and form: for example, sin is a defect, or an inclination, or an action, opposed to the law of God.

units.la: Actio nihil aliud est, quàm jus persequendi in judicio, quod sibi debetur. Lib 4. Inst.de actionib.
units.tr: An action is nothing other than the right to pursue in court what is owed to oneself (Institutes, book 4, on actions).

units.la: Ostende usum à Definitione argumen- tandi?
units.tr: How is the argument from definition used?

units.la: Cui congruit definitio, ei etiam Definitum. At concupiscentiæ congruit hæc Definitio: Inclinatio pugnans cum lege Dei. Ergo etiam cōcupiscentiæ congruit Definitum, nempe peccatum. Est syllogismus prorsus inexpugnabilis adversus Jesuvitas, qui nugantur concupiscentiam non esse verè peccatum.
units.tr: That to which the definition fits, to that the thing defined also fits. But this definition fits concupiscence: an inclination opposed to the law of God. Therefore the thing defined, namely sin, also fits concupiscence. This is a wholly unanswerable syllogism against the Jesuits, who trifle that concupiscence is not truly sin.

units.la: Qui jus non habet persequendi in judicio quod sibi debetur, actionem habere non potest. At Sempronius id non habet. Ergo Sempronius actionem habere non potest. Ratio: quia cui adimitur Definitio, ei etiam Definitum.
units.tr: He who has no right to pursue in court what is owed to himself cannot have an action. But Sempronius does not have this right. Therefore Sempronius cannot have an action. The reason: because from the one from whom the definition is taken away, the thing defined is also taken away.

units.la: Quid est Definitio imperfecta?
units.tr: What is an imperfect definition?

units.la: Est descriptio, eine <bl>beschreibung</bl>/ ex aliis etiam argumentis rem describens: ut,pontifex est,qui ex hominibus assumptus, pro hominibus constituitur in iis, quae sunt ad Deum: ut offerat dona & sacrificia pro peccatis,Hebræor.5.[?]
units.tr: It is a description, which, drawing also on other arguments, describes the thing: for example, "A high priest is one taken from among men and appointed on behalf of men in matters pertaining to God, to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins" (Heb. 5).

units.la: Ingenuus est is, qui statim ut natus est, liber est: sive ex duobus ingenuis matrimonio editus est, sive ex libertinis duobus, sive ex altero libertino & altero ingenuo, 1.Instit.4.
units.tr: A freeborn person is one who is free from the moment he is born, whether he was born of two freeborn parents in marriage, or of two freedmen, or of one freedman and one freeborn parent (Institutes 1, book 4).

units.la: Ostende usum a Descriptione argumen- tandi?
units.tr: How is the argument from description used?

units.la: Cui congruit Descriptio, ei etiam descriptum.
units.tr: That to which the description fits, to that the thing described also fits.

units.la: At qui Christo congruit descriptio pontificis.
units.tr: But the description of a high priest fits Christ.

units.la: Ergo Christo etiam congruit descriptum, nempe Pontifex.
units.tr: Therefore the thing described, namely high priest, also fits Christ.

units.la: Qui non statim ut natus est, liber est, ingenuus appellari nequit. At Titius non statim postquam in lucem editus est, liber est. Ergo Titius ingenuus appellari nequit. Ratio: quia cui adimitur Descriptio, ei etiam descriptum.
units.tr: He who is not free from the moment he is born cannot be called freeborn. But Titius was not free from the moment he was brought into the light. Therefore Titius cannot be called freeborn. The reason: because from the one from whom the description is taken away, the thing described is also taken away.

units.la: Hactenus argumenta artificialia, quae natura sua propria aliquid arguunt & demonstrant, expósita sunt.
units.tr: Thus far the artificial arguments have been set out, which by their own nature argue and demonstrate something.

units.la: Quid est Testimonium ostavum[?] argu- mentorum locum occu- pans?
units.tr: What is testimony, which occupies the eighth place among the arguments?

units.la: Testimonium, <bl>ein gezeugnuß</bl>/ est argumentum inartificiale, quod non sua natura, sed assumpta artificialis alicujus argumenti vi arguit: ut, testimonium ex Sacrosanctis Bibliis sumptum, apud Ethnicos, Turcas, Jesuitas[?] & similes incredulos, sua natura nihil arguit, sicut ex Platonis dicto apparet: Moyses multa dicit, sed pauca probat. Nos autem soli Christiani sine ulla dubitatione aut rei inquisitione Sacrofanctis Bibliis fidem adjungimus propter assumptam vim artificialis argumenti, nempe authoris ac principalis causae ipsius Dei omnipotentis, justi ac veracis. Hanc causam Sacrosanctorum Bibliorum cum Ethnici, Turcae & Jesuvitae nolint agnoscere, testimonium ex Moyse & prophetis, perrexiguam, imo nullam probationis vim apud eos habet.
units.tr: Testimony is an inartificial argument, which does not argue by its own nature but by the force of some artificial argument it has taken on. For example, testimony taken from the most holy Bible, among the heathens, Turks, Jesuits and similar unbelievers, argues nothing by its own nature, as appears from the saying of Plato: "Moses says many things but proves few." We Christians, however, without any doubt or inquiry into the matter, give faith to the most holy Bible, on account of the artificial argument it takes up, namely the author and principal cause, God Almighty himself, just and true. Since the heathens, Turks and Jesuits refuse to acknowledge this cause of the most holy Bible, testimony from Moses and the prophets has very little, indeed no, force of proof among them.

units.la: Quotuplex est Testimonium?
units.tr: How many kinds of testimony are there?

units.la: Divinum aut Humanum. Divinum ut e sacris literis apud Christianos: Humanum comprehendit legem scriptam & non scriptam, rumorem, testes, consessionem liberam vel expressam tormentis, jusjurandum, pueritiam, somnum, vinolentiam, philosophorum, oratorum, poetarum sententias, proverbia & dicta[?] illustria.
units.tr: Divine or human. Divine testimony is that from the sacred writings among Christians. Human testimony comprises written and unwritten law, rumour, witnesses, confession, free or extracted by torture, oath, the testimony of childhood, sleep, drunkenness, the sayings of philosophers, orators and poets, proverbs, and famous sayings.

units.la: Testimonio trium legum Aristotelicarum Petrus Ramus liberales artes reformavit.
units.tr: By the testimony of three Aristotelian laws Peter Ramus reformed the liberal arts.

units.la: Prima lex est καθ᾽ παντὸς[?], id est, de omni. Haec imperat, ut quodlibet artis praeceptum seu axioma necessario & generaliter de omnibus verum sit.
units.tr: The first law is kath' pantos [κατὰ παντός], that is, "of all." It requires that every precept or axiom of an art be necessarily and universally true of all things.

units.la: Secunda lex praecipit, ut quodlibet artis axioma sit καθ᾽ αὐτο[?] per se & homogencum, id est, artis, in qua docetur, proprium, & tanquam ejusdem corporis membrum.
units.tr: The second law prescribes that every axiom of an art be kath' auto [καθ' αὐτό], that is, "in itself" and homogeneous, that is, belonging to the art in which it is taught, and as a member of the same body.

units.la: Tertia lex est καθ᾽ ὅλω πρῶτον[?], haec sancit, ut omnia axiomata artium, non solum necessario vera & propria sint, verum etiam universaliter prima, id est, si generalia sint, generaliter doceantur, si specialia, specialiter.
units.tr: The third law is kath' holou prōton [καθ' ὅλου πρῶτον]; it establishes that the axioms of the arts be not only necessarily true and proper, but also universally primary, that is, if they are general they are taught generally, if specific, specifically.

units.la: Ostende usum a Testimonio Divino & Humano argumen- tandi.
units.tr: Show the use of argument from divine and human testimony.

units.la: Si Michæas prædixit, Christum Bethlehemæ in lucem editum iri: Hoc Judæi merito credidissent. At Michæas prædixit ex Bethlehem prodituru esse ducem, qui gubernaturus sit populum Israel. Ergo hoc Judæi merito credidissent. Ratio a testimonio prophetæ, qui instinctu Spiritus S. locutus est.
units.tr: If Micah foretold that Christ would be born at Bethlehem, the Jews ought rightly to have believed this. But Micah foretold that a leader would come forth from Bethlehem who was to govern the people of Israel. Therefore the Jews ought rightly to have believed this. This is an argument from the testimony of a prophet, who spoke by the impulse of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Septimo mense nasci perfectum partum jam receptum est propter auctoritatem doctissimi viri Hippocratis. l.2.ff.de statu hominum. Atqui Titius ex justis nuptiis septimo mense natus est. Ergo Titius persectus partus est, & justus filius.
units.tr: That a child born in the seventh month is a complete birth has already been accepted on the authority of the most learned man Hippocrates (l. 2, ff. de statu hominum). But Titius was born of a lawful marriage in the seventh month. Therefore Titius was a complete birth and a legitimate son.

units.la: Hactenus Inventio prima pars Dialecticæ exposi-ta fuit.
units.tr: So far the first part of Dialectic, Invention, has been set out.

units.la: Quid est Dispositio?
units.tr: What is Disposition?

units.la: Dispositio est secunda pars Dialecticæ de disponendis argumentis ad benè judicandum.
units.tr: Disposition is the second part of Dialectic, concerning the arrangement of arguments for sound judgment.

units.la: Quot sunt partes Dispositionis?
units.tr: How many parts does Disposition have?

units.la: Tres: Enunciatum, Syllogismus, Methodus.
units.tr: Three: the proposition, the syllogism, and method.

units.la: Quid est Enunciatum?
units.tr: What is a proposition?

units.la: Enunciatum seu propositio est dispositio, qua argumentum de argumento enunciatur: ut, Dialectica est ars. Homo est animal. Sutor est artifex.
units.tr: A proposition, or enunciation, is an arrangement by which one argument is stated about another, as: Dialectic is an art. Man is an animal. A cobbler is a craftsman.

units.la: Quot sunt partes Enunciatis?
units.tr: How many parts does a proposition have?

units.la: Tres: Antecedens, Vinculum, Consequens.
units.tr: Three: the antecedent, the link, and the consequent.

units.la: Quid est Antecedens?
units.tr: What is the antecedent?

units.la: Antecedens seu Subjectum est Nominativus, aut quod ejus loco ponitur, de quo aliquid prædicatur:
units.tr: The antecedent, or subject, is the nominative, or whatever is put in its place, of which something is predicated.

units.la: Quid est Vinculum?
units.tr: What is the link?

units.la: Vinculum seu copula, est vel verbum ipsum,quod etiam alterum argumentum facit: ut, Socrates ambulat: vel verbum Substantivum inter duos Nominativos interjectum: ut, Homo est mortalis.
units.tr: The link, or copula, is either the verb itself, which also makes the second argument, as: Socrates walks; or the substantive verb placed between two nominatives, as: Man is mortal.

units.la: Quid est Consequens?
units.tr: What is the consequent?

units.la: Consequens seu praedicatum, est vel verbum Nominativo attributum, vel descriptio sequens copulā.
units.tr: The consequent, or predicate, is either a verb attributed to the nominative, or a description following the copula.

units.la: Quomodo primò distribuitur Enunc- iatum?
units.tr: In what first way is a proposition divided?

units.la: In affirmatum aut negatum. Affirmatum est, cujus vinculum affirmatur: Negatum, cujus vinculum negatur.
units.tr: Into affirmative or negative. A proposition is affirmative when its link is affirmed, and negative when its link is denied.

units.la: Hinc nascitur axiomatum, id est, enunciatorum contradictio, quando Axioma seu Enunciatum ita affirmatur & negatur, ut alterum verum sit, alterum falsum: Si enim utrunq; verum est, contradictio nequaquam esse potest: ut, aliquis homo ambulat, aliquis homo non ambulat. Hic contradictio nulla est: quia simul vera esse possunt.
units.tr: From this arises the contradiction of axioms, that is, of propositions, when an axiom or proposition is affirmed and denied in such a way that one is true and the other false. For if both were true, there could by no means be a contradiction, as: some man walks; some man does not walk. Here there is no contradiction, because both can be true at the same time.

units.la: In his autem Enunciatis: Omnes peccaverunt: Nulli peccaverunt. Omnes homines sunt electi: Quidam homines non sunt electi. Quidam homines moriuntur: nulli homines moriuntur. tanta contradictio est, ut neDeus omnipotens quidem utramque partem simul veram efficiat: quia Deus est & dicitur omnipotens eò, quòd possit quæ vult, quæq; ejus veritati ac justitiæ non repugnant. Huic sententiæ suffragatur Dominus Philippus Melanchthon hisce verbis: pariter recipere contradictoria, est ordinem mentis divinæ turbare,& totam universitatem rerum confundere.
units.tr: But in these propositions: All have sinned; no one has sinned. All men are elect; some men are not elect. Some men die; no men die. The contradiction is so great that not even almighty God can make both parts true at once, because God is and is called almighty in that he can do what he wills, provided it does not conflict with his truth and justice. Philip Melanchthon supports this view in these words: to accept contradictories alike is to disturb the order of the divine mind and to confuse the whole universe of things.

units.la: Quomodo secundò distribuitur Enunc- iatum?
units.tr: In what second way is a proposition divided?

units.la: In verum aut falsum. Verum, quando pronuntiatur uti res est: ut, Dominus ex nihilo creavit terram. Falsum, quando pronuntiatur uti res non est: ut, Dominus ex atomis creavit terram.
units.tr: Into true and false. A proposition is true when it is stated as the thing is: as, The Lord created the earth out of nothing. It is false when it is stated as the thing is not: as, The Lord created the earth out of atoms.

units.la: Quomodo tertiò distribuitur Enunc- iatum?
units.tr: In what third way is a proposition divided?

units.la: In simplex aut compositum. Simplex seu categoricum quod verbi vinculo continetur: ut, ignis urit. ignis est calidus. Simplex Enunciatum est aut generale, aut particulare, aut proprium. Generale est quando generali Antecedenti Consequens attribuitur: ut, Omnes declinaverunt, simul inutiles facti sunt: non est qui faciat bonum, non est usque ad unum Rom.2. Particulare est quando particulari Antecedenti Consequens attribuitur: ut, quidam sunt electi. Proprium est quando proprio Antecedenti Consequens attribuitur: ut, Jesus est lachrymatus, Joh.11.
units.tr: Into simple and compound. A simple or categorical proposition is one contained by a verbal link, as: fire burns; fire is hot. A simple proposition is either general, particular, or singular. It is general when the consequent is attributed to a general antecedent, as: They have all gone astray, they have together become worthless; there is none who does good, no, not one (Rom.2.). It is particular when the consequent is attributed to a particular antecedent, as: some are elect. It is singular when the consequent is attributed to a singular antecedent, as: Jesus wept (Joh.11.).

units.la: Quid est Enunciatum Compositum?
units.tr: What is a compound proposition?

units.la: Quod conjunctionis vinculo continetur: Estq; aut Copulatum, Conditionale, Diversum, aut Adversum.
units.tr: One contained by a conjunction; and it is either copulative, conditional, diversative, or adversative.

units.la: Quid est Enunciatum Copulatum?
units.tr: What is a copulative proposition?

units.la: Cujus Conjunctio est Copulativa: ut, Tunc ergo apprehendit Pilatus Jesum, & flagellavit. Johan.19.
units.tr: One whose conjunction is copulative, as: Then Pilate took Jesus and scourged him (Johan.19.).

units.la: Quid est Enunciatum Conditionale?
units.tr: What is a conditional proposition?

units.la: Cujus Conjunctio est Conditionalis: ut, Si Pharao obtemperasset Moysi, non periisset.
units.tr: One whose conjunction is conditional, as: If Pharaoh had obeyed Moses, he would not have perished.

units.la: Quid est Diversum?
units.tr: What is a diversative proposition?

units.la: Cujus Conjunctio est Diversativa: ut, Nam etsi ambulavero in medio umbrae mortis, non timebo mala: quoniam tu mecum es, Psalm.22.
units.tr: One whose conjunction is diversative, as: Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me (Psalm.22.).

units.la: Quid est Adversum?
units.tr: What is an adversative proposition?

units.la: Cujus Conjunctio est Adversativa: ut, Nemo servus potest duobus Dominis servire : aut enim unum oderit,& alterum diliget : aut uni adhærebit,& alterum contemnet, Lucæ16.
units.tr: One whose conjunction is adversative, as: No servant can serve two masters; for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will cleave to the one and despise the other (Lucae 16.).

units.la: Quid sunt quinque Prædicabilia & decem Prædica- menta, quæ Dominus Philippus in pri- mo suæ Dialectices libro tradidit?
units.tr: What are the five predicables and the ten predicaments, which Master Philip handed down in the first book of his Dialectic?

units.la: Sunt Enunciata simplicia vel composita. Nam de individuo seu specie seu substantia enuntiantur seu prædicantur, aut Genus, aut Differentia, aut Proprium, aut Accidens, aut quantitas, aut qualitas, aut relatio, aut actio, aut passio, aut quando, aut ubi, aut situs, aut habitus, quæ omnia Enunciata efficiunt.
units.tr: They are simple or compound propositions. For they are predicated or stated of an individual, or of a species, or of a substance, either as genus, or difference, or property, or accident, or quantity, or quality, or relation, or action, or passion, or when, or where, or position, or habit; and all of these produce propositions.

units.la: Hactenus de Enunciatis dictum est.
units.tr: So far has been said about propositions.

units.la: Quid est Syllogismus?
units.tr: What is a syllogism?

units.la: SYllogismus, <bl>ein schlußrede</bl> / est dispositio trium Enunciatorum : quorum primum vocatur Propositio seu Major : secundum Assumptio seu Minor : tertium Complexio seu Conclusio.
units.tr: A syllogism (a conclusion-speech) is an arrangement of three statements. The first is called the Proposition or Major; the second, the Assumption or Minor; the third, the Complexion or Conclusion.

units.la: Quomodo est Syllogismus expedite conficiendus?
units.tr: How is a syllogism to be constructed conveniently?

units.la: Si homines de aliquo Enunciato dubitent: efficiatur Quæstio, ad cujus fidem tertio argumento opus est cum Quæstione collocato.
units.tr: If people doubt some statement, let it be made into a question, for whose proof a third argument is needed, placed alongside the question.

units.la: Argumentum autem dicitur tertium (vulgò me-dius terminus) quia in qualibet Quæstione seu enuntiato simplici duo sunt argumenta, ad quæ accedens probatio ex aliquo Inventionis loco deprompta, tertium argumentum constituit.
units.tr: The third argument is so called (commonly the middle term) because in any question, or simple statement, there are two arguments; a proof drawn from some place of invention, coming to them, constitutes the third argument.

units.la: Quæstio est an Jesus Nazarenus sit verus Messias?
units.tr: The question is: Is Jesus of Nazareth the true Messiah?

units.la: Christiani hoc affirmant : Judæi vero negant. Argumentum tertium ab Effectis: quia Iesus Nazarenus sua omnipotentia claudos, caecos & caeteros insanabiles morbos sanavit.
units.tr: Christians affirm this, but the Jews deny it. The third argument is from effects, because Jesus of Nazareth healed the lame, the blind and the other incurable diseases by his omnipotence.

units.la: Syllogismus hic est:
units.tr: This syllogism is:

units.la: Qui sua omnipotentia aeterna claudos, caecos & caeteros insanabiles morbos sanat: is est verus Messias.
units.tr: Whoever heals the lame, the blind and the other incurable diseases by his eternal omnipotence is the true Messiah.

units.la: Atqui id fecit Iesus Nazarenus.
units.tr: But Jesus of Nazareth did this.

units.la: Ergo Iesus Nazarenus est verus Messias.
units.tr: Therefore Jesus of Nazareth is the true Messiah.

units.la: Quot sunt Syllogismi affectiones?
units.tr: How many affections does a syllogism have?

units.la: Tres: Ellipsis, Redundantia, Inversio. Ellipsis, cum pars syllogismi deest, & dicitur Enthymema, <bl>ein vn-</bl> <bl>vollkommenes: schlußrede.</bl>
units.tr: Three: ellipsis, redundancy, inversion. Ellipsis, when a part of the syllogism is missing, and it is called an enthymeme (an imperfect conclusion-speech).

units.la: Redundantia, cum Propositioni vel Assumptioni subjicitur confirmatio, quae nuncupatur Prosyllogismus. Inversio, cum partium ordo confunditur ita ut primo loco apud Authores ponatur Conclusio, secundo Propositio, tertio Assumptio.
units.tr: Redundancy, when a confirmation is added to the proposition or the assumption, and this is called a prosyllogism. Inversion, when the order of the parts is confused, so that the conclusion is put first, the proposition second and the assumption third.

units.la: Quotuplex est Syllogismus?
units.tr: What kinds of syllogism are there?

units.la: Triplex: Simplex, Conditionalis aut Adversus.
units.tr: Three kinds: simple, conditional, or adversative.

units.la: Quid est Syllogismus Simplex?
units.tr: What is a simple syllogism?

units.la: Est, ubi pars Consequens Quaestionis disponitur cum argumento tertio in Propositione: pars Antecedens in Assumptione. Quando autem propositio vel assumptio est negata, tum Conclusio quoq; erit negata.
units.tr: It is one in which the consequent part of the question is placed with the third argument in the proposition, and the antecedent part in the assumption. When the proposition or the assumption is negated, the conclusion too will be negated.

units.la: Quot sunt figurae Syllogismi Simplicis?
units.tr: How many figures does the simple syllogism have?

units.la: Tres: Prima, secunda, tertia.
units.tr: Three: the first, the second, the third.

units.la: Quid est prima figura?
units.tr: What is the first figure?

units.la: Est, ubi argumentum tertium in propositione Quæstionis consequentem partem, in assumptione antecedentem partem semper antecedit. In prima Figura (quae Melanchthoni est tertia) possunt quidem esse octo modi, sed syllogismi omnibus partibus explicati apud Authores raro occurrunt.
units.tr: It is the figure in which the third argument always precedes the consequent part in the proposition of the question, and the antecedent part in the assumption. In the first figure (which is Melanchthon's third) there can indeed be eight moods, but syllogisms with all their parts spelled out rarely occur in the authors.

units.la: Quid est Syllogismus in Daraptipri- mo modo?
units.tr: What is the syllogism in the first mood, Darapti?

units.la: Cujus propositio & assumptio sunt affirmatæ ge-nerales: ut, Quædam confidentia est virtus.
units.tr: Its proposition and assumption are general affirmatives, as: Some confidence is a virtue.

units.la: Argumentum tertium: ut, Constantia.
units.tr: The third argument: as, steadfastness.

units.la: Syllogismus hic est:
units.tr: This syllogism is:

units.la: Constantia est virtus.
units.tr: Steadfastness is a virtue.

units.la: Constantia est confidentia.
units.tr: Steadfastness is a confidence.

units.la: Ergo quædam confidentia est virtus.
units.tr: Therefore some confidence is a virtue.

units.la: Quid est Syllogismus in Felapton secun- do modo?
units.tr: What is the syllogism in the second mood, Felapton?

units.la: Cujus propositio est generalis negata, & Assum-ptio generalis affirmata: ut Confidentia quædam non est virtus. Argumentum tertium: ut, Audacia.
units.tr: Its proposition is a general negative, and its assumption a general affirmative, as: Some confidence is not a virtue. The third argument: as, audacity.

units.la: Syllogismus hic est:
units.tr: This syllogism is:

units.la: Audacia non est virtus.
units.tr: Audacity is not a virtue.

units.la: Audacia est confidentia.
units.tr: Audacity is a confidence.

units.la: Ergo quædam confidentia non est virtus.
units.tr: Therefore some confidence is not a virtue.

units.la: Quid est Syllogismus in Disamis tertio modo?
units.tr: What is the syllogism in the third mood, Disamis?

units.la: Cujus propositio est affirmata specialis, & Assumptio affirmata generalis: ut, Quidam laudabilis est dives. Argumentum tertium: ut,quidam sapiens.
units.tr: Its proposition is a particular affirmative, and its assumption a general affirmative, as: Some praiseworthy person is rich. The third argument: as, some wise person.

units.la: Syllogismus hic est:
units.tr: This syllogism is:

units.la: Quidam sapiens est dives.
units.tr: Some wise person is rich.

units.la: Omnis sapiens est laudabilis.
units.tr: Every wise person is praiseworthy.

units.la: Ergo quidam laudabilis est dives.
units.tr: Therefore some praiseworthy person is rich.

units.la: Quid est Syllogismus in Datisi quar- to modo?
units.tr: What is the syllogism in the fourth mood, Datisi?

units.la: Cujus propositio est affirmata generalis, & assum-ptio affirmata specialis: ut, Quidam pauper est laudabilis. Argumentum tertium: ut,Sapiens. Syllogismus hic est:
units.tr: Its proposition is a general affirmative, and its assumption a particular affirmative, as: Some poor person is praiseworthy. The third argument: as, wise. This syllogism is:

units.la: Sapiens est laudabilis.
units.tr: The wise person is praiseworthy.

units.la: Quidam sapiens est pauper.
units.tr: Some wise person is poor.

units.la: Ergo quidam pauper est laudabilis.
units.tr: Therefore some poor person is praiseworthy.

units.la: Quid est Syllogismus in Bocardo quinto modo?
units.tr: What is the syllogism in the fifth mood, Bocardo?

units.la: Cujus propositio est negata specialis, & Assumptio affirmata generalis: ut, Quidam, qui norunt jus naturale non sunt boni. Argumentum tertium: ut, quidam docti.
units.tr: Its proposition is a particular negative, and its assumption a general affirmative, as: Some who know natural law are not good. The third argument: as, some learned people.

units.la: Syllogismus hic est:
units.tr: This syllogism is:

units.la: Quidam docti non sunt boni.
units.tr: Some learned people are not good.

units.la: Omnes docti norunt jus naturale.
units.tr: All learned people know natural law.

units.la: Ergo quidam, qui norunt jus naturale, non sunt boni.
units.tr: Therefore some who know natural law are not good.

units.la: Quid est Syllogismus in Ferison sexto modo?
units.tr: What is the syllogism in the sixth mood, Ferison?

units.la: Cujus propositio est negata generalis, & Assumptio affirmata specialis: ut, Quidam fortunatus non est beatus. Argumentum tertium: ut, Stultus.
units.tr: Its proposition is a general negative, and its assumption a particular affirmative, as: Some fortunate person is not blessed. The third argument: as, foolish.

units.la: Syllogismus hic est?
units.tr: This syllogism is?

units.la: Nullus stultus est beatus.
units.tr: No foolish person is blessed.

units.la: Quidam stultus est fortunatus.
units.tr: Some foolish person is fortunate.

units.la: Ergo quidam fortunatus non est beatus.
units.tr: Therefore some fortunate person is not blessed.

units.la: Quid est Syllogismus in septimo modo?
units.tr: What is the syllogism in the seventh mood?

units.la: Cujus propositio & Assumptio sunt affirmatae propriae: ut, Quidam discipuli defecerunt à Christo. Argumentum tertium: ut Judas & Petrus.
units.tr: Its proposition and assumption are affirmative singulars, as: Some disciples fell away from Christ. The third argument: as, Judas and Peter.

units.la: Syllogismus hic est.
units.tr: This syllogism is.

units.la: Judas & Petrus defecerunt à Christo.
units.tr: Judas and Peter fell away from Christ.

units.la: Judas & Petrus fuerunt discipuli Christi.
units.tr: Judas and Peter were disciples of Christ.

units.la: Ergo quidam discipuli defecerunt à Christo.
units.tr: Therefore some disciples fell away from Christ.

units.la: Quid est Syllogismus in octavo modo.
units.tr: What is the syllogism in the eighth mood?

units.la: Cujus propositio est negata propria, & Assumptio affirmata propria : ut, Quidam homo non est philosophus. Argumentum tertium: ut Therfites.
units.tr: Its proposition is a negative singular, and its assumption an affirmative singular, as: Some man is not a philosopher. The third argument: as Thersites.

units.la: Syllogismus hic est: Therfites non est philosophus. Therfites est homo. Ergo quidam homo non est philosophus.
units.tr: This syllogism is: Thersites is not a philosopher. Thersites is a man. Therefore some man is not a philosopher.

units.la: Quid est secunda Figura?
units.tr: What is the second figure?

units.la: EST, ubi argumentum tertium in Propositione Quaestionis consequente partem, in Assumptione antecedentem partem semper sequitur, & in Propositione, aut Assumptione negatur. Secunda Figura habet sex modos.
units.tr: It is the figure in which the middle term is the consequent part of the question in the major premise, always the antecedent part in the minor premise, and is negated in either the major or the minor premise. The second figure has six moods.

units.la: Quid est Syllogismus in Cesare pri- mo modo?
units.tr: What is the syllogism in the first mood of Cesare?

units.la: Cujus propositio est negata, & omnes partes sunt generales: ut, Fideles non damnabuntur. Argumentum tertium: quia esuriunt & sitiunt justitiam.
units.tr: Its major premise is negative and all its terms are general, for example: The faithful will not be damned. Middle term: because they hunger and thirst for righteousness.

units.la: Syllogismus hic est: Qui damnabūtur nō esuriunt, neqį sitiunt justitiā. At fideles esuriunt & sitiunt justitiam. Ergo fideles non damnabuntur.
units.tr: The syllogism is this: Those who will be damned do not hunger or thirst for righteousness. But the faithful hunger and thirst for righteousness. Therefore the faithful will not be damned.

units.la: Quid est Syllogismus in Camestres se- cundo modo?
units.tr: What is the syllogism in the second mood of Camestres?

units.la: Cujus propositio est tantùm affirmata, & omnes partes generales: ut, Veri Christiani dissolutè non vivunt. Argumentum tertium: quia non sunt infideles.
units.tr: Its major premise is only affirmative and all its terms are general, for example: True Christians do not live dissolutely. Middle term: because they are not unbelievers.

units.la: Syllogismus hic est: Dissolutè viventes, sunt infideles. At veri Christiani non sunt infideles. Ergo veri Christiani dissolutè non vivunt.
units.tr: The syllogism is this: Those who live dissolutely are unbelievers. But true Christians are not unbelievers. Therefore true Christians do not live dissolutely.

units.la: Quid est Syllogismus in Festino ter- tio modo?
units.tr: What is the syllogism in the third mood of Festino?
