units.tr: Moreover, if the lower digit exceeds the upper, put before the upper one carried in the mind, or one taken from the preceding number written above; and then subtract the lower.

units.la: Exemplum.
units.tr: Example.

units.la: Debeo tibi 7454, septies millenos quadringentos quinquaginta quatuor Thaleros : Et solvi 6545, sexies millenos quingentos quadraginta quinq;.
units.tr: I owe you 7454 Thalers, seven thousand four hundred and fifty-four; and I have paid 6545, six thousand five hundred and forty-five.

units.la: Quæritur quot tibi sint solvendi?
units.tr: The question is how many remain for you to be paid?

units.la: Scribo numerum directè sub numero: 7 4 5 4 6 5 4 5
units.tr: I write the number directly beneath the number: 7 4 5 4 / 6 5 4 5

units.la: Et dico 6 à 7 remanet unum, quod sequenti subtrahendæ notæ, à qua inferior subtrahi nequit, prepono, & pergo dicens: 5 à 14 remanent 9, quae supra scribo, 4 à 5 remanet unum, quod sequenti notae praepono, & pergo dicens, 5 à 14 remanent 9, quae supra scribo. Subductio sic est: 1 9 1 9 7 ·4 5 ·4 6 5 4 5
units.tr: And I say: 6 from 7 leaves 1, which I place before the next digit to be subtracted, from which the lower cannot be subtracted; and I go on saying: 5 from 14 leaves 9, which I write above; 4 from 5 leaves 1, which I place before the next digit, and I go on saying: 5 from 14 leaves 9, which I write above. The subtraction goes thus: 1 9 1 9 / 7 4 5 4 / 6 5 4 5

units.la: Aliud exemplum.
units.tr: Another example.

units.la: Mutuavi tibi 3634, ter millenos sexcentos triginta quatuor aureos: Et tu solvisti 2600, bis millenos sexcentos. Quaeritur quot mihi solvere debeas?
units.tr: I lent you 3634, three thousand six hundred and thirty-four gold coins; and you paid 2600, two thousand six hundred. The question is how many you owe me to pay?

units.la: Scribo numerum directè sub numero: 3634 2600
units.tr: I write the number directly beneath the number: 3634 / 2600

units.la: Et dico 2 à 3 remanet 1, quod supra scribo: 6 à 6, remanet o, quam supra scribo: o à 3 remanent 3, quae supra noto: o à 4 remanent 4, quae supra scribo. Subductio sic est: 1 o 3 4 3 6 3 4 2 6 o o
units.tr: And I say: 2 from 3 leaves 1, which I write above; 6 from 6 leaves 0, which I write above; 0 from 3 leaves 3, which I mark above; 0 from 4 leaves 4, which I write above. The subtraction goes thus: 1 0 3 4 / 3 6 3 4 / 2 6 0 0

units.la: Aliud Exemplum.
units.tr: Another example.

units.la: Mercatoris famulus accepit primū Thaleros 1029: Deinde 2101. Iterum 7068.
units.tr: A merchant's servant first received 1029 Thalers; then 2101; again 7068.

units.la: Exposuit verò prima vice 917: secunda 809: Tertia 8048.
units.tr: Indeed, he paid out the first time 917; the second time 809; the third time 8048.

units.la: Quæritur quot Thaleros retinuerit? primùm per Additionem numero, quot acceperit, hoc modo: 1029 2101 7968 11098
units.tr: The question is how many Thalers he has kept back? First, by addition, the sum of what he received, in this way: 1029 / 2101 / 7968 / 11098

units.la: Deinde, quot exposuerit, hoc modo: 917 809 8048 9774
units.tr: Then, what he paid out, in this way: 917 / 809 / 8048 / 9774

units.la: Iam majorem numerum primùm scribo: deinde minorem directè subnoto: 11098 9774
units.tr: Now I write the larger number first, then directly beneath it I set the smaller: 11098 / 9774

units.la: Et dico 9 ab 11 remanent 2, sed 1 suprà noto, & 1 sequenti notę, à qua inferior subtrahi nequit, præpono, & pergo dicens: 7 à 10 remanent 3: 7 à 9 remanent 2: 4 ab 8, remanent 4.
units.tr: And I say: 9 from 11 leaves 2, but I mark 1 above, and place before the next digit, from which the lower cannot be subtracted, a 1; and I go on saying: 7 from 10 leaves 3; 7 from 9 leaves 2; 4 from 8 leaves 4.

units.la: Subductio sic est: 1324 11098 9774
units.tr: The subtraction goes thus: 1 3 2 4 / 11098 / 9774

units.la: Aliud Exemplum.
units.tr: Another Example.

units.la: Quispiam natus est Anno Christi 1562. Nunc autem annus est Christi 1588. Quæritur quot annos natus sit?
units.tr: Someone was born in the year of Christ 1562, and now it is the year of Christ 1588. How old is he?

units.la: Scribo primùm numerum majorem: deinde directè minorem subnoto: 1588 1562
units.tr: I write the larger number first, then directly beneath it the smaller: 1588 1562

units.la: Et dico 1 ab 1 remanet nihil: 5 à 5 remanet nihil: 6 ab 8 remanent 2, quæ supra noto: 2 ab 8 remanent 6, quæ supra scribo.
units.tr: I say: 1 from 1 leaves nothing; 5 from 5 leaves nothing; 6 from 8 leaves 2, which I note above; 2 from 8 leaves 6, which I write above.

units.la: Inductio sic est: 2 6 1588 1562
units.tr: The setting out is thus: 2 6 1588 1562

units.la: Probatio Subductionis.
units.tr: Proof of Subtraction.

units.la: Si autem scire cupio an rectè subduxerim: addo inferiorem numerum superiori: Et si tum medius numerus redierit, rectè subductum est: ut, 9 9 7* 4 5* 4 6 5 4 5 7 4 5 4
units.tr: If, however, I wish to know whether I have subtracted correctly, I add the lower number to the upper. If the middle number then comes back, the subtraction has been done correctly, as in: 9 9 7* 4 5* 4 6 5 4 5 7 4 5 4

units.la: Quid est Multiplicatio?
units.tr: What is Multiplication?

units.la: Multiplicatio est numeratio, qua numerus augmentatur per numerum, & habetur Factus.
units.tr: Multiplication is a counting by which a number is increased by another number, and a product is obtained.

units.la: Multiplicatio initium sumit à dextra versus sinistram.
units.tr: Multiplication begins at the right and proceeds toward the left.

units.la: Porrò ad unguem te scire oportet multiplicationem Digitorum: Eamque ex subjecta tabula facilè discere poteris.
units.tr: Furthermore, you must know the multiplication of the digits perfectly, and you can learn it easily from the table below.

units.la: Dicimus autem: bis bina sunt quatuor: bis terna sunt sex: Et contrà, Ter bina sunt sex. Bis quaterna sunt octo: Et contrà, Quater bina sunt octo: Bis quina sunt decem: Et contrà, Quinquies bina sunt decem, &c. 2 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 4 6 8 10 12 14 16 18 3 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 9 12 15 18 21 24 27 4 4 5 6 7 8 9 16 20 24 28 32 36 5 5 6 7 8 9 25 30 35 40 45 6 6 7 8 9 36 42 48 54 7 7 8 9 49 56 63 8 8 9 64 72 9 9 81
units.tr: We say: twice two are four; twice three are six. And conversely, three times two are six. Twice four are eight; and conversely, four times two are eight. Twice five are ten; and conversely, five times two are ten, and so on. 2 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 4 6 8 10 12 14 16 18 3 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 9 12 15 18 21 24 27 4 4 5 6 7 8 9 16 20 24 28 32 36 5 5 6 7 8 9 25 30 35 40 45 6 6 7 8 9 36 42 48 54 7 7 8 9 49 56 63 8 8 9 64 72 9 9 81

units.la: Ex hac tabula discere quoque possunt adolescentes quoties numerus in numero contineatur: ut, Novem in octoginta uno continentur Novies: Et Novies Novena sunt 81. 9 autem in 80 continentur 8: Et octies 9 sunt 72: Et 9 in 72 continentur 8: Et octies 9 sunt 72.
units.tr: From this table young people can also learn how often one number is contained in another. For example, nine is contained in eighty-one nine times, and nine times nine are 81. Nine is contained in eighty eight times, and eight times nine are 72. Nine is contained in 72 eight times, and eight times nine are 72.

units.la: Exemplum in quo fit Multiplicatio per unum Characterem.
units.tr: Example of Multiplication by One Character.

units.la: Emit quis 89 ulnas panni, & ulnam aureis 2. Quæritur quot sint numerandi aurei?
units.tr: Someone buys 89 ells of cloth at 2 gold coins an ell. How many gold coins are to be counted?

units.la: Colloco sic: 8 9 / 2
units.tr: I set it out thus: 8 9 / 2

units.la: Et dico bis 9 sunt 18: scribo 8 sub 2, retinens mente 1. Et progredior dicens: bis 8 sunt 16, quæ, addito 1 reservato, efficiunt 17, hæc integrè scribo, hoc modo: 8 9 Multiplicandus.
units.tr: And I say twice 9 is 18: I write 8 under the 2, keeping 1 in mind. And I proceed, saying: twice 8 is 16, which, with the 1 carried over added, makes 17; these I write out in full, in this way: 8 9 Multiplicand.

units.la: 2 Multiplicator. 1 7 8 Multiplicatus.
units.tr: 2 Multiplier. 1 7 8 Multiplied.

units.la: Aliud exemplum in quo multiplicatio fit per duos Characteres.
units.tr: Another example in which multiplication is done by two characters.

units.la: Anni dies sunt 365. Quæritur quot sint anni horæ? Colloco sic:
units.tr: A year has 365 days. How many hours are in the year? I set it out thus:

units.la: Et dico quater quina sunt 20: scribo o sub 4, & 2 mente reservo: Et dico quater 6 sunt 24, additis 2 reservatis, sunt 26, scribo 6, & 2 reservo: pergo inquiens: Ter 4 sunt 12, additis 2 reservatis, sunt 14, quæ integrè scribo.
units.tr: I say: four times five are 20; I write 0 under the 4 and keep 2 in mind. I say: four times 6 are 24; with the 2 kept added, they are 26. I write 6 and keep 2. I go on saying: three times 4 are 12; with the 2 kept added, they are 14, which I write in full.

units.la: Deinde ad proximum multiplicatorem accedo inquiens: bis 5 sunt 10, scribo o directè sub nota secunda, 1 servato: pergo dicens: bis 6 sunt 12, 1 addito sunt 13, & scribo 3 retinens 1: ac progredior inquiens: bis 3 sunt 6, addito 1 servato, sunt 7. Quibus omnibus conjunctis per additionem, prodeūt[?] horæ anni 8760, hoc modo: 365 Dies anni. 24 Horæ diei. 1460 730 8760 Horæ anni.
units.tr: Then I come to the next multiplier, saying: twice 5 are 10; I write 0 directly under the second figure, keeping 1. I go on saying: twice 6 are 12; with the 1 added it is 13, and I write 3, keeping 1. I proceed saying: twice 3 are 6; with the 1 kept added it is 7. When all these are joined together by addition, the hours of the year come to 8760, thus: 365 days of the year. 24 hours of the day. 1460 730 8760 hours of the year.

units.la: Aliud Exemplum.
units.tr: Another Example.

units.la: A Christo nato sunt anni 1588. Quæritur quot sint septimanæ? Colloco sic: 1588 52 3176 7940 82576
units.tr: Years since the birth of Christ are 1588. How many weeks are there? I set it out thus: 1588 52 3176 7940 82576

units.la: A Christo nato sunt septimanæ octuagies bis millenæ quingentæ septuaginta sex. Quæritur quot sint dies? Colloco sic: 82576 82576 7 578032
units.tr: Weeks since the birth of Christ are eighty-two thousand five hundred seventy-six. How many days are there? I set it out thus: 82576 82576 7 578032

units.la: A Christo nato sunt dies quingenties septuagies octies millenæ triginta duo.
units.tr: Days since the birth of Christ are five hundred seventy-eight thousand and thirty-two.

units.la: Quæritur quot sint horæ?
units.tr: How many hours are there?

units.la: A Christo nato sunt horæ tredecies millenæ, millenæ, octingenties septuagies bis millenæ, septingentæ sexaginta octo.
units.tr: Hours since the birth of Christ are thirteen million, eight hundred seventy-two thousand, seven hundred sixty-eight.

units.la: Observatio.
units.tr: Observation.

units.la: Quando multiplicator est articulus, o non ponitur sub prima nota, sed digitus, & semel tantum dicitur o est o: deinde digitus multiplicatur, hoc modo: 13872768 60 832366080
units.tr: When the multiplier is a zero, the 0 is not placed under the first figure but the digit, and it is said only once, "0 times is 0"; then the digit is multiplied, thus: 13872768 60 832366080

units.la: Probatio multiplicationis.
units.tr: Proof of multiplication.

units.la: Si autem scire cupio an recte multiplicaverim: abjicio 9 a multiplicando, quoties potero, quicquid novenario minus remanserit, scribo ad dextrum latus X, & cum multiplicatore ad sinistrum latus posito, multiplico, ac supra X noto. Deinde abjicio novem a multiplicato, & si hoc residuum cum superiori numero supra X posito convenit, vera est multiplicatio: ut, 8 9 | 2 | 1 7 8
units.tr: If, however, I wish to know whether I have multiplied correctly, I cast 9 out of the multiplicand as often as I can, and write the remainder, whatever is left after the nines, at the right side of an X. With the multiplier placed on the left side, I multiply and note the result above the X. Then I cast nines out of the product. If this remainder agrees with the number written above the X, the multiplication is correct, as in: 8 9 | 2 | 1 7 8

units.la: Hic abjicio, & ad dextrum latus X 8 noto, multiplicatorem ad sinistrum collocas, & dico: bis 8 sunt 16, unum & 6 sunt 7, quae supra scribo.
units.tr: Here I cast out, and note 8 at the right side of the X. I place the multiplier on the left and say: twice 8 is 16, and 1 and 6 make 7, which I write above.

units.la: Deinde abjicio 9 a multiplicato, & remanent 7, quae infra noto.
units.tr: Then I cast 9 out of the product, and 7 remains, which I note below.

units.la: Probatio Multiplicationis fit etiam per Divisionem.
units.tr: Proof of multiplication is also made by division.

units.la: Multiplicatum per multiplicatorem divido: Et si in semicirculo redierit multiplicandus, bene numeratum est. * | * 7 8 (89 | * * | * 6 8 | *
units.tr: I divide the product by the multiplier. If the multiplicand comes back in the semicircle, the calculation is correct. * | * 7 8 (89 | * * | * 6 8 | *

units.la: Quid est Divisio.
units.tr: What division is.

units.la: Divisio est numeratio, qua numerus dividitur per nūmerum[?], & habetur Quotus.
units.tr: Division is a calculation by which a number is divided by a number, and the quotient is obtained.

units.la: Sumit autem Divisio à sinistra initium. Numerus qui dividitur dicitur Dividendus,is qui dividit, dicitur Divisor, Tertius q[?] ex Divisione provenit, dicitur Quoriens seu Quotus, & scribitur versus dextrâ post semicirculum.
units.tr: Division begins from the left. The number that is divided is called the dividend; that which divides is called the divisor; the third number, which comes from the division, is called the quotient or quotient figure, and it is written to the right, after the semicircle.

units.la: Quando Divisor Dividendo par est vel minor, ponitur primus sub primum, secundus sub secundum, & sic deinceps, à sinistra progrediendo ad dextram, hoc modo: 8 6 2 8 | 8 6 2 8 8 6 | 2 6
units.tr: When the divisor is equal to or smaller than the dividend, the first figure is placed under the first, the second under the second, and so on, proceeding from left to right, as here: 8 6 2 8 | 8 6 2 8 8 6 | 2 6

units.la: Cùm autem Divisor major est Dividendo, tum promovetur, hoc modo: 8 6 2 8 9 2
units.tr: When, however, the divisor is larger than the dividend, it is moved along, as here: 8 6 2 8 9 2

units.la: Si Divisor habet unam vel plures nullas eæ versus dextram in fine sub Dividendo ponuntur: Et quicquid supra o fuerit, est residuum, hoc modo: + 7 | (4 3 | (17 [?] + + | 0 0 7
units.tr: If the divisor has one or more noughts, these are placed at the right end under the dividend. Whatever remains above the nought is the remainder, as here: + 7 | (4 3 | (17 [?] + + | 0 0 7

units.la: Exemplum cum uno Divisore.
units.tr: Example with one divisor.

units.la: Tres mercatores lucrati sunt 5 4 3 1 2 Thaleros : Quæritur quot ex his quisq; accipiat? Colloco sic:
units.tr: Three merchants have won 54312 thalers. The question is how much each of them receives. I set it out thus:

units.la: Et dico tria continentur in 5 semel : noto 1 in semicirculo, inquiens : semel 3 sunt 3, quæ subtraho à 5 & remanent 2, quæ supra scribo.
units.tr: I say: 3 goes into 5 once. I write 1 in the semicircle, saying: once 3 is 3, which I subtract from 5, and 2 remains, which I write above.

units.la: Deinde transfero Divisorem sub 4, dicens: 3 in 24 continentur 8, & 8 in semicirculo noto, inquiens, ter 8 sunt 24, quæ subscripta subtraho, remanet nihil.
units.tr: Then I move the divisor under the 4, saying: 3 goes into 24 eight times, and I note 8 in the semicircle, saying: three times 8 is 24, which I write underneath and subtract. Nothing remains.

units.la: Tertiò transfero Divisorem sub 3, dicens: 3 in 3 continentur 1: scribo 1 in semicirculo, inquiens: semel 3 sunt 3, quæ subtraho & remanet nihil.
units.tr: Thirdly, I move the divisor under the 3, saying: 3 goes into 3 once. I write 1 in the semicircle, saying: once 3 is 3, which I subtract, and nothing remains.

units.la: Quartò transfero Divisorem sub 1, & dico: 3 in 1 non continentur: scribo igitur o in semicirculo, inquiens, ter o est o, quam subtraho ab 1 & remanet 1.
units.tr: Fourthly, I move the divisor under the 1, and I say: 3 does not go into 1. I therefore write 0 in the semicircle, saying: three times 0 is 0, which I subtract from 1, and 1 remains.

units.la: Quintò transfero Divisorem, & dico 3 in 12 continentur 4, 4 in semicirculo noto, dicens: ter 4 sunt 12, quæ subtraho remanet nihil, hoc modo: 5 4 3 [?] [?] (18104 3 3 3 3 3 3 4 3 [?] [?] [?] [?]
units.tr: Fifthly, I move the divisor, and I say: 3 goes into 12 four times. I note 4 in the semicircle, saying: three times 4 is 12, which I subtract, and nothing remains. Thus: 5 4 3 [?] [?] (18104 3 3 3 3 3 3 4 3 [?] [?] [?] [?]

units.la: Aliud exemplum cum Duobus Diuisoribus.
units.tr: Another example with two divisors.

units.la: Duodecim mercatores lucrati sunt 5643 aureos. Quaeritur quot ex hisce quisque accipiat? Colloco sic:
units.tr: Twelve merchants have won 5643 gold coins. The question is how many each of them receives. I set it out thus:

units.la: Et dico 1 in 5 habeo 4 : possem quidem habere 5, sed tum inferior numerus major foret numero supra directe posito. Nunquā autem inferior numerus productus debet esse major numero supra directe posito.
units.tr: And I say: 1 into 5, I have 4. I could indeed have 5, but then the lower product would be larger than the number directly written above. A lower product, however, must never be larger than the number directly written above it.

units.la: 4. igitur in semicirculo noto, dicens: bis 4 sunt 8, quae sub dextro Diuisore noto, & pergo dicens: semel 4 sunt 4, quae sub finistro Diuisore noto, & subtraho 4 à 5, & remanet 1, quod notae sequenti subtrahendae praepono, dicens, 8 à 16 remanent 8.
units.tr: I therefore note 4 in the semicircle, saying: twice 4 is 8, which I write under the right divisor, and I go on, saying: once 4 is 4, which I write under the left divisor, and I subtract 4 from 5, and 1 remains, which I place before the next figure to be subtracted, saying: 8 from 16 leaves 8.

units.la: Deinde transfero 2 sub 4, & 1 sub 8, dicens: 1 in 8 continetur 7 : scribo 7 in semicirculo, dicens: bis 7 sunt 14, & subnoto 4, 1 reservo, ac dico, semel 7 sunt 7, addito 1 servato sunt 8, & subtraho 8 ab 8, remanet nihil, à 4 remanet nihil.
units.tr: Then I move 2 under 4 and 1 under 8, saying: 1 into 8 goes 7. I write 7 in the semicircle, saying: twice 7 is 14, and I write 4 underneath and carry 1. And I say: once 7 is 7, plus the carried 1 makes 8, and I subtract 8 from 8, nothing remains; from 4, nothing remains.

units.la: Tertiò transfero 2 sub 3 & 1 sub 4 dicens: 12 in 3 non continentur : scribo igitur o in semicirculo, inquiens: bis o est o, semel o est o, quibus deletis, remanent 3, quae inclu-do semicirculo, hoc modo: ꝇ (3 ꝭ ꝺ 6 ɺ 4 ꝭ (470 ꝭ ꝭ ꝭ ꝭ ɺ ꝭ ɺ ꝺ ꝭ ꝭ ꝇ ꝺ
units.tr: Thirdly, I move 2 under 3 and 1 under 4, saying: 12 does not go into 3. I therefore write 0 in the semicircle, saying: twice 0 is 0, once 0 is 0. When these are cancelled, 3 remains, which I enclose in the semicircle, as here: ꝇ (3 ꝭ ꝺ 6 ɺ 4 ꝭ (470 ꝭ ꝭ ꝭ ꝭ ɺ ꝭ ɺ ꝺ ꝭ ꝭ ꝇ ꝺ

units.la: Aliud Exemplum.
units.tr: Another example.

units.la: Quidam scire cupit quot Thaleros faciant albi 3 6 4. Thalerus Marpurgensis valet albis triginta uno. Colloco sic: 3 6 4 ( 3 ı
units.tr: Someone wishes to know how many thalers make 364 albi. A Marburg thaler is worth thirty-one albi. I set it out thus: 3 6 4 ( 3 ı

units.la: Et dico 3 in 3 continetur semel, & unum in semicirculo noto. Per ı autem nō multiplico, sed statim subtraho, inquiens, 3 à 3 remanet nihil, ı à 6 remanent 5, quæ suprà noto. Deinde transfero Divisores, dicens: 3 in 5 continenturı, & ı in semicirculo noto: ac omissa multiplicatione, statim subtraho 3 à 5 remanent 2, ı à 4 remanent 3. Albi igitur 3 6 4 faciunt ıı Thaleros, & viginti tres albos. ꝇ 6 4 (ıı 3 ꝭ ꝭ 3
units.tr: And I say: 3 goes into 3 once, and I note 1 in the semicircle. I do not multiply by 1, but at once subtract, saying: 3 from 3 leaves nothing; 1 from 6 leaves 5, which I note above. Then I move the divisors, saying: 3 goes into 5, and 1 into the semicircle I note. Omitting the multiplication, I subtract at once: 3 from 5 leaves 2, and 1 from 4 leaves 3. So 364 albi make 11 thalers and 23 albi. ꝇ 6 4 (ıı 3 ꝭ ꝭ 3

units.la: Probatio Divisionis.
units.tr: Proof of Division.

units.la: Si autem scire cupio an recte primum exemplum diviserim, abjicio 9 a quoto in semicirculo, & 5 remanent, quae ad dextrum latus literæ X colloco, & Divisorem, nempe 3 ad sinistrum latus scribo, dices: Ter 5. sunt 15, 5 & 1 sunt 6, q; supra X noto. Deinde abjicio 9 a Dividendo, & remanent 6, q; sub X noto. [Division proof diagram: the cross-multiplication scheme of the first example, with the numbers (18104 and the quotient 3, 6, 5, 6 arranged around an X-shaped cross]
units.tr: If, however, I want to know whether I have divided the first example correctly, I cast 9 out of the quotient in the semicircle, and 5 remains. I write this to the right of the letter X, and I write the divisor, namely 3, to the left, and I say: three times 5 are 15; 5 and 1 are 6, which I note above the X. Then I cast 9 out of the dividend, and 6 remains, which I note below the X. [Diagram of the division proof: the cross-multiplication scheme of the first example, with the numbers 18104 and the quotient 3, 6, 5, 6 arranged around an X-shaped cross]

units.la: Probatio Divisionis fit vere per mul- tiplicationem.
units.tr: The proof of division is truly made by multiplication.

units.la: Quotum per Divisore multiplico. Quod vero in Divisione remansit, id directè subnoto à dextra versus sinistram procedens. Deinde per additionem numeros colligo: Et si tum Dividendus producitur, semper bene numeratum est. Examen primi exempli. 1 8 1 0 4 3 5 4 3 1 2 Examen secundi exempli. 4 7 0 1 2 9 4 0 4 7 0 (3 5 6 4 3
units.tr: I multiply the quotient by the divisor. What remained in the division I write down directly beneath, proceeding from right to left. Then I gather the numbers by addition. If the dividend is thereby reproduced, the calculation has always been done correctly. Check of the first example: 1 8 1 0 4 3 5 4 3 1 2. Check of the second example: 4 7 0 1 2 9 4 0 4 7 0 (3 5 6 4 3.

units.la: Hastenus quatuor numerationis species fuere traditæ: sequitur Aurea Regula.
units.tr: So far the four species of numeration have been set out; there follows the Golden Rule.

units.la: Quid est Aurea Regula?
units.tr: What is the Golden Rule?

units.la: EST, qua ex trib. oblatis numeris, quartus producitur. Vulgò vocatur Regula Detri, seu Mercatorum.
units.tr: It is that by which a fourth number is produced from three given numbers. It is commonly called the Rule of Three, or the Merchants' Rule.

units.la: Numerus primæ positionis notetur primo loco à sinistra progrediedo versus dextram, numerus secundæ positionis, secundo loco, numerus Quæstionis tertio ponatur loco. Primus autem numerus re & nomine cū tertio convenire debet, hoc est, si alter continet aureos, alter similiter continebit aureos.Si alter albos,dies,hebdomadas,menses,annos,&c. Alter eandē rem continebit.
units.tr: The number of the first position is written in the first place, reading from left to right; the number of the second position is written in the second place; the number of the question is placed in the third place. The first number must agree with the third in kind and name: that is, if one contains gold coins, the other will likewise contain gold coins; if one contains white coins, days, weeks, months, years, etc., the other will contain the same thing.

units.la: Si igitur in primo forte loco fuerint aurei : in tertio verò albi, erunt aurei similiter in albos resolvendi. Et sic de aliis. Secundus autem numerus est cum tertio multiplicandus.
units.tr: Therefore, if by chance there are gold coins in the first place but white coins in the third, the gold coins must likewise be resolved into white coins. And so with other cases. The second number is then to be multiplied by the third.

units.la: Productus numerus est per primum dividendus, & Quotus quaesitum numerum indicabit.
units.tr: The product is to be divided by the first number, and the quotient will show the number sought.

units.la: Exemplum.
units.tr: Example.

units.la: Emuntur 2 libræ Cerae 10 albis.
units.tr: 2 pounds of wax are bought for 10 white coins.

units.la: Quaeritur quot albis emantur 100 libræ?
units.tr: It is asked how many white coins 100 pounds will be bought for?

units.la: Colloco sic: lib. alb. lib. 2 — 10 — 100 10
units.tr: I arrange it thus: pounds, white coins; pounds 2 — 10 — 100 — 10.

units.la: Hic numerum Quaestionis per medium multiplico,dicens: o est o, semel o est o, semel o est o,1 est 1.
units.tr: Here I multiply the number of the question by the middle number, saying: 0 times 0 is 0; once 0 is 0; once 0 is 0; 1 times 1 is 1.

units.la: Iam productū ex multiplicatione divido per primum numerū, nempe 2, hoc modo: 1 0 0 0 ( 2 Duo in io continentur 5, & 5 in femicirculo noto,& dico:bis 5 sunt io,quæ subscripta subtraho. remanet nihil.
units.tr: Now I divide the product of the multiplication by the first number, namely 2, in this way: 1 0 0 0 ( 2. Two goes into 10 five times, and 5 I write in the semicircle, and I say: twice 5 is 10, which I write below and subtract. Nothing remains.

units.la: Promoveo Divisorem, inquiens: 2 in o non continentur: scribo o in femicirculo, ac subtraho 2 à o, & remanet nihil.
units.tr: I move the divisor along, saying: 2 does not go into 0; I write 0 in the semicircle, and I subtract 2 from 0, and nothing remains.

units.la: Transfero Divisorem, dicens:2 in o non continentur: scribo o in semicirculo, & subtraho 2 à o & remanet nihil. Centum ergo libræ emuntur 500 albis. ⊥ ·o· ·o· ·o· (500 [?] ⊥ ⊥ ⊥ [?] ⊥ ·o· [?]
units.tr: I move the divisor across, saying: 2 does not go into 0; I write 0 in the semicircle, and I subtract 2 from 0, and nothing remains. Therefore 100 pounds are bought for 500 white coins. [Division notation diagram: 500 with zeros and question marks]

units.la: Nunc albi in aureos sunt ducendi per duos Divisores, nempe 26 hoc modo: 5 o o ( 2 6
units.tr: Now the white coins are to be converted into gold coins by the two divisors, namely 26, in this way: 5 0 0 ( 2 6.

units.la: Duo in 5 continentur 1, noto 1 in semicirculo, & subtraho 2 à 5 & remanent 3, 2 scribo, unum sequenti notæ præpono, dicens,6 à 10,remanent 4, quæ supra noto.
units.tr: Two goes into 5 once; I write 1 in the semicircle and subtract 2 from 5, and 3 remains. I write 2, and I put the one before the next figure, saying: 6 from 10 leaves 4, which I note above.

units.la: Transfero Divisores, dicens 2 in 24 continentur 9,& 9 in semicirculo noto,dicens, Sexies 9 sunt 54. subnoto 4,& 5 retineo,ac pergo inquiens,bis 9 sunt 18, additis 5, sunt 23,quę subscripta subtraho,& 2 à 2 remanet nihil, 3 à 4 remanet 1, quod sequenti notæ præpono, inquiens, 4 à 10 remanent 6, quæ includo semicirculo, hoc modo: ♃ 4 (6 ♆ ·o· ·o· (19 ♃ ♄ ♄ ♃ 4 ♃ 3
units.tr: I move the divisors along, saying: 2 goes into 24 nine times, and I write 9 in the semicircle, saying: six times 9 is 54. I write down 4 and keep 5, and I proceed, saying: twice 9 is 18, and adding 5 makes 23, which I write below and subtract; 2 from 2 leaves nothing, 3 from 4 leaves 1, which I put before the next figure, saying: 4 from 10 leaves 6, which I enclose in the semicircle, thus: ♃ 4 (6 ♆ ·o· ·o· (19 ♃ ♄ ♄ ♃ 4 ♃ 3.

units.la: Centum igitur libræ ceræ emuntur 19 aureis, & 6 albis.
units.tr: Therefore 100 pounds of wax are bought for 19 gold coins and 6 white coins.

units.la: Probatio Aureæ Regulæ fit per inversionem.
units.tr: The proof of the Golden Rule is made by inversion.

units.la: Colloco tertium numerum primo loco, ac numerum Regula Detri inventum, medio, & primum numerum loco tertio: Et si per operationem Regulæ, numerus in medio supra locatus redierit, bene operatus sum. lib. aurei alb. lib. 100 ——— 19 ——— 6 ——— 2
units.tr: I place the third number first, the number found by the Rule of Three in the middle, and the first number in the third place. If, by the working of the Rule, the number placed above in the middle has come back, I have worked correctly. lib. aurei alb. lib. 100 ——— 19 ——— 6 ——— 2

units.la: Hic aureos in medio positos duco in albos per 26, inquiens: sexies 9 sunt 54, 4 subnoto, & ƒ mente reservo, ac pergo dicens: semel 6 sunt 6, quibus addo 5, & sunt 11, quæ subscribo.
units.tr: Here I multiply the gold coins placed in the middle by 26 into the white ones, saying: six times 9 is 54. I write down 4 and keep 5 in mind, and go on saying: once 6 is 6, to which I add 5, making 11, which I write under.

units.la: Deinde dico bis novena sunt 18, 8 scribo, 1 mente reservo, ac progredior dicens: semel 2 sunt 2, quibus addo 1, & sunt 3. Nunc producto subjicio 6 supra in medio positra, dicens: 6 & 4 sunt 10, subnoto o, servans 1.
units.tr: Then I say: twice 9 is 18. I write 8 and keep 1 in mind, and I proceed, saying: once 2 is 2, to which I add 1, making 3. Now I place 6 under the number above in the middle, saying: 6 and 4 make 10. I write under it 0, keeping 1.

units.la: 1 & 8 sunt 9, addito 1, sunt 10, scribo 0, seruans 1, quod tribus addo, & sunt 4, addito 1 sunt 5, quæ subscribo. Iam productum multiplico per 2 supra in fine posita, hoc modo: bis 0 est 0, quam subscribo, ac iterum, bis 0, est 0, quam subnoto, bis 5 sunt 10, quæ subscribo. lib. aurei alb. lib. 100 — 19 — 6 — 2 26 1 1 4 3 8(6 500 2 1000
units.tr: 1 and 8 make 9, adding 1 makes 10. I write 0, keeping 1, which I add to three, making 4, and adding 1 makes 5, which I write under. Now I multiply the product by 2 placed at the end, in this way: twice 0 is 0, which I write under; and again twice 0 is 0, which I write under; twice 5 is 10, which I write under. lib. aurei alb. lib. 100 — 19 — 6 — 2 26 1 1 4 3 8(6 500 2 1000

units.la: Postremò numerum productum divido per primum numerum supra positum, nempe per 100, inquiens: 1 in 1 continetur 1, & noto 1 in semicirculo, ac omissa multiplicatione, subtraho 1 ab 1, remanet nihil. Promoveo Divisorem, dicens: 1 in 0 non continetur, scribo 0 in semicirculo, deinde subtraho, remanet nihil, ac pergo dicens: 0 à 0 remanet nihil: ac iterum 0 à 0 remanet nihil. Iam in semicirculo sunt 10, quæ supra in medio loco fuerunt. Vera igitur est operatio. ⊹ ⊖ ⊖ ⊖ (10 [?] ⊹ ⊹ ⊖ ⊖ [?]
units.tr: Finally I divide the product by the first number placed above, namely by 100, saying: 1 in 1 goes 1; I mark 1 in the semicircle, and, omitting the multiplication, I subtract 1 from 1, and nothing remains. I move the divisor along, saying: 1 in 0 does not go; I write 0 in the semicircle, then I subtract, and nothing remains. I go on saying: 0 from 0 leaves nothing, and again 0 from 0 leaves nothing. Now in the semicircle there are 10, which were in the middle place above. The operation is therefore true. ⊹ ⊖ ⊖ ⊖ (10 [?] ⊹ ⊹ ⊖ ⊖ [?]

units.la: Aliud Exemplum.
units.tr: Another Example.

units.la: Venditur Cantharus vini 4 albis. Quæritur quot albis, 2. Canthari veneant?
units.tr: A jar of wine is sold for 4 white coins. It is asked how many white coins 2 jars will fetch?

units.la: Colloco sic: Canth. | alb. | Canth. 1 | 4 | 12 4 48
units.tr: I arrange it thus: jars | white | jars: 1 | 4 | 12 — 4 — 48

units.la: Nunc 48 albos duco in aureos per 26, sic: 22 48 (1 26
units.tr: Now I multiply the 48 white coins into gold coins by 26, thus: 22 48 (1 26

units.la: Duodecim igitur Canthari veneunt aureo & 22 albis.
units.tr: Therefore twelve jars sell for one gold coin and 22 white coins.

units.la: Si autem scire cupio, an recte numeraverim, exemplum inverto hoc modo: Canth. | aur. | alb. | Canth. 12 | 1 | 22 | 1 26 22 48 4 ·8 (4 + ‡ 4 8
units.tr: If, however, I wish to know whether I have counted correctly, I invert the example in this way: jars | gold | white | jars: 12 | 1 | 22 | 1 26 22 48 4 ·8 (4 + ‡ 4 8

units.la: Aliud exemplum.
units.tr: Another example.

units.la: Venditur Cantharus Cerevisiæ 4 numulis. Quæritur quot numulis, 16 Canthari veneant? Colloco sic: Canth. — Numul. — Canth. 1 — 4 — 16 4 64
units.tr: A jar of beer is sold for 4 pennies. It is asked how many pennies 16 jars will fetch? I arrange it thus: jars — pennies — jars: 1 — 4 — 16; 4 — 64

units.la: Nunc 64 numulos duco in solidos per 12, sic: (4 64 4 (5 + ‡ 64 o
units.tr: Now I multiply the 64 pennies into shillings by 12, thus: (4 64 4 (5 + ‡ 64 o

units.la: Sedecim igitur Canthari veneunt 5 solidis, & 4 numulis.
units.tr: Therefore sixteen jars sell for 5 shillings and 4 pennies.

units.la: Probatio.
units.tr: Proof.

units.la: Emit quis ulnam panni 2 Thaleris.
units.tr: Someone buys an ell of cloth for 2 thalers.

units.la: Quæritur quot Thaleri sint numerandi pro 34 ulnis? Colloco sic: uln. thal. uln. 1 — 2 — 34 2 68
units.tr: It is asked how many thalers are to be paid for 34 ells? I arrange it thus: ells, thalers, ells: 1 — 2 — 34; 2 — 68

units.la: Triginta quatuor ulnæ constant 68 Thaleris.
units.tr: Thirty-four ells cost 68 thalers.

units.la: Probatio.
units.tr: Proof.

units.la: uln. thal. uln. 34 — 68 — 1
units.tr: Ells — thalers — ells: 34 — 68 — 1

units.la: Hic non multiplico neque addo: sed 68 per 34 divido, sic: & 8 (2 3 4 & 8
units.tr: Here I neither multiply nor add, but divide 68 by 34, thus: & 8 (2 3 4 & 8

units.la: Aliud Exemplum.
units.tr: Another example.

units.la: Quidam palus erectus,1 2 pedes longus jacit umbram 18 pedum, eodem articulo temporis, quo vicina quædam turris projicit umbram pedum 168. Quęstio est quanta sit turris altitudo? Colloco sic: umbr. | ped. | umbr. 18 | 12 | 168 [illegible, ~6 letters] | | 12 (112 | [illegible, ~4 letters] | 336 [illegible, ~4 letters] | | 168 2016
units.tr: A certain upright pole twelve feet long casts a shadow of 18 feet at the same moment of time that a nearby tower casts a shadow of 168 feet. The question is how great the height of the tower is? I arrange it thus: shadow | feet | shadow: 18 | 12 | 168 [illegible, ~6 letters] | | 12 (112 | [illegible, ~4 letters] | 336 [illegible, ~4 letters] | | 168 2016

units.la: Differtne Regula Societatis à Regula Detri?
units.tr: Does the Rule of Partnership differ from the Rule of Three?

units.la: Regula societatis parùm aut nihil differt à Regula Detri, teste Gemma Frisio.
units.tr: The Rule of Partnership differs little or not at all from the Rule of Three, according to Gemma Frisius.

units.la: Exemplum.
units.tr: Example.

units.la: Quatuor mercatores inito consortio lucrati sunt 3000 aureorum, sed primus contulit tantùm 30 aureos, secundus 50, tertius 60, quartus 100, in quæstionem vocatur, quantum cedere debeat unicuiq; ex lucro pro pecunia forti commissa? Colligo omnium pecuniâ collatam in unam summam, per additionem sic: 30 50 60 100 240
units.tr: Four merchants, having entered into a partnership, made a profit of 3000 gold coins, but the first contributed only 30 gold coins, the second 50, the third 60, the fourth 100. The question is, how much of the profit should fall to each one for the money committed to the venture? I collect the money contributed by all into one sum, by addition, thus: 30 + 50 + 60 + 100 = 240

units.la: Nũc dico 240 aurei lucrati sunt 3000 aureorum, quantum 30, lucrantur? 240 — 3000 — 30 Operor secundum Regulæ morem, & colligo lucrum primi 375 aureorum.
units.tr: Now I say: 240 gold coins made a profit of 3000 gold coins; how much do 30 make? 240 — 3000 — 30. I work according to the custom of the Rule, and I obtain the profit of the first: 375 gold coins.

units.la: Rursum, pro secundi lucro dico, 240 lucrantur 3000, quantum 50?
units.tr: Again, for the profit of the second I say: 240 gain 3000; how much does 50 gain?

units.la: Ac sic pro singulis unam constituo Regulam Detri, ut semper primus sive divisor sit summa pecuniæ omnium, medius lucrum, tertius quæcum uni ex lucro cedere debeat.
units.tr: And so, for each one, I set up one Rule of Three, so that the first term is always the sum of all the money, the middle the profit, and the third the sum that is due to each one from the profit.

units.la: Habebit igitur primus 375, secundus 625, tertius 750, quartus 1250.
units.tr: The first will therefore have 375, the second 625, the third 750, the fourth 1250.

units.la: Hactenus de speciebus, Regula Detri & Societatis: sequuntur Fractiones.
units.tr: So far concerning the kinds, the Rule of Three and the Rule of Partnership; the Fractions follow.

units.la: Quid sunt Fractiones?
units.tr: What are Fractions?

units.la: FRactiones, minutiæ seu partes sunt numeri, integræ rei partes significantes, secundum Gemmam Frisium.
units.tr: Fractions, or fractional parts, are numbers signifying parts of a whole thing, according to Gemma Frisius.

units.la: Scribuntur autem duobus numeris: Superior, Numerator: Inferior, Denominator appellatur: ut Numerator 1 / Denominator 2. Dimidia alicujus rei pars. 1/3 una tertia. 1/4 una quarta. 3/5 tres quintæ, &c.
units.tr: They are written with two numbers. The upper is called the numerator and the lower the denominator, for example numerator 1 over denominator 2: half of a thing. 1/3: one third. 1/4: one quarter. 3/5: three fifths, and so on.

units.la: Porrò duæ tantùm Fractiones simul sumuntur sic: 1/3 1/5
units.tr: Moreover, only two fractions are added together, thus: 1/3 1/5

units.la: Si integris Fractiones annexæ sunt, procedendum est hoc modo: 1 1/4 2 3/8
units.tr: If fractions are attached to whole numbers, proceed in this way: 1 1/4 2 3/8

units.la: Hic priorem notam per inferiorem multiplico, & superiore addo, dicens: semel 4 sunt 4, addito 1, sunt 5, quæ infra scribo, & Denominatorem subnoto. Deinde dico bis 8 sunt 16, additis 3, sunt 19, quę infra scribo & Denominatore subnoto, hoc modo: 1 1/4 2 3/8 5 19 4 8
units.tr: Here I multiply the first whole number by the lower number and add the upper, saying: once 4 is 4, add 1, which is 5. I write this below and note the denominator underneath. Then I say: twice 8 is 16, add 3, which is 19. I write this below and note the denominator under it, thus: 1 1/4 2 3/8 5 19 4 8

units.la: Hæcres usui est in sequentibus, ut facilior fiat operatio.
units.tr: This is useful in what follows, to make the operation easier.

units.la: Cùm Fractio majoribus numeris scripta est, minimo quàm potest fieri numero exprimatur, inquire igitur numerum quemcunque, qui ambos, superiorem scilicet & inferiorem ita exacte dividat, ut nihil superfit, quotientes ad latus scribito. 14 / 24
units.tr: When a fraction is written with larger numbers, it should be expressed with the smallest number possible. Look for any number that divides both the upper and the lower number exactly, leaving no remainder, and write the quotients at the side. 14/24

units.la: Hic Numerator dividitur ꝑ 2, & 2 in 14 continentur 7: Denominator dividitur per 2, & 2 in 24 continentur 12. Iam Fractio minimo quàm potest fieri numero exprimitur, sic: (2 | 14 / 24 | 7 / 12
units.tr: Here the numerator is divided by 2, and 2 goes into 14 seven times. The denominator is divided by 2, and 2 goes into 24 twelve times. Now the fraction is expressed with the smallest possible number, thus: (2 | 14/24 | 7/12

units.la: Hujusmodi verò Fractionem 15 / 105 ad minimam sic redigo, dicens: 3 in 15 continentur 5, & 5 ex adverso noto, subjecta linea. Deinde dico tria in 10 continentur 3, & 3 ex adverso sub linea noto: remanet autem 1, quod 5 praepono, inquiens: 3 in 15 continentur 5, & 5 sub linea scribo, hoc modo: 3 1 5 | 5 1 0 5 | 3 5
units.tr: I reduce a fraction of this kind, 15/105, to its lowest terms in this way, saying: 3 goes into 15 five times, and I note 5 opposite, with a line drawn beneath. Then I say: 3 goes into 10 three times, and I note 3 opposite below the line. A remainder of 1 is left, which I put in front of 5, saying: 3 goes into 15 five times, and I write 5 below the line, thus: 3 1 5 | 5 1 0 5 | 3 5

units.la: Quando vero scire volo, quidnam duae tertiae, tres quartae, seu tres quintae, &c. alicujus rei sint: per Numeratorem Fractionis multiplico valorem ejus rei, quam habere cupio. Deinde multiplicatum divido per Fractionis Denominatorem: quo facto, sit 1, 2, vel 3, &c. & una tertia seu una quarta, &c. proveniant: denotantur 1, 2 vel 3 Thaleri seu aliae res, & 1/3 seu 1/5 ejusdem rei: Et si hanc quoque fractionem scire cupio, per valorem alterius minoris rei ago, ut dictu: Et hoc tantisper dum ulterius progredi nequeam.
units.tr: When I want to know what two thirds, three quarters or three fifths, etc., of something amount to, I multiply the value of the thing I wish to have by the numerator of the fraction. Then I divide the product by the denominator of the fraction. When this is done, there results 1, 2 or 3, etc., with one third or one quarter, etc., left over. These are reckoned as 1, 2 or 3 thalers or other things, and 1/3 or 1/5 of the same thing. If I want to know this remaining fraction as well, I work it out by the value of another, smaller unit, as stated, and I continue this for as long as I cannot go any further.

units.la: Quaeritur quot batzenis quatuor nonae Thaleri valeant?
units.tr: It is asked how many batzen four ninths of a thaler are worth.

units.la: Thalerus autem valet 19 batzenis. 4/9 · 19/4 76
units.tr: A thaler, however, is worth 19 batzen. 4/9 · 19/4 76

units.la: Hic per 4 multiplico 19, & proveniunt 76, quae divido per 9 proveniunt 8 batzeni, quatuor nonae.
units.tr: Here I multiply 19 by 4, which gives 76. I divide this by 9, which gives 8 batzen, four ninths.

units.la: Ulterius quaeritur quatuor nonae batzeni,quot numulis valeant?
units.tr: Further it is asked: how many numuli are four ninths of a batzen worth?

units.la: Batzenus autem Hafficus[?] valet 14 numulis. 1 4 / 4 / 9 / 4 / 5 6 [?]
units.tr: A Hafficus batzen is worth 14 numuli. 1 4 / 4 / 9 / 4 / 5 6 [?]

units.la: Nunc 56 divido per 9 & proveniunt 6 numuli & 2/9 numuli.
units.tr: Now I divide 56 by 9, and there result 6 numuli and 2/9 of a numulus.

units.la: De Additione Fractionum.
units.tr: On the Addition of Fractions.

units.la: Superior dextra nota per inferiorem finistram, ac inferior dextra per superiorem sinistram multiplicatur, peracta multiplicatione, numeri adduntur, quo facto, Denominator per alterum multiplicatur, & per multiplicatum, numerus per additionem collectus, dividitur: Et numerus qui in Divisione supra remanet, fit alterius fractionis numerator: Divisor fit Denominator: Et cum producta fractione, si plures quam duae fuerint, fractio reliqua conjungitur: ut,
units.tr: The upper right number is multiplied by the lower left, and the lower right by the upper left. Once the multiplication is done, the numbers are added. Having done this, the denominator is multiplied by the other denominator, and the number collected by the addition is divided by the product. The number that remains above in the division becomes the numerator of the other fraction, and the divisor becomes its denominator. If there are more than two fractions, the remaining fraction is joined to the product fraction in the same way, thus:

units.la: Primum dico ter 6 sunt 18, quae seorsim scribo, ac progredior dicens: quater 5 sunt 20, quae subscribo 18, & facta additione, proveniunt 38. Nunc Denominatorem per alterum multiplico, dicens: quater 6 sunt 24, per quae divido triginta octo, & provenit 1 ac 1 4/2 4, quæ per 2 in hanc fractionem rediguntur: 7/1 2
units.tr: First I say: thrice 6 is 18, which I write separately. I proceed, saying: four times 5 is 20, which I write under 18. When the addition is made, there come 38. Now I multiply the denominator by the other, saying: four times 6 is 24. By 24 I divide thirty-eight, and there results 1 and 14/24, which, reduced by 2, become this fraction: 7/12

units.la: Iam productæ Fractioni adjungo tertiam Fractionem suprà positam sic: 7/1 2 X 3/5
units.tr: Now I add the third fraction, placed above, to the product fraction, thus: 7/12 X 3/5

units.la: Et dico ter 12 sunt 36, quæ seorsim scribo, ac progredior dicens: quinquies 7 sunt 35, quæ subscripta & per additionem collecta, efficiunt 71. Nunc Denominatorem per alterum multiplico, dicens: quinquies 12 sunt 60, per quæ divido 71, & producitur 1 & undecim 60. Productę [?] fractioni adjungo quartam suprà positam sic: 1 1/6 0 X 3/7
units.tr: And I say: thrice 12 is 36, which I write separately. I proceed, saying: five times 7 is 35, which, written below and added together, make 71. Now I multiply the denominator by the other, saying: five times 12 is 60. By 60 I divide 71, and there results 1 and 11/60. I add the fourth fraction, placed above, to the product fraction, thus: 1 11/60 X 3/7

units.la: Et dico ter 60 sunt 180, quæ seorsim scribo, ac pergo dicens: septies 11, sunt 77, quæ subscripta & addita efficiunt 257. Nunc Denominatorem per alterum multiplico, dicens: septies 6, sunt 420, per quæ non possum 257 dividere: linea igitur interjecta, fit fractio sic: 2 5 7/4 2 0
units.tr: And I say: thrice 60 is 180, which I write separately. I proceed, saying: seven times 11 is 77, which, written below and added, make 257. Now I multiply the denominator by the other, saying: seven times 6 is 42. I cannot divide 257 by this, so with a line drawn between them the fraction is: 257/420

units.la: Aliud exemplum, in quo Fractiones primùm, ut suprà monstratum colliguntur: deinde adduntur. 1 1/4 2 3/8 7 6 ——— ——— 4 0 5/4 X 1 9/8 1 1 6
units.tr: Another example, in which the fractions are first collected as shown above, and then added: 1 1/4 2 3/8 7 6 ——— ——— 4 0 5/4 X 1 9/8 1 1 6

units.la: Nunc 119 divido per 32, & proveniunt 3, & fractions 2 0 over 3 2 quæ per 4 in hanc fractionem ducuntur: 5/8
units.tr: Now I divide 119 by 32, and there come 3, with a remainder of 20 over 32, which, reduced by 4, becomes this fraction: 5/8

units.la: De Subtractione Fractionum.
units.tr: On the Subtraction of Fractions.

units.la: In Subtractione Fractionū perinde procedītur ac in Additione, nisi quòd peracta multiplicatione numerus minor à majori subducatur, & qui remanet, si fieri potest per multiplicatum Denominatorem dividatur.
units.tr: In subtraction of fractions one proceeds just as in addition, except that once the multiplication is done the smaller number is subtracted from the larger, and what remains is divided, if possible, by the multiplied denominator.

units.la: Duæ quintæ à tribus quartis quot remanent? 2/5 X 3/4 1 5/8 7/20
units.tr: How much remains when two fifths are taken from three quarters? 2/5 X 3/4 1 5/8 7/20

units.la: Thalerus & tres septimę à quatuor Thaleris & quinq; nonis, quot remanent? 1 3/7 4 5/9 197 287 90 10/7 X 41/9
units.tr: One thaler and three sevenths, taken from four thalers and five ninths: how much remains? 1 3/7 4 5/9 197 287 90 10/7 X 41/9

units.la: Iam 197 divido per 63, & proveniunt 3 ac 8/63.
units.tr: Now I divide 197 by 63, and there come out 3 and 8/63.

units.la: De Multiplicatione Fractionum.
units.tr: On the Multiplication of Fractions.

units.la: Hic Numeratorem per alterū multiplico, multiplicatum seorsim noto: Deinde Denominatorem per alterum multiplicatum subnoto: Et si fieri potest per eum dividoʃin minus, linea interjecta fit fractio. 3/7 X 5/8 15/56
units.tr: Here I multiply the numerator by the other, noting the product separately. Then I write beneath it the denominator multiplied by the other, and if it can be done I divide the lesser by it; a line placed between them makes the fraction. 3/7 X 5/8 15/56

units.la: Aliud exemplum, in quo Fractiones primùm colliguntur: Deinde multiplicantur. 3 1/4 5 3/8 5 5 9 3 2 1 3/4 4 3/8
units.tr: Another example, in which the fractions are first added together and then multiplied. 3 1/4 5 3/8 5 5 9 3 2 1 3/4 4 3/8

units.la: Hic 5 5 9 divido per 3 2, & proveniunt 17 ac 1/3 5/2. [?]
units.tr: Here I divide 5 5 9 by 3 2, and there come out 17 and 1/3, 5/2. [?]

units.la: De divisione Fractionum.
units.tr: On the Division of Fractions.

units.la: In Divisione Fractionum superior finistra nota per inferiorem dextram, & superior dextra per inferiorem sinistram multiplicatur: Deinde fit Divisio. 4/7 X 3/1 [?] 2 4 4 (2 2/2 2 [?] 2 1 4 2
units.tr: In division of fractions, the upper left number is multiplied by the lower right, and the upper right by the lower left; then the division is made. 4/7 X 3/1 [?] 2 4 4 (2 2/2 2 [?] 2 1 4 2

units.la: De Regula Detri in Fractionibus.
units.tr: On the Rule of Three in Fractions.

units.la: Primò Fractiones colliguntur: Deinde Denominator Fractionis tertiæ multiplicatur per Denominatorem mediæ fractionis,&primis numeris subjectus denuò multiplicatur & habetur Divisor : Tertiò, primæ fractionis Denominator subjicitur numeris tertio loco positis, & multiplicatur: Quartò, fractio media in unā collecta, cum numeris tertio loco notatis multiplicata per primum inferiorem numerum, qui Divisor est,dividitur.
units.tr: First, the fractions are collected together. Then the denominator of the third fraction is multiplied by the denominator of the middle fraction, and this product is multiplied again by the first numbers placed beneath, and the divisor is obtained. Thirdly, the denominator of the first fraction is placed under the numbers in the third position and multiplied. Fourthly, the middle fraction, collected into one, is multiplied by the numbers noted in the third position, and divided by the first lower number, which is the divisor.

units.la: Exemplum. uln. Fl. uln. 1 1/2 — 3 1/4 — 36 2/3
units.tr: Example. uln. Fl. uln. 1 1/2 — 3 1/4 — 36 2/3

units.la: Hic dico semel 2 sunt 2, addito 1, sunt 3 quæ subnoto: Ter 4 sunt 12, addito 1, sunt 13, quæ subscribo : Ter 6 sunt 18, additis 2, sunt 20, scribo 0, & 2 mente retineo, ac dico ter 3 sunt 9, additis 2, sunt 11, quæ subnoto.
units.tr: Here I say: twice 2 is 2, add 1, makes 3, which I write beneath. Three times 4 is 12, add 1, makes 13, which I write below. Three times 6 is 18, add 2, makes 20; I write 0 and carry 2 in mind, and I say three times 3 is 9, add 2, makes 11, which I note below.

units.la: Deinde inquio, ter 4 sunt 12, quæ primis numeris subjicio, & multiplico , dicens: bis 3 sunt 6, semel 3 sunt 3, & habeo Divisorem.
units.tr: Then I say: three times 4 is 12, which I place under the first numbers and multiply, saying: twice 3 is 6, once 3 is 3, and I have the divisor.

units.la: Tertiò, transfero 2 primæ fractionis sub tertium numerum, dicens : bis o est o, semel 2 sunt 2,& rursum semel 2 sunt 2. Quartò, Fractionem mediam in unam collectam transfero sub tertium numerum, inquiens: tero est o, bis 3 sunt 6 & rursum bis 3 sunt 6: semel o est o, semel 2 sunt 2, & iterum semel 2 sunt 2. Jam per Additionem numeris collectis, proveniunt 2860, quae divido per primum infimum numerum. uln. | Flor. | uln. 1 1/2 | 3 1/4 | 36 2/3 3 | 13 | 110 12 | | 2 36 | | 220 | | 13 | | 660 220 2860
units.tr: Thirdly, I transfer the 2 of the first fraction under the third number, saying: twice 0 is 0, once 2 is 2, and again once 2 is 2. Fourthly, I transfer the middle fraction, collected into one, under the third number, saying: three times 0 is 0, twice 3 is 6, and again twice 3 is 6; once 0 is 0, once 2 is 2, and once more once 2 is 2. Now, by adding the collected numbers, there come out 2860, which I divide by the first lowest number. uln. | Flor. | uln. 1 1/2 | 3 1/4 | 36 2/3 3 | 13 | 110 12 | | 2 36 | | 220 | | 13 | | 660 220 2860

units.la: Hic divido 2860 per 36, & proveniunt 79, & 1/3 5/6 [?], quae ad minimam per 4 redigun- tur, hoc modo: 4/9 [?].
units.tr: Here I divide 2860 by 36, and there come out 79 and 1/3 5/6 [?], which are reduced to the lowest terms by 4, in this way: 4/9 [?].

units.la: Aliud Exemplum.
units.tr: Another Example.

units.la: Hîc divido 2135 per 32 & proveniunt 66 Thaleri, & remanent 23, quos per 19 in batzenos duco, sic: 23 19 207 23 437
units.tr: Here I divide 2135 by 32, and there come out 66 thalers, with 23 remaining, which I convert into batzen by multiplying by 19, thus: 23 19 207 23 437

units.la: Nunc 437 per superiorem Divisorem nempe 32, divido, & exurgunt 13 batzeni, ac remanent 21, quos per 14 in numulos resolvo, sic: 21 14 84 21 294
units.tr: Now I divide 437 by the upper divisor, namely 32, and there come out 13 batzen, with 21 remaining, which I resolve into small coins by multiplying by 14, thus: 21 14 84 21 294

units.la: Iam per divisorem divido, & proveniunt 9 numuli & 6/32, quae per 2 ad minimam ducuntur, sic: 3/16. Constant igitur ulnae 53 & 3/8, Thaleris 66, batzenis 13, numulis 9 & tribus 16 numuli.
units.tr: Now I divide by the divisor, and there come out 9 numuli and 6/32, which are reduced to lowest terms by 2, thus: 3/16. Therefore the total is 53 and 3/8 ells, 66 thalers, 13 batzen, and 9 numuli and three sixteenths of a numulus.

units.la: De Regula societatis in Fractionibus.
units.tr: On the Rule of Partnership in Fractions.

units.la: Tres mercatores inito consortio, lucrati sunt 288 aureos. Primus autem contulit 2/5:Secundus 3/4:Tertius 4/5. Quæstio est quantum cuiq; cedat? 2/5 3/4 4/5
units.tr: Three merchants entering into partnership gained 288 gold coins. The first contributed 2/5, the second 3/4, the third 4/5. The question is how much falls to each? 2/5 3/4 4/5

units.la: Hic Denominatores multiplico, dicens: quater 5 sunt 20, & quinquies 20 sunt 100, quæ seorsim noto.
units.tr: Here I multiply the denominators, saying: four times 5 is 20, and five times 20 is 100, which I note separately.

units.la: Nunc 2 subjectis centum, & multiplicatis exurgunt 200, quæ divido per 5, & proveniunt 40.
units.tr: Now I multiply 100 by the numerator 2, and there come out 200, which I divide by 5, and there come out 40.

units.la: Deinde 3 subjectis centum, & multiplicatis exurgunt 200, quæ divido per 4, & existunt 75.
units.tr: Then I multiply 100 by 3, and there come out 200, which I divide by 4, and the result is 75.

units.la: Tertiò 4 subnotatis centum, & multiplicatis, exurgunt 300, quæ divido per 5, & habeo 80.
units.tr: Thirdly, I write 4 beneath 100 and multiply, and there come out 300, which I divide by 5, and I have 80.

units.la: Iam per additionem numeris in unam summam collectis dico, 195 lucrati sunt 288 aureos. Quot lucrantur 40? Deinde quot lucrantur 75? tertiò quot lucrantur 80? Et semper secundum Regulam Detri operor. 2/5 3/4 4/5 100 | 100 | 100 2 | 3 | 4 200(40 | 300(75 | 400(80 5 | 4 | 5 40 75 80 195 195 — 288 — 40 75 80
units.tr: Now, by adding the numbers collected into one sum, I say: they gained 195 in total from the 288 gold coins. How much do they gain as 40? Then how much as 75? Thirdly, how much as 80? And I always work by the Rule of Three. 2/5 3/4 4/5 100 | 100 | 100 2 | 3 | 4 200(40 | 300(75 | 400(80 5 | 4 | 5 40 75 80 195 195 — 288 — 40 75 80

units.la: Aliud exemplum.
units.tr: Another example.

units.la: Duo mercatores societate inita lucrati sunt 146 ½. Alter autē contulit 136 ¼ : Alter vero 198 ⅓. Quæstio est quantum cuiq; cedat?
units.tr: Two merchants formed a partnership and made a profit of 146 ½. One contributed 136 ¼, and the other contributed 198 ⅓. The question is how much each should receive?

units.la: Primùm priori summæ subjicio alteram, & integros numeros per additionem colligo: Deinde fractiones: Tertiò secundùm Regulam Detri progredior. 136 ¼ | ¼ X ⅓ | 4/7 [?] 198 ⅓ 334 7/12 334 7/12 — 146 ½ — 136 ¼ 675 | 293 | 545 334 | 12 4015 | 1090 8 | 545 32120 | 6540 293 19620 58860 13080 1916220
units.tr: First I place the second sum beneath the first and add the whole numbers together. Then I deal with the fractions. Third, I proceed by the Rule of Three. 136 ¼ | ¼ X ⅓ | 4/7 [?] 198 ⅓ 334 7/12 334 7/12 — 146 ½ — 136 ¼ 675 | 293 | 545 334 | 12 4015 | 1090 8 | 545 32120 | 6540 293 19620 58860 13080 1916220

units.la: Nunc per primum inferiorem numerum fit Divisio.
units.tr: Now division is made by the first lower number.

units.la: Lecturi praecepta prolixiora videant Arithmeticam Lazari Schoneri, Gemmæ Frisii, Iohannis Monhemii vel aliorum.
units.tr: Readers who want fuller rules should consult the Arithmetic of Lazarus Schoner, Gemma Frisius, Johannes Monheim, or others.

units.la: Hactenus Arithmetica explicata est: sequitur Idea succincta Geometriae.
units.tr: So far the Arithmetic has been explained; there follows a brief outline of Geometry.

units.la: DE GEOMETRIA.
units.tr: ON GEOMETRY.

units.la: Quid est Geometria?
units.tr: What is geometry?

units.la: <bl>GEOMETRIA, die Meßkunst[?]</bl> / est ars bene metiendi: Cujus subjectum est magnitudo, quae dividitur in lineam & lineatum.
units.tr: GEOMETRY, the art of measuring[?], is the art of measuring well. Its subject is magnitude, which is divided into line and lined surface (lineatum).

units.la: Quid est Linea?
units.tr: What is a line?

units.la: Est magnitudo tantum longa. Lineae terminus est punctum. Est autem punctum signum in magnitudine individuum.
units.tr: It is magnitude only in length. The terminus of a line is a point. A point, moreover, is an indivisible sign in magnitude.

units.la: Quotuplex est Linea?
units.tr: How many kinds of line are there?

units.la: Duplex: recta aut Obliqua, Recta, quae intra suos terminos aequaliter interjacet: Obliqua, quae intra suos terminos inaequaliter interjacet.
units.tr: Two: straight or oblique. A straight line is one that lies evenly between its own termini; an oblique line is one that lies unevenly between its own termini.

units.la: Quotuplex est linea obliqua?
units.tr: How many kinds of oblique line are there?

units.la: Duplex: Peripheria, <bl>ein umbkreiß</bl> vel Helix, <bl>ein</bl> <bl>umbkreiß wie in den schnecken ist.</bl>
units.tr: Two: the periphery, a round circuit (ein umbkreiß), or the helix, a circuit such as is found in snails (wie in den schnecken ist).

units.la: Peripheria est linea aequaliter à medio comprehensi spacii distans: Helix est linea à medio comprehensi spacii distans inaequaliter.
units.tr: The periphery is a line equally distant from the middle of the space it encloses; the helix is a line unequally distant from the middle of the space it encloses.

units.la: Hactenus de linea.
units.tr: So much for the line.

units.la: Quid est Lineatum?
units.tr: What is a lined surface?

units.la: Est magnitudo plus quam longa. Lineati affectiones duae sunt: Angulus & figura. Anguli latera sunt termini comprehendentes angulum. Angulus rectus est cujus latera inter se sunt recta: Angulus obliquus est cujus latera inter se sunt obliqua.
units.tr: It is magnitude more than long. The affections of a lined surface are two: angle and figure. The sides of an angle are the termini enclosing the angle. A right angle is one whose sides are straight lines with respect to each other; an oblique angle is one whose sides are oblique with respect to each other.

units.la: Quid est Figura?
units.tr: What is a figure?

units.la: Figura est lineatum undique terminatum: Cujus partes quinque sunt: Centrum, <bl>ein mittelpunct in einem</bl> <bl>kreiß/</bl> Perimeter, <bl>der umbgang/</bl> Radius, <bl>die</bl> <bl>linien vom punct zum umbgang /</bl> Diameter, <bl>ein linien so die</bl> <bl>so die figuren mitten zertheilet</bl> / Altitudo, <bl>ein linien</bl> <bl>von oben der figur biß zum untersten.</bl>
units.tr: A figure is a surface bounded on every side by a line. Its five parts are: the centre, a point in the middle; the perimeter, the circumference; the radius, the lines from the centre to the circumference; the diameter, a line that cuts the figure through the middle; and the altitude, a line from the top of the figure down to the bottom.

units.la: Centrum est punctum in figura medium.
units.tr: The centre is the point in the middle of a figure.

units.la: Perimeter est comprehensio figuræ.
units.tr: The perimeter is the enclosing boundary of a figure.

units.la: Radius est recta à centro ad perimetrum.
units.tr: The radius is a straight line from the centre to the perimeter.

units.la: Diameter est recta inscripta figuræ per centrum, quæ in planis proprie Diagonius dicitur: in solidis vero Axis.
units.tr: The diameter is a straight line drawn through the figure's centre, which in plane figures is properly called the diagonal, but in solids the axis.

units.la: Altitudo est perpendiculum à vertice figuræ ad basim.
units.tr: The altitude is the perpendicular from the vertex of a figure to its base.

units.la: Quot sunt species Figuræ?
units.tr: How many kinds of figure are there?

units.la: Duæ: Superficies & Corpus. Superficies, <bl>die blosse</bl> <bl>eusserste am dinge/ est</bl> lineatum duntaxat latum.
units.tr: Two: surface and body. A surface, the bare outermost part of a thing (die blosse eusserste am dinge), is merely a lined surface of breadth.

units.la: Quotuplex est Superficies?
units.tr: How many kinds of surface are there?

units.la: Duplex: Plana vel Gibba. Plana superficies, <bl>die</bl> <bl>eben eusserste/ est</bl> in triangulo, <bl>im dreyeckigen / qua-</bl> <bl>drato, vierreckigen/ rhombo, ungleichem vierreckigen/</bl> <bl>trapezio, langem vierreckigen / multangulo, vielecki-</bl> <bl>gen/ circulo, im kreiß.</bl>
units.tr: Two: plane or curved. A plane surface, the flat outermost part (die eben eusserste), is found in the triangle (im dreyeckigen), the square (quadrato), the quadrilateral (vierreckigen), the rhombus, the irregular quadrilateral (ungleichem vierreckigen), the trapezium, the oblong quadrilateral (langem vierreckigen), the polygon (multangulo, vielecki­gen), the circle (circulo, im kreiß).

units.la: Gibba superficies, <bl>die gebogene eusserste / est</bl> in sphæra, <bl>an der kugel / cono, an dem das sich unden</bl> <bl>auff in ein spitz zeucht / cylindro, an dem das rund in</bl> <bl>die lenge ist.</bl>
units.tr: A convex surface, the curved outer surface, is found in a sphere; in a cone, which tapers to a point at the bottom; and in a cylinder, where the round surface runs lengthwise.

units.la: Hactenus de superficie.
units.tr: So much for surface.

units.la: Quid est Corpus?
units.tr: What is a body?

units.la: Corpus est lineatum latum & altum: Estque solidum planum vel solidum gibbum. Solidum planum, <bl>das ebene so inwendig ganz ist / est</bl> pyramis, <bl>ein vierreckig</bl> <bl>gebew / so sich in ein spitz zeucht /</bl> & cubus, <bl>ein</bl> <bl>vierreckig ding an allen orten wie ein würffel:</bl> Solidum gibbum, <bl>das gebogene so inwendig nit hol ist /</bl> <bl>est</bl> conus, cylindrus.
units.tr: A body is a lined surface having breadth and height; and it is either a solid plane or a solid curved. A solid plane, a flat thing that is entirely solid within (das ebene so inwendig ganz ist), is the pyramid (ein vierreckig gebew so sich in ein spitz zeucht), and the cube (ein vierreckig ding an allen orten wie ein würffel). A solid curved, a bent thing that is not hollow within (das gebogene so inwendig nit hol ist), is the cone and the cylinder.

units.la: Lecturus præcepta prolixiora, videat Euclidem Geometram insignem.
units.tr: Whoever wishes to read fuller precepts, let him consult the famous geometer Euclid.

units.la: Hactenus Geometriæ idea tradita fuit: sequitur Architectura.
units.tr: So much for the outline of geometry; there follows Architecture.

units.la: DE ARCHITE- CTURA.
units.tr: ON ARCHITECTURE.

units.la: Quid est Architectura?
units.tr: What is architecture?

units.la: Architectura, <bl>Die bawkunst</bl> / est ars domos & ædificia varia extruendi: Ejus Subjectum est Domus seu Ædificium, in quo tria consideranda sunt: Caussae, Species, Adjuncta.
units.tr: Architecture (the building art) is the art of constructing houses and buildings of various kinds. Its subject is the house or building, in which three things are to be considered: its causes, its kinds, and its accessories.

units.la: Quæ est caussa finalis ædificii?
units.tr: What is the final cause of a building?

units.la: Præcipua est defensio ab injuria cœli & tempestatum: Cujus gratia caussa Efficiens cæteras caussas ad effectum dirigit.
units.tr: The chief one is protection from the injury of the sky and of storms. For the sake of this, the efficient cause directs the other causes to their effect.

units.la: Lapis & lignum, duæ præcipuæ materiæ sunt. Ad has pertinent, Calx, falch & Cæmentum, <bl>kleine zer-</bl> <bl>schlagene steine damit man mawret</bl>[?].
units.tr: Stone and wood are the two chief materials. To these belong lime, sand and mortar, and small broken stones with which one builds walls (rubble).

units.la: Quot sunt species ædificiorum?
units.tr: How many kinds of buildings are there?

units.la: Duæ: Alia enim publica sunt, alia privata. Publica vel sacra, vel prophana sunt. Sacra, quæ ad religionem comparata sunt, ut templa, quorum forma est vel quadrangula, vel rotunda.
units.tr: Two. For some are public and others private. Public buildings are either sacred or profane. Sacred buildings are those prepared for religion, such as temples, whose shape is either square or round.

units.la: Quænam ædificia comparata sunt ad defensionem?
units.tr: What buildings are prepared for defence?

units.la: Portæ & turres cum muris, aggeribus, obliquis accessibus, & aliis quibus hostium impetus arcetur.
units.tr: Gates and towers with walls, earthworks, sloping approaches, and other things by which the attack of enemies is kept off.

units.la: Quænam comparata sunt ad oppor- tu-nitatem?
units.tr: What buildings are prepared for convenience?

units.la: Forum, <bl>das marckt</bl> / Aerarium, <bl>die schatzkammer</bl> / Carcer, <bl>etliche orth da die roßle gehalten werden</bl>[?] / <bl>ehe man</bl> <bl>sie zum thurnieren herauß lässt</bl> / Curia, <bl>ein rahthauß</bl> / Balneae, <bl>gemeine badstuben</bl> / Palæstræ, <bl>fechtschulen</bl> / Xysti, <bl>weite bedeckte gänge</bl> / <bl>darinn die fechter sich</bl> <bl>winters zeit üben</bl> / Portus, <bl>Meerhafen</bl> / Structuræ, <bl>gebew</bl> <bl>gebew</bl> im wasser/Theatrum, ein schawhauß : Cujus partes sunt, porticus, ein bedecktt orth zu spatzieren/ Orchestra, der fürnembsten Herrn brügge im schawhauß/Scena,ein hutt/zelt im schawhauß/Proscenium, das gerüst vor den zelten / Odeum, ein orth den sängeren/trummenschlagern/pfeiffern verordnet / Pulpitum, ein erhöhet gerüst / darauff die possen treiber seind / Cuneus, ein orth im schawhauß zwischen den <bl>bencken</bl>.
units.tr: The marketplace (forum); the treasury (aerarium); the prison (carcer), certain places where the horses are kept before being let out for the tournament; the council house (curia), a town hall; public baths (balneae); fencing schools (palaestrae); covered walks (xysti), where fencers practise in winter; the harbour (portus); structures (structurae), buildings built in the water; the theatre (theatrum), a playhouse, whose parts are the porticus, a covered place for walking; the orchestra, the place of the chief lords in the playhouse; the scena, a tent or booth in the playhouse; the proscenium, the platform in front of the tents; the odeum, a place assigned to singers, drummers and pipers; the pulpitum, a raised stage where the buffoons perform; and the cuneus, a place in the playhouse between the benches.

units.la: Quotuplices sunt partes ædificiorum?
units.tr: How many kinds of parts do buildings have?

units.la: Duplices: Sunt enim aut infra terram, aut supra terram. Infra terram sunt Fundamenta & Hypogea, <bl>Keller</bl>: Supra terram sunt podia pensilia (seu pergulæ, <bl>fürgehencfte gebew</bl> / <bl>darauß man schawet</bl> / exedræ, ein orth voll stüle/da man gesprach haltet/ hæ partes dicuntur exteriores: Interiores sequuntur.
units.tr: Two kinds. For they are either below the ground or above it. Below the ground are the foundations and the hypogea (cellars). Above the ground are the podia pensilia (or pergolas, projecting structures from which one looks out), and the exedrae, a place full of seats where people hold conversations. These parts are called exterior; the interior parts follow.

units.la: Quotuplices sunt interiores partes?
units.tr: How many kinds of interior parts are there?

units.la: Duplices : Aliæ ad fordidas actiones comparatæ sunt, ut Latrinæ : Aliæ ad honestas, quæ vel eundi gratia fiunt, ut oftia, vel habitandi. Ostium est aditus habitationum, quæ intra januam sunt : janua enim proprie primus ædium aditus est : cujus partes sunt, postes, <bl>thürpfoste</bl> / limina, <bl>thürschwellen</bl> / fores, <bl>thüren</bl>.
units.tr: Two kinds. Some are prepared for base functions, such as latrines; others for decent ones, which are used either for going out, such as doors, or for living in. A door (ostium) is the entrance to the rooms that lie inside the gate; for the gate (janua) is properly the first entrance to a building. Its parts are the posts (door-jambs), the thresholds, and the leaves (doors).

units.la: Quotuplex est habitatio?
units.tr: How many kinds of dwelling are there?

units.la: Duplex: Inferior aut Superior. Ad inferiorem habitationem pertinent: Vestibulum, ein <bl>vorhoff</bl> / Atrium, ein <bl>vorhoff</bl> / Porticus, ein <bl>spatziergang</bl> / Cavædium, ein unbedecktt orth mit gemachen umbgeben / Culina, die <bl>Küche</bl>: Cujus partes sunt, focus, ein <bl>feur-</bl> <bl>statt</bl> / & Caminus, ein <bl>gebew</bl> / da der rauch hinauß gehet.
units.tr: Two: the lower or the upper. To the lower dwelling belong: the vestibule, a forecourt; the atrium, a forecourt; the porticus, a walkway; the cavaedium, an open place surrounded by rooms; the kitchen (culina), whose parts are the hearth, a fireplace, and the chimney (caminus), a structure through which the smoke goes out.

units.la: Gymnasium,ein übe orth/ Balneum,ein eigen badstub / Apodyterium , <bl>ein abʒeuchstube</bl> [?] / Valetudinarium, <bl>ein ofth da francken ligen</bl> [?] / Stabulum, <bl>ein stall</bl>: Cujus species sunt: Equile, <bl>ein pferdstal</bl> / Bovile, <bl>ein</bl> <bl>rinderstal</bl> / Ovile, <bl>ein schaffstal</bl> / Caprile, <bl>ein ʒiegenstal</bl> / Agnile, <bl>ein lämmerstal</bl> / & Hara, <bl>ein schweinstal</bl>.
units.tr: The gymnasium, a place for exercise; the balneum, a private bathroom; the apodyterium, an undressing room; the valetudinarium, a place where the sick lie; the stabulum, a stable. Its kinds are: the equile, a horse stable; the bovile, a cattle stable; the ovile, a sheep pen; the caprile, a goat stable; the agnile, a lamb stable; and the hara, a pigsty.

units.la: Hactenus de partibus inferioris habitationis.
units.tr: So much concerning the parts of the lower dwelling.

units.la: Quid est superior habitatio?
units.tr: What is the upper dwelling?

units.la: Est contignatio, <bl>ein bune</bl> [?]: Ad quam ascenditur per scalas, quarum gradus ex ligno aut lapide fiunt: Scalæ vero, quibus per gyrum ascendimus, à cochleæ forma, cochlides dicuntur.
units.tr: It is the storey (contignatio), a floor: one goes up to it by stairs, whose steps are made of wood or stone. Stairs by which we ascend in a circle are called cochlides, from the shape of a snail's shell (cochlea).

units.la: In contignatione solent esse: Triclinium, <bl>ein saal</bl> <bl>darauff man isset</bl> / Cubiculum, <bl>ein schlaffkammer</bl> / Conclave, <bl>ein beschlossen gemach</bl> / Gynæceum, <bl>ein ge-</bl> <bl>mach da das frawenzimmer ist</bl> / Cœnaculum, <bl>ein gemach</bl> <bl>da man zu nacht isset</bl> / Bibliotheca, <bl>ein Libe-</bl> <bl>ren/ein buchstammer</bl>. Bibliothecæ ad orientem spectare debent, ita libri non putrescunt. In quibusdam locis Culina solet esse in superiori habitatione.
units.tr: Usually in the storey there are: the triclinium, a dining room where one eats; the cubiculum, a bedroom; the conclave, a closed chamber; the gynaeceum, a room where the women are; the coenaculum, a room where one eats supper; the bibliotheca, a library, a room for books. Libraries ought to face east, so that the books do not rot. In some places the kitchen is usually in the upper dwelling.

units.la: Hactenus de partibus inferioris & superioris habitationis dictum est.
units.tr: So much has been said concerning the parts of the lower and upper dwelling.

units.la: Quid est Tectum?
units.tr: What is the roof?

units.la: Tectum, <bl>das tach</bl> [?] est proprie ea pars, quæ domū tegit. Sub eo plærunque est granarium, <bl>ein tornbune</bl> [?]. Partes tecti duæ sunt: Fastigium & Culmen. Fastigium, <bl>die gebel</bl> à rota parietum latitudine sensim in acutum erigitur instar pyramidis. Culmen, <bl>die seite</bl> <bl>des dachs</bl> constat ex transtris, <bl>zwerchbalcken</bl> / capreolis, <bl>trampffen</bl> / tignis, <bl>latten</bl> / scandulis, <bl>dünne bretter</bl> / tegulis, <bl>ziegel der flach ist</bl> / imbricibus, <bl>außgehölet ziegel</bl> / vel stissilibus lapidibus, <bl>scheverstein</bl>. Stillæ sunt vel à tubulis teretibus, vel canalibus semirotundis excipiendæ, ne deorsum cadentes parietes corrumpant.
units.tr: The roof (tectum) is properly that part which covers the house. Under it there is usually a granary, a loft. The parts of the roof are two: the gable and the ridge. The gable is raised gradually from the width of the walls' base to a point, like a pyramid. The ridge, the side of the roof, consists of cross-beams, rafters, laths, thin boards, flat tiles, curved tiles, or split stones. The rainwater is to be received either by round pipes or by half-round gutters, so that it does not fall downward and damage the walls.

units.la: Quænam sunt Adjuncta ædificiorum?
units.tr: What are the adjuncts of buildings?

units.la: Horti & piscinæ, <bl>garten vnd fischteiche</bl>. Horti pensiles sunt, qui de fenestris appenduntur. Hortos circundant sepes structiles, vel vivæ seu naturales ex rubis & spinis.
units.tr: Gardens and fishponds, <bl>gardens and fishponds</bl>. Hanging gardens are those which are suspended from the windows. Gardens are surrounded by hedges, either built of construction, or living and natural ones made of brambles and thorns.

units.la: Quid est Machina?
units.tr: What is a machine?

units.la: Machina, <bl>ein rüstzeug</bl> / est pars Architecturæ subveniens desperatis actionibus, qua etiam contra naturam agere licet.
units.tr: A machine, <bl>a contrivance</bl>, is a part of architecture that comes to the aid of desperate undertakings, by which it is also permitted to act against nature.

units.la: Quid est Machina tractatoria?
units.tr: What is a hauling machine?

units.la: Cùm onera machinis trahuntur, aut ad altitudinem sublata deponuntur: Cujus species fere sunt: Fistuca, <bl>ein schlegel/ so man auff zeucht vnd laßt wieder herab fallen / daß</bl> <bl>die pfäle in den boden gehen/</bl> Trochlea, <bl>ein welle vber die ein seil oder kette gehet</bl> <bl>an einem zug</bl> / Tympanum, <bl>ein zugrad/ ein kranich/</bl> Succula, <bl>ein zugwahl/ die man mit stangen vmbtrei-</bl> <bl>bet</bl> / Vectis, <bl>ein stang</bl>.
units.tr: When burdens are drawn by machines, or raised to a height and set down: its kinds are roughly these: the fistuca, <bl>a mallet which one hauls up and lets fall again, so that</bl> <bl>the piles go into the ground</bl>; the trochlea, <bl>a pulley over which a rope or chain runs</bl> <bl>on a haul</bl>; the tympanum, <bl>a hoisting wheel, a crane</bl>; the succula, <bl>a windlass which is turned with poles</bl>; the vectis, <bl>a lever</bl>.

units.la: Lecturus præcepta prolixiora videat Vitruvium, Grapaldum & alios.
units.tr: Whoever wishes to read fuller precepts should see Vitruvius, Grapaldus and others.

units.la: Hactenus exposita est Architectura: sequitur Ethica.
units.tr: So much for architecture has been set out; ethics follows.

units.la: DE ETHICA.
units.tr: ON ETHICS.

units.la: Quid est Ethica?
units.tr: What is Ethics?

units.la: ETHICA, <bl>die tugentkunst</bl> / est ars secundum virtutem vivendi: Cujus Subjectum est Virtus.
units.tr: Ethics, <bl>the art of virtue</bl>, is the art of living according to virtue; its subject is virtue.

units.la: Quid est virtus?
units.tr: What is virtue?

units.la: Est habitus animi in mediocritate consistens. Cujus species sunt quatuor: Justitia, Fortitudo, Prudentia, Temperantia.
units.tr: It is a habit of the mind consisting in a mean. Its species are four: justice, fortitude, prudence, and temperance.

units.la: Quid est Justitia?
units.tr: What is justice?

units.la: Est virtus, quæ in hominum societate tuenda, tribuendoq; suum cuique, & rerum contractarum fide versatur. Justitiæ fundamentum est fides dictorum, conventorumq; constantia, & veritas: Dicta, quia fiat quod dictum est.
units.tr: It is the virtue which concerns the preservation of human fellowship, the giving to each his due, and the keeping of faith in contracts. The foundation of justice is the faithfulness of words and the constancy and truth of agreements: faithfulness of words, so that what has been said is done.

units.la: Injustitiæ duo sunt genera : Unum eorum, qui inferunt injuriam: Alterum eorum qui ab iis, quibus infertur, non propulsant si possunt.
units.tr: There are two kinds of injustice: one of those who inflict injury; the other of those who do not ward off injury from those to whom it is inflicted, when they can.

units.la: Quorsum refert Cicero liberalitatem?
units.tr: To what does Cicero refer liberality?

units.la: Ad justitiam. Habet autem liberalitas tres cautiones: Quomodo dandum sit, quantum & quibus.
units.tr: To justice. Liberality, however, has three cautions: how it is to be given, how much, and to whom.

units.la: Quomodo dandum est?
units.tr: How is it to be given?

units.la: Ita, ne obsit benignitas & iis, quibus benignè videbitur fieri, & cæteris.
units.tr: So that kindness does no harm either to those to whom it seems to be done, or to others.

units.la: Quantum dandum est?
units.tr: How much is to be given?

units.la: Cuiquè pro dignitate, in qua consideranda sunt quatuor: Mores ejus in quem beneficium confertur: Animus & benevolentia erga nos: Officia nobis ante collata: Communitas & Societas vitæ.
units.tr: To each according to his worth, in which four things are to be considered: the character of the person on whom the benefit is conferred; his disposition and goodwill towards us; the services previously rendered to us; and community and fellowship of life.

units.la: Quot sunt gradus Societatis humanæ?
units.tr: How many degrees of human society are there?

units.la: Sex: primus est universi generis humani : Secundus ejusdem gentis: Tertius ejusdem civitatis : Quartus propinquorum: Quintus consanguineorum: Sextus patriæ.
units.tr: Six: the first is that of the whole human race; the second of the same nation; the third of the same state; the fourth of relatives by marriage; the fifth of blood relatives; the sixth of the homeland.

units.la: Quibusnam plurimum officii est tri- buendum?
units.tr: To whom is the greatest measure of duty to be rendered?

units.la: Imprimis patriæ & parentibus : proximè liberis: Deinde consanguineis.
units.tr: Above all to the homeland and parents; next to children; then to blood relations.

units.la: Quid est fortitudo?
units.tr: What is fortitude?

units.la: Est virtus, quæ in animi excelsi & invicti magnitudine dine ac robore versatur.Fortes habendi sunt qui propulsant injuriam.
units.tr: It is the virtue which lies in the greatness and strength of a lofty and unconquered mind. Those are to be counted brave who ward off injury.

units.la: Quid est prudentia?
units.tr: What is prudence?

units.la: Est virtus, quae in perspicientia veri, solertiaq; versatur. Huic duo vitia contraria sunt: Unum, incognita habere pro cognitis: Alterum, nimis magnum studiū in rebus obscuris,iisq; non necessariis adhibere.
