units.tr: It is the virtue which lies in the clear perception of truth and in skill. Two vices are opposed to it: one, to hold unknown things as known; the other, to apply too great zeal to obscure matters and to those that are not necessary.

units.la: Quid est Temperantia?
units.tr: What is temperance?

units.la: Est virtus in omnium, quae fiunt, quaeq; dicuntur, ordine & modo versans.
units.tr: It is the virtue governing the order and measure of all the things that are done and said.

units.la: Quænam sunt præcepta hîc tenenda?
units.tr: What precepts are to be held here?

units.la: Adhibenda est munditia non odiosa, neq; exquisita nimis, tantum quae fugiat agrestem & inhumanam negligentiam.
units.tr: A cleanliness is to be practised that is not offensive, nor excessively refined, but only such as avoids rustic and inhuman neglect.

units.la: Lecturus præcepta prolixiora videat Ethicam Domini Philippi Melanchthonis, Aristotelis, Domini Doctoris Scribonii vel aliorum.
units.tr: Whoever wishes to read more extended precepts should consult the Ethics of Master Philipp Melanchthon, Aristotle, Doctor Scribonius, or others.

units.la: Hactenus est Ethica declarata: sequitur de Oeconomica.
units.tr: Thus far Ethics has been set forth; there follows the section on Economics.

units.la: DE OECONO-MICA.
units.tr: ON ECONOMICS.

units.la: ECONOMICA[?] est ars bene rem fa-miliarem administrandi: Cujus subjectum est ars familiaris, in qua tria consideranda sunt: Fuga vitiorum, Ars qua vitae necessaria acquirantur,& Conjugiu. <bl>Die haußhaltenskunst ist eine kunst wol das heusliche gut</bl> <bl>zu verwalten: Diese kunst gehet auffs heusliche gut/Da-</bl> <bl>rin dreyerley müssen betrachtet werden: Die vermei-</bl> <bl>dung der laster/Die kunst damit des lebens nothurff-</bl> <bl>tige ding müssen erworbē werde/ vnd der Ehestād.</bl>
units.tr: Economics is the art of managing household property well. Its subject is the art of the household, in which three things are to be considered: the avoidance of vices, the art by which the necessities of life are acquired, and marriage. Household management is the art of managing the household's goods well. It concerns household property, and three things must be considered in it: avoiding vices, the art by which the necessities of life are acquired, and the married state.

units.la: Quænam vitia Oeconomo sunt fugienda?
units.tr: What vices must the steward avoid?

units.la: <bl>Desidia, pigritia, negligentia, lusus, gula, libido,</bl> <bl>ebrietas, ambitio.</bl>
units.tr: Idleness, sloth, negligence, gambling, gluttony, lust, drunkenness, ambition.

units.la: <bl>Was für laster muß ein Haußhalter vermeiden?</bl>
units.tr: What vices must a householder avoid?

units.la: <bl>Faulheit / trägheit / versaumniß / spilleren / die begird</bl> <bl>lecker speise / vnkeuschheit / truncken heit / chiget-</bl> <bl>igkeit[?].</bl>
units.tr: Laziness, sloth, neglect, gambling, a craving for dainty food, unchastity, drunkenness, and [?] greed.

units.la: Quænam ars est Oeconomo scitu necessaria, qua victum honeste quærat?
units.tr: What art is necessary for the steward to know, by which he may honestly seek his livelihood?

units.la: Cicero inquit: Omnium rerum ex quibus aliquid exquiritur, nihil est agricultura melius, nihil uberius, nihil dulcius, nihil homine libero dignius. Hoc quidem verum est: sed tamen artibus mechanicis, ut arte pistoria, arte fabrili, arte sutoria, & reliquis, victum suum homines pii ac diligentes largiter sibi comparare queunt.
units.tr: Cicero says: "Of all the things from which some gain is sought, nothing is better than agriculture, nothing more fruitful, nothing sweeter, nothing more worthy of a free man." This is indeed true. Yet pious and diligent people can also obtain their livelihood in abundance by mechanical arts, such as baking, smithing, shoemaking, and the rest.

units.la: <bl>Was für eine kunst ist einem Haußhalter zu-</bl> <bl>wissen nötig, damit er seine nahrung</bl> <bl>ehrlich suchen möge?</bl>
units.tr: What art should a householder know, so that he may honestly seek his livelihood?

units.la: <bl>Cicero sagt : unter allen dingen / darauß man</bl> <bl>etwas bekompt / ist nicht bessers / dann der Ackerbaw /</bl> <bl>nicht fruchtbares / nicht lieblichers / nicht wirdigers</bl> <bl>einem freyen menschen. Dieses ist zwar also : aber</bl> <bl>doch mit den handwerckes künsten / als mit der becker-</bl> <bl>kunst / schmiedekunst / schusterkunst / und andern /</bl> <bl>können ihre narung Gottsförchtige und fleissige leute</bl> <bl>sich reichlich verschaffen.</bl>
units.tr: Cicero says: among all the things from which one gets something, none is better than farming, none more fruitful, none more pleasant, none more worthy of a free man. This is true. Yet by the crafts, such as baking, smithing, shoemaking and others, God-fearing and diligent people can procure their livelihood abundantly.

units.la: Quænam consideranda sunt in Conjugio?
units.tr: What must be considered in marriage?

units.la: Officia mariti & uxoris. Mariti duo sunt præcipua officia: precatio & labor.
units.tr: The duties of husband and wife. The husband has two principal duties: prayer and labour. The labour of the head of the household consists in acquiring and preserving goods, honour and goodwill.

units.la: Labor patrisfamiliās consistit in acquisitione & conservatione opum,honoris,benevolentiæ.
units.tr: The labour of the head of the household consists in acquiring and preserving wealth, honour and goodwill.

units.la: <bl>Was</bl>
units.tr: What

units.la: <bl>Was muß betrachtet werden im</bl> <bl>Ehestande?</bl>
units.tr: What must be considered in the married state?

units.la: <bl>Die dienste des Ehemannes vnnd der Haußfrawen. Zween fürneme dienste sind des Ehemannes: das gebett vnd die arbeit. Die arbeit eines Haußv-</bl> <bl>atters stehet in erwerbung vnd bewahrung der güter/der ehr/ der gutwilligkeit.</bl>
units.tr: The duties of the husband and the housewife. The husband has two chief duties: prayer and work. The work of the head of the household consists in acquiring and keeping goods, honour and goodwill.

units.la: Quomodo acquiruntur opes?
units.tr: How are goods acquired?

units.la: Diligentia & honesta parsimonia, quae magnum vectigal est, ut Cicero inquit.
units.tr: By diligence and honest thrift, which is a great income, as Cicero says.

units.la: <bl>Wie werden die güter erworben.</bl>
units.tr: How are goods acquired?

units.la: <bl>Durch fleiß vnnd ehrliche sparsamkeit / welche ein</bl> <bl>grosser zoll ist/ als Cicero sagt.</bl>
units.tr: By diligence and honest thrift, which is a great source of revenue, as Cicero says.

units.la: Quomodo acquiret Paterfamilias honorem & benevolentiam?
units.tr: How shall the head of the household gain honour and goodwill?

units.la: Si neminem injuria affecerit.
units.tr: If he does injury to no one.

units.la: <bl>Wie soll ein Haußvatter erlangen ehr</bl> <bl>vnd gutwilligkeit?</bl>
units.tr: How shall a householder gain honour and goodwill?

units.la: <bl>Wenn er niemand vnrecht thun wird.</bl>
units.tr: If he will do wrong to no one.

units.la: Quodnam exemplum Paterfamilias suis praebere debet?
units.tr: What example ought the head of the household give to his own?

units.la: Sit diligens, primus cubitu surgat, postremus cubitum eat, ac meminerit adagiorum: Ager nulla alia re stercoratur melius, quàm stercore, quod de calceis Domini cadit. Et oculus Domini saginat equum.
units.tr: Let him be diligent; let him rise first from bed and go to bed last, and let him remember the proverbs: "A field is manured by nothing better than the dung that falls from the master's shoes," and "The eye of the master fattens the horse."

units.la: <bl>Was für ein exempel sol ein Haußvatter</bl> <bl>den seinen geben?</bl>
units.tr: What example should a householder give to his own?

units.la: <bl>Er soll fleissig sein / zum ersten sol er auffstehen/</bl> <bl>zum letzten sol er zu bette gehen / vnnd sol gedencken</bl> <bl>der Sprichwörter: Der acker wird mit keinem dinge</bl> <bl>besser gedünget / dann mit dem miste/ so von den schuhen des Herzen</bl> <bl>fällt. Vnd / das aug des Herrn machet das pferd feist.</bl>
units.tr: He should be diligent: he should rise first and go to bed last, and he should remember the proverbs: no field is better manured than with the dung that falls from the master's shoes. And: the eye of the Lord makes the horse fat.

units.la: Quænam sunt officia Uxoris?
units.tr: What are the duties of the wife?

units.la: Uxoris est domi manere, & ea quae domum comportantur, suscipere, quae consumenda sunt, promere:quæ vero servanda, providè condere & custodire,ne uno mense consumantur, quae in annum reponi debebant: non debet moleste ferre si maritus plus oneris sibi imponat, quàmulli de familia. Nam familiae custodia duntaxat & cura rerum commissa est: Uxor verò etiam usumfructum ut domina in domo habet.
units.tr: It is the wife's part to stay at home, to receive what is brought into the house, to bring out what is to be consumed, and to store carefully and keep what is to be kept, so that what should be laid by for a year is not used up in one month. She should not take it amiss if her husband imposes more work on her than on any of the household servants. For the servants are entrusted only with the keeping and care of things, whereas the wife, as mistress in the house, also has the use and enjoyment of them.

units.la: <bl>Was sind für dienste der Hausfrawen?</bl>
units.tr: What are the duties of the housewife?

units.la: <bl>Der hausfrawen stehet wol an zu hauß bleiben/</bl> <bl>vnnd das welches zu hauß gebracht wird / auffnem-</bl> <bl>men/vnd was man verzehren sol/ herfür geben: was</bl> <bl>man aber bewahren sol / fürsichtiglich beylegen vnnd</bl> <bl>behalten / Das nicht in einem Monat verzeret</bl> <bl>werde / das man auff ein Jar solte beylegen: sie muß nit</bl> <bl>für vngut auffnemmen / wenn der Ehemann mehr</bl> <bl>würde jr auffleget/als einem vom hausgesind. Deñ</bl> <bl>dem hausgesind ist allein die bewahrung vnnd</bl> <bl>sorg der Dinge befohlen: Die hausfraw aber hat auch den</bl> <bl>nießbrauch auch als eine Herrin im hauß.</bl>
units.tr: It becomes the housewife to stay at home, to receive what is brought into the house, to bring out what is to be used up, and to lay aside and keep carefully what is to be kept, so that what should last a year is not spent in a month. She must not take it amiss if her husband lays more work on her than on any of the servants. For the servants are entrusted only with the keeping and care of things, but the housewife, as mistress of the house, also has the enjoyment of them.

units.la: Præcepta lecturus prolixiora, videat Xenophontem,& alios.
units.tr: Whoever wishes to read more extended precepts should see Xenophon and others.

units.la: Tantùm de Oeconomica: sequitur
units.tr: That is all on economics; what follows is:

units.la: DE POLITICA.
units.tr: ON POLITICS.

units.la: Quid est Politica?
units.tr: What is politics?

units.la: POLITICA, <bl>die Staatregierens kunst</bl>/ est ars in civili societate bene gubernandi: Cujus Subjectum est Civitas.
units.tr: POLITICS, <bl>the art of government of the state</bl>, is the art of governing well in civil society; its subject is the commonwealth.

units.la: Quid est Civitas?
units.tr: What is a commonwealth?

units.la: Civitas est civium eodem jure viventium collecta multitudo.
units.tr: A commonwealth is a multitude gathered together of citizens living under the same law.

units.la: Quid est Politia?
units.tr: What is a polity?

units.la: Idem quod Respublica seu Status civitatis. Politia est duplex: Recta aut aberrans. Recta ut Monarchia, <bl>ein einige herrschung</bl>/ Aristocratia, <bl>der fürnem-</bl> <bl>men vnd frommen regiment</bl>/ Timocratia, <bl>des volcks</bl> <bl>herrschung</bl>: Aberrans, ut Tyrannis, <bl>wütereÿ</bl>/ Oligarchia, <bl>ein regiment da etliche Reichen den nutze allein</bl> <bl>haben</bl> / Democratia seu Anarchia, <bl>ein herrschung des</bl> <bl>volcks/so ihm selbs Amptleut erwehlet</bl>.
units.tr: The same as a republic or state of the commonwealth. A polity is twofold: right or deviant. Right polities are: monarchy, <bl>rule by one</bl>; aristocracy, <bl>the rule of the leading and pious men</bl>; timocracy, <bl>the rule of the people</bl>. Deviant ones are: tyranny, <bl>tyrannical rage</bl>; oligarchy, <bl>a rule in which some rich men have the benefit alone</bl>; democracy or anarchy, <bl>the rule of the people, who elect their own officials</bl>.

units.la: Quid est Monarchia?
units.tr: What is monarchy?

units.la: Est imperium unius, ad communem utilitatem spectans.
units.tr: It is the rule of one, aiming at the common good.

units.la: Quid est Aristocratia?
units.tr: What is aristocracy?

units.la: Est imperium paucorum ad communem utilitatem spectans: qualis est status civitatis Norinbergæ.
units.tr: It is the rule of a few, aiming at the common good: such is the state of the city of Nuremberg.

units.la: Quid est Timocratia?
units.tr: What is timocracy?

units.la: Est imperium populi, ad communem utilitatem spectans.
units.tr: It is the rule of the people, aiming at the common good.

units.la: Quid est Tyrannis?
units.tr: What is tyranny?

units.la: Est imperium ad utilitatem unius spectans.
units.tr: It is rule aiming at the advantage of one man.

units.la: Quid est Oligarchia?
units.tr: What is oligarchy?

units.la: Est imperium ad utilitatem paucorum, scilicet divitum spectans.
units.tr: It is rule aiming at the advantage of a few, namely the rich.

units.la: Quid est Democratia?
units.tr: What is democracy?

units.la: Est imperium ad utilitatem multorum, scilicet tenuiorum spectans: qualem statum somniabat Anno Christi 1525. Germanica plebs in tumultu rusti-corum.
units.tr: It is rule aiming at the advantage of the many, namely the lowly: the kind of state the German common people dreamed of in the peasants' uprising of the year of Christ 1525.

units.la: Quot sunt partes Reipublicae?
units.tr: How many parts does a commonwealth have?

units.la: Tres: Magistratus, Senatus, Judicium.
units.tr: Three: the magistracy, the senate, and the judiciary.

units.la: Lecturus praecepta prolixiora videat Politica Aristotelis, & Thomae Freigii Quaestiones politicas.
units.tr: One who wishes to read fuller precepts should look at the Politics of Aristotle and Thomas Freige's Political Questions.

units.la: Hactenus est Politica declarata: sequitur de Apo-demica.
units.tr: So far politics has been explained; there follows the section on travel (Apodemica).

units.la: DE APODEMICA.
units.tr: CONCERNING APODEMICS.

units.la: Quid est Apodemica?
units.tr: What is Apodemics?

units.la: APODEMICA, <bl>die reisekunst/</bl> est ars bene peregrinandi ad consequendam politicam rerum cognitionem. Haec cognitio consistit in regionibus, urbibus, politia, & incolis cognoscendis.
units.tr: Apodemics, the art of travel, is the art of travelling well in order to gain a political knowledge of things. This knowledge consists in knowing regions, cities, the polity and the inhabitants.

units.la: Quot sunt in Regionibus consideranda?
units.tr: What must be considered in regions?

units.la: Tria: aër, aqua, terra. Aër, utrùm salubris an pestilens sit, qui venti, quae aves, quae infecta. In aqua consideranda, Flumina perpetua, torrentes, lacus, balneae, thermae, piscinae, fontes, rivi, aquaeductus.
units.tr: Three things: air, water and earth. For air: whether it is healthy or pestilential, which winds, which birds, which infections. In water are to be considered: perennial rivers, torrents, lakes, bathing places, hot springs, fish ponds, springs, streams and aqueducts.

units.la: In terra sunt consideranda, Agri, pagi, vici, arces, fodinae, metalla, frumenta, plantae, villae, animantia domestica & fera, frequentia urbium, res gestae, appellatio.
units.tr: In earth are to be considered: fields, villages, hamlets, citadels, pits, mines, grain, plants, country houses, domestic and wild animals, the population of the cities, the deeds done there, and the names of places.

units.la: Quaenam sunt consideranda in urbibus?
units.tr: What must be considered in cities?

units.la: Ambitus, <bl>der[?]</bl> umbkreis / centrum, <bl>das mittel in der</bl> <bl>Statt</bl> / & radii, <bl>die strassen</bl>. In ambitu seu circuitu sunt navalia, portus, portae, carceres & muri. Centrum est medium urbis punctum, ubi plærunq; forum esse solet. Forum est frumentarium piscarium, suarium, boarium, vinarium, olitorium, scrutarium, lignarium.
units.tr: The perimeter, the centre (the middle of the town) and the radii (the streets). In the perimeter or circuit are the shipyards, harbours, gates, prisons and walls. The centre is the middle point of the city, where the market square usually is. The market consists of the grain market, fish market, pig market, cattle market, wine market, vegetable market, second-hand market and timber market.

units.la: Radii a centro exeuntes sunt plateæ & viæ stratæ.
units.tr: The radii running out from the centre are the squares and the paved roads.

units.la: In urbibus præterea consideranda sunt, Curia, ærarium, <bl>Schatzkammer</bl>, armamentarium, <bl>harnisch kam-</bl> <bl>mer</bl>/cella vinaria, cerevisiaria, pharmacopolia, theatrum, porticus, basilica, Xenodochiū, <bl>ein gasthauß</bl>/ nosodochium, <bl>ein Frankenhauß</bl> / thermæ, balneæ, templa cum cœmiteriis & epitaphiis, cœnobia, collegia cum Bibliothecis, & parœciæ, <bl>Die Gei[?] samlung</bl> <bl>Derer so in eine Kirche gehö:en</bl>.
units.tr: Besides these, the following are to be considered in cities: the council house, the treasury, the strong room, the armoury, the armour chamber, the wine cellar, the beer cellar, the apothecary's shop, the theatre, colonnades, the basilica, the xenodochium, an inn, the nosodochium, a house of the Franks, baths, bathhouses, temples with their cemeteries and epitaphs, monasteries, colleges with their libraries, and parishes, and the collection of those who belong to one church.

units.la: Quot sunt in Politia consideranda?
units.tr: What must be considered in the polity?

units.la: Species politiæ: utrum Monarchia sit, an Aristocratia, an Timocratia. Item leges, judicia, genera nummorum argenteorum & aureorum.
units.tr: The kinds of polity: whether it is a monarchy, an aristocracy or a timocracy. Likewise the laws, the courts of justice, and the kinds of silver and gold coins.

units.la: Quænam in incolis sunt considerandæ?
units.tr: What must be considered in the inhabitants?

units.la: An cives sint an advenæ: qui eorum mores, qui ritus, qui habitus, quæ ratio victus: quinam sint insignes divitiis, nobilitate, artibus vel bellicis, vel Mechanicis. An sint multi Theologi, Philosophi, Jurisconsulti, Medici.
units.tr: Whether they are citizens or foreigners; what their manners, their rites, their dress and their way of life are; who are distinguished by wealth, by nobility, or by skill in the arts, whether military or mechanical; whether there are many theologians, philosophers, jurists and physicians.

units.la: Lecturus præcepta prolixiora, videat Zvingerum, Hilarium, Pirckmajerum vel alios.
units.tr: Whoever wishes for fuller rules should consult Zwinger, Hilarius, Pirckmayer or others.

units.la: Hactenus fuit Apodemica exposita: sequitur de Polemica.
units.tr: So much for the exposition of Apodemics; follows Polemics.

units.la: Quid est Polemica?
units.tr: What is Polemics?

units.la: POLEMICA, die kriegekunst / est ars bellum recte administrandi.
units.tr: Polemics, the art of war (the art of war-making), is the art of conducting war rightly.

units.la: Quid est bellum?
units.tr: What is war?

units.la: Bellum est legitima poena, suscepta ab ordinaria potestate, propter justam causam, adversus sceleratos publicae pacis turbatores, seditiosos & contumaces, propter hunc finem, ut publica pax, aut conservetur, aut recuperetur, & in pace vera doctrina de Deo, & aliae artes & linguae utiles & necessariae propagentur.
units.tr: War is a lawful punishment, undertaken by the ordinary authority, for a just cause, against wicked disturbers of the public peace, seditious and obstinate people; its end being that the public peace may either be preserved or recovered, and that in peace the true doctrine of God and other useful and necessary arts and languages may be spread.

units.la: <bl>Der Krieg ist ein rechtmäßi-</bl> <bl>ge straffe/von der verordneten Oberkeit geübet/umb</bl> <bl>gerechter sache willen / wider die boßhafftigen zer-</bl> <bl>störer gemeines frieden / vnd die aufrürischen/vnnd</bl> <bl>halßstarrigen/zu diesem ende/daß der gemeine friede</bl> <bl>entweder erhalten oder wider erlanget werde / vnnd daß im friede die wahre</bl> <bl>lehr von Gott / vnnd andere künste / vnd sprachen nützlich vnd nohtwendig er-</bl> <bl>weitert werden.</bl>
units.tr: War is a lawful punishment, carried out by the appointed authority, for a just cause, against the wicked destroyers of the common peace, and against the rebellious and stiff-necked, to this end: that the common peace either be maintained or be won back, and that in peace the true teaching of God and other arts and languages be usefully and necessarily extended.

units.la: In quibus versatur Polemica?
units.tr: In what does Polemics consist?

units.la: Versatur in Apparatu, Castris & Congressu.
units.tr: It consists in the preparation, the camp and the engagement.

units.la: In quo est apparatus belli?
units.tr: In what does the equipment for war consist?

units.la: In legione, cohortibus legionis, Imperatoribus, Tribunis, centurionibus, militibus, civibus robustis & armorum peritis, in pilo, scuto, galea, lorica, manicis, ocreis, gladiis, hastis, tormentis, nummo, commeatu, & vestibus.
units.tr: In the legion, the cohorts of the legion, the commanders, tribunes, centurions, soldiers, and sturdy citizens skilled in arms; in the javelin, shield, helmet, cuirass, arm-guards, greaves, swords, spears, siege engines, money, supplies and clothing.

units.la: <bl>Woh in stehet die rüstung zum Krieg?</bl>
units.tr: Wherein does the readiness for war consist?

units.la: <bl>In außerlesem kriegesvolck / in rotten deß</bl> <bl>kriegsvolcks/in Obersten Feldherrn/ Hauptleuten/ Rott-</bl> <bl>meistern / Soldaten / starcken bürgern die der waf-</bl> fen wissen zugebrauchen / in drey spitzigem spiesslin/ schildte / eisenhut / panzer / eisen ermelen / stifflen/ schwertern / spiessen / büchsen / geldt/proviand unnd kleidungen.
units.tr: In chosen troops; in the companies of the army; in the commanders-in-chief, captains, company commanders, soldiers, and strong citizens who know how to use weapons; in the three-pointed spear, shields, iron hats, breastplates, iron sleeves, greaves, swords, pikes, guns, money, provisions and clothing.

units.la: Quaenam sunt in castris consideranda?
units.tr: What is to be considered in camps?

units.la: Progressus agminis in castra, intervalla locorum, viarum genera, diverticula, montes, flumina, duces viarum fideles & probati, architectura castrorum, locus idoneus frumentationi: pabulationi, aquationi, lignationi, valetudini militum, victoriæ si dimicandum sit: Decursio, lustratio: praemia, ut torques, equi, agri, honores: Supplicia, ut fustigatio, decimatio.
units.tr: The advance of the column into camp; the distances between places; the kinds of roads; side-tracks off the main road; mountains; rivers; trusty and proven guides of the roads; skill in laying out camps; a place suitable for gathering grain, fodder, water and wood; the health of the soldiers; victory, if a battle must be fought; sallies and reviews; rewards such as neck-chains, horses, fields and honours; and punishments such as flogging and decimation.

units.la: Was muß man in den Kriegslägern bed- encken?
units.tr: What must one consider in the military camps?

units.la: Die fürrückung des Kriegesvolcks ins Läger/ die weite der örther / die art der wege / die abweglin von der landstrassen/berge/wässer/ getrew unnd bewehrte führer der wege / die wissenheit läger zu bawen / der orth dem Kornsamlen bequem / der Fute[?]rung/der holtzung/der gesundtheit der Kriegesleute/ der überwindung wenn man streitten soll: das außlauffen / die beschawung: die besoldung/ als / halßketten/pferde/ äcker/ ehre: die straffe/als das schlahen mit steckēn / unnd wenn je der zehende getödtet wird.
units.tr: The advance of the army into the camp; the distances of the places; the nature of the roads; the side-tracks from the highway, mountains, waters; faithful and tried guides of the roads; the knowledge of how to build camps; a place convenient for collecting grain, for fodder, for wood; the health of the soldiers; victory, when one must fight; the sallies and the inspections; the pay, such as neck-chains, horses, fields, honour; the punishment, such as beating with sticks, and when every tenth man is put to death.

units.la: Quae sunt in Congressu consideranda?
units.tr: What things are to be considered in the engagement?

units.la: Vires, locus aut natura aut arte superior, acies simplex, duplex, triplex, quadruplex, cuneata, quadrata, rotunda: cohortatio, vinea, agger, turris ambulatoria.
units.tr: Strength; a place superior either by nature or by art; the line of battle, single, double, triple, quadruple, wedge-shaped, square, round; exhortation; the mantlet (vinea); the mound (agger); the movable tower.

units.la: Was muß man bedencken so man sich in den streit begibt?
units.tr: What must one consider when entering into battle?

units.la: Die kräffte/der orth von natur oder auß küst hoch/ <bl>Die schlachtordnung</bl> <bl>einfacht/zweyfacht/dreyfacht/vierfacht/gespitzet/vierecket/rund: die vermanung</bl> <bl>zum streit/eingeflochten schirmtach/unter dem die</bl> <bl>stürmenden stehen/ein thurn auff rädern gemacht/</bl> <bl>darauff die Kriegsleute die Städte bestürmen.</bl>
units.tr: The strength of the forces; a place high by nature or by the lie of the ground; <bl>the battle order: single, double, triple, quadruple, wedge-shaped, square, round; the exhortation</bl> <bl>to battle; the interwoven shelters under which</bl> <bl>the storming troops stand; a tower made on wheels,</bl> <bl>from which the soldiers assault the cities.</bl>

units.la: Lecturus praecepta prolixiora, videat Aelianum, Frontinum, Ramum de disciplina militari Caesaris vel alios.
units.tr: A reader who wants fuller precepts should consult Aelian, Frontinus, Ramus on the military discipline of Caesar, or others.

units.la: Hactenus est Polemica expositia: sequitur de Historia.
units.tr: So much for the Polemica expositio; there follows the part on History.

units.la: DE HISTORIA.
units.tr: ON HISTORY.

units.la: Quid est Historia?
units.tr: What is History?

units.la: HISTORIA est rerum gestarum expositio, versatur circa res gestas: Estque aut universalis aut particularis.
units.tr: History is the exposition of things done; it is concerned with actions performed. It is either universal or particular.

units.la: Quid est Historia universalis?
units.tr: What is universal history?

units.la: Quæ commemorat res universas: Eaque est rursus vel Ecclesiastica, omnium prima & antiquissima, quæ præcipuè commemorat res Ecclesiæ: Vel politica, quæ Monarchiarum, Imperiorum & rerumpublicarum initia, constitutiones, incrementa, gubernationes & conversiones exponit.
units.tr: It is that which recounts all things. This is in turn either ecclesiastical, the first and oldest of all, which chiefly recounts the affairs of the Church; or political, which sets out the beginnings, constitutions, growth, governments and changes of monarchies, empires and commonwealths.

units.la: Quid est Historia particularis?
units.tr: What is particular history?

units.la: Quæ commemorat res particulares.
units.tr: It is that which recounts particular things.

units.la: Quænam sunt in Historia consideranda?
units.tr: What things are to be considered in history?

units.la: Synopsis, <bl>ein ansichtiger kurtzer begriff</bl> / Authores, Ordo, Locus, Tempus.
units.tr: The synopsis, a clear and brief summary; the authors, the order, the place, the time.

units.la: Quænam est Synopsis Historiæ?
units.tr: What is the synopsis of history?

units.la: Historia post diluvium dividitur in quatuor Monarchias, Assyriorum, Persarum, Macedonum & Romanorum ex oraculo Danielis cap.7. Videbam in vifione mea nocte, & ecce quatuor venti cœli pugnabant in mari magno. Et quatuor bestiæ grandes ascendebant de mari diversæ inter se. Prima quasi Leæna, & alas habebat aquilæ: Aspiciebam donec evulsæ sunt alæ ejus, & sublata est de terra, & super pedes quasi homo stetit, & cor hominis datum est ei.
units.tr: After the Flood, history is divided into four monarchies: those of the Assyrians, Persians, Macedonians and Romans, according to the oracle of Daniel, chapter 7: "I saw in my vision by night, and behold the four winds of heaven strove upon the great sea. And four great beasts came up from the sea, diverse one from another. The first was like a lion, and had eagle's wings. I beheld till its wings were plucked, and it was lifted up from the earth, and stood upon its feet as a man, and a man's heart was given to it."

units.la: Et ecce bestia alia similis ursō in parte stetit: & tres ordines erant in ore, & in dentibus ejus, & sic dicebant ei, Surge, comede carnes plurimas.
units.tr: "And behold another beast, like a bear, stood up on one side; and it had three ribs in its mouth between its teeth, and they said thus to it: Arise, devour much flesh."

units.la: Post hæc aspiciebam, & ecce alia, quasi pardus, & alas habebat quasi avis quatuor super se, & quatuor capita erant in bestia, & potestas data est ei.
units.tr: "After this I beheld, and lo, another like a leopard, which had upon its back four wings of a fowl; the beast also had four heads, and power was given to it."

units.la: Post hæc aspiciebam in visione noctis, & ecce bestia quarta terribilis atque mirabilis & fortis nimis, dentes ferreos habebat magnos, comedens atq; comminuens, & reliqua pedibus suis conculcans, dissimilis autem erat cæteris bestiis quas videram ante eam, & habebat cornua decem. Considerabam cornua, & ecce cornu aliud parvulum ortum est de medio eorum, & tria de cornibus primis evulsa sunt à facie ejus, & ecce oculi, quasi oculi hominis erant in cornu isto, & os loquens ingentia.
units.tr: "After this I saw in the night vision, and behold a fourth beast, terrible and wonderful and exceedingly strong; it had great iron teeth, devouring and breaking in pieces, and treading the rest under its feet. It was diverse from all the beasts that were before it, and it had ten horns. I considered the horns, and behold there came up among them another little horn, before which three of the first horns were plucked up by the roots; and behold, in this horn were eyes like the eyes of a man, and a mouth speaking great things."

units.la: Quartam bestiam omnes intelligunt Monarchiam Romanam, & decem cornua, decem regna Imperio Romano subjecta, ut sunt Syria, Aegyptus, Asia, Græcia, Italia, Gallia, Hispania, Africa, Germania, Anglia. Per parvum cornu intelligunt Turcicum im-perium.
units.tr: All understand the fourth beast to be the Roman monarchy, and the ten horns to be the ten kingdoms subject to the Roman Empire: Syria, Egypt, Asia, Greece, Italy, Gaul, Spain, Africa, Germany and England. They understand the little horn to be the Turkish empire.

units.la: Quis fuit primus Rex Assyriorum & ultimus?
units.tr: Who was the first and the last king of the Assyrians?

units.la: Ninus fuit primus: ultimus Sardanapalus.
units.tr: Ninus was the first; Sardanapalus the last.

units.la: Quis fuit primus & ultimus Persarum?
units.tr: Who was the first and the last of the Persians?

units.la: Cyrus fuit primus: Darius ultimus.
units.tr: Cyrus was the first; Darius the last.

units.la: Quis fuit primus Monarcha Ma-cedonum?
units.tr: Who was the first monarch of the Macedonians?

units.la: Alexander Magnus.
units.tr: Alexander the Great.

units.la: Quis fuit primus & ultimus Rex Ro- manorum?
units.tr: Who was the first and the last king of the Romans?

units.la: Romulus fuit primus : ultimus Tarquinius Superbus.
units.tr: Romulus was the first; the last was Tarquin the Proud.

units.la: Quis fuit primus Imperator Romanus?
units.tr: Who was the first Roman emperor?

units.la: Julius Cæsar, quem secutus est Augustus.
units.tr: Julius Caesar, whom Augustus followed.

units.la: Quis fuit primus Imperator Constan- tinopolitanus?
units.tr: Who was the first emperor of Constantinople?

units.la: Constantinus Magnus : ultimus fuit Constantinus Palæologus, sub quo Constantinopolim Turcæ ceperunt. •
units.tr: Constantine the Great. The last was Constantine Palaeologus, under whom the Turks took Constantinople.

units.la: Lecturus tractationem Historiarum pleniorem videat Chronica Philippi Melanchthonis, quæ D. Doctor Pezelius teutonicè reddidit : Et Martyrologium Fochsi. •
units.tr: Let the reader who wants a fuller treatment of histories look at the Chronicle of Philip Melanchthon, which Doctor Pezel rendered into German, and at Foxe's Martyrology.

units.la: Hastenus est de Historia dictum : Sequitur de Rudimentis juris.
units.tr: So much has been said about history. Follows: on the rudiments of law.

units.la: DE RUDIMENTIS IURIS.
units.tr: DE RUDIMENTIS IURIS.

units.la: Quibus rebus Imperatorem decoratum esse oportet?
units.tr: What qualities should an emperor be adorned with?

units.la: IMPERATORIAM Majestatem non solùm armis decoratam, sed etiam legibus oportet esse armatam, ut utrunque tempus, & bellorum & pacis, rectè possit gubernari. In princip.procem.instit.
units.tr: The imperial majesty should be adorned not only with arms but also armed with laws, so that both kinds of time, of war and of peace, may be governed rightly. In the beginning of the Preface of the Institutes.

units.la: Fuitne Justinianus armis & legibus decoratus?
units.tr: Was Justinian adorned with arms and laws?

units.la: Fuit : ipse enim inquit §.1.in procem.inst. Quorum utranq; viam cum summis vigiliis, summaque providentia, annuente Deo, perfecimus. Et bellicos quidem sudores nostros, Barbaricæ gentes sub juga nostra redactæ cognoscunt. Et cùm Sacratissimas constitutiones antea confusas in luculentam ereximus consonantiam, id est, cùm tam trium veterum Gregoriani, Hermogeniani atque Theodosiani Codicum constitutiones, quam plurimas alias post eosdem Codices à Theodosio Divinæ memoriæ, cæterisque post eum retrò principibus, à nostra etiam clementia positas, in unum (Justinianeum) Codicem, fœlici nostro vocabulo nuncupandum, colligi præcepimus, ut dicitur in Cōstitut.[?] Summa de Justinian. Cod. confirmand. Tunc nostram extendimus curam ad immensa veteris prudentiæ volumina: & opus desperatum, quasi per medium profundum cuntes, cœlesti favore jam adimplevimus. §. 2. in*procem. institut. Id est, postea verò maximum opus aggredientes, ipsa vetustatis studiosissima opera jam pene confusa & dissoluta, viro excelso (Triboniano) permisimus tàm colligere, quàm certo moderamine tradere. Sed cùm omnia percontabamur, à præfato viro excelso suggestum est, duo pene millia librorum esse conscripta, & plus quàm trecentiens decem millia versuum à veteribus effusa, quæ necesse esset omnia & legere & perscrutari, & ex his si quid optimum fuisset, eligere. Quod cœlesti fulgore & summæ Trinitatis favore confectum est secundum nostra mandata, quæ ab initio ad memoratum virum excelsum fecimus: & in quinquaginta libros, omne quod utilissimum erat, collectum est: & omnes ambiguitates decisæ, nullo seditioso relicto: nomenque libris imposuimus Digestorum seu Pandectarum: qui omnes Disputationes & decisiones in se habent legitimas, ut refert Imperat. in Constit. Tanta. §. omnia. versic. postea vero de Confirmat. Digestor.
units.tr: He was. For he himself says, §1 in the Preface of the Institutes: "Having brought both of these paths to completion with the greatest vigilance and the greatest foresight, by the will of God, our sweated labours in war are known to the barbarian peoples brought under our yoke. And when we had brought our most sacred constitutions, previously confused, into a clear harmony, that is, when we ordered the constitutions of the three older codes, of Gregory, Hermogenian and Theodosius, together with the very many others laid down after those codes by Theodosius of divine memory and the other emperors before him, and also by our own clemency, to be gathered into one code, to be called by our fortunate name, the Justinianic Code, as is said in the constitution Summa on the confirmation of the Justinianic Code. Then we turned our care to the immense volumes of ancient wisdom, and, going as it were through a deep sea, we have now accomplished by heavenly favour a work thought desperate." §2 in the Preface of the Institutes: "That is, afterwards, undertaking the greatest work, we entrusted to the excellent man Tribonian the task of gathering and of setting out with a sure guidance the very studious works of antiquity, now almost confused and dissolved. But while we were inquiring into everything, it was reported by the aforesaid excellent man that about two thousand books had been written, and more than three million verses had been poured out by the ancients, all of which it would be necessary both to read and to examine, and from them to choose whatever was best. This was accomplished, according to our commands which we first gave to the said excellent man, by the heavenly splendour and the favour of the most holy Trinity; and everything most useful was gathered into fifty books, all ambiguities were settled, and no seditious matter was left behind. We named the books the Digests, or Pandects, which contain all the lawful disputations and decisions," as the Emperor reports in the constitution Tanta, §omnia, at the words "but afterwards" on the confirmation of the Digests.

units.la: Cumque hoc (inquit Imperator, §. 3. in proœm. in-fit[?].) Deo propitio peractum est, Triboniano, nec non Theophilo & Dorotheo convocatis, mandavimus specialiter, ut ipsi nostra authoritate, nostrisque suasionibus institutiones componerent, ut liceat vobis prima legum cunabula seu totius legitimæ scientiæ prima elementa, non ab antiquis fabulis discere, sed ab imperiali splendore appetere.
units.tr: When this had been done, by God's favour (the Emperor says, §3 in the Preface of the Institutes), Tribonian, Theophilus and Dorotheus having been summoned, we specially commanded them, by our authority and under our guidance, to compose the Institutes, so that you may learn the first cradle of the laws, or the first elements of the whole legal science, not from old fables, but may aim at them from imperial splendour.

units.la: His ita absolutis Imperator priorem Codicem Iustinianeum appellatum emendavit, atque ipsum longè emendatiorem, quàm antea edidit. Et is est Codex, quæ hodie inter reliquos juris libros habemus: prior vero Codex ex tribus Codicibus Gregoriano, Hermogeniano & Theodosiano factus, hodie non extat.
units.tr: With these things thus finished, the Emperor amended the earlier code called the Justinianic, and published it far more corrected than before. This is the code which we today have among the other books of law; the earlier code, made from the three codes of Gregory, Hermogenian and Theodosius, no longer exists.

units.la: Postremò Authenticas seu Novellas Constitutiones, præstantissimam & maximè necessariam juris civilis partem protulit: quæ solæ reliquo juri civili authoritate addunt, solæ detrahunt, solæ novam formam & normam attribuunt, teste Dom. Mynsinger.
units.tr: Lastly, he produced the Authentic or Novel Constitutions, the most outstanding and most necessary part of civil law; these alone add authority to the rest of civil law, these alone take it away, these alone give it a new form and rule, as Dr. Mynsinger attests.

units.la: His prædictis juris libris, sunt Feudorum consuetudines additæ, & aliæ quædam Constitutiones Imperiales adjectæ.
units.tr: To these aforesaid books of law have been added the customs of the fiefs, and certain other imperial constitutions have been appended.

units.la: Quare prædicta à Tyronibus juris sunt diligenter notanda?
units.tr: Why must the aforesaid things be carefully noted by beginners in law?

units.la: Ut sciant, quæ sit librorum juris series, ne illis objiciatur, quod Quintus Mutius Servio dixit: Turpe esse patricio & nobili & causas oranti jus in quo versaretur ignorare, l.2. §. Servius 43. ff. de origin. juris.
units.tr: So that they may know what the sequence of the law books is, and so that the objection of Quintus Mucius to Servius may not be raised against them: that it is shameful for a patrician and a noble, who pleads cases, to be ignorant of the law in which he is engaged; Law 2, §Servius 43, Digest, on the origin of law.

units.la: Quare Digestorum seu Pandectarum aliquem locum allegaturi, librum ipsum per du- plex ff. signamus?
units.tr: Why, when we are going to cite some passage of the Digests or Pandects, do we mark the book itself with a double ff.?

units.la: Cùm Tribonianus responsa jurisprudentum tanquam in Centonem quendam redegisset, operi & Digestorum & Pandectarum nomen imposuit: Et quoniam Græci ipsi confarctores fuerant, verisimile est, eos solitos sub græco nomine pandectarum librum ipsum adducere. Cùm itaque primam tantùm notam π cum accentu circumflexo scriberent, nostri Latini eos imitabantur: sed criptores librarii, qui literam ignorabant, existimaverunt esse binas ff. in quam figuram facilè fuit græcam notam depravare. Hæc dicit Mynsingerus ex Alciato.
units.tr: Since Tribonian had reduced the responses of the jurists into a kind of patchwork, he gave the work the name of Digests and also of Pandects. And since the Greeks themselves had been the compilers, it is likely that they were accustomed to cite the book itself under the Greek name of Pandects. Since they wrote only the first sign, the Greek letter [π] with a circumflex accent, our Latin writers imitated them; but the scribes, who did not know the letter, thought that there were two ff.'s, and it was easy to corrupt the Greek sign into that shape. So says Mynsinger, from Alciatus.

units.la: Quis est verus Jurisprudentiæ scopus & finis?
units.tr: What is the true aim and purpose of jurisprudence?

units.la: Imperator quidem inquit: Nullus manebit non audiens legem, quæ neque in paupertate vivere, neq; mori in anxietate permittit cap 4. in sin. Auth. de hæredib. & Falcid. Ac vulgò dicitur:
units.tr: The Emperor indeed says: "No one will remain who does not hear the law, which permits him neither to live in poverty nor to die in anxiety," at the end of chapter 4 of the Authentic constitution on heirs and the Falcidian law. And it is commonly said:

units.la: Dat Galenus opes, & Justinianus honoresEx aliis paleas ex istis collige grana.
units.tr: Galen gives wealth, and Justinian gives honours; from other things gather the chaff, from these gather the grain.

units.la: Tamen principalis finis non spes lucri esse debet, sed ut gloria Dei in Administratione Reipublicæ, illustretur, inquit Schneidevvinus.
units.tr: Yet the principal end must not be the hope of gain, but that the glory of God be made illustrious in the administration of the commonwealth, says Schneidewin.

units.la: Quænam in studiosò ad jus anhelanti requiruntur?
units.tr: What is required of a student who aspires to the law?

units.la: Si quis forte velit, Jurisconsultus haberi, Continuet studium: velit à quocunq; doceri, Invigilet, nec vincat eum tortura laboris, Fortior insurgat cunctisq; recentior horis.
units.tr: If anyone wishes to be called a jurist, let him keep at his studies. Let him wish to be taught by anyone at all, let him be vigilant, and let not the torment of labour overcome him; let him rise stronger, and fresher than the hours themselves.

units.la: QUOT SUNT TITULI IN PRIMO libro Institutionum Juris?
units.tr: HOW MANY TITLES ARE THERE IN THE FIRST BOOK OF THE INSTITUTES OF LAW?

units.la: Viginti Sex.
units.tr: Twenty-six.

units.la: QUIS EST PRIMUS TITULUS? De Justitia & Jure. <bl>Von Gerechtigkeit und Recht.</bl>
units.tr: WHAT IS THE FIRST TITLE? On Justice and Law. <bl>Von Gerechtigkeit und Recht.</bl>

units.la: Quotuplex est Justitia?
units.tr: Of how many kinds is justice?

units.la: Duplex : Spiritualis aut Civilis. Spiritualis ad Theologiam spectat. Civilis justitia est, quae pertinet ad formandos in hac vita politicos mores, & exigit exteriorem quandam honestatem, ut in tuto sit Reipublicæ tranquillitas. Civilis justitia est duplex: universalis aut particularis.
units.tr: Of two kinds: spiritual or civil. Spiritual justice belongs to theology. Civil justice is that which concerns the forming of political morals in this life, and it requires a certain outward decency, so that the tranquillity of the commonwealth may be secure. Civil justice is of two kinds: universal or particular.

units.la: Quid est Justitia universalis?
units.tr: What is universal justice?

units.la: Est obedientia juxta omnes leges. Hanc Imperator in Institutionibus non definit.
units.tr: It is obedience to all the laws. The Emperor does not define this in the Institutes.

units.la: Quid est Justitia particularis?
units.tr: What is particular justice?

units.la: Est constans & perpetua voluntas, jus suum cuique tribuendi. In princ. Inst. cod.
units.tr: It is a constant and perpetual will to render to each his own right. In the beginning of the same Institutes.

units.la: In hac Imperatoris definitione voluntas nihil aliud est, quàm naturalis notitia omnium hominum animis insita, quæ tàm in scelveratis, quàm probis semper hortatur ut unicuique suum tribuatur: neque enim, si quis recedat à naturali illa notitia, quæ justitia appellatur, id fit vitio justitiæ, sed pravi ac sceleratí hominis perversa natura, inquit Mynsingerus.
units.tr: In this definition of the Emperor, "will" means nothing other than the natural knowledge implanted in the minds of all men, which always urges, in the wicked as in the upright, that each be given what is his. For if someone departs from that natural knowledge, which is called justice, this does not happen through a fault of justice, but through the perverse nature of a wicked and criminal man, says Mynsinger.

units.la: Quotuplex est Justitia particularis?
units.tr: Of how many kinds is particular justice?

units.la: Duplex : Distributiva aut Commutativa. Distributiva pertinet ad præmia & pœnas distribuendas pro ratione & varietate meritorum. Commutativa versatur circa contractus, & æqualium rerum permutationes.
units.tr: Of two kinds: distributive or commutative. Distributive justice concerns the distribution of rewards and punishments according to the proportion and variety of merits. Commutative justice is concerned with contracts and with the exchange of equal things.

units.la: Quid est Jurisprudentia?
units.tr: What is jurisprudence?

units.la: Jurisprudentia est Divinarum atque humanarum rerum notitia, justi atque injusti scientia. §. 1. inst. cod.
units.tr: Jurisprudence is the knowledge of divine and human things, the science of what is just and unjust. Section 1 of the same Institutes.

units.la: Quid est Jus?
units.tr: What is law?

units.la: Jus est ars boni & æqui. l. 1. in princip. ff. de iustit. & jur.
units.tr: Law is the art of what is good and equitable. Law 1, at the beginning, in the Digest on justice and law.

units.la: Quomodo Jura Tyronibus commodè expo- ni tradiq; possunt?
units.tr: How may the laws be explained and handed down to beginners conveniently?

units.la: Si primò levi ac simplici via, post deinde diligentissima atque exactissima interpretatione singula tradantur. §.2.inst.cod.
units.tr: If they are first delivered by a light and simple way, and afterwards each point is taught by the most diligent and exact interpretation. Section 2 of the same Institutes.

units.la: Quæ sunt Juris præcepta?
units.tr: What are the precepts of law?

units.la: Juris præcepta sunt hæc: Honeste vivere, alterum non lædere, suum cuiq; tribuere. §.3.inst.cod.
units.tr: The precepts of law are these: to live honourably, not to harm another, to give each his own. Section 3 of the same Institutes.

units.la: Quot sunt hujus studii positiones seu species?
units.tr: How many divisions or kinds does this study have?

units.la: Hujus studii duæ sunt positiones, publicum & privatum. Publicum jus est, quod ad statum rei Romanæ spectat: privatum, quod ad singulorum utilitatem. Dicendum est igitur de jure privato, quod tripertitum est: Collectum est enim ex naturalibus præceptis, aut gentium aut civilibus. §.4.inst.cod.
units.tr: This study has two divisions, public and private. Public law is that which concerns the condition of the Roman state; private law is that which concerns the advantage of individuals. It must therefore be said of private law, which is threefold, since it is gathered from the natural precepts, from those of the nations, or from civil ones. Section 4 of the same Institutes.

units.la: QUIS EST SECUNDUS Titulus?
units.tr: What is the Second Title?

units.la: De Jure naturali, Gentium & Civili. Von natürlichem Recht / der Völcker und Bürgerlichem. Quotuplex est Jus naturale?
units.tr: On Natural Law, the Law of Nations and Civil Law. How many kinds of natural law are there?

units.la: Duplex: Primarium aut Secundarium. Jus naturale primarium est, quod natura omnia animalia docuit. Nam jus istud non humani generis proprium est: sed omnium animalium, quæ in cœlo, quæ in terra, quæ in mari nascuntur. Hinc descendit maris atq; fœminæ conjunctio, quam nos matrimonium appellamus: hinc liberorum procreatio, hinc educatio. in princ.inst.cod.
units.tr: There are two kinds: primary and secondary. Primary natural law is that which nature taught to all animals. For this law is not peculiar to the human race but belongs to all animals born in the heavens, on the earth and in the sea. From it descends the union of male and female, which we call marriage; from it comes the procreation of children, and from it their upbringing. in princ.inst.cod.

units.la: Jus naturale secundarium est notitia mentibus hominum Divinitus insita, de bonis moribus optimam vivendi rationem proponens.
units.tr: Secondary natural law is the knowledge implanted in human minds by God, which sets forth the best rule of living in matters of good morals.

units.la: Quotuplex est Jus Gentium.
units.tr: How many kinds of the Law of Nations are there?

units.la: Duplex : primarium aut secundarium. Jus Gentium primarium nihil aliud est, quàm jus naturale secundarium, illa scilicet notitia Divinitùs mentihumanis insita, qua naturalis ratio judicat, quid deceat.
units.tr: There are two kinds: primary and secondary. Primary law of nations is nothing other than secondary natural law, namely that knowledge implanted in human minds by God, by which natural reason judges what is fitting.

units.la: Hujus juris gentium effecta sunt, veluti erga Deum religio : ut parentibus & patriæ parcamus. l. 2. ff. de juft. & jur. ut vim atque injuriam propulsemus. Nam jure hoc evenit, ut quod quisq; ob tutelam corporis fui fecerit, jure fecisse existimetur. l. 3. ff. cod.
units.tr: Among the effects of this law of nations are: religious reverence toward God; that we spare parents and fatherland; that we repel force and injury. For by this law it comes about that whatever a person has done to defend his own body is considered to have been done lawfully. l. 2. ff. de just. & jur.; l. 3. ff. cod.

units.la: Jus Gentium secundarium est, quod naturalis ratio inter omnes homines constituit : id apud omnes peræque custoditur : vocaturque Jus Gentium, quasi quo Jure omnes Gentes utantur, §. 1. inst. cod. Interdum jus naturale & jus Gentium secundarium pro eodem sumuntur. §. singulor. inst. de rer. divis.
units.tr: Secondary law of nations is what natural reason has established among all men; it is observed equally by all, and it is called the law of nations, as if it were the law which all nations use. §. 1. inst. cod. Sometimes natural law and secondary law of nations are taken to be the same. §. singulor. inst. de rer. divis.

units.la: Ex hoc Jure Gentium secundario intiodu&a sunt bella : discretæ gentes : regna condita : Dominia distin&a : agris termini positi : ædificia collocata : commercia, emptiones & venditiones, locationes, conductiones, obligationes institutæ : Exceptis (stipulatione, literarum obligatione, sponsalitia largitate seu donatione propter nuptias, & contractu Emphyteutico, Mayer[?] contract) quæ à jure civili introductæ sunt. l. 5. ff. eod.
units.tr: From this secondary law of nations wars were introduced, nations were separated, kingdoms founded, dominions distinguished, boundaries set on fields, buildings erected, and commerce, buying and selling, leases, hirings and obligations instituted. Excepted are those (stipulation, obligation by letter, the betrothal gift or donation on account of marriage, and the emphyteutic contract, the Mayer contract) which were introduced by civil law. l. 5. ff. eod.

units.la: Quid est jus Civile?
units.tr: What is civil law?

units.la: Quod quisq; populus ipse sibi jus constituit : id ipsius proprium civitatis est : vocaturq; jus civile, quasi jus proprium ipsius civitatis. §. jus autem. inst. cod.
units.tr: Whatever law a people establishes for itself is that people's own law, and it is called civil law, as if it were the law proper to the state itself. §. jus autem. inst. cod.

units.la: Quotuplex est Jus Civile?
units.tr: How many kinds of civil law are there?

units.la: Duplex[?] : Publicum aut Privatum. Publicum dividitur in scriptum & non scriptum. Jus civile publicum scriptum est Lex, Plebiscitum, Senatusconsultū Principum placita, Magistratuum edicta, responsa Prudentum.
units.tr: There are two kinds: public and private. Public law is divided into written and unwritten. Public written civil law consists of: the statute (lex), the plebiscite, the senatorial decree, the decrees of princes, the edicts of magistrates, and the responses of jurists.

units.la: Quid est Lex?
units.tr: What is a lex?

units.la: Lex est jus, quod populus Romanus Senatorio magistratu interrogante (veluti Consule) constituebat,§.lex est,inst.eod.
units.tr: A lex is law which the Roman people enacted when a senatorial magistrate (such as a consul) put the question. §. lex est, inst. eod.

units.la: Quid est Plebiscitum?
units.tr: What is a plebiscite?

units.la: Plebiscitum est, quod plebs, plebejo magistratu interrogante (veluti Tribuno) constituebat,§.plebiscitum.inst.eod.
units.tr: A plebiscite is what the plebs enacted when a plebeian magistrate (such as a tribune) put the question. §. plebiscitum. inst. eod.

units.la: Quid est Senatusconsultum?
units.tr: What is a senatorial decree?

units.la: Senatusconsultum est, quod senatus jubet atque constituit,§.Senatusconsultum inst.eod.
units.tr: A senatorial decree is what the Senate orders and establishes. §. senatusconsultum. inst. eod.

units.la: Quid est Principis placitum?
units.tr: What is a prince's decision?

units.la: Est quod principi placuit, sive per epistolam constituit, vel cognoscens decrevit, vel edicto præcepit,§. Sed & quod. inst. eod.
units.tr: It is what pleased the prince: whatever he established by letter, decided upon examination, or prescribed by edict. §. sed & quod. inst. eod.

units.la: Quid est prætoris edictum?
units.tr: What is the praetor's edict?

units.la: Est quod Prætor edixit.Hoc etiam jus honorarium solemus appellare,§.prætorum.inst.eod.
units.tr: It is what the praetor has decreed. We are accustomed to call this also honorary law. §. praetorum. inst. eod.

units.la: Quid sunt responsa prudentum?
units.tr: What are the responses of jurists?

units.la: Responsa prudentum sunt sententiæ & opiniones eorum, quibus permissum erat de jure respondere.§. responsa.inst.eod.
units.tr: The responses of jurists are the judgments and opinions of those who were permitted to give legal answers. §. responsa. inst. eod.

units.la: Quid est Jus Civile publicum non scriptum?
units.tr: What is unwritten public civil law?

units.la: Est generalis consuetudo, qua omnes omnium ordinum homines hodiè in imperio Romano utuntur, ut sunt Consuetudines Feudorum, quæ licèt memoriæ caussa in Corpore Juris scriptæ sint: tamen nō sunt jus scriptum, quod sanctione aliqua principis, puta constitutione, lege, Senatusconsulto, introductum est: sed sunt jus Consuetudine fundatum.
units.tr: It is the general custom which all people of every rank today use throughout the Roman empire, such as the customs of feuds. Although these are written down in the Body of Law for the sake of memory, they are not written law, since they were not introduced by any sanction of a prince, such as a constitution, statute or senatorial decree; they are law founded on custom.

units.la: Quid est Jus Civile privatum scriptum?
units.tr: What is written private civil law?

units.la: Est illud quod unaquæq; civitas cum expresso cosensu populi sibi constituit : Et appellatur alias jus municipale, seu statutum, vulgo <bl>Wilkhür</bl> / <bl>Weic-</bl> <bl>hbild/oder Stattrecht.</bl>
units.tr: It is that which each city establishes for itself with the express consent of the people. It is also called municipal law or statute, commonly Willkür, Weichbild or Stadtrecht (town law).

units.la: Quis autem possit condere statuta, dicit Schneidevvinus ad §.jus autem civil.inst.hoc titulo.
units.tr: Who may draw up statutes, Schneidewin discusses at §. jus autem civile, this title.

units.la: Quid est Jus Civile privatum non scriptum?
units.tr: What is unwritten private civil law?

units.la: Est quod usus approbavit. Nam diuturni mores, consensu utentium comprobati, legem imitantur. §. sine scripto, inst. cod. Et dicitur Consuetudo Specialis. Quomodo autem consuetudo introducatur, docet Schneidevvinus hic.
units.tr: It is what usage has approved. For long-standing customs, approved by the consent of those who observe them, imitate law. It is called special custom. Schneidewin teaches here how custom is introduced. §. sine scripto, inst. cod.

units.la: Quae jura non mutantur?
units.tr: Which laws are not changed?

units.la: Naturalia quidem jura, quæ apud omnes gentes peræque observantur. Divina quadam providentia constituta, semper firma atque immutabilia permanent. Ea vero quæ ipsa sibi quæque civitas constituit sæpe mutari solent, vel tacito consensu populi, vel alia postea lege lata.§.sed natural.inst.eod.
units.tr: Natural laws, indeed, which are observed equally among all nations and were established by a certain divine providence, remain always firm and unchangeable. But those laws which each state establishes for itself are often changed, either by the tacit consent of the people or by another law passed later. §. sed natural. inst. eod.

units.la: Quorsum pertinent jura?
units.tr: What is the relevance of rights?

units.la: Omne jus, quo utimur, vel ad personas pertinet, (quibus jus redditur) vel ad res (de quibus jus redditur) vel ad actiones (per quas jus redditur.) Et prius de personis videamus. Nam parum est jus nosse, si personæ, quarum causa constitutum est, ignorentur. §.final.inst.eod. Vide Vvesenbecium[?] super institut.
units.tr: Every right we use either pertains to persons (to whom the right is rendered), or to things (concerning which the right is rendered), or to actions (through which the right is rendered). Let us first look at persons. For it is of little use to know the law if the persons for whose sake it was established are unknown. See the final section of the same Institutes. See Wesenbeck on the Institutes.

units.la: QUIS EST TERTIUS Titulus?
units.tr: WHAT IS THE THIRD TITLE?

units.la: De Jure Personarum. <bl>Vom Recht</bl> <bl>der Personen.</bl>
units.tr: On the Law of Persons. <bl>Of the law</bl> <bl>of persons.</bl>

units.la: Quae est summa Divisio personarum?
units.tr: What is the chief division of persons?

units.la: Summa divisio personarum hæc est, quod omnes homines aut liberi sunt, aut servi. in princ.inst.eod. l.3. de statu hominum..
units.tr: The chief division of persons is this: all men are either free or slaves. Inst. eod. in princ.; D. de statu hominum, l. 3.

units.la: Quid est Libertas?
units.tr: What is Liberty?

units.la: Libertas quidem ( ex qua etiam liberi vocantur) est naturalis facultas ejus, quod cuique facere libet, nisi si quid vi aut jure prohibetur. §.1.inst.cod.l.4.ff.de stat. hom.
units.tr: Liberty (from which free men are also so called) is the natural power of doing what each person pleases, unless something is forbidden by force or by law. Inst. cod. §.1; D. de statu hominum, l. 4.

units.la: Quid est Servitus?
units.tr: What is Servitude?

units.la: Servitus est constitutio juris gentium, qua quis Domino alieno contra naturam subjicitur. Servi autem ex eo appellati sunt, quòd Imperatores captivos vendere, & per hoc servare, nec occidere solent: qui etiam mancipia dicti sunt, eò quòd ab hostibus manu capiuntur. §.Servitus.inst.cod.
units.tr: Servitude is an institution of the law of nations, by which someone is made subject, against nature, to another's lordship. Slaves, moreover, have been so called because commanders were accustomed to sell captives rather than kill them, and so to keep them alive; they are also called mancipia, because they are taken by hand from enemies. Inst. cod., §. Servitus.

units.la: Quot modis fiunt servi?
units.tr: In how many ways do people become slaves?

units.la: Servi aut nascuntur aut fiunt. Nascuntur ex Ancillis nostris: fiunt aut jure gentium, id est, ex captivitate, aut jure civili, cùm liber homo major viginti annis ad pretium participandum se venundari passus est. §. Servi autem. inst.cod.
units.tr: Slaves are either born or made. They are born of our female slaves. They are made either by the law of nations, that is, through captivity, or by civil law, when a free man over twenty years old has allowed himself to be sold so as to share in the price. Inst. cod., §. Servi autem.

units.la: Estne differentia inter liberos & servos?
units.tr: Is there any difference between free persons and slaves?

units.la: In servorum conditione nulla est differentia: in liberis autem multæ: aut enim sunt ingenui aut libertini. §.final.inst.cod.
units.tr: In the condition of slaves there is no difference; among free persons, however, there are many: for they are either freeborn (ingenui) or freedmen (libertini). Inst. cod., §. final.

units.la: QUIS EST QVARTVS Titulus? De Ingenuis. <bl>Von den Frengebornen.</bl>
units.tr: WHAT IS THE FOURTH TITLE? On Freeborn Persons. Von den Frengebornen.

units.la: Quis est Ingenuus?
units.tr: Who is a freeborn person?

units.la: INgenuus est is, qui statim ut natus est, liber est: sive ex duobus ingenuis matrimonio editus est, sive ex libertinis duobus, sive ex altero libertino & altero ingenuo. Sed & si quis ex matre nascitur libera, patre vero servo, ingenuus nihilominus nascitur. in princ. inst. cod.
units.tr: A freeborn person is one who is free from the moment of birth, whether he is born of two freeborn parents in lawful marriage, of two freed parents, or of one freed parent and one freeborn. Moreover, even if a child is born of a free mother and a slave father, he is nonetheless born freeborn. Beginning of the Institutes, Code.

units.la: Quot temporibus prodest matris liber- tas infanti?
units.tr: At what time does the mother's freedom benefit the infant?

units.la: Sufficit liberam fuisse matrem eo tempore, quae[?] nascitur, licet ancilla conceperit. Et e contrario si liberam conceperit, deinde ancilla facta pariat: placuit[?] eum, qui nascitur, liberum nasci: Quia non debet calamitas matris ei nocere, qui in ventre est. §. Sed & inst.cod.
units.tr: It is enough that the mother was free at the time the child is born, even though she conceived while a slave. And conversely, if she conceived while free and afterwards, having become a slave, gives birth, it has been decided that the child who is born is born free, because the misfortune of the mother ought not to harm the one who is in the womb. Section "But also," Institutes, Code.

units.la: Officitne ingenuo nato manumissio?
units.tr: Does manumission harm a child born freeborn?

units.la: Cùm ingenuus aliquis natus sit, non officit ei in[?] servitute fuisse, & postea manumissum esse: saepissime enim constitutum est natalibus non officere manumissionem. §. final. inst. cod.
units.tr: When someone has been born freeborn, it does not harm him that he was in servitude earlier and was afterwards manumitted; for it has very often been established that manumission does not detract from birthright. Final section, Institutes, Code.

units.la: QUIS EST QUINTUS Titulus?
units.tr: What is the fifth title?

units.la: <bl>De Libertinis. Von Frengegebenen.</bl>
units.tr: <bl>On Freedmen. Of those set free.</bl>

units.la: Quid sunt Libertini?
units.tr: What are freedmen?

units.la: Libertini sunt, qui ex justa servitute manumissi sunt[?] in princ. inst. cod. & l.6. ff. de stat. hom.
units.tr: Freedmen are those who have been released from lawful servitude (Inst. de Iure Personarum, in princ.; and Dig. 1.6, de statu hominum).

units.la: Quid est Manumissio?
units.tr: What is manumission?

units.la: Manumissio est de manu datio. Nam quamdiu aliquis in servitute est, manui & potestati suppositus est: & manumissus liberatur potestate. in princip. inst. cod.
units.tr: Manumission is the giving of freedom from the hand. For as long as someone is in servitude, he is placed under the hand and power of another; but the one who is manumitted is released from power (Inst., in princ.).

units.la: Ubi & quibus modis procedit Ma- numissio?
units.tr: Where and in what ways does manumission take place?

units.la: Aut ex Sacris Constitutionibus in Sacrosanctis Ecclesiis, aut vindicta, aut inter amicos, aut per Epistolam, aut per testamentum, aut per aliam quamlibe[?]t ultimam voluntatem. §. multis. inst. cod.
units.tr: Either in the holy churches by sacred constitutions, or by the rod (vindicta), or among friends, or by letter, or by will, or by any other last declaration of intent (Inst., §. multis).

units.la: Quotuplex erat olim libertinorum status?
units.tr: What was the former status of freedmen, of which there were several kinds?

units.la: Libertinorum status tripertitus antea fuer[?]t. Nam qui manumittebantur, modò majorem & justam libertatem consequebantur & fiebant cives Romani: Modò minorem & Latini ex lege Julia Norbana fiebant: Modo inferiorem: & fiebant ex lege Aelia Sentia Dediticii. §.libertinorum.inst.eod.
units.tr: The status of freedmen was formerly threefold. For those who were manumitted either obtained the greater and full liberty and became Roman citizens; or the lesser, and became Latins under the Julian Norbanan law; or the inferior, and became Dediticii under the Aelian Sentian law (Inst., §. libertinorum, same title).

units.la: Hodie vero est unum tantum genus libertinorum, qui fiunt cives Romani: Reliqua duo genera Imperator duabus Constitutionibus sustulit.l.cùm dediticii. C.de Latin.libert.tollend.& l.deditilia[?]. C.de deditilia liber.tollend.
units.tr: Today, however, there is only one kind of freedman, who become Roman citizens; the Emperor abolished the other two kinds by two constitutions (C. de Latinis libertis tollendis, l. cum dediticii; and C. de dediticiis libertate tollenda, l. dediticia).

units.la: QUIS EST SEXTUS Titulus?
units.tr: WHAT IS THE SIXTH TITLE?

units.la: Quibus ex causis manumittere non licet. Auß was vrsachen nicht zugelassen wirt loß zugeben. Qui non potest manumittere?
units.tr: On what grounds it is not permitted to manumit. Who cannot manumit?

units.la: NOn tamen cuicunque volenti, manumittere licet. Nam is qui in fraudem creditorum manumittit, nihil agit: quia lex Aelia Sentia impedit libertatem. in princ.inst.eod.
units.tr: Yet manumission is not permitted to just anyone who wishes it. For a man who manumits in fraud of his creditors accomplishes nothing, because the Aelian Sentian law prevents the freedom. Beginning of the Institutes, same title.

units.la: Potestne Dominus, qui solvendo non est, in tes- tamento manumittere?
units.tr: Can a master who is not solvent manumit in his will?

units.la: Licet Domino qui solvendo non est, in testamento servum suum cum libertate haeredem instituere, ut liber fiat, haeresque ei solus & necessarius: si modò ei nemo alius ex eo testamento haeres extiterit. §. licet.inst.eod.
units.tr: A master who is not solvent may, in his will, institute his slave as heir with freedom, so that he becomes free and is his sole and necessary heir, provided that no one else has come forward as heir under that will. §. licet, Institutes, same title.

units.la: Si fine libertate servus hæres institutus est, quid juris?
units.tr: If a slave is instituted heir without freedom, what is the law?

units.la: Tunc ex ipsa scriptura institutionis etiam libertas ei competere videtur: quum non sit verisimile, eum quem hæredem sibi elegit, si prætermiserit libertatis dationem, servum remanere voluisse, & neminem sibi hæredem fore. §. idemq; inst. eod.
units.tr: Then, from the very wording of the institution, freedom seems to belong to him as well, since it is not likely that the one whom he chose as heir, if he omitted the grant of freedom, would have wanted him to remain a slave and would have no heir. §. idemque, Institutes, same title.

units.la: Quis in fraudem creditorum ma- numittit?
units.tr: Who manumits in fraud of creditors?

units.la: In fraudem creditorum manumittere videtur, qui vel jam eo tempore, quo manumittit, solvendo non est: vel qui datis libertatibus defuturus est solvendo esse. Prævaluisse tamen videtur, nisi animum quoque fraudandi manumissor habuerit, non impediri libertatem, quamvis bona ejus creditoribus nō sufficiant: sæpe enim de facultatibus suis amplius quàm in his est, sperant homines. Itaq; tunc intelligimus impediri libertatem, cùm utroq; modo fraudantur Creditores, id est, & consilio manumittentis & ipsa re, eò quòd ejus bona non sunt suffectura creditoribus. §. in fraudem. inst. eod.
units.tr: A man seems to manumit in fraud of creditors if, already at the time he manumits, he is not solvent, or if by granting freedoms he will be unable to remain solvent. It has, however, prevailed that freedom is not impeded merely because his goods are not sufficient for the creditors, unless the manumitter also had the intention of defrauding them, since people often hope for more from their resources than they actually have. Therefore we understand freedom to be impeded only when the creditors are defrauded in both ways, that is, both by the intention of the manumitter and by the fact itself, because his goods will not suffice for the creditors. §. in fraudem, Institutes, same title.

units.la: Potéstne minor viginti quinq; annis testa- mento manumittere?
units.tr: Can a minor under twenty-five manumit by will?

units.la: De jure Digestorum manumittere non potest. l.1. ff.de manumissionibus.Nisi justæ manumissionis causæ sunt, veluti si quis patrem aut matrem, filium, filiamve, aut fratres sororesque naturales, aut paedagogum, aut nutricem, aut educatorem, aut alumnum alumnamve, aut collactaneum manumittit. §. justæ. inst.eod.
units.tr: By the law of the Digest he cannot manumit, unless there are just causes for manumission, as when he manumits his father or mother, son or daughter, or natural brothers and sisters, or a tutor, or a nurse, or a foster-parent, or a foster-child, or a milk-brother or milk-sister. §. justae, Institutes, same title.

units.la: De jure verò Institutionum, major septendecim annis manumittere potest. §. final. inst. eod.
units.tr: But by the law of the Institutes, one who is over seventeen may manumit. §. final, Institutes, same title.

units.la: Sed ista dispositio hodie per jus novissimum in Authenticis est sublata. cap.2. Authent. ut Sponsalit. largit. speciali. sit contract. Ubi Impetator inquit: Et hoc quoq; præsenti constitutione sancimus, ut licentia sit minoribus in ipso tempore, in quo licet eis testari de alia substantia, etiam suos servos in ultimis voluntatibus manumittere. Hodiè verò decimoquarto anno ætatis completo masculus testari potest: Fœmina duodecimo. Ergo eodem tempore manumittere possunt, inquit Gothofredus.
units.tr: But this arrangement has today been abolished by the newest law in the Authentics: chapter 2, Authentic "ut sponsalitia largitas", where the Emperor says: "And by this present constitution we also decree that minors may, at the very time when they are permitted to make a will concerning other property, manumit their own slaves in their last wills as well." Today, however, a male may make a will once he has completed his fourteenth year of age, and a female her twelfth. Therefore, says Gothofredus, they may manumit at the same time.

units.la: QVIS EST SEPTIMVS Titulus?
units.tr: WHAT IS THE SEVENTH TITLE?

units.la: De Lege Fusia Caninia tollenda. Von dem Gesetz Fusia Caninia aufzuheben.
units.tr: On Repealing the Lex Fusia Caninia. On the repeal of the Fusian-Caninian law.

units.la: Unde dicta est Lex Fusia Caninia?
units.tr: Whence is the Lex Fusia Caninia so named?

units.la: NON à cane, ut Accursius comminiscitur, sed à Fusio Caninio ejus latore sic dicta est, qui post Aelium Sentium libertatum conferendarum jus ita restrinxit, ut à duobus usq; ad decem pars dimidia, à decem usq; ad triginta pars tertia, à triginta usque ad centum pars quarta, à centum usque ad quingentos pars quinta manumitti posset: nunquam autem plures quàm centum etiam ex grandi familia manumittendi jus erat in testamento, ut refert Schneidevvinus ex Mynsingero.
units.tr: It is not named from a dog (canis), as Accursius invents, but from Fusius Caninius, its proposer. After the Aelian Sentian law, he restricted the right of granting freedom in this way: from two to ten slaves, half could be manumitted; from ten to thirty, a third; from thirty to a hundred, a quarter; from a hundred to five hundred, a fifth. But in a will a master could never free more than a hundred slaves, even from a large household, as Schneidewin reports from Mynsinger.

units.la: QVIS EST OCTAVVS Titulus?
units.tr: What is the eighth title?

units.la: De his qui sui vel alieni juris sunt. Von denen so jres oder eines andern Rechten seind.
units.tr: On those who are under their own right or under another's right.

units.la: Quæ est alia personarum Divisio?
units.tr: What is the other division of persons?

units.la: SEquitur de jure personarum alia divisio. Nam quædam sui juris sunt, quædam alieno juri subₒ jectæ. Rursus earum, quæ alieno juri subjectæ sunt, aliæ sunt in potestate parentum, aliæ in potestate dominorum. Videamus itaque de his, quæ alieno juri subjectæ sunt. In princ. inst. eod.
units.tr: Next follows another division concerning the right of persons. For some are under their own right (sui juris), and some are subject to another's right (alieno juri subjectæ). Again, of those who are subject to another's right, some are in the power of parents and some in the power of masters. Let us therefore look at those who are subject to another's right. In the beginning of the Institutes, same title.

units.la: Qui sunt in potestate Dominorum?
units.tr: Who are in the power of masters?

units.la: In potestate Dominorum sunt servi. Quæ quidem potestas juris gentium est. Nam apud omnes peræq; gentes animadvertere possumus, Dominis in servos vitæ necisq; potestatem fuisse. §. in potest inst. eod.
units.tr: Slaves are in the power of masters. Indeed this power belongs to the law of nations. For among all nations alike we can observe that masters had the power of life and death over their slaves. §. In potest, Institutes, same title.

units.la: Num etiam hodie Dominis servos occi- dere licet?
units.tr: Is it still lawful today for masters to kill their slaves?

units.la: Hoc tempore, inquit Imperator, nullis hominibus, qui sub imperio nostro sunt, licet sine causa legibus cognita, in servos supra modum sævire. §. Sed hor. eod.
units.tr: At this time, says the Emperor, no one who is under our rule may rage against slaves beyond measure without a cause recognised by the laws. §. Sed hodie, Institutes, same title.

units.la: Coguntúrne Domini servos suos vendere?
units.tr: Are masters compelled to sell their slaves?

units.la: Antoninus consultus à quibusdā præsidibus provinciarum de his servis, qui ad ædem sacram, vel ad statuam principum confugiunt, præcepit, ut si intolerabilis videatur sævitia Dominorum, cogantur servos suos bonis conditionibus vendere, ut pretium Dominis daretur. Et recte: Expedit enim Reipublicæ, ne suæ re quis male utatur. §. Nam ex, inst. eod.
units.tr: When some governors of provinces consulted Antoninus about those slaves who flee to a sacred temple or to the statue of the emperors, he ruled that if the cruelty of the masters appears intolerable, they should be compelled to sell their slaves on good terms, so that a price be paid to the masters. And rightly so: for it is in the interest of the commonwealth that no one should misuse what is his own. §. Nam ex, Institutes, same title.

units.la: QUIS EST NOVUS TITULUS? De patria potestate. <bl>Von Vätterlicher</bl> <bl>gewalt.</bl>
units.tr: WHAT IS THE NEW TITLE? On paternal power. Von Vätterlicher gewalt.

units.la: Qui sunt in potestate patris?
units.tr: Who are in the power of the father?

units.la: IN potestate nostra sunt liberi nostri, quos ex justis nuptiis procreavimus. in princ. eod.
units.tr: Those children are in our power whom we have begotten from lawful marriage. Beginning of the same title.

units.la: Quid sunt Nuptiæ?
units.tr: What is marriage?

units.la: Nuptiæ sive Matrimonium est viri & mulieris con-junctio, junctio, individuam vitae consuetudinem continens. §. Nuptiae. inst. cod.
units.tr: Marriage, or matrimony, is the joining of a man and a woman, containing an indivisible partnership of life. The paragraph "Nuptiae", Institutes, same title.

units.la: Habentne alii etiam homines in liberos ta- lem potestatem, qualem cives Romani?
units.tr: Do other men also have such power over their children as Roman citizens have?

units.la: Jus potestatis, quod in liberos habemus, proprium est civium Romanorum: nulli enim alii sunt homines, qui talem in liberos habeant potestatem, qualem nos habemus. §. jus autem. inst. cod.
units.tr: The right of power that we have over children is peculiar to Roman citizens; for there are no other men who have such power over children as we have. The paragraph "Jus autem", Institutes, same title.

units.la: QUIS EST DECIMUS Titulus?
units.tr: WHAT IS THE TENTH TITLE?

units.la: De Nuptiis. vom Ehestande. Sed cum Sponsalia Nuptias antecedant, quae- ritur quid sint Sponsalia?
units.tr: On Marriage. But since betrothals precede marriages, the question arises: what are betrothals?

units.la: Sponsalia, <bl>Eheberedungen/ Ehegelübd/</bl> sunt mentio & repromissio nuptiarum futurarum. l. 1. ff. de sponsalibus. Sponsalia autem dicta sunt à spondendo. Nam moris fuit veteribus stipulari & spondere sibi uxores futuras. l. 2. ff. eod. unde & sponsi sponsaeque appellatio nata est. l 3 ff. eod. Ideo etiam sine arrhis, <bl>ohne trawpfennung/</bl> sponsalia cotrahi possunt, sed datis arrhis sponsalia dicuntur firmata.
units.tr: Betrothals (mutual engagements and vows to marry) are a mention and promise of future marriage. L. 1, ff. de sponsalibus. The word "sponsalia" is derived from "spondere" (to promise), for it was the custom of the ancients to stipulate and promise to take wives for themselves in the future. L. 2, ff. eod. Hence also the names "sponsus" and "sponsa" (betrothed man and woman) arose. L. 3, ff. eod.
